Upcoming Walking tours of Downtown Mountain View http://mvhistory.eventbrite.com/ FALL As we come to the end of 2026, the year in which we commemorate 250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence, it is still worth contemplating the document. Despite the obvious "flaws" in the Declaration, the radical notion that people can govern themselves (instead of a monarch) is an idea that carried our nation, and many others that followed, to a new place in the history of human civilization. History is full of "what ifs." The events surrounding the Declaration of Independence and the American Revolution are no different. What if King George III and the British government had been more accommodating to the concerns and complaints of the people living in the 13 colonies? In reading the Declaration, there is a long list of 27 complaints against the King. Or was the split with the King and the British government destined to happen anyway (perhaps a few years later)? What if Thomas Paine hadn't written the pamphlet "Common Sense"? It is considered by many scholars to be a catalyst that captured public opinion and helped propel the Colonists toward independence. What if Thomas Jefferson (the primary author of the document) had not participated? Would the Declaration have the same eloquence if written by someone else? What if some of the signers of the Declaration been arrested and punished by the British for treason? Would this have delayed the Revolution? A person can go on and on imagining the various twists and turns that might have occurred. But whatever we can imagine, it probably won't compare to the actual drama, communities and alliances that formed to create the United States that our ancestors were lucky to enjoy. And that we today and those that follow have a responsibility to maintain and enhance. The special exhibit "Spirit of '76" at the Los Altos History Museum covers the Declaration, its influences and the reaction of historical figures. It also chronicles the Bicentennial activities in Mountain View and Los Altos. The last day to view the exhibit is November 8, 2026. www.losaltoshistory.org/exhibit/commemorating-americas-250th/ "Mention Mountain View and most people think about dinner. At 7 p.m. ...Castro Street is jammed with the hungry….But by 10 p.m. the crowds evaporate" wrote Kathleen Donnelly, Mercury News Entertainment Writer in 1991. The story was Mountain View's bold plan to keep people downtown. After years of work, a new downtown anchor was about to open. Our city's downtown revitalization planning ran through the 1980s to 1990. It started with a $11.7 million face lift of Castro Street and included a $44.5 million new city hall and live theater complex. Planning for the downtown makeover began when the existing city hall was deemed unsafe due to new tighter earthquake building codes. Local leaders pushed the idea of building a theater as well to anchor a spiffed up downtown. There was a need. Sunnyvale was considering a large theater but ultimately dropped their plans. Nearby venues included Cupertino's Flint Center built in 1971, Palo Alto's Lucie Stern Theater, and Stanford University theaters on campus. Local high school orchestras had no place to perform where acoustics were good. The Community School of Music and Arts had no permanent place to showcase its musicians and students. Affordable theater space was tight. Ben DeBolt moved from San Francis co to Mountain View in 1954 and did not want to go to San Francisco to experience live performances in large venues. He joined the boards of local performing arts groups and worked to change that. DeBolt was joined by others to organize efforts to fill the void. Mountain View launched a design contest for the city hall and theater complex. Five architecture firms were invited to submit entries in a competition for the design and engineering contract for Mountain View's largest building project to date—a city hall, theater and parking structure. Three submitted designs. Each entry included a model of the Civic Center and color renderings of the buildings plus a detailed cost estimate for the project. City Council and city staff weighed in. Several days of public comment also contributed to the selection process. Competing models were displayed at the Art & Wine Festival and the library. The public vote resulted in the selection of William Turnbull Associates of San Francisco. The salmon stucco and teal tile were considered emblematic of a relaxed California style. In the original design, City Hall and the Center for the Performing Arts were planned at different heights. "Mention Mountain View and most people think about dinner . For many of us, the 2023 regional banking crisis may be a hazy recollection. While its potential harm was largely avoided, the collapse of First Republic and Silicon V alley Banks, and the resulting economic concerns were a reminder of the instability inherent in the /f_inancial networks that run our modern world. In looking back at our past, the story of the First National Bank of Mountain View is impressive and one that few people know. /T_he institution weathered the growing pains of early twentieth-century Mountain View, the Great Depression, and the 1930s economic policy changes and challenges. /T_he National Banking System /T_he First National Bank of Mountain View was one of over 10,000 nationally chartered but locally run banks, having their origin in the /f_inancial constraints the Union faced during the Civil W ar. Despite the superior industrial technology and production capacity of the North, the early months and years of the war dragged on with no end in sight. Unprepared to /f_ight a lengthy war, the Union government quickly began running low on money, thus prompting Congress to pass legislation to counteract the budget de/f_icit. By 1863, however, the combined public mistrust of the non-specie money (banknotes unbacked by precious metals) issued as a temporary means to /f_inance the war, and the expanding debts of the Union proved the necessity of establishing an entirely new banking system. /T_he National Banking Act of 1863 was introduced to establish a program that gave individuals the authority to establish government-chartered banks provided they met certain requirements. A minimum of $50,000 had to deposited into the U .S. T reasury which could be used to guarantee their bank notes. Up to 90% of this money (in the form of government bonds) could be used to back any notes the bank issued. By all measures, the National Banking System was extremely successful. /T_he new system allowed the Union to /f_inance the war and provide a trustworthy national money supply. National Banks could be found in almost every city and unincorporated communities in the country. Most moderately sized to large cities had at least two such institutions. A provision in the Gold Standard Act of 1900 stipulated that banks in towns with a population of less than 3,000 could organize with a capitalization amount of $25,000. /T_his stimulated the organization of numerous small-town banks across the country and began what is now called "/T_he Golden Age of National Banking." /T_he most tangible artifacts of these banks are their banknotes, each prominently featuring the town name and the signatures of the bank officers on the front. /T_he National Banking System continued to operate in this same basic form until 1935. Mountain View In January 1913, the First National Bank of Mountain View was organized with the minimum capitalization of $25,000. (In 1910, the U .S. census listed the population of Mountain View at 1,161 people). /T_here were two original officers for the bank. Bert W. Holeman (1875–1951), served as cashier from 1913–15 and then president starting in 1917. According to his obituary, Holeman sold his stake in the company in 1925 and moved to Bishop, CA where he worked for the national banks there until about 1946, when he moved to San Jose. Charles C. Minton (born 1850) was president until his death in September 1914. Before moving to Mountain View, Minton worked at the Marion, Kansas State Bank, where, according to his obituary, he was very highly esteemed. /T_he fact that both Holeman and Minton came from Kansas at around the same time suggests they may have known each other prior to moving to Mountain View. Beginning in 1913 the First National Bank of Mountain View was housed at the corner of Castro and Villa Streets in an impressive Greek Revival styled building. Its prominence would have been conspicuous in early Mountain View. In a 1939 newspaper article in the Mountain View Register-Leader, the bank's long-time cashier John J. T aylor (who started as the only assistant cashier) recalled its grand opening reception. /T_he building was decorated with /f_loral arrangements sent by neighboring banks, whose leaders all made appearances at the event. /T_hroughout the day, boys and girls guided many interested visitors through the building. /T_he First National Bank of Mountain View quickly achieved success. In a December 1916 advertisement in the Register-Leader, the bank reported a nearly 220% increase in total deposits, from $53,570 at its opening to $170,674 in November 1916. In 1916 the bank gained 174 new bank accounts. Banknote circulation also increased quickly. /T_hese notes could be used the same as US currency. In 1913, the bank had $6,250 worth of their banknotes in circulation. By 1915, that number had increased to $25,000. Only two years later, $1, $2, $5, $10, $20, and $100 notes in circulation had reached its cap of $50,000. /T_he bank would maintain this strong balance amount throughout the 1920s and early 1930s. /T_he end of banknote issuances by nationally chartered banks occurred in 1935. /T_he bank was not immune to the effects of the Great Depression. T otal assets decreased from $887,375 in 1929 to $711,028 in 1932, and $688,844 in 1934. Los Altos School District School Board Trustee Bryan Johnson belongs to a family who has made significant contributions to computer technology and progress through multiple generations. Bryan's great-grandfather, John Alfred Johnson, was born in Bitterna, Skraborg, Sweden in 1863. In 1868, he immigrated to Meeker County, Minnesota with his parents, Swan and Mary Johnson. John was the fifth of ten children. He married Elizabeth Erickson, another Swedish immigrant, in 1888, and had ten children with her. Both John and Swan were farmers. John and Elizabeth's ninth son Reynold Benjamin Johnson, was to follow a different path. On the farm, he displayed a keen talent for mechanics, inventing a submersible submarine, which he displayed in a horse trough. He graduated with a B.S. in education administration, from the University of Minnesota in 1929. He started teaching math and science at Ironwood High School in Michigan, and became convinced that there must be a way to automate the testing and grading of his students. He invented a machine that could automatically score tests where the answers were marked by students, first by punching holes into paper, and later using pencil marks. Thomas Watson, the president of IBM, purchased Reynold's invention and hired him as a senior engineer, moving him to Endicott, New York, helping him develop his idea into the IBM 805 test scoring machine. After being issued 53 patents, Reynold left for San Jose, California, in 1951, to manage IBM's West Coast Laboratory, where he led a research team that developed the first disk data storage technology in 1956. In retirement, Reynold developed the micro-phonograph technology used in Fisher-Price "Talk to Me" books. Reynold received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation from President Reagan in 1986. Reynold and his wife Beatrice married in 1934 and had three children, a daughter Karen and twin boys Phillip and David. David graduated from Yale Law School in 1972, moving to Washington, D. C., joining the law firm Wilmer, Cutler, and Pickering, where he was named a partner in 1980. An electronic commerce expert, he helped write the Electronic Communications Privacy Act in 1986. He later co-founded the Cyberspace Law Institute and after that was the founding director of the Aspen Institute Internet Policy Project. David and his wife Judith became the parents of LASD Trustee Bryan and his sister Kathryn. Bryan met his wife Jocelyn Goldfein while they were both computer science majors at Stanford. They lived in the same dorm and worked overlapping shifts at the computer science center. Bryan worked as a software engineer at a variety of companies, the latest of which was Guidewire Software. He and Jocelyn had two daughters: Maya and Madelyn. After Madelyn was born, Bryan decided to be a stay-at-home dad. This is when he got involved in the Santa Rita PTA. Being PTA president gave Bryan a lot of interaction with the LASD Trustees. He was first elected to fill a vacancy, then was re-elected in 2018 and 2022. He is seeking reelection this fall. Bryan was President of the LASD School Board when the COVID-19 crisis hit, and is proud of the district's ability to pivot to remote learning faster and more effectively than many other school districts in the state. He also notes the district's financial situation has consistently improved over the last decade, and the coming campus modernization work made possible by the Measure EE facilities bond will further reduce repair and maintenance costs. This will also allow the school PTAs to focus less on fundraising and more on the vital work of strengthening school communities. Bryan's wife Jocelyn is a managing director at an AI-focused venture capital fund. Their oldest child Maya is an anthropology major at Brandeis University, while younger sibling Madelyn will start college this fall at Johnson and Wales University, planning to major in Baking and Pastry Arts. Bryan's advice to young people is "Don't assume that you can achieve your goals by just checking the right boxes; figure out how to acquire the experiences and skills you will need, and then work diligently to achieve real mastery." Dr. Amy Ellison, Curator and Director of Exhibitions, speaking about the development of the special exhibit. 6 7 Mountain View was a dynamic hub in an early California transit network that depended on the stagecoach. The town, in its formative days, was a key stop on the pioneering stagecoach line between San Francisco and San Jose; a link in the first regular trans-continental mail route; and, after the railroad arrived, a strategic transfer point, so the story goes, from train to stagecoach (or stagecoach to train) for passengers traveling to and from the coast over the rugged Santa Cruz mountains. In the mid-19th century, the influx of new people and a rapid increase in industry and commerce demanded enhanced means of transportation. In autumn 1849, Mountain View pioneer John Whisman started California's first stagecoach line, running between San Francisco and San Jose along the muddy Lower San Francisco Road (near today's Highway 101). The trip took nine hours (in good weather), and fare was two ounces of gold or $32, an exorbitant amount (over $1,000 today). The service provided by Whisman was quite rudimentary, based on an old French omnibus pulled by poorly cared-for mustangs and mules. During the heavy winter rains of 1849–50, the road became so soft and muddy that stage wheels sank to their hubs. Whisman was forced to redirect his route, which ran temporarily from San Jose to Alviso as the northern terminus; passengers then made steamboat connections for San Francisco. The original route was restored in spring 1850. But Whisman's stagecoach enterprise was slow and inefficient, and in fall 1850 he sold out to the firm of Hall and Crandall. The Hall and Crandall line ran along the Upper San Francisco Road (El Camino Real). While passengers still endured a rough and jarring ride over the rutted, unpaved road, these proprietors were more experienced and had better horses and infrastructure. According to H.C. Ward, an early driver on the line, in March 1851 500 mares and 14 stallions were delivered to the firm, which they "immediately commenced to break to harness." The vehicles were also upgraded. Early passenger coaches used in the area were often make-shift wagons of various sorts. Beginning in 1850 larger and more solidly constructed coaches came into use. One of the most common was the New Hampshire-built Concord coach, and in 1851 Hall and Crandall bought a supply specifically intended for the El Camino route. Building on this foundation, in May 1851 the firm was awarded a four-year contract to carry the U.S. mails between San Francisco and San Jose, ensuring a steady, reliable income. According to historian Mary Jo Ignoffo in Milestones: A History of Mountain View, the Hall and Crandall stagecoaches made a rest stop in the shade of a large laurel tree about a half a mile southeast of Stevens Creek within today's Sunnyvale. Ignoffo notes that the location was a natural stopping point to switch horses. " As yet there was no bridge over Stevens Creek," she writes, "and coaches and wagons had to negotiate the slippery banks and ford the rock stream." In April 1853, Hall and Crandall sold their line to Dillon, Hedge and Company, interests that subsequently passed into the California Stage Company. The Daily Alta California for December 6, 1851, described the condition of the road between San Francisco and San Jose as "wretched." Heavy winter rains spawned relentless mud. If a coach bogged down in the muck, passengers might have to climb out and push. In dry weather, billowing dust stirred up by the hammering horses permeated the coach. Travelers, including ladies wearing capacious skirts, were cramped inside sharing hard benches with random and sometimes unfriendly strangers. Wayside rest stops offered a few minutes' reprieve from the incessant shaking and jolting and a much-needed opportunity to stretch while the horses were changed (every ten or twelve miles). Starting around 1852, a stage stop was constructed on El Camino west of Stevens Creek, near today's Grant Road, and gradually evolved into the village of Old Mountain View. A single huge oak tree marked the site. The location seemed a natural stopping point, where southbound stages might have to prepare to ford the creek. When the stagecoach pulled up, the scene must have (cont'd p.7) Historical placard at intersection of El Camino and Grant Road For the next twenty years First National Bank weathered both tough and later robust /f_inancial times. /T_he First National Bank of Mountain View was absorbed as a branch of the Central Bank of Oakland in May 1954, with assets of $250,000. Since then, the neoclassical exterior has been replaced by the current façade. /T_he building is now occupied by the Independent Order of the Odd Fellows. Y et, the legacy of the First National Bank lives on through the physical banknotes it issued, which are in high demand in the collector market (and typically sell for $2,000 to $4,000). More importantly, it serves as a reminder of the /f_inancial origins of Silicon V alley, when the area was a successful farming community. When Mountain View was a Stagecoach Town Lower Road (near 101) Upper Road (near today's El Camino) The two San Francisco stage roads c. 1850 been a lively one, as sounds of commerce and community mixed with the bustle of sweating, snorting horses. A blacksmith shop serviced horses and coaches. At the hotel, passengers were picked up and discharged and could eat or stay overnight. Shumway's store also served as the post office, where local mail pouches were dropped off and collected. The curved ash body of the commonly-used Concord rested on long leather, shock-absorbing thorough-braces. The braces reduced the road's sharp jolts and allowed the vehicle to rock back and forth and swing sideways, providing forward thrust for the team. Nine to twelve passengers rode inside, and up to a dozen or more could journey precariously on the roof. Stagecoaches were drawn by four or six horses, which required expert, sometimes entertaining and occasionally intimidating drivers, or 'whips.' From 1858 to 1861, Mountain View was also an official station along the legendary Butterfield Overland Mail stage route. Mail to California from the rest of the country was painfully slow, and Californians clamored for a through line. The 2,800 mile trans-continental service eventually mandated by Congress carried both passengers and mail, running twice a week from St. Louis and Memphis to San Francisco. The trip took about 25 days, and coaches traveled day and night. Lighter mud (celerity) wagons were used on the section from Arkansas to Los Angeles, while the classic Concords were employed from Los Angeles to San Francisco. The route in California ran via Pacheco Pass, Gilroy and San Jose. The Butterfield coaches then merged onto the established thoroughfare along El Camino, sharing this vital corridor with local and regional lines. The Overland Mail almost certainly used the thriving Grant Road settlement as its Mountain View station, utilizing the infrastructure already developed by local pioneers. Given the line's strict, round-the-clock timetable, station stops for the Butterfield stages were usually quick, to swap mail-pouches and obtain a fresh relay of horses. Travelers could transfer between the trans-continental route and the regular line, and "through" passengers could take a brief break. The Butterfield coaches were painted in brilliant colors, usually red, green or canary yellow. Imagine Old Mountain View around 1859: dusty El Camino, scattered buildings, routine business mixed with the saloon's occasional hubbub, the troublesome Stevens Creek crossing—and then a large, brightly decorated Concord coach drawn by four or six horses is spotted coming up the road. It must have been quite a spectacle! The San Francisco & San Jose Railroad was completed in 1864, with a stop at Mountain View that bypassed the old Grant Road settlement. The center of civic and commercial life now shifted to the new town that coalesced around the railroad stop, and the primary stagecoach line that had operated along El Camino since 1849 wound down. But while the railroad's arrival reconfigured the area's transport framework, it did not erase Mountain View's importance as a stagecoach town. See the Winter 2027 issue for the story of the likely stagecoach link between New Mountain View and the lumber and tourist town of Pescadero on the Pacific coast, with a notable nexus to the railroad. Pamela Baird, MVHA President and Carol Donahue, MVHA Board Member, at the Harvest Festival Finding Your Family History More on Court Records By Robert Cox Sometimes, we get the deepest look into our relatives' lives by looking at the court records in which they appear. Unfortunately, most court records document an incident where someone did wrong to someone else. If your relative was the wrongdoer, discovering the information in the court record can be embarrassing. One thing to remember is if you cast a wide enough net in your search for distant relatives, you are bound to find someone who is a wrongdoer. I'm a fan of Alfred Hitchcock, but the kinds of wrongdoing I have seen while tracing distant relatives is more amazingly varied than what I have seen in watching many episodes of old Al's TV show. So as not to cast aspersions on my distant relatives as a whole, I will illustrate how valuable court records can be in family history research by selecting an incident where a distant cousin of mine, Thelma Cox, was the unfortunate recipient of bad fortune. According to court records, Thelma "came to her death in the village of Garfield Heights, Ohio, due to an automobile in which she was riding being overturned in said village, sustaining injuries which resulted in her death." Thelma's mother Eva Cox "brought suit against the village, resulting in a judgment against the village of $1500." The court records also include a distribution of the $1500 as follows. Note that names and relation to the deceased are listed as well as the amount due to each of the recipient. Even the street addresses of the recipients are provided in the application for letters of administration for Thelma. For my research, the most interesting new fact was the address of Sterling Cox. I knew Sterling had gone to New York City, but I did not have any idea where he lived there. This information was not available anywhere else. However, a majority of voters opted to remove the theater's top floor so that City Hall would appear more prominent. As a result of that decision, the theater's fly loft ended up 20 feet shorter than what is typically required for a fully functional professional stage. Features that made the Turnbull design stand out were city hall and theater buildings set facing one another diagonally. Carl Smith, a Turnbull partner, told City Council "We wanted to open the plaza to Castro and Mercy Streets and make it a gateway to Pioneer Park." Over the years many parades, cultural and holiday celebrations, and other events have flowed from the streets into the plaza and the park and served as a community gathering hub. In late 1989, the Performing Arts Advisory Committee began work on fundraising and planning the gala opening. The gala was a black tie event at the Center. The evening included a reception, tours and formal dinner. In its early years, the Center for the Performing Arts showcased a diverse calendar of local and national names of the day, including Della Reese, Dizzy Gillespie, and John Tesh. The National Theater of the Deaf offered its original presentation of Ophelia, a retelling of Hamlet from the heroine's point of view. Storyteller Brenda Wong Aoki was an early act. She went on to be a founding faculty member of the Institute for Diversity in the Arts at Stanford University. Queen Ida and the Bon Temps Zydeco Band brought New Orleans to Mountain View. International acts Mahlathini and Mahotella Queens, considered the Supremes of South Africa and Shanghai Acrobats and Dance Theater also performed on the mainstage. Closer to home, San Francisco's a cappella vocal ensemble Chanticleer and Mountain View High School Music Department's Winter Fest had an opportunity to perform in a venue with good acoustics. Thanks to the foresight of civic leaders and community support in the 1980s, today the Center for the Performing Arts has more requests for dates from performing groups than it can accommodate. The Center is planning its 35th Anniversary Celebration in January 2027. The Harvest History Festival held September 26 was a wonderful way to explain MVHA and the local history. Carol Donahue and Pamela Baird enjoyed sharing stories with visitors to our table. summer-2026.text: Official newsletter of the Mountain View Historical Association. Volume XV Issue 3 Summer 2026. Sunday, August 9, 2026, 4:30 p.m., Los Altos History Museum. Sharing the Spirit 1776 1976 2026. President's Message by Pamela Baird, MVHA President. This year the national, state and local celebrations and commemorations recognizing 250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence have been modest or insignificant. This started me wondering about other milestone anniversaries — 1826, 1876, 1926 and 1976. In 1826, about 11 million people lived in 24 states, almost all east of the Mississippi river. The 50th anniversary, or jubilee, was marked with many small local events, including speeches and bonfires. A celebration was held in Washington DC on July 4, primarily marked by a special program in the chamber of the House of Representatives. In an odd coincidence, both John Adams and Thomas Jefferson, original signers of the Declaration, died on July 4, 1826. The centennial anniversary in 1876 was marked with nationwide celebrations. The population had grown to about 45 million people living in 38 states. The centerpiece was the Centennial Exposition, May 10 to November 10, in Philadelphia, attended by an estimated 10 million visitors. Proudly displayed was new technology including the typewriter and telephone. Attendees were introduced to novelties such as root beer, popcorn and bananas. After a ceremonial reading of the Declaration of Independence, Elizabeth Cady Stanton pushed forward to present the Declaration of the Rights of Women to Acting Vice-President Thomas W. Ferry. She was not authorized to speak at the Exposition. Women distributed printed copies of their declaration to those attending. In 1926 the Sesquicentennial of the signing was observed with another Exposition in Philadelphia. One of the most impressive attractions was the gateway entrance, an 80-foot replica of the Liberty Bell that people, cars and trucks passed under. President Calvin Coolidge spoke to an estimated 200,000 visitors, noting that the historical importance of this immortal document is measured by the progress of the Republic. The Bicentennial in 1976 had wide support across the nation, led by the American Revolution Bicentennial Administration (ARBA), funded by congress. 284 national programs covered a wide range of civic and cultural topics. A 26 car American Freedom Train brought a documentary to 138 cities on a 24,000 mile journey. Nearly 100 sailing ships paraded through New York Harbor over the Bicentennial weekend, the largest gathering of world navies in history. Cities that established programs could qualify to be designated an official Bicentennial city. Mountain View qualified for the designation. A committee was started in March of 1975 to plan the many events scheduled for 1976. A kite flying contest, special city medallions, a rodeo, lectures, fire hydrant painting and a special day-long 4th of July celebration were among the programs created. History Happening Now, June 11, 2026. On a very hot June 11 afternoon eight new historic art panels were officially dedicated. Located on both sides of the train station, the panels represent a two year journey led by Anita Rosen. It was a complicated endeavor because three agencies were involved. Caltrain owns the land, Mountain View owns the building and VTA is the tenant. Anita Rosen heads a non-profit organization called Arts Mountain View. Created by artist John Patrick Thomas, Mountain View through Time: Eight Windows into our History, the panels depict local history as well as flora and fauna. The Mountain View Historical Association and the Visual Arts Committee consulted with the artist on themes and details. Each panel has a QR code that explains the content of the panel. A majority of the funding came from a grant from VTA, 30 percent from the city and a small remainder from Arts Mountain View. Mountain View Family History Spotlight: MVLA Trustee Catherine Vonnegut, by Robert Cox, MVHA Vice President. Mountain View Los Altos School Board Trustee Catherine Vonnegut hails from a prominent Indianapolis, Indiana family which valued both business acumen and education. Catherine's father, George Lewis Vonnegut, was a second cousin to Kurt Vonnegut Jr., best-selling author of Cat's Cradle and Slaughterhouse-Five. Catherine's and Kurt's common ancestor, Clemens Vonnegut, was born in Muenster, Germany, in 1824. Originally apprenticed to an importing and banking house in Muenster, he later became a traveling salesman, and in 1851 he was entrusted with establishing trading posts in America. On one trip to America he decided to visit an old friend, Charles Volner, who had immigrated to Indianapolis. Charles persuaded Clemens to settle in Indianapolis. In 1853 Clemens married Katarine Blank, a German immigrant from Baden. In 1857 Clemens founded the Vonnegut Hardware Company. Clemens also founded the Indianapolis Free Thinkers' Association, the Indianapolis Turner Verein, an athletic association, and the German-English School Society, which promoted the teaching of German in local schools. Catherine's great-grandfather George and her grandfather Carl also worked in the family hardware business. Carl died at the age of 36, leaving a widow Marjorie and two children, George, Catherine's father, and Nancy. Carl's surviving brothers Erwin and Ralph helped support Carl's family. George became a metallurgical engineer after graduating from Purdue University. George married Jean Ann Bates, a Butler University beauty queen. They had two daughters, Catherine and Marjorie. Catherine earned a B.S. in math then an M.S. in Computer Science at Purdue. In grad school she met her future husband, Gary Winiger. Gary and Catherine relocated to the Bay Area, where Catherine worked at Control Data and Argo Systems. They married in 1979 and their son Evan was born in 1987. Catherine's first foray into volunteering in local education came when she helped establish the computer lab at the old Mountain View High School on Castro Street. She later became a leader in the Mountain View High School Parent Teacher Student Association. She has been serving as a Mountain View Los Altos Trustee since 2018. Spring program recap: Settlers and Saints, The Naming of Streets in Mountain View. Robert Cox and Melanie Kaye shared the origins and historical significance of many of Mountain View's well-travelled avenues at the Mountain View Public Library on May 3rd. Santa Rosa Avenue honors St. Rose of Lima, canonized 1671, the first person from the Americas to be canonized by the Roman Catholic Church. Sullivan Drive: John Grove Sullivan, born 1824 in County Limerick, Ireland, came to California in 1847. He and his wife Ada Kenna Sullivan donated land on El Camino Real for the first St. Joseph's Church in 1868. We still drive along Ada, Alice, Gladys and Stella. Whisman Road: John W Whisman, proprietor of the Willigrove Inn. In 1849 he started the first stagecoach line in California, between San Jose and Yerba Buena, now San Francisco. Easy Street: In 1912 William Seppich bought four acres on Dean Street to build a home. After seeking a fortune in various failed ways, he petitioned county supervisors to rename his street. His request was granted and he could at last claim to live on Easy Street. 100 Years of Kiwanis in Mountain View by Mark Lindberg. On August 8 the Kiwanis Club of Mountain View will celebrate its 100th anniversary with a Gala at the Don Giovanni Restaurant in Mountain View. The club was founded just a few years after the first Kiwanis International Club was established in Detroit, Michigan, in 1919. As Mountain View evolved from a small agricultural town into a center of innovation and technology, the Kiwanis Club remained committed to its mission of service, supporting local charities, community programs and scholarships for graduating high school students. Back and Forth in Time: the 1976 time capsule. A popular program developed in 1976 by the MV Bicentennial Committee was the establishment of a time capsule. Originally envisioned to be buried on the 4th of July in Rengstorff Park, it was later decided to bury it in January 1977 so that all of the Bicentennial efforts could be included. The committee invited contributions from residents, civic groups, schools and city departments including the Fire and Police Departments, as well as NASA, Moffett Field, Lockheed and other companies. So many items were contributed that a large capsule was needed. Its dimensions are 39 inches long, 20 inches wide and 23 inches deep, with sides 1.5 inches thick. The committee consulted with NASA about the best way to seal the contents. Jean Holtzclaw, the city historian, oversaw the collecting of items. The 1976 yearbooks from Mountain View, Awalt and St. Francis High Schools were selected, as were items donated by students at Bubb Elementary School. Notable items included a letter from the White House and the Bicentennial Flag that flew over Moffett in 1976. Local and national newspapers published on July 4 were included, along with early maps of Mountain View, a copy of the 1902 incorporation paperwork and other city documents. A few churches included histories of their congregations. Civic groups such as Kiwanis, the Oddfellows and the Eagles provided reviews of their organizations. The permits issued for the painting of the fire hydrants were also included. It was decided to place the time capsule outside the entrance to the Library instead of the Community Center. The ceremony was the last official action of the city's Bicentennial committee, headed by former Mayor Joe Cusimano. The burial took place at noon on Friday January 7, 1977. The Fort Ord Army Bicentennial Color Guard Unit posted the colors and the band from St. Francis High School provided the music. A fun component was the inclusion of information from the last two children born in Mountain View in 1976, Joshua Lee Craig and Tracey Lorraine Bagley, both born on December 31, who are to be invited to the 2026 unveiling. It was stipulated that the capsule be buried for 50 years, at which time it would be unburied in 2026 in a ceremony open to the public. The contents are to be placed on display in the library and then resealed for another 50 years. Color Me Patriotic: the 1976 Bicentennial call for hydrant artists. One of the programs that was popular and fun during the Bicentennial in 1976 was painting fire hydrants with a patriotic theme. The project was primarily a decentralized grassroots phenomenon driven by local civic groups, Cub Scouts and garden clubs rather than a federal program. It is estimated that tens of thousands were painted nationwide. Called Paint a Plug, the program was locally organized by members of the Mountain View Bicentennial Committee. Led by Grant and April Huberty, the Committee developed a program where about 180 fire hydrants were painted in Mountain View, over 20 percent of the fire hydrants located in Mountain View at the time. To participate a person needed to get a permit at the Community Center on Rengstorff Street. The fee to paint one hydrant was $6.00, $17.76 for three or $19.76 for four. The needed paint, up to five colors, was included with the fee, along with two brushes, a drop cloth and a wet paint sign. Those painting hydrants used their creativity to paint soldiers, historic figures and even Abraham Lincoln. In Mountain View participants ranged in age from 3 to 83. Scout troops, families, senior citizens, church groups and businesses all participated. The Blossom Valley News, no longer published, and the San Jose Mercury News published articles about the hydrant program. Map created by Neil Hendin and IdaRose Sylvester. We will meet at the Los Altos History Museum for a private viewing of the special exhibit The Spirit of 76, reflecting on America's 250. Afterwards Amy Ellison, Director of Exhibits, will speak about the exhibit. Finding Your Family History: DNA Matches and Chromosome Browsers. DNA services like those provided by Ancestry or MyHeritage can help fill out your family tree by providing shared matches or DNA matches. Two profiles are shared matches if they share a segment of DNA along some chromosome, indicating a common ancestor. If profiles A and B are shared matches and profiles B and C are shared matches, do the people represented by A, B and C share a common ancestor? Not necessarily. A chromosome browser can tell you. Robert Cox, his first cousin Larry Cox and their third cousin Franklyn Cooke all share a pair of common great-great-grandparents, George and Sarah Ward Cox. While MyHeritage does offer a chromosome browser, Ancestry does not. First Presbyterian Church of Mountain View celebrates 175 years of Ministry by Cindy Newman. From March to October 1850 a wagon train traveled 2,000 miles from the Midwest to a tiny settlement on the banks of Stevens Creek and El Camino Real. The travelers sought to spread the word of God, not fill their pockets with gold. The settlement became known as Mountain View. On April 4, 1851, three residents, all Cumberland Presbyterian ministers, formed the Cumberland Presbyterian Church. It was the first Protestant congregation between San Jose and San Francisco, and one of only two Presbyterian churches on the Pacific Coast. In 1860 the first church building was constructed at the corner of what would become Castro and Mercy, now City Hall, on land donated by Maria Trinidad Peralta de Castro. She also gave adjacent land for use as a cemetery for all faiths, now Pioneer Memorial Park. This building was destroyed in a fire in 1911. Members were able to save the new organ, pews, pulpit and the Dale bell with the help of others from nearby St. Joseph's Church. The congregation built a much larger church, which survived until 1948 when it was declared unsafe and condemned. A third building was constructed in 1951 on the same property bounded by Castro, Mercy, Franklin and Church. In 1959 the decision was made to move to the corner of Miramonte and Cuesta, where the congregation remains today. The location was formerly part of the 165-acre Benjamin T. Bubb ranch. A celebration of 175 years in ministry was held on Sunday July 19. Who loves Ice Cream? Our Founding Fathers. Thomas Jefferson acquired a taste for ice cream while serving as ambassador in France. He hand copied a recipe for vanilla ice cream and had his staff at Monticello prepare it. Ice houses on the property kept ice ready. George Washington's love of ice cream was well known. He purchased elaborate molds used to shape ice cream, some in the shape of a basket of fruit. Martha liked to add pureed fruit from their farm to the mixture. James Madison also was a lover of ice cream. His wife Dolley famously served a strawberry ice cream creation at President Madison's second inaugural banquet at the White House in 1813. Box 252, Mountain View, CA 94042 www.mountainviewhistorical.org MVHA Board of Directors President: Pamela Baird Vice-President: Robert Cox Secretary: Jamil Shaikh Treasurer: Anthea Chung Past President: Nicholas Perry Historical Data: David Salinero Membership: Position Open Newsletter: John Cortez Director-at-Large: Carol Donahue Director-at-Large: IdaRose Sylvester Director-at-Large: Melanie Kaye Newsletter Design & Layout by Nicholas Perry, Melanie Kaye and Pamela Baird MVHA Board of Directors Email: info@mountainviewhistorical.org Pamela Baird News & Notes This year we are commemorating the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Also known by the tongue twisters- Semiquincentennial, Bisesquicentennial, the Sestercentennial, or the Quarter Millennium. As we know , the most memorable sentence contains the phrase "that all men are created equal". Over the past few months, I've been thinking about this famous document and what it means to me as an individual, to history and to our nation. As a member of the Los Altos History Museum exhibit committee, we have been discussing the upcoming 250th exhibit and what should or should not be included. Exhibit curator Amy Ellison, PhD, has been exploring and expanding the scope of the exhibit- pushing us to think about its impact, the groups of people not mentioned and how the document has been interpreted over the past 250 years. The new exhibit will be on display June 18–-November 8. Recently I was interviewed by Rachel Burnstein, a local historian and educational researcher. She is working on a Declaration of Independence project- talking to local people about their thoughts. In our discussion she asked about my earliest knowledge (which was elementary school) of the Declaration. As a young student, I studied the lists of Grievances contained in the Declaration and I remember thinking- "wow- that' s a long list. No wonder the people were upset with the British government." But it takes more study to understand the full scope of the Declaration. In my opinion, the most dramatic reference to the Declaration is that by Abraham Lincoln in the Gettysburg Address. Lincoln ties the document to the founding and ideals of our nation "Fourscore and seven years ago, our fathers brought forth upon this continent a new nation, conceived in liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal". T oday those remain powerful words. Let us hope that we as a people, can continue to pursue that mutual pledge to each other as contained in Declaration. Upcoming Walking tour of Downtown Mountain View April 26th, 2 pm http://mvhistory.eventbrite.com/ 3 by Robert Cox, MVHA Vice President Former Mayor and current Vice Mayor Chris Clark's family tree has branches almost all of which reach back to colonial America. Chris has ancestors from England, Scotland, Wales, Ulster, France, Germany, and Sweden. His fourth greatgrandfather Charles Edgar Clark, Sr. was born in 1795 in Perthshire Scotland, immigrating first to Pennsylvania, then later finding his way to Henderson County, Illinois. Charles's son, Charles Edgar Clark, Jr. married Mariah Cox in 1862. So, who knows, Chris and I may be distant relatives! One of Chris's eighth great-grandfathers, Rev. Nathaniel Jenkins, was a Baptist minister and an early advocate of religious liberty. Born in 1678 in Tyngraig, Wales, he immigrated to colonial New Jersey in 1710, and was elected a member of the colonial council. In 1721, a bill was introduced "to punish such as denied the doctrines of the Trinity, the Divinity of Christ, and the inspiration of the Scriptures" . Jenkins spoke passionately against the bill, declaring "although I believe these doctrines as firmly as the warmest advocate of the bill, yet I would never consent to oppose those who rejected them with law or with any other weapon than argument." One of Chris's fourth great-grandfathers, Benjamin Coleman Coghill, was likely his first ancestor to live in Rozetta, Illinois, where Chris was born. Coghill was born in 1803 in Henrico County, Virginia. Coghill had three wives, Millicent, Mary, and Loucie. Chris is descended through Mary. Loucie was a school teacher in Hannibal, Missouri, where Samuel Clemens (a.k.a. Mark Twain) was one of her students. Loucie was not fond of the Clemens family, referring to them as "inveterate liars." I suppose a world-renown author of fiction needs to start somewhere! Like many Virginians of the time, Coghill owned slaves. Shaken by the Nat Turner rebellion of 1831, he decided to liberate his slaves and relocate to a Free State. Coghill wrote, "I procured good homes as I could for the aged and sent all who were young to Liberia." Then in the spring of 1836, Coghill and his family set out for what is now Henderson County, Illinois, arriving in May. Chris's family has had a strong and continuous presence in the county since then. Chris was born in 1983 and developed an interest in politics at a young age. He watched CNBC and CNN from a giant motorized satellite dish on the family farm. Seeking broader life experiences, he learned about the Congressional Page Program, and was nominated to the program by Democratic Congressman Lane Evans. At age 16, Chris was off to Washington, D. C.! Chris was encouraged by the Page School counselor to apply for college summer school programs and so ended up Stanford, both for the summer program and later as an undergraduate. After graduation, Chris joined AT & T's rotational management program, working on the IPhone launch team. Chris came to Mountain View when he joined Loopt, a startup company providing smartphone location services. Chris writes, "I rented an apartment off Whisman Road, and I quickly found the community welcoming and accessible. Mountain View felt like a place where I could put down roots after years of Clark, continued on page 8 Treasurer's Report Through Q1 2026 —Anthea Chung, Treasurer The Mountain View Historical Association is a nonprofit organization focused on preserving and promoting local history. Mariah (Cox) Clark (1843-1919) Benjamin Coleman Coghill (1803-1880) Vice Mayor Chris Clark Mountain View Family History Spotlight 4 A visit to the Mountain View Police Department, located inside the Police and Fire Administration building at Villa and Franklin streets, reveals contrasts with its history and its present. A display along a hallway showcases outdated equipment the MVPD has used over the decades, which is situated just around a corner from the department's state-of-the-art communications center. Also presenting a contrast is that the 1980 Police and Fire Administration building, which has gotten a bit long in the tooth to sufficiently accommodate the needs of two public-safety departments serving a city at the heart of Silicon Valley modernity. It's not just the agency operations that are located in the easily recognizable building, which has been a fixture of downtown for more than 45 years. An emergency dispatch center, fire department administration, emergency operations, and support staff all work out of the same location. However, plans are underway to replace and modernize the entire complex, expanding it more fully across the 4.3-acre site -- including sleeping quarters for police and fire personnel who live far from Mountain View – and address the city's evolving public-safety needs. The city council is presently reviewing those plans. It won't be the first time the MVPD, established in 1902, has moved into larger and updated facilities. Doug Johnson, the department's resident historian who's a veritable fountain of information on the subject, wrote an excellent history of the MVPD. In it he points out that the department's first station was "….just an office within the 1909 City Hall at Castro and California Street. That office was divided into two rooms, one of which was the jail. The jail consisted of an iron cage within a slightly larger room, and most of the jail's 'tenants' were transients passing through town looking for a warm, dry place to sleep." By 1952, the MVPD force of 11 officers were working out of an increasingly crowded office within City Hall – so crowded interviews often had to be conducted outside in patrol cars. These conditions necessitated the construction of a new police station at 947 Villa St. Over following years, additions made to that building weren't sufficient for a department that was, in Doug's words, "bursting at the seams." Mountain View, in the late 1970s, finally approved plans for what is now the present Police and Fire Administration building, constructed kitty-corner from the previous home of MVPD. Certainly, Mountain View's finest will welcome their eventual new home – a vast change and improvement over the department's humble beginnings more a century and a quarter ago. MVPD's Home Has Evolved for over a Century by Jerry SteachEditor's note: A version of this article appeared in November 2025 issue of The Lamppost, the quarterly newsletter of the Old Mountain View Neighborhood Association (OMVNA.org). History Happening Now Don Hershman reacts to a question from Moderator David Garcia History Happening Now continues on page 9 Carol Donahue & Pamela Baird 6 Burma Calling: One Woman's Journey — by M. Elena Lopez It was a time of fear and uncertainty. Peasant rebellions, ethnic violence, strikes, and riots convulsed the British colony of Burma (Myanmar) throughout the 1930s. Amid this unrest, a young Baptist teacher from Mountain View arrived in Rangoon on February 20, 1934. Elizabeth Margery Taylor was born in Puyallup, Washington in 1908. By 1914, her father J. J. Taylor had moved the family to Mountain View, where he worked for the First National Bank. The Taylors were active in the Baptist Church, whose Foreign and Home Missionary Society likely inspired Taylor's interest in overseas service. Mountain View residents also learned about Asian religions from a1926 lecture by the Rev. W. Hopkins, who served at the Baptist mission in India. As a student at Mountain View Union High School, Taylor consistently made it to the honor roll. She belonged to the Girls Glee Club and to the Orchestra, where she played the cello and piano. She accompanied the Glee Club in its presentations, played "countless piano solos," and performed one of the leading roles in the Dramatic Club's "Penrod." The caption next to her 1925 graduating class photo reads, "Her voice was always soft, gentle and low…" Taylor pursued higher education with determination. She earned a Bachelor of Music degree from the University of Redlands and a Bachelor of Arts from San Jose State Teachers College, and also studied at the Baptist Divinity School in Berkeley. In December 1933, she received her formal commission to teach missionary children at the American School in Taunggyi. Taunggyi, located at an elevation of 4,712 feet, had grown from a small Shan village into a British administrative center. Known as the "City of Music," it offered a vibrant cultural scene that suited Taylor's musical passions. In a 1936 letter to her Mountain View friends, she described Saturday military band performances, noting drummers "twirling their sticks and making all sorts of fancy designs in the air." Taylor was deeply committed to music education. She asked friends to send prizes for her piano students, preferring books about music and musicians. She also sought ideas for children's plays and operettas, expressing a longing to spend hours in a well-stocked music or book store. In 1937, a lady tourist persuaded Taylor to travel with her to India. Within four days, she had arranged her journey and departed Taunggyi. Her travels took her from the Himalayan north to southern India. From the Hotel Mount Everest in Darjeeling, she wrote,"The world's 'forehead' is just being veiled by a cloud curtain! Kangchenjunga, 28,156 ft. high, only appears at dawn and sunset." When Taylor's initial term in Burma ended in 1939, she returned to the United States. Although she planned to go back, World War II interrupted travel. She resumed teaching in Burma in 1946 but between 1953-1959 was not on active duty. Illness forced her return to the United States in 1964. She later served in the Philippines before retiring in 1973. At the Central Philippine University she organized a Bell Ringers choir that continues to perform today. Elizabeth Margery Taylor died in Fresno in 1991, leaving behind a life marked by dedication to education, music, and international service. "Her voice was always soft, gentle and low…" 7 The Bicentennial recognition of the signing of the Declaration of Independence was a year long effort, both locally and nationally. Congress created the American Revolution Bicentennial Administration (ARBA) in 1973, which it charged with encouraging and coordinating locally sponsored events. A look at the Wikipedia website reveals a huge number of events that were conducted around the country in 1976. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Bicentennial The city of Mountain View formed a volunteer committee of at least 16 members to organize efforts to be held throughout 1976. Local planning efforts (and some events) commenced in 1975 and took up most of that year. The committee, led by Joseph Cusimano, a prominent resident and council member, created subcommittees to develop ideas and programs. In 1975 outreach began to recruit volunteers and raise awareness of the upcoming events. On May 4, 1975, a marker to recognize John W. Whisman, an early settler in the north Bayshore area, was placed inside the main gate at Moffett field. Two flags, one created for the American Revolution Bicentennial Administration (ARBA) and the famous Betsy Ross flag, were raised in a ceremony on July 4,1975, at Rengstorff Park. The city could raise the ARBA flag because Mountain View met the requirements to be an official Bicentennial city. Later in July the Moffett Field Naval Air Station hosted an open house and air show. The city sponsored a booth to provide information about the Bicentennial. On August 24,1975, the Filipino-American Senior Citizens of the Bay Area presented a daylong event. Held at Rengstorff Park, the festivities included a fashion show, music, dancing and food. In November the Bicentennial committee hosted a booth at the three day holiday bazaar for the MV Cultural Arts Council (precursor to the Visual Arts Committee) held at the Community Center. In the next two issues of this newsletter, we will explore the planning and events held in 1976. Stay tuned—some are really fun and creative! A year of commemoration & celebration1976 The Betsy Ross Flag at San Francisco City Hall Local WWI Soldier becomes a Museum Greeter After President Pamela Baird and Board Member David Salinero visited the World War I exhibit at the Moffett Field Museum, they remembered MVHA has an authentic U.S. Army uniform from 1917. David's project to catalog artifacts in the History Center at the library and and Senior Librarian James Thadjudeen easily located Glenn Wilson's perfectly preserved WW1 uniform. Glenn's son, also named Glenn, had wisely decided to have it cleaned and professionaly packed away before donating it to the Mountain View Historical Association. In addition, Glenn donated a copy of his father's memoir to accompany his uniform and document the family's history as early residents and business owners of Mountain View. When you decide to pay a visit to the Moffett Field Museum, be sure to explore the World War I trench. And thanks to MVHA stop by to greet Glenn in full uniform at the entrance to the museum, along with a brief biography and excerpt from his memoir. His uniform is on loan. The WWI Exhibit runs through May, 2026. Hours are Wednesday through Saturday, 10am–3pm. moffettfieldmuseum.org Glenn William Wilson, was born January 2, 1887 in Dover, Minnesota, to William and Bertha Wilson. He came to California after college to attend Stanford University, where he received a master's degree in electrical engineering in 1917. He married Mary Chadwick Eastwood on 30 July 1917 and left for the Army two days later. After training at what was then Camp Fremont in Menlo Park, he shipped out on a troop train to New York. He arrived in France three months before the Armistise was signed, and spent the winter building and maintaining housing for soldiers returning to the U.S. from the trenches in France. He and his family lived in Mountain View, where, in 1923, he started Valley Electric, specializing in wiring and electrical contracting. He ran the business until 1964, when his son, Glenn E. Wilson, took over. Glenn William Wilson, founder of Valley Electric in Mountain View, died Dec. 17, 1985 in Los Altos Hills, California. He was 98 years old. Glenn W. Wilson 1917 Valley Electric, Castro Street 1924 8 bouncing around for school and work." Realizing how much local government impacts daily life, Chris applied for, and was appointed to, the city's Human Relations and Planning Commissions, and served on the council from 2013–2021. He served as mayor in 2014. Chris was reelected for a third term in 2024. Looking back on his public service in our city, Chris is most proud of completing the Community Center, Aquatics Center, and extensions to the city's trail systems. As the first gay mayor, Chris also cherishes the first time the city flew the Pride flag at the Civic Center Plaza. After the event, city staff handed Chris a box filled with deeply personal notes that had been spontaneously left at the base of the flagpole by community members sharing their journeys and thanking the council for making them feel safe. Chris notes, "Even seemingly small, symbolic actions can matter more than you expect." Chris offers the following advice to young people pursuing a career in tech or politics: "Take calculated risks while time is still on your side, especially when rare and exciting opportunities arise. Don't be afraid to make mistakes, learn from them, and adjust course. Ask for help. Mentors are often closer and more accessible than you think. And when you succeed, pay it forward. That's how careers—and communities—are built." The Clark Family: Adults: Chris, his sister Megan Gullberg, his grandmother Beverly (Sprout) Clark, his brother-in-law Karl Gullberg. Karl & Megan's four children: Reese, Elijah, Adalyn, and Kynzie. A fifth is on the way! The Clark Family Farm Where there's a Will, there's a Way! Finding Your Family Historyby Robert Cox Some of the most detailed information that you can discover about family relationships are in court records. Among the most valuable for genealogical research are wills and the associated probate records. In particular, in the years before census records recorded individuals by name, these records are among the few official government records that explicitly include family relationships. A will typically begin with a statement that the testator (the one making the will) is of sound mind and body, that this is his last will and testament, and that all previous wills are revoked. After that, the testator typically says that he intends his debts to be paid. Finally, the testator lists each item of personal property and to whom that item is willed. There are usually provisions indicating to whom each item would go in case the person willed the property passes away. When property is willed to a minor, there are often stipulations on how much the minor will inherit and under what circumstances. For example, the will could indicate that a minor would only receive certain money when he reaches a certain age. When family members are willed property, their relationship to the testator is usually specified. In the absence of a will, an application for letters of administration is generally filed. This document will list information about the deceased's next of kin and his property. For example, when my father's uncle, Clinton Cox, passed away, with no widow or children, his brothers filed a document with the judge of the probate court stating: The undesigned hereby makes application to be appointed as administrator of the estate of Clinton A. Cox late of the City of Cleveland in said county, deceased, and on oath states that said Clinton A. Cox died on or about the 6th day of April 1928, intestate, leaving no widow and the following named persons, his next of kin: Applicant further states that there is not to his knowledge and last will and testament of said decedent in existence. That the whole personal estate of said decedent consists of: one Studebaker Automobile coupe 1921; two Boston Bull Terriers; Eighteen Dollars in Cash; Household Furniture. The real estate of said decedent consists of house and lot at No. 1507 E. 65th St., Cleveland, Ohio. A great place to find wills and other probate records is by using the free FamilySearch "Full Text" feature. Go to www.familysearch.org and click on the "Search" drop down menu. From there select "Full Text." This will bring up a form where you can enter and name, place, and year range: Putting the name in quotes let's you indicate that the first and last name should appear together in the searched document. It was designed by staff architects and engineers of the Department of the Navy's Bureau of Yards & Docks, with Rear Admiral A.L. Parsons in charge. The principal designer was Ernest L. Wolf, a civil engineer employed by the Goodyear-Zeppelin Corporation of Akron, Ohio. Originally constructed by the U.S. Navy as the centerpiece of NAS (Naval Air Station) Sunnyvale, the U.S. Army took over the administration of the base in 1935 following the destruction of the dirigible U.S.S. Macon. The base remained under Army control until 1942 when the Navy reassumed control. The Navy retained ownership of NAS Moffett Field until 1994, when the base was closed as part of the Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) process. At that time, the Navy turned NAS Moffett Field over to NASA. Until NAS Moffett Field was decommissioned in 1994, the Navy used Hangar 1 to house a variety of aircraft, in particular P2 and P3 Orion surveillance aircraft. Box 252, Mountain View, CA 94042 www.mountainviewhistorical.org MVHA Board of Directors President: Pamela Baird Vice-President: Robert Cox Secretary: Jamil Shaikh Treasurer: Anthea Chung Past President: Nicholas Perry Historical Data: David Salinero Membership: Vacant Newsletter: Melanie Kaye Director-at-Large: Carol Donahue Director-at-Large: IdaRose Sylvester Director-at-Large: Melanie Kaye Newsletter Design & Layout by Melanie Kaye and Pamela Baird MVHA Board of Directors Email: info@mountainviewhistorical.org e Pamela Baird News & Notes National Archives Over the recent holidays my family and I stayed near the Fisherman's Wharf area. The San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park is located nearby. A 50-acre park has grown around the Aquatic Park Cove, which hosts historic sailing vessels, (which currently are not on display because of renovations to the Hyde Street Pier) a visitor center and a museum. The Visitor Center is in a large brick building https://www.nps.gov/safr/ planyourvisit/the-visitor-center.htm. We have walked by the entrance numerous times without noticing it. This time we saw the entrance and were rewarded with a wonderful exhibition covering the history of ship building, the growth of San Francisco and the many groups of people who have contributed to the story of San Francisco and the Bay area. A person could easily spend two–three hours exploring the exhibits. This made me wonder—are there stories and history for local parks on the peninsula? The city of Los Altos has a page on their website listing the names of the parks and photos for each. A map is also available. None of the parks have any history noted. The website for Los Altos Hills is similar. The city of Sunnyvale also has a a listing of the parks on their website, as well as a map. One listing has information about the history behind the name of the park. Only Palo Alto has information about the history of the parks on their website. An interactive map contains a drop-down option for each park. https://www.paloalto.gov/Departments/Community- Services/Parks-Open-Space-Golf-Division/ Neighborhood-Parks. Another click explains the history of the park—who was the namesake, when the park was developed, etc. It's a great way to learn about the history of Palo Alto. The city of Mountain View has a listing of parks but no map https://www.mountainview.gov/our- city/departments/community-services/parks-and-trails/parks/city-parks. No historical information is provided. Several Mountain View parks have historical panels (Heritage Park and Eagle Park), but many more could be enhanced by including historical information (Wyandotte, Varsity, Thaddeus and more). The MVHA hopes that the city can be encouraged to include historical panels at city parks. This would be a wonderful way to give residents and visitors a better idea of the history of Mountain View. Looking for History—visit a park! The San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park Visitor Center The City of Palo Alto has a multi-layer website with information that covers the history of their city parks The MVHA is looking for someone to lead the membership efforts! Reach out to new members, maintain membership rosters and encourage early renewals for existing members. Sound like your specialty? Email us! info@mountainviewhistorical.org. 3 e Mountain View Family History Spotlight by Robert Cox, MVHA Vice President The known family history of former Police Chief and Mayor Robert Schatz begins in the German village of Ehlenbogen. Hanss Shatz, Robert's seventh great-grandfather, was born here in 1608. The village is situated in a mountainous area at the bend in a small stream. The geography gave rise to the village's coat-of-arms, which depicts a bent man's arm in a blue sleeve. One might even think that this coat-of-arms foreshadowed Chief Schatz's career with the Mountain View Police Force! The people of Ehlenbogen and the surrounding district of Wuerttemburg, including the Schatz family, were primarily Protestants. Records show that five generations of Robert's Schatz ancestors, from 1600-1800, were all named either Johannes or Hanss (both German variants of "John"). Around 1800, Robert's third great-grandfather Andreas Schatz lead his family to the Banat area of Hungary, and with a number of other Germany families founded the village of Liebling. But less than a generation later, the family relocated to an area near Odessa, Russia (now Ukraine), called Neu Freudental. Catherine the Great, Empress of Russia, was of German origin. She was eager to see more of her countrymen settle in Russia, and granted them privileges such as the free exercise of their religion and language within their communities, as well as exemption from military service and taxation. Germans living in these communities were known as Black Sea Germans. After Catherine's reign, Russians were less kind to the Black Sea Germans living on their territory. Many, including Robert's great-grandfather Johannes Schatz, immigrated to the USA. Johannes and his bride Katharina set sail on the ship Augusta Victoria from Hamburg, Germany, and arrived in New York City in 1889. From there, they found their way to South Dakota and then North Dakota, to where many other Black Sea Germans had come. It is estimated that about one-third of North Dakotans today are descended from Black Sea Germans. Around 1920, Johannes's son, also named Johannes, resettled his family in Idaho, to take up potato farming. In fact, Robert Schatz was born in 1927 in Pocatello, Idaho. A few years later, Robert's father, John, followed some cousins to Oakland, California, to work as a grocery manager. Robert would spend most of his childhood years in Oakland. After graduating from San Jose State University in 1955, Robert was first a seaman in the US Navy and then a captain in the US Army. In 1950, he began a 34-year career as a Mountain View police officer, becoming Police Chief in 1971. He was Mountain View's first police chief to earn a college degree and the initiator of Mountain View's progressive policing policy. Robert Schatz also served eleven years on the city council, with two terms as mayor. During that time, the city gave Shoreline Park the form it has today. He was instrumental in the design and approval of Mountain View's current police and fire building, which bears his name.
