Certainly not big news, but the Mockbee Building, located on the northeast corner of Castro and Villa Streets, was recently repainted. The handsome c. 1906 building's new gray and white scheme freshens up this venerable Downtown landmark. Bryant Street Building Boom. A new chapter of Downtown Mountain View's long history is being built along Bryant Street. The City Council recently approved a new office building on the former site of Dunn's Automotive. Charles "Chuck" Dunn opened the auto shop in 1975. Mr. Dunn recently passed away at the age of 90. The new office building is one of three under construction along Bryant Street, including Bryant Park Plaza where the historic Pearson House and Immigant House once stood. Immigrant House Update. In May the City Council selected 771 North Rengstorff Avenue as their first preference for a permanent home for the "Immigrant House." The 1.2 acre property was recently sold to the City by longtime owner Frances Stieper in hopes it would be turned into a City Park. We'll continue to provide updates on this project as it moves forward. Stay tuned for more updates on the future of this iconic structure. 4 By Barbara Kinchen Historical Data Chair Howard Lane, Mountain View High School class of '58, was in the History Center talking about people, places, and events and mentioned that Lane Avenue was named for his family. The street is only a couple of blocks long and comes into El Camino Real between Castro and Boranda. Clark's Charcoal Broiler is at the corner of El Camino and Lane Avenue. William, Hurcial, and Wilbur Lane came from Texas in the early 1930's and were prominent businessmen in our area for almost forty years. They had creameries in Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale, as well as furniture and appliance stores, a coin shop, and a drive-in restaurant. The restaurant at 1313 El Camino Real opened in 1947, but soon after was operated by Johnny Mac's. After a fire in 1961 it again was Lane's Drive-In. When I was in high school, the popular place for food, fun and gossip was just across Castro Street from the school at Bill Lane's Air Base Creamery. He made and sold something we called a "milkshake on a stick." Sometime in the 1940's Lanes operated a creamery right close to the Mountain View Theatre. Share your Mtn. View Memories! Box 252, Mountain View, Ca 94042 www.mountainviewhistorical.org BOARD MEMBERS & CHAIRS President: Patricia Figueroa Vice-President: Cliff Del Carlo Secretary: Jamil Shaikh Treasurer: John Figueroa Past President Bob Weaver Historical Data: Barbara Kinchen Membership: June Casey Newsletter Editor: Nick Perry Ways & Means: Richard Espinosa Director-at Large: Nick Galiotto Hospitality: Helene Hughes Memorial & Remembrances: Trudi Tuban Programs: Bob Weaver Publicity: Jes Casey n Memoriam Updates from Around Town By Nick Perry Newsletter Editor Happy 110th Birthday to the City of Mountain View! On November 7,2012 the City will celebrate its 110th anniversary of incorporation. Hard to believe it has already been a decade since the city was busy celebrating its Centennial! Some interesting facts about the city's incorporation: • The vote to incorporate was held on 11/1/1902 and 58% of voters (152 men) voted for incorporation. 64 voted against. • The 1902 town limits were the railroad, Pettis Avenue, El Camino Real and Calderon Avenue with a slight jog encompassing the elementary school on El Camino Real. • Mountain View is the 5th oldest incorporated city in the county, but the 6th to incorporate. How's that? Alviso incorporated in 1852 but became part of San Jose in 1968. Although there are not any official City sponsored-events scheduled to mark the city's 110th, the MVHA's Fall meeting just three days before will be a great way to mark the occasion. I'm looking forward to sharing some of the fascinating photos and stories uncovered while researching and writing my new book, Mountain View Then & Now. See page 6 for more information on the book and the MVHA meeting! In other news, a new Downtown office building was approved by the City Council at 902 Villa Street, currently the location of the circa 1880s Pearson House. In August the Mtn. View Voice reported that a couple of parties have offered to have the house relocated to their private properties. Marina Marinovich is leading a campaign to relocate and restore the 130+ year old residential cottage on the same property, pictured above at 166 Bryant Street. Her idea is to have the structure relocated, restored, and opened to the public as an "Immigrant House" - an educational resource that tells the story of early laborers who came to Mountain View from around the world to start a new life. Stay tuned for updates. 2 New to the History Center By Barbara Kinchen Historical Data Chair From Kevin Duggan — Copy of an undated postcard showing the Trinity Methodist Church Aid Society The ladies, all in long dresses or skirts, are on the porch of a large home. Newsletter Editor: Nick Perry Ways & Means: Richard Espinosa Director-at Large: Nick Galiotto Hospitality: Helene Hughes Memorial & Remembrances: Trudi Tuban Programs: Bob Weaver Publicity: Jes Casey Updates from Around Town By Nick Perry Newsletter Editor In this new column, we offer a brief digest of modern-day news related to Mountain View's history. First, an update on Moffett Field's iconic Hangar One. As the photo above shows, toxic siding has been removed by the government, exposing the impressive steel structure of the landmark dirigible hangar for the first time since its construction in the 1932. The steel is being coated to withstand effects of weathering while the Federal Government continues to ponder whether they'll accept an offer from Google's founders to restore the hangar. We'll keep you posted on any future updates. After over 60 years downtown, Meyer Appliance is relocating to the former Ethan Allen building at 861 East El Camino Real near the Sunnyvale Border. As far as we know, Meyer's downtown location (originally built to house JC Penney) features the only publically accessible escalator in the entire City! Given how hopping Downtown is these days it'd be surprising to see the space vacant for long. Across town, San Antonio Center is experiencing some major changes. If you haven't been there recently you'll be surprised to see new residential and commercial buildings rising where Sears once stood. When complete, the "Village at San Antonio Center" will replace the oldest portion of the center with mix of shopping and housing akin to San Jose's Santana Row. A couple historic community events are occurring this summer. Mountain View's 60th annual Obon Festival and Bazaar will be held at the Mountain View Buddhist Temple on the weekend of July 20-21. The popular summer festival celebrates and honors the lives of lost loved ones with Japanese music, dance, food, and games. Our neighbor Sunnyvale is celebrating the centennial of its incorporation on the weekend of August 25-26. The website www.sunnyva1e100.com has more information on the festivities. Finally, the Rengstorff House is hosting numerous arts and music events this summer- see page 4 for details! 2 New to the History Center By Barbara Kinchen Historical Data Chair • From Katie Hambly of Long Beach, a 1916 Blue and Grey Mountain View High School yearbook. The school was located on El Camino Real at Calderon Avenue. There were seven teachers and principal, E.L. Zahn, and 25 graduates. In addition to the usual pictures of students, faculty, buildings and organizations, there are many poems and essays, news of alumni, business advertisements, and seven pages of the sorriest "joshes" (jokes) ever. A reception to meet the artists will be held on Thursday, August 2, 5:00-7:00 in Rengstorff House. A New Park's Rich History By Nick Perry Newsletter Editor Have you been to Mtn. View's newest (37th!) park? On Saturday, June 9, Mariposa Park opened between Mariposa Street and West Dana Street. "Mariposa" means "butterfly" in Spanish, and the park's design by Robert Mowat Associates carries that theme in many unique and playful ways such a butterfly garden and benches shaped like caterpillars. Within the butterfly garden are four pillars that might be of special interest to MVHA members; Each pillar features an interpretive panel on the history of the surrounding area, one of Mountain View's oldest neighborhoods. Each of the four history panels is paired with a separate panel drawing parallels between the neighborhood's growth and the four life-stages of a butterfly. The park was built on land formerly occupied by a collection of cottages and a Victorian-era home and barn. Although these structures had to be removed to build the park, there history is commemorated on the fourth pillar. MVHA's leadership supported the creation of these pillars and newsletter editor Nick Perry helped the park's landscape architect write and review text, as well as pick out photos to use on each pillar. So next time you're in the vicinity of Mariposa Park - be sure to check out this new tribute to our city's history. 4 By Barbara kinchen Historical Data Chair In 1963 the City Council approved plans for a new housing development for the Frank Ormonde farm property at Stierlin Road and the proposed new Middlefield Road extension. View Police Captain January 25, 2012 Faye Taylor June 13,2011 THE LAST OF THE PRUNE PICKERS A PRE-SILICON VALLEY STOR\ News &Notes Spring Meeting Preview By Bob Weaver Past President and Programs Chair Not long before the Santa Clara Valley of California was known for silicon, the Valley was largely covered with orchards. There were orchards of pears, apricots, cherries, walnuts and the king of them all—prunes. Most of the orchards were part " of small family farms, and there 4 were thousands of them. This - , is the story of how those farms * ,41 4" came into being and thrived. It is also the story of one of the last of those farms, of the farmer and of some of the young boys and girls who had the privilege of working for him. We were among the last of the prune pickers. Tim Stanley grew up in Saratoga, and during his teens worked on one of the last fruit farms there. When he married, he and his wife moved to Los Gatos and later to Irvine. After running a construction business for thirty years, Tim is now working as a free-lance writer. He has published a local history book titled, The Last of the Prune Pickers: A Pre-Silicon Valley Story. His web site is: www.2timothypublishing.com Mr. Stanley will give a brief overview of the book with visual aid. He will divide the presentation into two parts: the Historical Background for the orchard farms that once graced the Santa Clara Valley and the Way of Life of the orchard farmers. The Historical Background presentation will include a little about Mission Santa Clara agricultural operations, the Californios and cattle ranching, early American farming successes and failures, and highlights of the technology stories that transformed the Valley into "The Garden of the World."In the Way of Life presentation, Mr. Stanley will discuss orchard farming, market challenges and the Sunsweet story the end of the orchard era, and some lessons learned. Mr. Stanley has traveled a great distance to speak with us, and others who have heard him speak have found him quite entertaining. Please don't forget that our spring meeting will be one week earlier than usual, April 29, so double check your calendars as you won't want to miss this program. Mr. Stanley will have a few books available for sale at our meeting. Memories of a MV Prune Picker By Eugene Darrell Sharp MVHA Member Young MV Prune Pickers: Warren Goff, Nolan, Eugene, and David Sharp, Harry Goff, and Sylvia Sharp. In front of the great oak tree at El Ranchito Avenue behind the Sharp home. In August of 1947 I picked my first prunes at the orchards of Ernest and Fanny Powell on the corner of Alma Street (now Central Expressway) and Rengstorff Avenue. The Powells were members of the Trinity Methodist Church, which my family also attended. There were about 10 acres of orchard on their property; over one-half were prune trees along with a few plum trees next to Alma. The apricot trees were on the other side of the long driveway from Rengstorff to the Powell home. On a Monday morning early in August I biked to work through town on Villa Street. I passed the Castro home (Villa Francesca) and I biked across the railroad tracks on Rengstorff and into the Powell driveway. I took two buckets into the orchard, kneeled down in the soft smooth dirt and started picking prunes with both hands. I usually had one foot on the ground in front of me so that I could rest my chest on my knee. It was easy to advance by moving the other foot forward and resting the other side of my chest on the other knee. I usually ate several prunes when I started picking. Having grown up on a farm west of Eaton Colorado there was something very satisfying about being in that wonderful Santa Clara Valley dirt. Mr. Powell would precede us by shaking the tree branches to increase the number of prunes on the ground. I carried the two buckets heaped with prunes and poured them into the lugs nearby. I could usually pick about 20 lugs of prunes a day at 20 cents a box. I earned about $50 that August, the first money that I ever earned. I opened a savings account at the Bank of America on the corner of Castro and Villa Streets and put almost all of my earnings there. The bank building now houses the Red Rock Cafe. I picked prunes at the Powell's for three of four years. At noon I ate the lunch my mother made for me and would watch Mr. Powell pour a lug box into a wire basket at the end of a 20-foot four-inch diameter wooden pole. The pole was suspended in the middle about eight feet above ground. Mr. Powell would then take the far end of the pole and lift the basket into a tub containing boiling lye (NaOH.) After maybe 30 seconds, he would lift the basket, let the lye drain for a minute and rotate the basket above a drying tray so that he could pour the prunes onto the tray and smooth them in one layer. The boiling hot lye bath broke the skins of the prunes so that they would dry in the sun and not spoil. About a week later, the prunes would be ready to sell. [imagine that the lye never bothered any prune eater, because the sugars in the prunes and the slightly acidic prune skins would neutralize the lye. My cousins Warren and Harry, and their mother, Eva Mae Goff, came to visit several summers. They stayed with my grandparents in a former field office—still standing on El Ranchito Way—that my father used to supervise the installation of the Westinghouse equipment at the 40 by 80 NASA Wind Tunnel. We picked prunes at the Popovich orchard at the southern boundary between Mountain View and Sunnyvale on El Camino Real. Warren and Harry joined me and my siblings Nolan and Sylvia Sharp picking prunes there. I was docked pay for a box of prunes because I picked some worthless prunes that every one else said were no good. I also picked prunes with a couple of buddies: Dickie Eglington and Ubaldo Maxwelliano St. Jovenine Tonella. We biked out Grant Road across the railroad tracks (now Foothill Expressway) where we often paused to lay one of our bikes across the tracks to cause the wig wags and red light to flash. A pickup truck stopped to wait for the coming train. When the driver saw us young punks, he shook his head and crossed the tracks. We picked prunes and goofed off, pissing into the smudge pots, and had lunch sitting in an oak tree on Fremont Avenue. We watched the steam engine stop to take on water from a tank next to the track. We went to get paid at a home next to the Boy Scout Hall, a former fire house, next to the home where Louise and Will Jordan lived for a time on the Hope and Villa corner. The former Boy Scout House is now a MV parking lot and the two houses at 191 Hope Street are now dental offices. With all the summer work in the orchards there was no time to get into mischief. 5 On the Web In this new occasional feature we will share some of the best comments, memories and stories shared by "fans" of the Mountain View Historical Association's facebook page. Givich June 19, 1911-June 12,2011 By Bob Weaver Past President and Programs Chair The Museum Project Team has been extremely busy with the final details of the Pearson House proposal that would add a history house to our museum site at Cuesta Park. The Pearson House dates from 1888 and will be a grand 1st step toward the establishment of our History Museum. The feeling of "a sense of place" is challenging in an urbanized area and especially difficult if one has no knowledge of the area's evolution. The inclusion of the Pearson House with our History Museum would preserve a rich layer of local history, a snapshot in time. Like the Gilbert Smith House at the Los Altos Museum, the Pearson House would be a window into the past. This is an exciting opportunity and our project team members have put in hundreds of hours of their time and talent to make it a reality. It would be very encouraging to us if members of this association would publicly support our efforts by writing letters of support for the Pearson House and the History Museum, and send them to the Mountain View Voice and the Los Altos Town Crier for publication. Use your voice to keep the dream moving forward. F I Memon-es Remembering John J. Pear On April 7, 2011, longtime MVHA member and life-long Mountain View & Los Altos resident John Pear passed away. His son Matt Pear shares with us this account of his father's life. My father, John Pear was born in 1928 at his family's ranch on Ortega Avenue, then named Calderon Avenue, to Martin and Milica Pear. The Pears were one of Mtn. View's pioneer families, having emigrated from Austria, now Croatia, in the late 1800s. During his childhood John experienced the deprivation of the Great Depression first hand and learned the values of hard work, capriciousness, and inherent risks in farming. As a child he was put to work irrigating strawberries where venture capital companies on Sandhill Road now stand. This experience was a constant influence throughout his life and molded his investment principles, work ethic, and political perspective. John J. Pear c. 1937 with dog Scotty Courtesy Matt Pear John graduated from Mtn. View High School where he was Student Body President, was selected for Boys State, and excelled in football. The San Jose State Spartan Daily heralded his arrival by writing, "With his reputation as 'Lineman of the Year' in 1946, and his selection as All Santa Clara Valley Athletic League tackle in 1945 and 1946, John Pear, 190 pounder, comes from Mtn. View High School, and appears to have won himself a starting berth on 'Bud' Winters' freshman football squad." After earning an AA degree in business, he worked for an advertising firm in San Francisco that required business trips to Hollywood quite an experience for someone from this area. In high school he met his beloved wife of 56 years, Edna, and they had two sons, myself (Matt) and my brother Mark. Shortly after being married, he was drafted into the US Army and stationed in Berlin, Germany. After completing his tour of duty he became a contractor whose crew worked on Silicon Valley construction projects, including his own developments. As a landlord, he constantly worried about tenants and keeping expenses at an absolute minimum so he could pass the savings on them; he saw far too many families lose their land due to financial hardships and escalating property taxes and assessments. My father insisted that my brother and I work on the ranch tending to crops and that we learn the construction trades, in particular concrete construction, which he remembered being a good trade even during the Depression. From 1964 to 1994 my father and his brother Joe augmented the sale of eggs, cherries, and apricots with fireworks, pumpkins, and Christmas trees at the corner of California and Ortega, where the lot remains today. They donated Christmas trees to local parishes such as Saint Athanasius and Saint Joseph's, as well as El Camino Hospital on several occasions. My father's ties to the family ranch remained throughout his life with the planting of an annual vegetable garden and his wish to see the remaining parcel on Ortega developed. As many of you know, he was a member of the Mountain View Historical Association, Napredak Club, Native Sons of the Golden West, and SIRS, from which he drew camaraderie and a connection to his heritage and agricultural and construction past. The Allis-Chalmers Model M Tractor and Meyers Sprayer on display at the Los Altos Heritage Museum are from the ranch and were donated by John in recognition of The Valley of Heart's Delight. 4 Life on Central Avenue By Gladys Robinson A rural Central Avenue c. 1964 with Moffett Blvd. on the left and Stevens Creek on the right. Mountain View Public Library Photo Archives Gladys Robinson is an MVHA member and retired painter of local landscapes. The following are selected excerpts from her written memories of life on Mountain View's Central Avenue. For the full version of her essay, e-mail mvha.newsletter@gmail.com. After our MVHA meeting on November 8, 2011, I drove one block north and turned right. For memory's sake I wanted to see where I crossed the ford of Stevens Creek at the end of Central Avenue so many times. From the berm that has been set up at the end of the Avenue and the new Stevens Creek Trail bridge I could find no trace of the old road bed down and up the steep bank across the creek. Grandpa and Grandma' place and walnut orchard was located nearby at 59 Central Avenue. When Moffett Field brought the sailors to Mountain View the family remodeled our tank house into a rental, my uncle Pete's bunk house became a rental, and a garage was moved and remodeled into a small apartment. The place became Anderson Court. I still remember our phone number, just 626. Across the road lived our friends the Alfreds. They were old people who didn't farm their place so they had a glorious field of California poppies in the spring. I picked all the poppies my hands could hold to put in a jar on my bedroom dresser but they just wilted. Every day I carried a quart jar of our cow's milk across the road to their front porch. I never could stomach the warm milk right out of the cow. It didn't seem clean somehow, but through the cream separator and in the ice box it tasted good. Down the street lived a Mexican man named Bailey, who lived with his family in a shack across the creek on the other bank. The junior Chamber of Commerce hired him to make adobe bricks for the Adobe Building. I remember seeing dozens of bricks drying on the ground right out there in his yard. I used to think the junior Chamber of Commerce was the most important organization in Mountain View because they were responsible for building the Adobe. They liked to party there - my mother told me one party got a little out of hand and a hunk of bread landed in the coffee cup of the Mayor's wife. The mayor disbanded the junior Chamber of Commerce. I have never heard of any junior Chamber of Commerce since. The bank of Stevens Creek was a pleasant picnic spot in summer. My mother told me years ago she saw her mother spear a salmon in the creek. My Grandfather started a gravel business selling sand and gravel from the dry creek bed. After a storm, Stevens Creek was my rain gauge. I once saw the creek an angry torrent of muddy water that must have been five feet deep. On Sunday morning once a year I woke up to the sound of parade drums coming from Stierlin Road. I would run down Central Avenue to see the beautiful dark haired Portuguese Queen and her princesses in their white satin gowns with sparkling silver crowns marching downtown to the Catholic church. How I longed to be a Portuguese princess; I was just a homely towhead. These are some memories of my little world on Central Avenue, now "Gone with the Wind." 5 Membership Membership Report Join us today! Rendering of the Mountain View Cohousing Project from Calderon Avenue, with the Abbot/Bakotich house on the left Courtesy Mountain View Cohousing Community New Life for an Old House By Susan Burwen Member of the Mountain View Cohousing Community Susan Burwen, member of the Mountain View Cohousing Community, shares with us the history of the Abbot/Bakotich House at 445 Calderon Avenue, and her group's plans for the property's future. The farmhouse located at 445 Calderon Avenue sits on land purchased by a group of local residents who want to create the first Cohousing Community in Mountain View. Cohousing is a type of collaborative housing in which residents are consciously committed to living as a community, actively participating in the design and operation of their own neighborhood. We envision the Mountain View Cohousing Community as a new 'old-fashioned' neighborhood consisting of 19 energy-efficient condominium homes plus common facilities for shared activities. Parking will be underground to maximize open space in a park-like setting with a garden, orchard and network of pedestrian pathways. The farmhouse will be an integral part of our community. It was originally constructed in 1885 by Charles Abbot, making it ones of the oldest homes in Mountain View. At the time, Calderon Avenue was a rural street and the house was surrounded by a 12-acre plot planted with apricot, walnut, and cherry trees. Remnants of the walnut orchard are still visible, although the trees are no longer viable. In 1926, the house was purchased by the Bakotich family. Ann Bakotich, born in 1917, grew up in the house and lived there until she passed away in 2007. Many residents of the Old Mountain View Neighborhood have fond memories of Ann. 4 New Life for an Old House (continued from page 4) Over the years, several changes to the property have taken place. The farmhouse was moved an unknown distance sometime between 1926 and 1956, relocated from elsewhere on the original 12 acre parcel to its current location. Its original orientation on the site is unknown. In the early 1950s, the original 12 acre parcel was subdivided and sold off, including the land now occupied by Landels School as well as the adjacent apartment buildings. Besides relocation, the farmhouse itself has undergone several alterations including additions to the rear of the building and replacement of original parts. Looking toward the future, we plan to make the farmhouse an integral part of the Mountain View Cohousing Community. It will be used as a gathering place to share community activities and for accommodations for guests and a possible future on-site caregiver. In its present form and location, the house does not contribute to the neighborhood—it is barely visible in its present setting. Our plans for incorporating the farmhouse into our community include: • Rotating the house 90 degrees clockwise from its present orientation and relocating it to the southwest corner of the property. The facade with the existing front porch and original front door will face Calderon Avenue. It will be placed in a park-like setting visible to the neighborhood. • Removing the addition at the back of the building that was not part of the original farmhouse. • Reconfiguring the back of the original farmhouse, by removing 11 feet and reusing the original siding, windows, moldings, and trim to enclose the hole made by the removal of the addition. In this way, the characteristics of the exterior of this simple farmhouse, with light touches of Victorian flourish in the details and materials, will be preserved. • Restoring the hip roof, that was altered when the addition was put on, to its original configuration, by moving the hip back and removing the flat part of the roof that was not part of the original house. This preserves the original roof overhang, eave and bracket design. Not only is most of the farmhouse being retained and rehabilitated, it will be devoted to a lasting and valuable use; it will have a new life and purpose as a vital part of our cohousing community. Historical consultants refer to this as "adaptive reuse" and value it highly as a means of merging the past and the future. With the original front porch and front door facing Calderon Avenue, the Old Mountain View Neighborhood will now be able to see and enjoy this house in a well-landscaped park-like setting. The farmhouse offers a wonderful interface between the neighborhood and our cohousing community, providing a link between past and future. Very truly yours, Pat thero-a, mountainviewhistorical.org info@mountainviewhistorical.org 1 INTRODUCING OUR FEBRUARY SPEAKER JOHN TOMAC By Bob Weaver John Tomac will share with us the history of the Mountain View Police Department from 1902 until 1973. This covers a time from having the Marshall sitting on a keg of nails at the intersection of Castro and Villa watching for speeders and trouble makers to the modern police department developed by Arthur C. Nielson with modern patrol cars with two way radios. John joined the Mountain View Police Department in August 1956 and served for 30 years with the department and going through the ranks. He served as a Patrol Officer, Sergeant, Lieutenant and retired in 1986 with the rank of Captain. He was born in New Mexico and his family moved and settled in San Francisco where he attended Galileo High School and City College in San Francisco where he attained an AA Degree in Law Enforcement. John moved to Mountain View in 1940. He Transferred to San Jose State College where he received a Bachelor of Arts Degree in Police Science. He later received a Masters of Arts Degree in Criminal Justice Administration from San Jose State University. During the four years he served in the Air Force he specialized in Air Intelligence and served in Germany and France during the Korean conflict. After he was discharged in May 1956 his next step was to join the Mountain View Police Department Join us to hear from John Tomac on February 6th at 1pm, Adobe House, 157 Moffett Blvd, Mountain View. STREET TALK By Barbara Kinchen A 1929 map shows three different Central Avenues in our area. Must have been a little confusing! One ran between Miramonte and Springer Road and became a part of the present Cuesta Drive. The second was west of San Antonio Road running from El Camino Real to the railroad tracks. At some point in time the name was changed to Del Medio Avenue. Still in existence is Central Avenue, north of the railroad, between Stierlin Road and Orchard Avenue. 2 VICTOR CAL VO, LIFE LONG MOUNTAIN VIEW RESIDENT, FORMER, MOUNTAIN VIEW MAYOR, COUNTY SUPERVISOR, & STATE LEGISLATOR PASSED AWAY IN SEPTEMBER 2010 Victor Calvo was born in Mountain View on Feb. 13, 1924. He graduated from Mountain View High School in 1942, as a valedictorian, and the same year volunteered for the U.S. Army Air Corps. He flew top-secret bomber missions in the Army Air Force during World War II. When he returned he earned a degree in political science from Stanford University in 1948. Victor was married to Nellie Quintero for 62 years and they had five children, Suzanna, Victor, Peter, Theodore and Mary, who gave Vic and Nellie the joy of 12 grandchildren. Victor is also missed by his brother and two sisters. He began his political career as a Mountain View City Council Member in 1961 and later served as Mayor for 3 terms. In 1968 he began his service as a 5th District Santa Clara County Supervisor until 1974 when he was elected to the 21st State Assembly District. Later he served as a State Public Utilities Commissioner; and from 1987 until he served on the California Coastal Commission, retiring in 1989. It was said that Calvo recognized early on that there had to be a balance with development in order to preserve marshland. He became a strong advocate for the voterapproved bonds needed for the development of Cuesta, Rengstorff and Shoreline Park developments. In 1979 Victor Calvo was recognized as "Environmental Legislator of the Year" by the California Planning and Conservation League. When he left the Assembly in 1980 he had established himself as an environmental expert. As an avid golfer Calvo continued to provide suggestions, some of which were used at Shoreline Park Golf Course, to help deal with the ever present problem geese & coots on the golf course. —LOCAL HISTORIAN BEN DeBOLT PASSES AT AGE 83 Ben DeBolt served as President of the Mountain View Historical Association during that difficult time in 1994 when Moffett Field was decommissioned. He served as the founding President when Mountain View and Sunnyvale Historical Associations worked together to help preserve the historical artifacts that were in the Naval base. Ben formed the Board of the Moffett Field Historical Society and served as its founding President. He was a Principal and Assistant Principal in the 1960's and 1970's at a variety of Mountain View Elementary Schools. When he retired he devoted time to a variety of Mountain View Community volunteer projects that included serving as a City Commissioner on the Community Cable Access Board. In 1988 was one of the founding Board Members of the Mountain View Community Television (KMVT). In fact the 3 Mountain View Community benefited in many ways because of Ben's willingness to give — from 1976 until 1985 he served on 14 boards and community groups. Until his death he was president of the Henry and Maria Holt Memorial Scholarship Foundation, which awarded scholarships to promising young opera singers. Ben is survived by his sons Geoff and Chris, his grandsons Daniel and Jason greatgrandson Isaac as well as the family of his wife Carol Harris; Cyrus Harris, Roxanne Boyle, Eric Boyle and Quincy Boyle. fall-2010.text: Mountain View Historical Association Newsletter ACTING PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE By Robert Weaver Our November meeting is the bi-annual election of our Board of Directors. The current board began under the leadership of president Honor Spitz, who served the membership with distinction. One of her major accomplishment was the adoption of new by-laws and standing rules, which now allows the board more flexibility to conduct the association's business. With more of the board's business centered on the new History Museum, the updating is a welcome relief. The board deserves a lot of thanks for all the time and effort that they have given to the association. We will miss those who are retiring and welcome those who will be joining us for the first time. THE DUES FOR 2011 ARE NOW DUE. (SEE 2ND TO LAST PAGE.) PLEASE FILL OUT THE VOUCHER, CUT YOUR CHECK AND SEND IT IN. ALSO, CHECK YOUR MAILING LABEL TO SEE IF YOU OWE FOR PRIOR YEARS. The History Museum accepted three plaster busts from the collection of the late Anna Knapp Fitz. The sculptures are of Crisanto Castro and his wife Francisca Armijo and Catholic Father Bixio. Anna, a local artist and a long time member of our association as well as the Los Altos History Museum, created the sculptures. Anna was born in San Francisco in 1912 to German emigrants who later moved down the Peninsula and bought an 8.5 acre farm in the area of present Los Altos Avenue near El Camino Real. We are looking forward to including the sculptures in our permanent collection. I have enjoyed filling in as acting president this last year, and hope to see each of you at our November meeting. October/November Newsletter November 7, 2010 Meeting NOVEMBER SPEAKER By Robert Weaver We are presenting a fascinating speaker for our November program, Nelson W. "Bill" Hyler. Bill will tell us about his mother -- the late Elmarie Leslie Hurlbert Hyler Dyke, of Pacific Grove. She was a very dynamic woman who accomplished many major projects throughout our state. Bill is a wonderful speaker and will keep you entertained. Nelson William "Bill" Hyler, is a WWII US Navy veteran who saw action in the South Pacific and Guadalcanal and the New Hebrides Islands. He was a teacher for 14 years, an elementary school principal, a high school teacher, and a college teacher. He was also a plastics manufacturer on Cannery Row, Monterey, a sea shell dealer, a merchant on Old Fisherman's Wharf in Monterey for some 60 years, and the owner of "The Wharf's General Store" and building. He is now retired, widowed and living in Pebble Beach, California. 89 years young! Bill will be telling about how Elmarie decided the California Bear Flag with the 'so called Grizzly Bear' looked more like a pig than a bear, and how she changed it. How she heard of some 1000 acres of Sequoia gigantean trees were going to be cut down in Kern County and how she saved them. There are more stories to tell. The list is almost endless. Elmarie was an energetic person of many talents. A graduate of Pacific Grove High School in 1915, of San Jose Normal School in 1918 [a two year teacher training school at this time] and later an AB graduate "with Great Distinction" of San Jose State College in 1940. She started her teaching career in Sutter Creek, Arnador County, California in 1919; met and married Nelson William Hyler, Mayor of Sutter Creek, gold mine owner, garage owner, and Superintendent of Mine Rescue for the Mother Lode. Hyler passed away in 1927 of tuberculosis and Elmarie returned to Pacific Grove, her childhood and her parent's home, with two small boys, Nelson William Hyler, Junior 6 years old and Robert Elgin Hyler 4 ½. In 1934 she married a local pharmacist, Clyde Franklin Dyke, owner of a small drug store chain. She continued her teaching career, and became the Monterey County Supervisor of some 32 schools of Monterey County. She also was an in-demand teacher at San Jose State College and other school meetings, and groups concerned with elementary education. She served on several state panels, appointments, and traveled the United States to a number of educational events as a lecturer. Her work in education led her to several national conventions and she was known and recognized as an authority of reading and art for elementary schools. 2 NOMINATING COMMIT ILE REPORT OFFICERS FOR THE 2010 — 2012 TERM (Election effective at close of the November 7th meeting): President Pat Figueroa Vice President Cliff Del Carlo Secretary Jamil Shaikh Treasurer John Figueroa Standing Committee Chairs recommended by the Nominating Committee to the Incoming President and Executive Committee: Historical Data Barbara Kinchen Membership June Casey Newsletter Trudi Tuban Ways & Means Richard Espinosa Immediate Past President Robert Weaver STREET TALK Submitted by Barbara Kinchen Crittenden Lane is between Shoreline Boulevard and Stevens Creek, about opposite the Shoreline Amphitheatre. It carries the name of one of our early families of that North Bayshore area. Reverand Orrim Crittenden (1814 — 1903), a Baptist minister who was important in early Mountain View churches, and other churches in Northern California, acquired 160 acres on the East side of Stevens Creek in 1853. His adopted son, Albert M. Crittenden (1861 — 1958), then owned the ranch until it was purchased to become part of Moffett Field in the early 1930's. Albert was a student in the earliest years of Whisman School and his father served on the School Board. For many years, Albert was also a school board member and was honored in 1949 by the opening of the Albert M. Crittenden School on Rock Street. 3 MVHA'S INCOME St EXPENSE STATEMENT Beginning balance At 6/29/2010: $ 9,470.26 Income: 1,853.92 Expenses: - 2,588.45 Ending balance as of 9/28/2010: $ 8,735.73 Certificates of Deposit = $81,313.63 with $30,565.96 designated for the Museum NEW TO THE LIBRARY'S HISTORY CENTER Submitted by Barbara Kinchen * Three photos of workers on Hangar One at Moffett Field — from Betty Mendoza Bridges. * Items from the Glumaz-Mardesich family. * Punch tags used to keep track of boxes of fruit cut for drying. * 1958 receipt from Growers Hardware, 160 Castro Street, included 10# nails for $2.10. In 1943, my parents and my Mother's parents, purchased a ten acre apricot Ranch. The Ranch was originally part of the Rancho de las Borregas patented to Martin Murphy Jr. Coming from San Francisco, we moved into a big two story, brown shingle Ranch house. The house, gardens, garages, tank house, cutting shed, chicken house and rabbit pens covered about an acre. The gardens became Daddy's delight. His begonias bloomed under the old, old oak tree whose limbs were secured with cables. However, the old, old oak fell over one day! Flowers included begonias, gladiolus, daphne, hydrangeas, fuchsias and tree roses along the long driveway to the house and gardens. We three children always took bouquets to the teachers at Highway Elementary! Daddy made a two-seater swing for us in the large pepper tree. A wine press was stored nearby; grapes were crushed each year making the family wine. Daddy took his vacation during the apricot season. The fruit was usually sold to the same Stockton salesman (who was a teacher) for the Wood (then Fernwood) Canneries. We all worked on the Ranch during apricot season; we punched the picker's tally tickets, picked up fallen "cots" and cut "cots" for drying. The cut apricots were put on trays, placed in the smoke house overnight; the trays were then spread to dry. The dried apricots were then scraped off the trays using old license plates. We'd roller skate on the concrete cutting shed floor, but we really learned to skate in the downstairs back hallway; it made for an easier fall and we could hold onto the walls! On Sundays, Daddy's brothers and their families would "come down the country" to help. The men would work with Daddy, the women talked and cooked, and we children played with our cousins. We enjoyed family dinners that evening around the dining room table. We children ate in the kitchen as there was never enough room for us too at the big table. Oh, the tank house. In order to fill the water tank, you had to switch on the water pump and then watch the tank's water gauge. When it reached the top of the gauge, you ran to turn off the pump. If you were playing and not watching, you heard the 5 sound of water cascading over the tank house down to the ground near the back door. Oh, my!! That meant Daddy would know you had let 1the tank overflow!! Because of the apricot season, we had one vacation trip during our time on the Ranch in a rented Capitola cabin. It was a special event for us all. The Ranch was sold in 1956 near the end of the Santa Clara Valley farm era. I have such fond memories growing up on the Ranch. And to this day, I can't get enough of apricots! MEMORIUM CRAIG HOLDEN passed away September 6, 2010 at the age of 86. He is survived by his wife of 63 years, Marjorie and his son John. MVHA'S INCOME & EXPENSE STATEMENT Beginning balance as of 3/23/2010: $10,374.70 Income: 1,609.03 Expenses: -2,513.47 Ending balance as of 6/29/2010: 9,470.26 Note: This does not include the certificates of deposit funds 3 I REMEMBER: MEMORIES OF MOUNTAIN VIEW — 1930 THROUGH 1936 Going Back in Time Submitted by Margaret Nakamura Cooper When I was in college I had the idea to return to the old place I lived in Mountain View on Dale Avenue from 1930 to 1936. I turned onto the road from the El Camino Real and knew it was the right road since it was still called Dale Avenue. My parents, Nellie and Harry Nakamura, moved there from Los Angeles after losing their dry cleaning business when the Great Depression hit in 1929. When I turned left onto a dirt road where I thought the long driveway used to be (it was dirt then too), I went as far as I could before there was a dead end. There was still a cherry orchard all around. A young man with a shovel over his shoulder asked me what I was looking for and I told him that I had lived somewhere around here 14 years ago. He told me his name and I figured he must be the grandson of Jimmy Dale, my father's landlord. I returned to the El Camino but not before being transported for a short few moments back to the dusty raspberry fields of the 1930's rural depression. I don't know what I was expecting, but it wasn't the wiped out feeling of not finding even a hint of what used to be there. I knew the house wouldn't be there since Papa had it moved to the Calvo's ranch on San Antonio Road near the railroad tracks. Mr. Calvo sub-let a small piece of his property to my father and we grew raspberries there too until World War 2 and the evacuation of all Japanese and Japanese Americans from the West Coast. I'm still glad I made the attempt to find the past but was unaware that Nature has a way of erasing the landscape in a few short years so that even traces are hard to find. It's the same way I felt after looking at the land where the internment camp used to located, at Heart Mountain, Wyoming. It was 50 years later and the dusty barbed wire enclosure with tar papered barracks lined up row after row was now a beautiful meadow of green grass waving in the breeze. It was hard to believe. Yet it was the place because the iconic shape of Heart Mountain looked the same as before in the distance. Eugene and Emily Calvo came from Spain and through hard work and persistence succeeded and left a legacy of success with children and grandchildren anyone could be proud of. He represents the epitome of what any immigrant strives for. 4 I met Trini Calvo in first grade and we became friends for a few short weeks when I had to return home since someone told the principal that I was a few months underage. Imagine my delight and surprise the following year when I learned that my old friend and I would be living on the same ranch even though she'd be a year ahead of me at school. We've been friends ever since and still correspond at least yearly through Christmas cards to keep each other informed about various members of our families. Those early years seem even more distant since I turn 80 this year and I don't know where all those years have gone. Mountain View In Review by Ed Ritter CATHOLIC CHURCH The graceful Romanesque architecture of St. Joseph Catholic Church adds beauty and dignity to the church district of Mountain View. St. Joseph's Church is the house of worship for about 2600 members of its parish. It Is one of the newest and largest of the city's Important structures and stands in sharp contrast to the church in which the first Catholics of this vicinity worshipped, That first local Catholic church was a little one-room, frame building almost hidden from view by tall cypress trees. It stood on the spot where the Wells Trailer Camp is now located. Jesuits, who were the early teachers, and missionaries, had been sent out from the Santa Clara Mission in the '60s to establish that church. One fortunate day in 1901, Father Cullin, who has since been honored by having been given the title of monsignore, was sent from S a n Francisco to be the administrator of the little church, The church prospered under Father Guilin, and two years after his arrival the large parish house immediately north of the new church was built. By 1904 plans were being made Mountain Viow,-(TaTir(irnia, Thursd for the erection of a new Catholic Church on the property that had been donated by Crisanto Castro. To help finance the project, Father Guilin sponsored a fair in old Olympic Hall, a large building that fell in the earthquake. The occasion was more than "just another fair"; it was one of the headine events in the history of Mountain View. Programs with outstanding speakers were nightly attractions and booths were operated by Mrs. R. W. McDonald, Mrs. B. Distel, Mrs. T. Miller, Mrs. B. Farrell and Mrs. C. Swall. The booths offered many prizes, most of which had been donated, and they were raffled off on the "Wheel of Fortune." "The success of this fair and many later ones," W. P. Wright tells us, "was due to the popularity of Father Cunha." It has been estimated by those who helped promote the project that the proceeds ran well over $3,000. Father Cullin was the administrator when the church was erected in 1905, and Mrs. R. W. McDonald had the distinction of being the first organist. After 1906, many notable fairs were held in the basement of the church, one of them netting proceeds of over $3800. In 1928 the cherch was burned to the ground, the origin of the fire having been incendiary. "Scarcely had the ashes of St. Joseph Church cooled before Father Galvin, the indefatigable pastor of 1Y1r. and Mrs. George Ricketts and family of Santa Barbara arrived on Sunday for a week's visit at t h e home of Mrs. Rickett's brother and sister-in-law, Mr. and Mrs. George Geus. This week they are also attending the World's F-air. On Sunday, Mr. and Mrs. Geus entertained as dinner guests NIT. and Mrs. Hareld Geus of Oakland. Harold is a son of George Geus. the parish, had begun to lay plans for a new fire proof structure," recorded the Register-Leader of July 20, 1928.The new St. Joseph Church, erected at a eoSt of $64,000, maintained the Spanish Mission legend, becoming the third important building of the community to follow the Spanish Mission pattern. Its predecessors in that style had been the elementary school on the highway and the local high school. The present administrator of the St. Joseph Church is the Reverend Father Kennedy, and he is assisted •by the Reverend Father Karrigan. spring-2010.text: Mountain View Historical Association Newsletter PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE: By Honor Spitz Someone far wiser than I was quoted once as having said, "Every end is a new beginning." As I've struggled the past few months with an elegant way in which to announce my "early retirement" as President of the Mountain View Historical Association, I couldn't find anything that said it better than that. While I have known for some time that I would be moving within the next year, I hadn't expected all of the pieces to fall into place as quickly as they have. I had fully intended and hoped to serve out my term, but now I will be handing off the baton much sooner than anticipated. PLEASE CHECK YOUR MAILING LABEL TO SEE IF YOUR DUES ARE OVERDUE (If you are two years in arrears, you will be dropped from our mailing list) There have been some noteworthy events in the past year and a half in which I have been President. While I cannot take direct credit for any of them, I am nonetheless very proud. Most exciting, of course, is the status of the History Museum. The tireless and expert work of Bob Weaver and Nick Galiotto has paid off, and we are now ready to go forward with the fund raising campaign. Membership has increased, and we have begun to see new interest in the association due to our advertising in the "Preview" publication, as well as our wonderful up-to-date website created and maintained by Suzette Spencer. The Chamber of Commerce has taken note of the MVHA and become a valuable ally, giving us lots of "air time" on their "I Love MV" website as well. When I think about my association with the MVHA, I am flooded with a myriad of thoughts and memories too great to mention specifically or in detail. However, if I were to narrow down the list and sum up my thoughts, I would say: friendship, respect and support, generosity, and connection to the community. Topmost would be, of course, all of the stories that so many of you have shared with me personally as well as putting your memories down in writing for the enjoyment and edification of future generations. Thank you from the bottom of my heart for everything! Our Association is a dynamic force in the Mountain View community, moving forward with the History Museum & Education Center, our most ambitious undertaking in over 50 years. We need people on our board that will continue the progress we have made, and lead us on to the next level. If you believe that Mountain View is a wonderful and dynamic city, then you must also believe that its history is worthy of celebrating as well. This may not be your 2 hometown but it is your children's. What will they know of it if you don't get involved now? Make your stand for Mountain View, Sunday, November 7. History Museum Update By Bob Weaver May is California Museums Month. We have many fine museums in our area just waiting for your visit, and soon we will have one of our own here in Mountain View. During the last several months we have made great headway with our History Museum. We have invested in software to help create a solid business plan that we will utilize in our Capital Campaign. The business plan is a document that outlines the groundwork for, and creates a path to, the successful development and operation of the History Museum. I attended the California Association of Museums conference in March, which was held in San Jose. Their programs and lectures provided information that will open many doors for us within the museum community. Information regarding new products and services currently available has proven invaluable. I was able to network with representatives from other museums who have gone down the path we are currently on, and gained insight from their journeys. I met with representatives of companies that provide material and other support for museums, and came away with many new and exciting ideas that may be incorporated into our own History Museum. Also, a meeting was held with representatives of John Viscovich's family to formulate a plan on how best to move the historic "Goose Neck" wagon and windmill, which John so generously donated to our museum, from John's property to our storage container, where they will reside with other historic memorabilia until our museum opens. The storage container is being prepared to accept and properly store those items selected for our museum, prior to the museum's opening. Tom Erichsen, Ruth & Wallace's son, spent a Saturday morning cutting holes and installing vents to accept the solar-powered ventilation system we will be installing in the container. Tom is also fabricating the mounting fixture for the two solar panels to be placed on the roof of the container. He is doing a great job and we deeply appreciate his time and talent. The Mountain View Firefighters Local 1965 has given us a strong show of support with their generous donation of $800 to cover the cost of the solar vent system and the new paint for the exterior of the container. Not only will Local 1965 be paying for the paint, they will be painting the storage container for us as well! Many thanks to our own Cliff Del Carlo, Battalion Chief, who facilitated the deal, and to the men and women of Mountain View Firefighters Local 1965 for their very generous support of our project. 3 NEW TO THE LIBRARY'S HISTORY CENTER Submitted by Barbara lUnchen Thank you to the Los Altos Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution (D.A.R.), and especially Ellen Osborn, Dorothy Demange, Roberta Kure and Shiela Mahler for producing and donating a copy of their new book, "Mountain View Cemetery, Pioneer Park, Mountain View, California." Contents of the over 200 page book cover history of the site, records of burials, removals, pictures of tombstones, newspaper articles and maps. From author, Mrs. Margaret Beltran Duran, a 34 page booklet about a house she lived in during the 1950s with her parents, sisters and brother. The large, elaborate home stood just off El Camino until the 1960s and today it would stand behind the present Chevy's Restaurant. Mrs. Duran calls the house "Oakwood Hall, the Duran Estate's Not Quite Forgotten House and Ranch in Mountain View." The book includes photographs, maps, drawings, and descriptions of the home bought by J. T. Dunn in 1892. The research about the land and house is remarkable, covering history back to the Spanish land grant period and through the development into commercial property. Jeff Fitzgerald from Palo Alto liked to hang out around MVUHS. He drove a ModelT that had no license plates or muffler or things like that. Naturally, Motorcycle Officer Art Nielsen pulled him over, stopping between Lanes Creamery and the Spangler Mortuary during the lunch hour. All the guys gathered around to watch the action probably in 1945. While Nielsen was busy giving the ticket, some of the seniors put his motorcycle in the Mortuary. After Nielsen had finished giving the ticket, his motorcycle was nowhere to be seen. Fitzgerald and Nielsen walked around the car looking for the motorcycle. Then Officer Nielsen marched into Principal Charles Crooke's office and asked for help. Mr. Crooke delivered a notice over the loud speaker system asking if anyone knew anything about the location of Officer Nielsen's Motorcycle. About this time Martin Spangler, who was President of the School Board, called to say that a motorcycle was leaking oil all over his garage floor. Paul Nichols, MVUHS '46, remembers being stopped by Officer Nielsen and another much less qualified Police Officer at different times on Castro Street, when he was driving his '33 Plymouth. (2) Submitted by Fern Wright McLaggan I REMEMBER MY GRANDMOTHER'S HOUSES It was the year 1916, when my Grandpa and Grandma, John Lloyd and Lillian Tidrow Wright, brought their four children from Paso Robles, California to Mountain View, California, to live in the house on the corner of California and Oak Street. The two story house was on a large corner lot which included a chicken coop, a large brown shed/garage and several trees (one being a special large fig tree). The house consisted of three bedrooms, two upstairs and one on the first floor, as well as a dining room, living room and a very large kitchen with a pantry. The kitchen had a large stove and several chairs for visiting with company, a hooked rug and several quilts. The bathroom was on the back screen porch. 6 My parents and I moved into Grandma and Grandpa's house when I was three years old because Grandpa was quite ill and Mother was needed to assist in his care. Grandma helped me gather the eggs from the chicken coop and I became friends with all the neighbors. I was told that Grandpa really enjoyed having me around and called me "bright eyes." He passed away while we lived there. Several years after Grandpa passed away, the house became too large for Grandma to take care of, so my Uncle and Aunt bought the house from her. Grandma then moved into the Tank House on California Street. This was a fascinating house to me because it was small and tall and the best thing about it was that it was around the corner from the house where we lived. Miss Bessie Bates lived next door to us and I was able to walk several times a day through her yard to my Grandma Wright's house. Grandma lived on the first floor which had a kitchen, bathroom and a living room/bedroom combination. Mr. Thompson, Grandma's boarder, lived upstairs. I loved this house and having Grandma living so close. I would help her cook and bake pies. She was a good cook and could make a special meal out of very little. Her big black stove/oven made me always think about the stove the witch had in the Hansel and Gretel story. The tank house still stands to this day and I always love driving by it and remembering those good times. In 1957, Grandma's first house on the corner of Oak and California made headlines after a Jet plane from Moffett Field crashed into it. At the time, my Aunt and Uncle lived there. My Aunt was home at the time of the crash and had to climb out of the downstairs bedroom window. It is sad to me that that dear house is gone forever, but my memories are still alive. PLEASE CHECK YOUR MAILING LABEL TO SEE IF YOUR DUES ARE OVERDUE (If you are two years in arrears, you will be dropped from our mailing list) It's a new year already!! Not only that, it's almost a new decade!! So — where did the time go?!! Wasn't it only a few years ago that all of us were worrying about and consumed with the dire predictions about Y2K2?!! Surely you haven't forgotten about that!! Well, just as quickly as a decade will slip by, so will another and then another after that. While you and I most assuredly will not be around to usher in the next millennium, others will. And while I cannot even begin to imagine what their world will look like, I can say with a fair degree of certainty what some of them will have to look forward to. Bob Weaver and Nick Gahotto continue to work fervently behind the scenes to insure that Mountain View will have a first class museum. Soon we will be forming an Acquisition and Gift Committee with the museum in mind. And, as always, I will continue to "bug" you to jog your memories and contribute a story or two about a favorite Mountain View event in your life. The coming year promises to bring another star-studded roster of programs for our quarterly meetings. For the up-coming February meeting on Sunday, the 7th, our starting time will be one hour earlier than usual and start at 1PM in order to allow everyone plenty of time to get home and tune in the Super Bowl. How's that for an auspicious start to the new year?!! January/February Newsletter February 7, 2010 Meeting FEBRUARY SPEAKER: By Bob Weaver THE RENGSTORFF FAMILY, THEIR HOME & "THE FRIENDS OF R HOUSE" Presented by Charles Grant February 7, 2010 The Rengstorff House, circa 1867; Mountain View's mansion on the meadow and the City's oldest house, was built from lumber felled from Mr. Rengstorff's 1,200 acres in the highlands of San Mateo County. The house is one of the finer examples of Victorian Italian architecture on the west coast. One characteristic of that style is the widow's walk, a platform on the roof of a house, dating back to Colonial times, so named because many a whaler's wife trod the boards watching to the horizon for a vessel that never returned. How many schooners do you think drove into view of this farm house in Mountain View? Four a week, and they all came to do business with Mr. Rengstorff. More on that later. Charles Grant, a moving force with the Friends of R House, will be our featured speaker for the February meeting. He has prepared a Power Point presentation for us with dazzling historic images. If you have ever met Charles, you will know he is a dynamic speaker and his enthusiasm for the Friends of R House is contagious. Come, be entertained and learn more about our sister organization here in Mountain View. Voting will take place at a subsequent meeting of the membership. 2 MVHA'S INCOME & EXPENSE STATEMENT Beginning balance as of 8.07.09: $11,511.64 Income: 1,116.22 Expenses: (1,653.05) Ending balance as of 12.15.09: $10,974.81 MYSTERY SOLVED Submitted by Barbara Kin chen At the last meeting, we asked for help with several photos from the Eva Mockbee estate. Clearly shown was a number of American Legion members, a flag pole and a plaque. It read: For God, Honor, Country. This flag flying today is in honor and memory of Earl Mockbee. Plaque dedicated by United Veterans Council of Santa Clara Co. We wanted to identify the location. Thanks to a number of people, especially Richard Espinosa, Honor Spitz, Vincent Cortez, and the staff worker on duty that Sunday, we now know the pictures were taken at San Jose's Oak Hill Cemetary. Richard was so positive about the location that he drove there after the meeting. He reported that on the plaque, in place of Bud's name, the line read "all veterans." 3 Honor also made a trip to Oak Hill and talked to office personnel. They verified that on flag ceremonies honoring a special veteran's death, that his or her name replaces the "all veterans" line. Bud Mockbee served in the U.S. Navy during World War II and was active in the local American Legion Post as well as the Mountain View Historical Association. He died in 1993 at age 84. NEW TO THE LIBRARY'S HISTORY CENTER Submitted by Barbara Kincben From the Lawson family: High School year books, 1949 Centennial program, scale for weighing fruit and bulk items from the Lawson Grocery. From Eileen O'Halloran: Several 1950-1960s quadrangle maps from the Menlo Park location of the United States Geological Survey. MEMBERSHIP Submited by June Casey Life members: 119 Honored: 2 A/S (single): 104 A/F (family): 74 TOTAL MEMBERS 299 New A/F: Ysidoro and Susan Cortinas. 4 IN MEMORIUM JOHN (JOHNNY) VISCOVICH passed away on November 28, 2009 at age 86. He leaves his long-time companion, June Casey, his brother, Charles, and his sister-in-law, Kay. He was preceded in death by his parents, Anton and Filomena, sister, Eva Sisk, and brothers, George and Steven. John was born and raised on Grant Road and lived there all his life. He attended Mountain View High School and then was a Sgt in the Armed Forces in World War II. After the war, he went into business with his brother, Charles and wife Kay, to operate and own the "T & C," a Los Altos night club. The family also sold cherries and Christmas trees on the family property on Grant Road. John was a member of the Napredak Club, the Native Sons of the Golden West and the Mountain View Historical Association. 5 I REMEMBER: MEMORIES OF MOUNTAIN VIEW Submitted by Barbara Kinchen THE POTATO STORY A number of years ago, there was a midget in Mountain View — a woman. Today, we call them "little people." She was often seen in downtown as she lived on Dana Street, not far from Castro Street. However, I never did know her name. One afternoon, in the Lucky market at the Palm Plaza, I saw her in the produce department. She had a shoe in one hand and a potato in the other hand. She would slip the potato into the shoe, reject it, and then she would try another potato. This was rather interesting and I asked her about it. She replied that the shoe was too tight in one or two spots and if she could just find the right size and shape potato, it could be left in the shoe long enough to stretch it. I laughed a lot as I then went about my shopping, but thought the potato might very well do the job. But, since that time, I have yet to see any one of any size, or gender, or nationality selecting potatoes by shoe size. Box 252 Mountain View, CA 94042 Truth Tuban - Editor !MS THE HISTORY OF MOFFETT FIELD AND HANGAR ONE - PRESENTED BY BERNIE McDONOUGH NOVEMBER 2, 2008 @2 PM Bernie McDonough, of the Moffett Field Historic Society, will 9ive a presentation of the history of Moffett Field as well as Hangar One. ***URGENT NOTICE*** Our History Museum and Education Center needs your help NOW. Please see page 3 for our message. * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE: BY ROBERT WEAVER This month's newsletter is bigger than usual, as we have included proposed Bylaws revisions. We have simply out grown the current Bylaws and the proposed revisions will make it easier for the Executive Committee to conduct the business of the Association. The most noteworthy part of the revision is the creation of "Rules of Procedure." They are the standing rules to implement Bylaws where there should be flexibility in the procedures to promote the organization's programs and activities. Through the Rules of Procedure, the 1 Executive Committee can make changes in procedure as the need arises. Please review the proposed changes and bring any thoughts or questions that you may have to the November meeting. Patricia Figueroa has put considerable time and effort into these revisions and we owe her a large debt of gratitude for her efforts. I am thrilled with our Associations new web site,Mountainviewhistorical.org. We have updated information about our meetings, membership and the History Museum, with links to other local Historical Associations and Museums. Thanks to the generosity of Katia Kamangar, of SummerHill Homes, we now have a beautiful watercolor rendering of the proposed History Museum and Education Center posted in the Museum area of the site. Many thanks also to our Museum's Architect, Lewis Alvernas, of HDR, for the colorful site plans and hours of work on the drawings also posted there. We will be adding several more images to this area during the next month so stay tuned. The Executive Committee also voted to establish a phone number with Voice Mail for the Association so we can connect there as well. Our storage container arrived in August and is ready to accept items donated to the Association until the Museum is opened. Shelving needs to be installed and we have been asked to give the exterior a coat of paint so that it blends in with its nzighb3rs, so we will be having a painting party soon. This will be my final message as your President, as I leave office with the elections in November. The two years have gone by quickly, but not so fast that I haven't made many new friends and learned so much from them. I wish to thank my Executive Committee for all the time and hard work they gave to the Association. Without their tireless dedication the Mountain View Historical Association wouldn't exist. The Nominations Committee has proposed this slate of officers for the next term: President, Honor Spitz; Vice-President, Vivian Schatz; Secretary, Margaret Peterson; Treasurer, Patricia Figueroa. Please support them with your votes and your attendance during their term. It has indeed been an honor to serve this Association as President. From the ranks I emerged and to the ranks I now return. Best Wishes to you all. 2 ***URGENT NOTICE*** Our History Museum and Education Center needs your help NOW. The Mountain View Historical Association's plan to establish a History Museum and Eduational Center for our community is facing two critical votes. The first Vote will be at the Parks and Recreation Commission meeting, in early November, and the second will be with the City Council, in early December. I know that many of you cannot attend these meetings; however you can help by writing a quick note or sending an email expressing your support for our project. Please take a minute to do this, as it will have impact. Please visit our web site at www.mountainviewhistorical.org to learn more about the Museum and what it will bring to our community. Two Castro Street hardware stores were closing. Harley Hardware, after more than 20 years at Castro and Villa Streets, was selling out and Walter Doust was closing Growers' Hardware in order to purchase an interest in the Air Base laundry. 5 50 YEARS AGO (1958): A gas war has spread from the Berkeley-Oakland area clear down to Mountain View where prices have dropped four or five cents to 30 cents a gallon for regular and 35 cents for premium. Jack Isadore, 35, is the new Assistant City Manager, replacing Ted Craig. Isadore attended local schools and San Jose State before entering the Navy. The salary for this position is $6,212 per year. Open house was held Sunday, October 19, 1958, at the new 8,438 square foot library at 585 Franklin Street. The previous location was at 939 Dana Street with only 2,000 square feet. Even so, Librarian, Edith Duke, predicts that an addition will be needed within five years. Staff now consists of five plus Ms. Duke and her assistant, Ruth Lawson. 25 YEARS AGO (1983): A Mountain View resident is the bad guy in the Minuteman Spy Case, which has been called "the biggest espionage operation in US history." James D. Harper, 49, of 1931 California Street, admitted that he and his late wife, Rub Louise Schuler, sold missile defense information to Polish agents, who in turn, passed it to the Soviets. The FBI believes Harper may have received One Million dollars. An unbeaten season earned the St. Francis' Lancers, coached by Ron Calcagno, the West Catholic Athletic League Championship and then the Central Coast championship. With 25 consecutive wins, the Lancers have the longest winning streak in California prep football. Mel Inouye, Mountain View rose grower, reported that 17% of roses in the Bay Area are now coming from Columbia, Israel, Holland and Mexico; all with good weather and lower labor costs. Local growers are feeling the pressure. Contour Medical Systems of Mountain View, working with Collagen Corporation of Palo Alto, is working to find materials, other than human bone, for use in implants. STREET TALK: BY BARBARA KINCHEN Old Middlefield Way is the original portion of Middlefield Road. It wasn't until late in 1983 that the City Council decided on the route for an 6 extension of Middlefield Road from the San Antonio Road area, across the city and beyond Alviso Road. NEW TO THE MOUNTAIN VIEW LIBRARY'S HISTORY CENTER: BY BARBARA KINCHEN [Note: Call for local High School Yearbooks—Remember the History Room accepts donations of yearbooks when you are at a yard sale or sorting and cleaning.] From member, Audrey Jarvis Hoke of San Diego: "90 Years of Mountain View Fire Department History" by James S. Graham, Audrey's cousin (of the Isaac Newton Graham family, (one of the pioneer families). An 8.5 x 11 inch, 1935 or 1936, photo of Junior Woodman of the World. Included in the picture is Audrey, her brothers, Leland and Harold, and their father, Fred Jarvis, and cousin Ruth Marie McKinley of Sunnyvale. Also identified is one of the Telmont boys, either Hip or Des. From member Richard M. Smith of Mountain View: "Now and Then, Exploring Mountain View's Architectural Heritage" and several items which belonged to his late wife, Nancy King, a local high school graduate. Included were yearbooks for 1957 and 1981; a brochure of the 1957 class reunion with pictures and names; a photo of attendees at the 1953-1958 reunion; colored photo of the high school; several short histories of the school; words for the Alma Mater and an obituary for Mrs. Frances Kagawa, long-time assistant to the school nurse. I REMEMBER: MEMORIES OF MOUNTAIN VIEW 80 YEARS AGO SENT IN BY WALTER FRIGERIO I attended the Dana Street School, High Way School (at Calderon) and the Mountain View High School on Castro Street. I was gone from Mountain View from 1941 until 1945. The "Mountain View Hotel" was my home until 1941; from 1945-1947 a house on Villa Street. At the hotel, we rented rooms for 50 cents a night, unless you wanted a room with a window and then it was 75 cents a night. The charge for room and board was $7 a week. My 7 mother sold homemade ravioli with sauce for 50 cents a quart; I shined shoes on Castro Street for 5 cents and sold papers for 3 cents each. I remember: a bank explosion at Villa and Castro Street; a murder at a restaurant on Villa Street (China town); a chicken thief that I caught in our back yard; a Mountain View cop taking me home (too much partying); receiving a special driver's license at 13 (man of the house); five of us jumping onto a train freight car to San Jose to see a hanging at St. James Park. In 1946, I went into Thrower's Fountain to buy a milk-shake and later (1947) married the girl that had been behind the counter that day. [Please share your memories with us. We would like to hear what you remember. Send your entries to: MVHA, P.O. Box 252, Mountain View, CA 94042-0252]. Along with her husband, former Los Altos Mayor Bob Grimm, Marion was a major financial contributor and visionary in the formation of the Los Altos Museum. Bob is currently very active in assisting with the formation of the future Mountain View History Museum. Marion was a life member of the Mountain View Historical Association.
