Box 252 Mountain View, CA 94042 Trudi Tuban - Editor 116e4ni4 &cat L Ind THE EL CAMINO REAL MISSION BELLS PRESENTED BY JOHN KOLSTAD SUNDAY, MAY 4, 2008 AT 2PM INTRODUCTION--BY HONOR SPITZ We are indeed fortunate to have John Kolstad as our guest speaker for the May 4th meeting. John is the owner of the California Bell Company, a local enterprise that is responsible for the manufacturing and placement of the replica Mission bells seen along the El Camino Real from Los Angeles to San Francisco. Please join us for what promises to be a most enjoyable and educational presentation. Refreshments and good conversation will be "served" after John's talk. PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE--BY ROBERT WEAVER Part of growing an organization is coalition building. Reaching out to other groups that share common interests and goals is a great way to share information and attract new members. Over the past year, the Mountain View Historical Association has successfully established connections with the Friends of "R" House and the Los Altos History Museum. As these relationships strengthen, we are continuing our outreach to other groups in the area. One of my goals as president is to provide the membership with meetings that offer more than just a social event. Former Program chair Wallace Erichsen, and current 1 chair Honor Spitz, have done a wonderful job of providing informative and stimulating programs for our members. Our May meeting upholds that standard and takes it one step further. We have invited all the 4th grade teachers in Mountain View to attend our May meeting on the "El Camino Bells". The 4th grade is when students learn about California History, and the "El Camino Bells" are symbolic of the Mission Trail. Our ultimate goal is to establish a program with the schools, where the 4th grade students raise funds toward the purchase of a bell. At the base of that bell will be a plaque acknowledging the efforts of the 4th graders of Mountain View. It is our hope that this will instill in every student a strong sense of place and the feeling of being a stakeholder in the community. The History Museum / Education Center is moving ahead. We have a crucial City Council meeting on Monday, April 21 at 6:00 P.M. to have the Cuesta Annex Master Plan adopted for the 2008/2009 Council Goals. Our Museum Steering Committee has put together a very strong proposal, and once the specific siting has been confirmed we will begin our Capital Campaign. I look forward to seeing you at the May meeting. SPECIAL BOOK SIGNING AT THE MEETING Ginny Kaminski, author of "Henry Rengstorff and His Family," will be at the meeting and available for book signing. The books are $5 each. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS—COMPILF:D BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1908): Mountain View Skating Rink (roller skates) reopened under management of Professor E.E. Kitching, a champion skater. The Mountain View Brass Band provides the music. The old winery on the Distel place (El Camino Real) has been converted into a summer school for convent girls. The salary for the Postmaster has been raised from $2,200 to $2,300 per year. George Spicer, retired merchant now living on Villa Street, is raising pigeons for recreation and profit. 2 75 Years Ago (1933): The USS Akron, the dirigible which visited here a year ago, went down in a storm off the coast of New Jersey on April 4, 1933 with only three survivors. Over 70 perished, including Rear Admiral William A. Moffett, Chief of the Navy Bureau of Aeronautics. Over 5,000 attended the formal commissioning ceremonies on April 12, 1933 for the US Naval Air Station Sunnyvale at Mountain View, now 80% completed. Adult admission is 25 cents at Blanco's Mountain View Theatre on Castro Street. The new 3.2 beer cannot be sold within the city limits of Mountain View. In 1912, the town adopted the local option law banning liquor sales. 50 YEARS AGO (1957): Dedication ceremonies were held for Holy Cross High School at 1030 McKelvey Drive (now Miramonte). Sylvania Electrical Products needing extra space while expanding its EvelynWhisman site, has leased two buildings: Number 301 Castro Street, which was occupied by Bank of America from 1946 to 1955 and a warehouse in the 100 block of Calderon. At the suggestion of the Historical Association, an elementary school, to be constructed on Ortego, will be named in honor of Miss Victorine Klein, teacher in local schools from 1902 to 1934. Ad for Lucky Stores: Tomato Soup, 10 oz can... 10 cents; Corned Beef Hash, 16 oz can... 39 cents; Salad Oil, 1 quart... 59 cents; Pork Chops, center cut... 98 cents per pound. 25 YEARS AGO (1982): Description of the bandit who robbed the Quick Stop Market, 161 West Evelyn, at midnight: black man in his 20's, 5 feet 7 inches tall, clean shaven, full makeup, shoulder length black wig, wearing a full length red plaid coat with fur trim. Malcolm "Max" Darroch Aitken, science teacher at Mountain View Union High School from 1928 to 1958, died in Pacific Grove at age 88. As a young man, he lived at Mt. Hamilton where his father was the director. The Portuguese IFES Society on Stierlin Road expects over 1,000 people to attend on Memorial Day for the last "bloodless" bullfight. While California law prohibits bullfights, an exception can be made when they are a part of religious observances. The arena will be turned into a parking lot. 3 Guest of honor at the Navy's celebration for Moffett Field's 50th birthday was Retired Rear Admiral W. E. Moffett, Jr., son of the station's namesake. A large stone monument, supporting a huge anchor, commemorates those lost in the crash of the dirigible USS Shenandoah in 1925, has been installed and now marks the area as Shenandoah Plaza at Moffett Field. STREET TALK--BY BARBARA KINCHEN Am I correct in assuming that the three short Los Altos streets named Eastwood Court, Eastwood Drive and Eastwood Place, all near the intersection of Miramonte and Covington, are named for the Joseph Eastwood family whose home was on Miramonte where St. Francis High School is? NEW TO THE MOUNTAIN VIEW LIBRARY'S HISTORY CENTER--BY BARBARA KINCHEN From Mrs. Margaret Sideroff (nee Garliepp): A beautifully framed 8" by 40" photograph of Highway Grammar School of pupils and teachers in 1937, Margaret's graduation year. From member Kevin Duggan: From his collection of Mountain View items, a 7" by 9" enlargement of the first high school, built in 1902 at El Camino and Calderon Avenue. I REMEMBER CIRCA 1940--By Yvette N. Polizzi Regarding Railroad Crossing Arms: Five members of the Highway Elementary School PTA monitored and recorded ALL traffic coming and going on each of the streets converging on the railroad track crossing. After many days of monitoring and MANY contacts with the railroad executives, we WON traffic arms to make the crossing safer. I will always remember that experience! I was the current PTA President and one of the five monitors. [Please share your memories with us. We would like to hear what you remember. Send your entries to: MVHA, P.O. Box 252 Mountain View, CA 94042 Trudi Tuban - Editor io.a.Aawn '4,4,at Vi , 1..i.te 78J8 ORAL HIS STORIES BY ROBERTA BUBB SWEENEY, DORIS AWALT EBERE AND ANNE BAKOTICH PRESENTED BY HONOR SPITZ SUNDAY, NOVEMBER 4,2007 AT 2PM INTRODUCTION BY WALLY ERICHSEN Three long standing Twentieth Century residents of Mountain View, all recently deceased, tell stories of their early days in the city. We will watch a video with their "oral histories." Our new Program and Publicity Chairperson, Honor Spitz, will set the stage for this presentation. PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE BY ROBERT WEAVER This fall has been very exciting and productive. Under Eugene Sharp's leadership, we hosted an Eagle Shack Reunion that brought together many old friends for a smashing party at the Adobe Building. There was great coverage in the Mountain View "Voice" regarding the event and from what I observed, everyone had a great time. I just spent the day at a conference on "Building Museums," hosted by the Western Museums Association, which was at the De Young Museum in San Francisco. I was able to make some solid contacts and acquire information that will help guide us along in the establishment of our new museum. A museum steering committee of business leaders and community leaders has been formed and will soon meet giving us the benefit of their professional expertise and experience during this formative development period. A welcome to Honor Spitz who replaces Wallace Erichsen as Program and Publicity chair for our Association. Please take time to meet Honor and offer your suggestions for future programs, at our November meeting. See you there. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA .KINCHEN 125 Years Ago (1882): Republican nominees for county offices were welcomed at the train station and escorted to Margoes Hall with a band, anvil salutes and bonfires. The Hall was decorated with flags, flowers and "even canary birds scattered throughout the room." A banquet followed the speeches. 100 Years Ago (1907): Barbers in Mountain View got together and agreed to raise the cost of hair cuts to 35 cents. Mr. Sanguinetti, of the Sanguinetti Canning Company, will be planting the Bailey property at Castro Street and San Francisco Road to tomatoes next season. 75 Years ago (1932): New businesses in Mountain View included the State Market at 124 Castro; McCormick Heating and Sheet Metal at 143 Castro and Ugo Mancini's Flying A Service Station, at the corner of Castro and Church Street, with Phil Rice as Manager. Honors for local boys: Henry Norman, a baritone, was elected to sing in the famous Pomona College Glee Club. Gordon Chandler and Dick Glyer were winning praise as actors. Glyer was lead in a Eugene O'Neill play at San Jose State. Snow fell in Mountain View on December 11, 1932, for the first time in the 30 years since newspaper editor, Pop Smith, has lived here. The grammar school was closed the following day as many children were "home sick." Work at the Air Station is almost half complete. The helium tank will be the largest structure of its kind in the world. Jesse Grant, son of Ulysses S. Grant, President from 1869-1876, lives in Los Altos. MVHA, 11/07 Newsletter, page 2 50 YEARS AGO (1957): The Asian Flu epidemic caused closure of schools and the cancellation of many gatherings. Carl E. Anderson, owner of Anderson Sand and Gravel Company, and Mountain View's first Eagle Scout (31 years ago), presented an Eagle Scout pin to his own son, Carl Anderson, Jr. The Mountain View Pioneer and Historical Association erected and dedicated its Wild Cherry tree marker at Grant and Cuesta on land owned by the Bubb family. This tree was used as a Witness tree to establish boundary lines. 25 YEARS AGO (1982): The City Council endorsed a proposal for a five to ten acre "Mountain View 80th Birthday Grove" of redwood trees in Big Basin. Mr. and Mrs. Tony Bondi were the first subscribers to use cable TV in Mountain View. Rengstorff House, sitting up on blocks in Shoreline Park, awaiting permanent placement and restoration, has been again vandalized in spite of a protective chain-link fence with barbed wire. A 12 year-old boy was charged with throwing lighted matches at 81 year-old Mrs. Shina Shigemura of Kittoe Drive and setting her clothing and hair on fire. Almost completed at NASA-Ames, the $85 Million new addition to the world's largest wind tunnel was seriously damaged during a test. Diverter vanes broke up and fragments damaged fan blades and motors. It may take more than a year to repair the $12 Million in damages. STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN Leong Drive honors Samuel Leong, Sr., who opened the Moffett Food Center in 1950 at or near Highway 101 and Moffett Boulevard. Mr. Leong was born in China, at age nine came to Arizona with family and then to the Bay Area in 1947. He was active in Kiwanis and the Chamber of Commerce and in 1974 was named the Chamber's Citizen of the Year. Mr. Leong died at age 81 at Anacordes, Washington in 1993. summer-2007.text: k uc7r '2-00 -7Mountain View Historical Association Newsletter P.O. Box 252 Mountain View, CA 94042 Trudi Tuban - Editor iliountain Oditoorn.... Inaiit in 1 Mg ANNUAL BARBEQUE AND RAFFLE AUGUSTS, 2007, SUNDAY, DOORS OPEN AT 1 PM PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE BY ROBERT WEAVER For those who could not attend our May quarterly meeting at the beautiful Los Altos History Museum, you missed a tremendous program. Mr. Robert Grimm gave an excellent presentation on how the Los Altos museum was established. Offering insight into the Los Altos process, Robert helped us understand what we will need to do to establish our own museum here in Mountain View. Joining us at the presentation were members of the Mountain View City Council and the City Manager who, along with our members, explored the exhibits, displays and gift shop. The Mountain View Voice published a follow up article about the meeting along with a positive editorial. We deeply appreciate the hospitality extended to us by Laura Bajuk, Executive Director of the Los Altos Museum, and Emily Lewis, her assistant. We just received assurance from the City Council that our museum will definitely be included in the forthcoming master plan for Cuesta Park Annex. With this assurance, we can now begin the planning and fundraising for the museum. Our Association has been invited by the Friends of Rengstorff House to participate in their History Day celebration on Sunday, September 30 at the Rengstorff House. Participants dress in period attire and perform tasks from the period. The tasks need to be interactive so that the members of the public can participate. Any ideas? Page 1, MUM, August 2007 Newsletter Bring those ideas and your appetite to our Summer BBQ at the Adobe Building, Sunday, August 5. The Association will be celebrating its 50th birthday. Along with our traditional "zesty" hamburgers we will be having birthday cake and ice cream. There will be beer and wine for sale at the event (bring your ID's -- you may have to prove you are over 21!), raffle prizes and good fellowship. Lastly, it is with sadness that I mention the passing of Anne Bakotich, a life-long resident of Mountain View and life member of our Association. Anne's passing is a personal loss to us all and we shall deeply miss her. In a larger sense, our loss of Anne symbolizes the passing of an era, a generation of early pioneers settling here, raising their families and building the great city we love. With each loss, our community is diminished, but let us be thankful for, and never forget, all they have given us while they were here. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1907): A high grade of wine is produced in Mountain View due to a perfect combination of soil, climate and altitude. One acre of vines will produce, on an average, 500 gallons of wine. The cost of making, including shrinkage, should not exceed 10 cents a gallon, while the price received is 20 to 30 cents per gallon. Seventh Day Adventists are now holding services in their new church on Bailey Avenue. The grammar and high school buildings are located on five acres surrounded by evergreen oaks in old Mountain View. Fourteen teachers are employed. Frank Huff, principal of the grammar school, receives $110 each month while his teachers get $70. High School Principal, L. Dornbeerger, is paid $150 a month and his teachers earn $90-$100. 75 Years ago (1932): John Puppo, the talented young accordionist of Mountain View, is spending his two weeks of vacation in San Francisco. While there, he is engaged for performances at both the Fox Theatre and the Milano Theatre. New mail rates, effective June 6, require 3 cents per ounce, or fraction of an ounce, for letters and first class mail, while airmail will need 8 cents per ounce. Page 2, MVIIA, August 2007 Newsletter Chief of Police, W. Evans, reminds residents that fireworks must not be sold or 4.1S. exploded within the city limits. An average of six iced railroad cars of apricots are leaving for eastern markets each night from the Ice and Pre-cooling Plant at Villa and Mariposa Streets. More than 100 people are employed there. 50 YEARS AGO (1957): Business Closings: Diaz's Mountain View Shoe Store, 212 Castro Street, announced a "going out of business sale" with all merchandise 25% off. Mountain View Feed and Fuel lost its lease at 1058 Villa Street and closed. Mrs. Edith Duke is Mountain View's new head librarian. Mountain View Recreation Department sponsored a six week class teaching 10 to 18 year olds how to train their dogs. Traffic officer, Marvin Marty, received special FBI recognition for his capture of a bank robber. Hearing that a robbery suspect had just fled the San Jose crime scene in a taxi, Marty headed for Bayshore Highway figuring that might be the get away route. It was and the officer successfully stopped the taxi and arrested the robber. 25 YEARS AGO (1982): The Flag Team from Mountain View High School (formerly called Await) won a "superior" trophy in competition with 40 other teams at a four-day event in Santa Barbara. Dan Navarro took over as head football coach in place of Rich Ryerson who was with the district for 16 years. Two hundred irate golfers appeared at a Council meeting to protest the proposed closing of Cherry Chase Golf Course. Two years ago, Dividend Development Company received permits to construct 170 housing units surrounding the greens and promised to continue operating the course. To date, nothing has been built. Insisting that income is too low, the company announced it is closing the 9-hole course and is considering plans for nearly 400 units on the 30 acre site. The City has to pay an extra amount of money to not accept a new name and logo for the 10-year-in-the-making baylands park. A graphic design firm recommended the name "Seagrass," which was accepted by a sub-committee and recommended to the full Council. Upset that they had been left out of the decision, Parks and Recreation Commissioners said the name was "unimaginative, indistinctive and inappropriate for a park 60 miles from the sea." It took two months and several votes before the great debate was settled. With "Shoreline" the official name, the graphics firm had to redesign logos, signs and literature and their contract went from $14,000 to almost $21,000. STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN No doubt you are familiar with Levin Avenue because of the publicity about the "Pumpkin Patch" location at Grant Road and Levin. But, do you know it was named for Joel Levin (1824 — 1909), an 1852 pioneer whose home ranch was on Charleston Road? In 1883, he bought additional land on the east side of Grant Road. The property extended clear to Stevens Creek, contained 160 acres, for which he paid a total of $16,000. In 1900, Mr. Levin divided the land into five portions, one for each of his five children. Two continued to own their orchard properties for many years-Ulysses Levin, and at the end of Levin Avenue, Mrs. Mame (Levin) Huff. She was the wife of Frank L. Huff, an early grammar school principal and later postmaster in Mountain View. Their home was moved from its original site and is now located at 2715 Dierix Drive. NEW TO THE MOUNTAIN VIEW LIBRARY'S HISTORY CENTER From Charles Huff, a retired teacher from the Palo Alto School District, a beautiful framed print of his watercolor painting of the dirigible Macon, which features one of the Sparrowhawk airplanes. From member Joseph Sweeney, a 1909 songbook of about 100 songs and hymns, which had belonged to Mrs. Roberta (Bubb) Sweeney. Pasted in the back are the words of two Mountain View High School songs. One has the name D. Dale, which would seem to indicate that Dorothy Dale may have written the words. There are also the names: Vera Dean, Dorothy Theurkauf, Ruth Hollingsworth and Pearl Foster (all of the class of 1926). Ralph Faravelli, who with others was instrumental in saving the Adobe Building, plans to attend and maybe say something at the beginning. Charlie Olsen of C. J. Olsen Cherries is coming and remembers being driven with friends to the Shack in a special bus from Sunnyvale. Aig 18d8 THIS MEETING IS AT THE LOS ALTOS HISTORY CENTER AT 10:00 AM, Sunday, May 6, 2007 -PLEASE NOTE TIME AND LOCATION CHANGEThe Association of the Los Altos Historical Museum has invited us to visit their Museum in the Los Altos Civic Center. It will be an opportunity to learn how the Los Altos Museum evolved. The current exhibit, "Scene from Above," shows maps and aerial photos of the Los Altos and Mountain View area. Robert Grimm will tell the history of how the Los Altos Museum developed. He will unfold the success story of the Los Altos Museum which will be of value with our project to develop our own heritage center in Mountain View. We will also have the opportunity to explore the museum attractions by taking a journey back in time with the Ohlone Indians, early California settlers, farmers and orchardists in the transformation from a portion of the "Valley of Hearts Delight" to the now culturally diverse community of Silicon Valley residents. There will be Docent led tours of the 1905 J. Gilbert Smith furnished house, historic gardens and the permanent exhibit gallery. The Museum entrance and parking is at the rear of the library with facilities accessible from San Antonio Road or Hillview Avenue (please see map on page 2). PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE BY ROBERT WEAVER e'N This is proving to be an exciting year for our association. The Los Altos History 00"N Museum has generously agreed to host our May meeting, and we are grateful indeed to have Mr. Robert Grimm as our speaker. Robert stands as a major force in the establishment of the Los Altos History Museum and has given generously of his time and talent in working with our museum committee. Please come, bring your family and friends and hear the story of the Los Altos Museum and enjoy its beauty. After our meeting, docents will be conducting tours of the museum, its grounds and the History House next door. ooN PLEASE MAKE NOTE OF THE LOCATION AND TIME CHANGE FORTHI,S MEETINGSunnyvale Historical Association will soon break ground for their new museum. We were fortunate to meet with Laura Babcock, Association Chair, who shared a wealth of information with us regarding the establishment of their museum, a replica of the Murphy family home. With the help of our friends in Los Altos and Sunnyvale, the Mountain View Museum is off to a good start and on solid footing. Long time museum supporters, Wallace and Ruth Erichsen, became the first to back up their convictions with a pledge of $10,000.00 to the museum fund! Rebecca Galiotto has also shown her support for the museum and pledged $5,000.00 as well! We are deeply grateful that your strong belief in the museum project are to be backed up by such generous financial contributions. The Eagle Shack will soar again thanks to Eugene Sharp. For young people in post World War II Mountain View, the hot place to spend a Saturday night was the Adobe Building, known then as the Eagle Shack. Join your friends on Sunday, October 7, from 2 to 4, when the Eagle Shack returns. This event is the day after the high school reunion so the gang will be in town. Mark your calendars as dance cards are filling fast. ....N Page 3, MVHA, May Newsletter I am quite happy to report that Pat Figueroa, association Treasurer, is recuperating nicely at home after a stay in the hospital. Pat's absence brings to point the need for additional depth in our ranks. As the museum and other projects move forward, we will need new faces on the board and in our ranks to sustain the association. A few hours of time, four times a year is not a lot to ask, and the same few who carry the load now can have back-up. Please volunteer to help at the meetings or go for a seat on the board. As you can see, this is going to be an exciting year for the Mountain View Historical Association. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1907): "About three miles west of the town of Mountain View, in one of the most beautiful spots in the Santa Clara Valley, is to be built a new town, to be called Los Altos. Situated at an elevation of 225 feet above sea level, partly in the valley and partly in the foothills, commanding a charming view of the Bay of San Francisco on the north and the evergreen Coast Range Mountains on the south, with the oakdotted valley extending to the east and west, is to be established a town that will be the Pasadena of Central California." 75 Years ago (1932): California Supply (Pickle Works) is now producing sauerkraut in its new building which has 40 tanks, each with a capacity of 2,000 gallons. Mr. Otto Uhrhammer is in charge with 20 men under his direction. A large and colorful flashing neon sign was installed at the theatre on Castro Street identifying it as BLANCO'S THEATRE. Between 6 and 7 pm on Friday, May 13, 1932, the world's largest airship moored at the Naval Air Station, Mountain View. Built by Goodyear Zeppelin Corporation, Akron, Ohio, the dirigible was christened the USS Akron by Mrs. Herbert Hoover. Over the several days the Akron was here, crowds of people came to see it and the local newspaper reported it was "the largest collection of cars that has ever been at any one place at one time in California, or on the whole West Coast." In spite of the numbers, refreshment stands did not have the business they had expected, neither did the downtown merchants. Page 4, MVHA, May Newsletter 00"N ern\ 50 YEARS AGO (1957): In April 1957, there were two special grand openings: The Crossroads and the Sears store, both located near San Antonio Road and El Camino Real. Lt. Robert Schatz of the Mountain View Police Department was in charge of crowd control, directed 50 officers from Mountain View and neighboring cities. Sakura Gardens, a unique and beautiful Japanese restaurant, opened at 2116 El Camino Real. Roy Watanabe was the Architect and George Tsukagama the Manager. The garden and fish pond was designed by Nagao Sakura, Head Landscape Architect for 20 years at the Japanese Imperial Palace. 25 YEARS AGO (1982): Marine World Africa USA, Redwood City, is looking at land in the North Bayshore area for a larger park. The restored Mockbee building, on the North East corner of Castro and Villa Streets, was recognized by the Santa Clara County Historical Heritage Commission with its Award of Excellence. STREET TALK BY BARBARA K1NCHEN Someone inquired about the origin of the street where he lives -- Thompson Avenue, between Central Expressway and Middlefield Road. At one time, Thompson Avenue was part of Calderon Road. (Do not confuse this with our present Calderon Avenue.) By 1950, this part of Calderon Road from El Camino Real to the railroad tracks was renamed Ortega Avenue. But, an 1952-53 map still showed Calderon Road north of the tracks. Monta Loma School opened in 1956 on Thompson Avenue. So who was Thompson and who were the side streets named for? Jane, Jewel, Lida, Laura, Louis and Adele? Box 252 Mountain View, CA 94042 Trudi Tuban - Editor SOI•d11.44 4.4pel viabw, Calitoww...a, kat in !Sid THE 1930 CENSUS AS A MOUNTAIN VIEW TIME CAPSULE Presented by DON McDONALD, Sunday, February 4,2007 at 2 Don McDonald is the History Editor of the Los Altos History Museum Newsletter. He is often seen at the History Room of the Mountain View Library digging into the history of Los Altos through the records and newspaper articles about Mountain View, Los Altos and unincorporated areas surrounding Mountain View during an earlier period of time. His presentation will cover the time when the population of Mountain View was slightly above 3,000. He will tell some interesting facts about changes that came about. The talk may tweak your interest in land development in this area. An exhibit at the Los Altos Museum, telling this story through maps and aerial photos, will give you further information. The exhibit is open until April 15. PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE BY ROBERT WEAVER The New Year is traditionally a time to reflect on the past year and plan for the new one. I would like to take a moment to express my gratitude to the members of the Board, who worked so long and hard last year to keep this association going. Many of these folks have been serving in their positions for years, and I feel honored that many are staying on for my term as well. Thank you, I deeply appreciate your support and guidance. However, even the most dedicated workers need to rest, and there are no replacements stepping forward to relieve them. This fact brings me to the first goal of my term; getting new members. At the last board meeting we discussed publicizing our programs to attract non-members. This is a small thing, but a big step toward getting new members. One way that you can help is for each of you to invite a family member or neighbor to accompany you to our meetings. We will be doing our part to keep the interest level high by making future programs fresh and interesting. I welcome any suggestions that you may have. The second goal of my term is the establishment of a history museum/education center at Cuesta Annex. The city council approved a concept plan for the Annex that includes the museum/education center, heritage orchard and open space. We must next obtain from the city council a site plan that formalizes the size and location of the Museum site. Once we have that directive, it is the intent of the museum committee to begin raising --funds as soon as possible. We have gained valuable knowledge from Los Altos Historical as to the ways and means of establishing a museum. We will soon be meeting with both Sunnyvale and Palo Alto Historical groups for their insight as well. It is going to be an exciting year for our association and I look forward to the challenges and rewards that lie ahead. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 75 Years ago (1932): Public Food Store on Castro Street specials: Sugar, 10 pounds, 39 cents Large eggs, 1 dozen, 29 cents Butter, 1 pound, 29 cents S&W Coffee, 1 pound, 32 cents. The first Marines arrived at the new air base. They will furnish security and will act as the ground crew when the dirigible AKRON visits in April. In case of very stormy weather, they will stay in the Redwine warehouse on Dana Street (later remodeled for Cinema Theatre) rather than in tents on base. The new American Legion Civic Building at Church and Franklin Streets was completed and dedicated. Post No. 2421: Veterans of Foreign Wars, was organized with 47 charter members. George Cooper will serve as the first commander. The bicentennial of George Washington's birthday was celebrated with planting of over 40 young redwood trees at the high school, new Legion building and City Park. Alan Cranston was writing a column, "School Daze," for the high school section in the local newspaper, "Register-Leader." Formway Machine Shop, on Almond Avenue, began to manufacture small cast metal zeppelins, attached to a mooring mast. They are exact miniatures of the dirigible now being built for the new air base. These toys can be used for radiator ornaments or paper weights. 50 YEARS AGO (1957): A jet plane coming into Moffett Field crashed in downtown Mountain View, killing the pilot, scattering debris over a large area and starting several fires. The home of Mr. and Mrs. Les Wright, 1093 California Street, at the corner of Oak, sustained the most damage. Mrs. Wright was slightly injured climbing out a window to escape. Don Bellew of Don's Camera Shop on Castro Street, rushed to the crash and his photos were used by United Press all around the world. This accident sparked requests to have all jets moved away from Moffett Field. CALIc. ?bate 3160 Mrs. May Armanini was named 'Citizen of the Year' by the Chamber of Commerce. She was honored for her service to United Community Fund, City Recreation Commission, Girl Scouts, Community Chest, American Red Cross, Pet Parade, Quadalco Club and Parent Teacher Association. Mrs. Armanini, mother of four daughters, graduate of the UC College of Pharmacy, is the wife of Lawrence Armanini and a 25 year resident of Mountain View. A first for the city -- an official dog catcher with an animal impound truck for transporting animals to the Humane Society in Santa Clara. Mrs. Edna Lauer Roth retired after nearly 13 years as City Librarian. Age 78, she had previously taught 27 years for the elementary school district. A Franklin Street site was located for a new library. Complaints by residents about the noisy, early morning garbage collections led to an order from City Hall to start pick up rounds no earlier than 0600 am. Investigations into contracts and operations revealed that the collectors were saving the profitable, salvageable items for their company instead of delivering everything to the dump. The dump operator, by contract, was to profit from everything which could be sold. In turn, a suit was filed against the City to recover thousands of dollars thought to have been diverted by the garbage collection company. 25 YEARS AGO (1982): The minimum hourly wage was $3.35. Over objections by the City Council and many residents, County Supervisors selected a building at 595 E. Middlefield Road, near Highway 237, for a work-furlough jail for minimum-security prisoners. Mrs. Eva Cooke Kankel celebrated her 100th birthday on February 7th. Mr. and Mrs. Kankel moved to Mountain View from Minnesota in 1927. Of their six sons, three survive Mrs. Kankel, as well as 10 grandchildren, 81 great-grandchildren and three great-great grandchildren. Mr. Ugo Mancini applied for a patent on a pasta-making machine. He uses a filling made from prosciuto in one of his products, called Ugolini. Foothill College has published a 180-page book on its history in celebration of 25 years in existence. It started in Mountain View in the former Highway Grammar School on El Camino Real at Calderon with 1,500 students. Mountain View hopes to deliver to all homes a blend of water from five active wells (hard water) and Hetch-Hetchy water from the Sierras (soft water) in hopes to persuade the 7000-8000 users of water softeners to give up their equipment. Sodium used in the softeners makes wastewater unsuitable for uses such as golf course watering. STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN Thanks to Betty Lamica Evans for information about the street named Marich Way. The Lamica family lived on property at El Monte and El Camino Real and also at the old Junction Inn Hotel structure. Betty remembers a neighbor, Mr. Louis Marich, possibly from Yugoslavia, who took care of the surrounding apricot orchards. As that area was opened for development, apparently a street through the Marich property was named for him. NEW TO THE MOUNTAIN VIEW LIBRARY'S HISTORY CENTER Given by William and Jean Pawek: booklet by the Paweks, "St. Joseph's Parish, Mountain View, Centennial Scrapbook, Part 1, 1850-1928." Betty Lamica Evans brought this item over to the Library (someone had given it to her): A small block of wood, 2-2/4" x 1-1/4" x 5/8" thick with a metal chain for keys through a hole at one end. The interesting part is the inscription: "Mountain View High School, 1923 Eagles 1987, original trophy case shelf, your last piece of MVHS." There is also an eagle printed or stamped on the surface. Mendoza James N. Porter, Anne Bakotich Donald Holt, Dominic Patti, Nancy L. Smith Roberta Bubb Sweeney DONALD MUIRLE HOLT, a native of Mountain View, passed away from a stroke on October 16, 2006. He is survived by his wife of 61 years, Virginia McClaine; sons Ronald Holt and Donald Holt and daughter Donna Hendee. Don was a Mountain View mail carrier from 1941 to 1974. He graduated from Mountain View Union High School in 1937 and was a member of the Mountain View Historical Association. ROBERTA BUBB SWEENEY died January 8, 2007. She was from a pioneering family and Past President of the Mountain View Historical Association. A more extensive obituary will be in our next Newsletter. We regret that we do not have obituary information for Dominic Patti or Nancy Smith. EAGLES SHACK Was the Eagles Shack a real structure? The Eagles Shack seemed to be an imaginary place disguised inside the solid Adobe Building only coming to life on selected Saturday evenings in a town recently founded in a place where eagles have flown for millennia. Early in the second year, Feb. 1943, of World War lithe Adobe building was used as a Service Men's Club. As reported in the MV Register-Leader, "The first order of business undertaken by the city council last night," (Feb. 3, 1943) "when a full board, together with City Clerk E. B. Erichsen and City Attorney Kenneth R. Malovos, was present, was hearing of arrangements made the executive committee recently organized to handle the affairs of the Service Men's Hospitality House and accept its petition for the use of the Adobe Building as a recreation center for service men either stationed or visiting here."' Within two weeks support blossomed: Wood was donated for the huge fireplace, bookcases were provided for either side of the fireplace, other donations included "coffee, sugar, shortening and other items so that cookies can be baked in plain sight and—smell—of boys that miss the home kitchen,--- coins for the juke box, records, ping pong table. "Articles needed included writing tables, 'sitting' chairs for our men and women guests, not those heartless things that are offered at the chamber of commerce meetings and in large part account for the poor attendance at the infrequent membership meetings."2 The EAGLES SHACK, coexisting with the Service Men's Club at the Adobe, was conceived at, "A meeting attended by nearly four score residents, representing nearly all active organizations of this community, was held Tuesday", Dec. 5, 1944, "evening in the Women's Club House... Judge J. M. Atkinson acting as temporary chairman explained the aims and objects of the project, giving it as his opinion, based upon much court dealings with youth, that supervised recreation is a big force in combating youthful delinquency."3 By Dec. 11, 1944 "Saturday night at the Adobe was another indication of the interest the young folks of the community are taking in the matter of suitable recreation. The following EAGLES SHACK Constitution has been drawn up and all participants must abide by it."4 4 Eagles Shack Constitution Articles I thru V are listed. In early 1949 a four-page folder titled "The Eagle Shack" was published "dedicated to youth by youth." ,6 About 2,800 copies of "The Eagle Shack" were distributed to principal towns in Northern California and recreation leaders in the state. ANYONE KNOWING OF A COPY of "The Eagle Shack" PLEASE NOTIFY the MVHA. The Eagles Shack or Eagle Shack, as MVUHS `49ers knew it, continued into the early 1950's. Around 1956 the Eagle Hut began meeting in the Surmyview Club. Plans are afoot to bring the Eagle Shack back on May 6, 2007. Box 252 Mountain View, CA 94042 Trudi Tuban - Editor DEER HOLLOW FARM SUNDAY, NOVEMBER 5,2006 g 2 PM A VCR titled "Life at Deer Hollow Farm," by Beverly McChesney, will be shown with •••••• an introduction and historical background by Barbara Kinchen, Mountain View's City Historian. Deer Hollow Farm, now a Mountain View farm park, evolved from the Grant Family Ranch. The Perham Family then occupied the ranch from 1937 through 1974. The VCR has an interview of George Perham who was eight years old when he moved to the ranch. There is also an interview of Mountain View Park employee and docent, John johnigan, during a tour of the property and Jasper's cabin with its period furnishings. PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE BY NICK GALIOTTO The Association's Annual Barbeque had a great turn-out and it looked like everyone enjoyed themselves. That was the second Barbeque of my two year term as President and the November membership meeting brings my term to an end (how quickly the time goes by). What is not ending is the Association's effort to prevail on the City for a Museum at the Cuesta Annex. Committee Chairman, Bob Weaver, is asking members to show support by attending the Council Study Session on October 24. I was at the Firefighters' fund raiser for their children's burn center recently and saw the old Model T fire truck that they're restoring. It is the first motor-driven fire vehicle that Mountain View had. Captain Cliff Del Carlo said displaying it in the proposed Museum would complement other artifacts and agricultural implements that reflect the actual history of Mountain View. Nearly all the cities in Santa Clara County have a museum, shouldn't we? Our Executive Committee met on September 27. It was noted that the Nominating Committee is proposing candidates for election at the November meeting. They are: Bob Weaver for President, Vivian Schatz for Vice President, Margaret Peterson for Secretary, and Pat Figueroa for Treasurer. Also, purchase was authorized for a quantity of the Mountain View and Moffett Field Pictorial history books that the Association can sell along with our own book. Well, it's time to turn over the reins, so I'll close with my usual comment. Join us at our meeting and bring a friend. You'll enjoy learning about Mountain View's rich history and conversing with many of those who have lived it. See you on November 5th! The new "Opera House" is almost completed. Adjacent to the Farmers and Merchants Bank (now Red Rock Coffee House) on Castro Street, it has three stores on street level with a large upper auditorium and stage. 75 Years ago (1931): Henry and Ernest Powell, in the grocery business on Castro Street since 1911, are retiring. Minton Company, 599 Front Street (now Evelyn Avenue), sold the lumber mill and plumbing business to Builders Service Company. Mr. Earl Minton, former owner, will operate as a contractor from a Palo Alto office and will continue the development AIMS of Palmta Park subdivision at Loreto and Velarde Streets. As recommended by the Chamber of Commerce Road Committee, Council approved a study for a road to run from the Castro Street-Railroad crossing directly to the new Naval Air Station. Only a short portion would be within the City limits. Moffett Boulevard had already been chosen as the name in honor of Rear Admiral William A. Moffett, Chief of The Bureau of Aeronautics, who had done so much for locating the Air Station in the Bay Area. (Later, the base also carried the Moffett name. The Admiral went down in the Atlantic with the dirigible AKRON in 1933.) 50 YEARS AGO (1956): Local businesses are now giving the new Blue Chip stamps, one for each 10 cents purchase. These stamps can be redeemed for special merchandise. Mr. Blue Chip chipmunk says, "Be wise, economize with Blue Chip stamps." Vice President Richard M. Nixon and wife, Pat, flew into Moffett Field in a charter plane, one stop in a 14 state campaign tour. They were met by a crowd of 300 and escorted to San Jose for speeches at FMC and San Jose State College. Mountain View Feed and Fuel, 1058 Villa Street, advertised a one-week special -- one IIMEN• free parakeet with purchase of a cage. November 1956 saw the grand opening of the New Palm Plaza Shopping Center, Castro Street between Mercy and Church Street (current Kaiser Health Foundation Clinic location). Anchored by Lucky Market, other merchants included Palm Variety, Rita Mari Fashions, Barber Shop, Basting's Sewing Center, Bert's Donut Bar, Careful Cleaners and Yorkshire Clothes. 25 YEARS AGO (1981): Mountain View High School on Castro Street, closed in June, has been renamed as the Continuing Education Center. Buildings and facilities are now used by the City, YMCA, Mood Disorder Clinic, Headstart Program, Adult Education, Karate Studio and Foothill College. Kathy and Karl Meier operate Mountain View's first and only bed and breakfast facility at 938 Villa Street, the former Julius Weilheimer home (now the Chez TJ Restaurant). The Peninsula Lace Mavericks have a Lace Museum at the Old Mill Shopping Center on California Street. San Francisco is negotiating to extend its contract to bring garbage to Mountain View, offering to pay $9 per ton, much higher than the $5.69 which neighboring cities will pay. The 66-year old Dunshee house was moved from Ferguson Drive, near Central Expressway, to the corner of Calderon Avenue and Eldora Drive and will be extensively remodeled by two local school teachers (now again being remodeled). Two Worlds is now open at El Camino Real and Calderon Avenue. Shops and professional offices are at street level facing El Camino with housing above and on the rest of the former Highway Grammar School property. STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN Several members contacted us with information about Showers Drive, so we know you are reading the newsletter. Nick Perry's new picture book on Mountain View, page 19, has photos taken of Showers Lane/Showers Drive in 1960 and 1961, with some facts about James Showers who owned property where the street is. He served as street superintendent, grammar school trustee from 1895 until 1898 and died in 1910. Showers Drive bordered the eastern side of the beginning-to-be developed San Antonio Shopping Center. BAZA'R occupied the large commercial building on the eastern side of the new street. (Target is located there now.) Hereafter, there will only be a street question when we truly do not know the answer. STREET QUESTION A gentlemen living on Marich Way wants to know the origin of that name. Can you help supply that information? IN MEMORIAM HARRY PINTO passed away August 26. He predeceased his wife IDA (noted below) by only 12 hours. Predeceased by son, Mark in 1977, and survived by daughters, Cheryl Sullivan and Denise Pinto. He was predeceased by his sister, Doris Seibert, and his brother, Neal Pinto. Harry was raised in Mountain View and graduated from Mountain View High School in 1932. As a Marine during WWII, Harry became a prisoner of war at Cabanatuan in the Philippines. He also served in Korea during the "Peace Action." He later worked as a tax assessor for Santa Clara County and was the proprietor of Hallmark Stationary on Castro Street. Member of Mason Lodge 194, A&FM, SIRS Branch 35, Life member of Defenders of Batan & Corregidor, DAV and the Mountain View Historical Association. IDA PINTO was born in Vacaville and was a star basketball player at the Vacaville High School. She later moved to Mountain View and worked as an assistant city clerk and head bookkeeper for her family's grocery store chain, Escano. Ida and Harry were married for 67 years. She was a volunteer with the Christmas Food Bank and El Camino Hospital and was past president of Quadalco Club. WARREN "SWEDE" NELSON passed away in Colorado Springs, Colorado on July 31. He is survived by his wife of 59 years, Betty Castle; three daughters, Susan Larson, Linda Ribary, Peggy Bryd and son Craig Nelson. Swede was an Aeronautical Research Scientist at the NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field. He was involved in many organizations including the Mountain View Historical Association. Historical Museum Update Your museum committee has been working diligently to keep the Historical Museum proposal on track, during the public hearing process. When the city began its public discussion regarding the future of Cuesta Annex, the association had concerns that our proposal would be lost in the smoke of battle between the open spade group and the playing field group. We were assured that the process would be based on the merit of ideas presented, and not on the volume or intensity of the rhetoric. Quality over quantity would be the order of the day. However well intended, that goal has not as yet been realized, and we felt compelled to assemble a document and re-present our proposal to the city council as it was in the beginning. The document includes a rendering by local artist Robert Schick, of the Annex as it would appear with the museum, barn and orchard in place, a pointby-point synopsis of our proposal, beautiful letters from some of our members expressing in their own words the desire for a museum, an editorial from the Mountain View Voice favorable to the establishment of a museum at the Annex and an article from the Town Crier on environmentally sensitive "green building" techniques. Your committee has done their homework and created a very well thought out museum proposal, but ideas alone, regardless of how good they may be, will not carry the day on their own. There are other groups with their visions for the annex, and they don't include a museum. They attend the meetings in great numbers and have dominated the discussions there. We have less than a month before the City Council will set the plan for the Annex, and your help is needed for the museum plan to prevail. There will be a City Council study session for the Annex on Tuesday, October 24, at 5:00 P.M. in the Council chambers. This will present our best opportunity to influence the Council. The decisions made at this meeting will form the final Annex usage proposals to be voted on in November. Please support the museum plan and your c—nn, ittee by attending this study session at 5:00 P.M. October 24, in Council chambers. You do not need to speak. Your attendance at this vital meeting is all we ask. I look forward to seeing you then, Robert H. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 YEARS AGO (1906): There were six graduates from Mountain View High School. The school opened in 1902 and these were the first students to have attended for four years. The Seventh-Day Adventists opened a primary school with 40 students. It was supported by tuition and church funds. Julius Weilheimer, President of the Town Board, requested that there be no fireworks on the Fourth of July as the water system was still under repair from the April earthquake. A local hotel proprietor was charged with assault with a deadly weapon. Because there was no proof that the gun was loaded, he was instead fined $40 for exhibiting a deadly weapon. 75 Years ago (MP: The Native Sons of the Golden West held their annual barbeque at "Ye Old Trout Farm," on Stevens Creek with "one of the finest barbeque cooks in the Santa Clara Valley" in charge -- Mark Espinosa. Vernon LeRoy Gardiner was elected president of the newly-organized 40 member Junior Chamber of Commerce. The United States government took title to 1,000 acres for a West Coast dirigible base. Owners of the land will receive the $470,000 subscribed by bay area organizations. Contracts for a dirigible hanger are ready to go out for bid, with an estimated cost of more than $1,500,000. It will be the second largest dirigible hanger in the United States, closely rivaling that of the Goodyear Zeppelin Company at Akron, Ohio, where ZR54 is now being built (USS Akron). Until permanent buildings are constructed on the base, headquarters will operate out of the new Owler building on Castro Street just opposite the High School. NEW IN TOWN: Air Base Laundry at 954 Villa Street (now Tied House), Airbase Tailors at 254 Castro Street and Beardslee Mortuary at the corner of Castro and Yosemite (now Spangler Mortuary). 50 YEARS AGO (1956): Safeway's produce prices: Tomatoes, 2 lbs for 25 cents Celery, 23 cents Lettuce, 2 heads for 19 cents Carrots, 2 lbs for 19 cents Corn, 5 ears for 39 cents. June building permits were at "all-time high" and included a Sears-Roebuck store on San Antonio Road, U.S. Armory, a $39,000 animal hospital on El Camino Real, a drive in restaurant at El Camino and Escuela and a $31,000 church for St. Timothy's Episcopalian parish. Monte Vista Drive In advertised a Fourth of July "Sundown to Sunrise" bash with five movies and sparklers for the kids. Chrysanthemums are being shipped nation-wide from the new Mt. Eden Mums plant at 525 E. Evelyn Avenue. A special cooling process lowers the temperature of the flowers to 35 degrees Fahrenheit which protects them during shipment. Children from the various summer playground programs participated in the annual Pet Parade on Castro Street, led by a King and Queen and their court riding in the Model T fire truck Prizes were awarded for costumes as well as pets. 25 YEARS AGO (1981): A memorial plaque honoring the late Joe Perez, councilman and former mayor, was installed in the Plaza de Pea f:e at the Two Worlds new business and residential complex at El Camino Real and Calderon Avenue. Two local elementary school teachers purchased the 1915 era, two story, Colonial revival style Dunshee home on Alviso Road for $2,000 and had it moved to Calderon Avenue at Eldora Drive (this house is now being completely remodeled). Whisman School District received a government grant to help create a better racial and ethnic balance within its schools. An innovative, year-round, K-6th grade, "Magnet" school was opened on San Pierre Way at the Stevenson School site. In order to attract non-minority students, the school was open to children both within and outside the district boundaries, offered special classes, labs and child care was available from 7-8 am and 4-6 pin for $1 per hour. Ruth Lawson retired after 23 years with the library after serving as the library director the last nine years. She was succeeded by her assistant director, Ruth Stillwell. July was dubbed "Month of the Medfly." Finding Mediterranean fruit flies in the Santa Clara Valley resulted in orders to strip and bag all fruit for collection by city workers. Residents and officials debated the safety issues of possible Malathion spraying. Governor Edmund Brown, Jr. ordered aerial spraying to begin the night of July 13th. That evening he made a surprise visit to Mountain View's Council meeting to thank the city for the fruit stripping program and announced he was staying the night to help allay fears about Malathion spraying. For two months, helicopters, flying out of Moffett Field, covered areas of Santa Clara and San Mateo counties. Residents tried to protect their families, pets and possessions, especially autos. Other residents left town when their areas were due to be sprayed. STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN Inigo Way is the name of the new and very short street joining Pear Avenue and La Avenida. The name is that of the Indian who received a Mexican land grant of nearly 1,600 acres, part of which became Moffett Field. Ynigo is another spelling of this name. Lazo New Family Members: Arleen and Allan Fink New Life Member: Keith Hendley July 13, 2008 Museum Committee Report The Mountain View Historical Association has had an active committee this past year (since May 2005) pursuing the establishment of a museum for the Mountain View area. Visits and contacts have been made to 10 museums in surrounding towns which have provided valuable information. In October 2005 the City Council initiated planning for the development of the Cuesta Park Annex site. Thus, it was a logical move for our committee to examine the possibility of establishing a museum on the site. This idea has already been presented to the City Council at their study sessions in October 2005 and January 2006. The City goals to develop a master plan are underway with opportunity for broad public input and participation. MVHA Committee Chairman Robert Weaver and member Wally Erichsen will meet with representatives of the project team Wednesday, July 19, 2006 to discuss MVHA ideas concern:ng developent of the Cuesta Park Annex site. Other interested groups will be interviewed on July 18 and 19. Subsequently, two community meetings will be held on Saturday, July 29 and Saturday, August 19. We encourage your support of a museum on the Cuesta Annex site and attendance at both meetings in July and August to show the City Council our interest in pursuing our goals. Please mark your calendar, just your presence at the meetings will be of value in helping us meet our goal. The concept of a museum on the Cuesta Annex site includes a heritage orchard, a museum building and a barn/museum for displaying historical agricultural equipment and other large items, also providing space for maintenance and production from the heritage orchard. This could be accomplished with a minimal impact on open space and preservation of native trees. The committee is currently identifying the collection of items and artifacts from early times to the present which could be considered for a museum. Items for display would include those of historical interest along with the stories about them. They would include the pre-orchard period, the orchard and agricultural period and the changes in the 20th century. We need your support. Be sure to attend the community meetings July 29 and August 19. They will be held in City Hall from 10 am to 12:30 pm. Her 44 years as a teacher ended after one year at the school named in her honor. She devoted her life to creating an eagerness for learning in her kindergarten children. Students to this day remember her with great affection. Don was a U.S. Navy meteorologist at Moffett Field during WWII and later a Supervisor in the Mountain View Post Office. PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE BY NICK GALIOTTO On Saturdqy, February 4, many of our members enjoyed a tour of the Computer History Museum, which took the place ofour regular _Quarterly membership meeting. We saw what a great asset the Computer History Museum is for Mountain View. For many of us, the tour demonstrated the importance of preserving and displaying history and reinforced our purpose as members of the Mountain View Historical Association. 110 Also in February, I had the pleasure of presenting a Mayor's Proclamation at a commemorative event marking Mountain View as the birthplace of Silicon Valley. The Computer History Museum and the MVHA sponsored the recognition of the 50th anniversary of the establishment of the Shockley Semiconductor Lab in Mountain View. Our Executive Committee met on March 22 and approved participating again in the Arts & Ala Carte Festival in May. Please consider assisting Hip Telmont with our booth. This contributes to our organization's "presence" in the community. Wally Erichsen reports that his ad hoc committee members, consisting of Wally, Anne Bakotich, Al Jehning, Barbara Kinchen, Vivian Schatz, John Viscovich and Bob Weaver, are moving forward with a proposal to establish a Heritage Orchard and History Museum in the Cuesta Park Annex. A 3-D layout needs to be prepared which will be submitted to the City during its master planning process for this site. The committee is looking for some "pro bono" assistance from someone with architectural skills. The membership meeting program in May will feature first-hand memories of Edith Landels, a teacher that touched the lives of many in Mountain View. Encourage your friends to attend our meetings. They will learn of Mountain View's colorful past and mingle with some of those that have lived it. That's what we're about. See you on Sunday, May 7th!! OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 YEARS AGO (1906): From the Mountain View Register of April 20, 1906, just after the great earthquake. "Mountain View certainly presents a sorry sight. The east and west walls of the Pacific Press are down. Mr. Weilheimer's building, occupied by Farr's implement business, is skewered over to the south and is in danger of collapse. Mr. Swan's brick building, occupied by Allen & Co.'s furniture store, now is a shapeless pile of bricks and Merchant's State Bank is cracked and is in danger of losing the top coping on the north side; the beautiful D.T. Ames brick block building is merely a pile of unsteady bricks ready to fall at any time; the Carlin frame building is tipped and unsteady; the Roger's block building and the Post Office is a pile of bricks on top of $30,000 stock of goods; Olympic Hall is debris with Wm. Neuroth's handsome fixtures and stock on the under side; the Bank of Mountain View building is cracked; the huge town water tanks tower is a pile of splintered timber; the Mountain View Fruit Exchange lies as a brick pile with an unsure roof over it; the tall chimney at the Whelan Brick Works is a thing of the past; besides much other damage; broken water tanks throughout the town and county; the man who has a chimney left is envied by his neighbors; plastering down; buildings off their foundations; broken china and knick.•••, knacks; and what is worse in many instances, the fear of danger to loved ones in less fortunate and unhappy San Francisco." 50 YEARS AGO (1956): New to Mountain View: --Lindy's Jewelers opened by Bob Lindberg at 166 Castro Street. --A&W Root Beer Drive-In on Moffett Boulevard. --Ivy's Gift Shop at 220 Castro Street. --Whisman District's Monta Loma School on Thompson Avenue. --Blossom Plaza Supermarket, 1750 Miramonte Avenue. (The first business to open in the new Blossom Plaza development.) Over 800 kids participated in the annual Easter Egg Hunt sponsored by the City and Lion's Club and held at both the park and Women's Club on Castro Street. Prizes included bikes, Easter bunnies and theatre passes. Honored for 35-year- membership in Leon Robart Post of the American Legion were: Frank Glann, James Graham, Ray Lorecks, H. C. Sayre, Maurice Daubin, Glenn Wilson and Everett Lawson. 25 YEARS AGO (1981): Stan Thompson, business services manager, retired after 35 years with Mountain View-Los Altos Union High School District. Marilyn Perry is the new Mayor and Pat Figueroa the Vice-Mayor. The first time both positions have been held by women. Thieves used a car to break through the reinforced steel back door of Eddy's Sport Shop on Castro Street and stole 14 guns. Police state the store has been broken into seven times in the last five years. Three times a week, "bug bomber" planes, flying out of Moffett Field, drop millions of sterile Mediterranean fruit flies over Santa Clara County. Gilda Kabbani, operator of hot dog wagons in Sunnyvale, San Jose and Mountain View, will open a restaurant, Gilda's Big Apple at 126 Castro Street. This was formerly the Working Man's Clothing Store, with a massage parlor at the back alley. After 35 years in Mountain View producing amusement rides such as the Bat, Corkscrew and Boomerang, the former Arrow Development Corporation is moving to Utah. A Switzerland company purchased the business in January. Karl and Kathy Maier opened Mountain View's first bed and breakfast establishment in the Julius Weilheimer house at 938 Villa Street (now Chez TJ). STREET TALK BY BAI?BARA KINCHEN Wild Cherry Lane and Blossom Lane are elegant names for two downtown alleys. They are at the rear of Castro Street businesses; each beginning at Evelyn Avenue and go south for only a few blocks. NEW QUESTION What is the name and exact location of Mountain View's newest street? It is north of Highway 101, very short and there are questions about the spelling and pronouncing. Patricia was born in Santa Cruz on January 30, 1910. When she was 2-1/2, she moved into the Southern Pacific Depot in Mountain View with her father Chester F. Await, then depot master, her brother Robert and sister Doris. Patricia graduated from Mountain View Union High School in 1927. She then began working as a stenographer for Hartey Hardware. In 1932 she married Harlan Reyburn, who was the son of a former local Cumberland Presbyterian Church pastor. During the years her husband was in the Navy or they lived elsewhere, Patricia and family returned to Mountain View often to visit family on Bailey Avenue and Sierra Avenue. Patricia was predeceased by her husband Harlan (1979) and daughter Barbara (Bernie) Selna of El Granada. She is survived by her son Alan (Loretta) Reyburn of Stockton and daughter, Jean Weston of Waikoloa, Hawaii. She was a life member of the Mountain View Historical Association. Shoreline Blvd., Mountain View SATURDAY- -- February 4,2006 at 2:30 pm Note: This is a change of meeting date and time John Toole, Executive Director and CEO of the Computer History Museum, has extended an invitation to MVHA members to tour the museum. The museum was moved from Moffett Field in 2002 after acquiring the Silicon Graphics (SGI) property on North Shoreline Boulevard between L'Avenida Avenue and Pear Avenue. The 120,000 sq. ft. building arrangement and exhibits are being developed in stages. Docent led tours of the visible storage and exhibit areas will be featured. We will be able to socialize together after the tour. Directions to the Museum: From Freeway 101, take the N. Shoreline exit. From downtown, take Shoreline and go over Freeway 101. Shortly after passing L'Avenida, enter the driveway from N. Shoreline into the Computer Museum parking lot; or turn on to Pear Avenue and then into the parking lot. The tour entrance is noted on a sign as you enter the parking lot. PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE BY NICK GALIOTTO Here we are at the end of the first month of the new year -- already. Your Executive Committee met on January 4 to plan the special gathering of our members on SATURDAY, February 4, at the Computer History Museum. There are many facets to Mountain View's history and certainly the development of the computer industry is a very significant one. Along these lines, and on behalf of the MVHA, Wally Erichsen is working on a program with the Computer History Museum that will commemorate the contribution of the Shockley Labs of Mountain View to the beginnings of the Silicon Valley we have today. This is an opportunity for our Historical Association to expand its contacts and become more visible within the community. This leads to our current goal of studying the feasibility of establishing a Heritage Orchard and History Museum in the Cuesta Park Annex. Wally reports that his ad hoc committee, consisting of Wally, Anne Bakotich, Al Jehning, Barbara Kinchen, Vivian Schatz, John Viscovich and Bob Weaver, has begun a site layout of these potential utilizations that will be submitted to the City during its master planning process. Obviously, if these concepts prove viable, there will need to be strong support to make it happen. Our members provided such support in achieving the preservation of the Adobe Building. Maybe we can be the catalyst once again. IMPORTANT: Encourage your friends to attend our meetings. They will learn of Mountain View's colorful past and mingle with some of those that have lived it. That's what we're about. See you on SATURDAY, February 4th!! OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 YEARS AGO (1906): Mountain View now has a night watchman. The downtown merchants pay most of his salary and the town the rest. National Ice Company is building an ice house on the railroad track "below the depot." Methodists are putting in a cement sidewalk in front of the church property in the 400 block of Castro Street. Reverend Orr raised the $100 cost by "soliciting" downtown businesses. Frank L. Huff, principal of the elementary school, and Mountain View native, has been awarded a state grammar school certificate for life. 75 YEARS AGO (1931): Perry Askam, star of the operetta THE DESERT SONG, is visiting his Aunt, Mrs. Elise (Rengstorff) Haag of Stierlin Road. A new mortuary was built for George Beardslee at the corner of Castro Street and Yosemite Avenue. Total cost for land, buildings and ambulance is approximately $25,000.00 (purchased by Martin J. Spangler in 1934). City Council ordered that all stones, monuments and markers in the Mountain View Cemetery (now Pioneer Park) be buried flat, two feet under the surface of the ground. A record will be made of the location of each marker and a photo taken of each. Congress has authorized acceptance of 1,000 acres of Mountain View for a Navy dirigible base. Mountain View Theatre: Show times: Daily, 7 pm and 9 pm Sunday, 4 shows, 2:30 pm - 11 pm Admission: 4-10 years 10 cents 10-12 years 15 cents Adults 35 cents Loges 50 cents 50 YEARS AGO (1956): Plans for extending Bailey Avenue across El Camino to connect with Miramonte Avenue have been approved. Foster's Old Fashioned Freeze featured six hamburgers for $1.00. Winter storms (1955-56) and record high tides caused levee breaks which marooned the sewage treatment plant at the end of Stierlin Road. A blimp has landed at Moffett Field for repairs; the first since the base was changed from lighterthan-air to airplanes in 1947. 25 YEARS AGO (1981): The average interest return on invested city money was 11.8%. The I.E.D. building at Castro and Mercy Streets has been renamed Mountain Bay Plaza, but is not yet occupied because the available parking spaces do not meet city requirements. Because of the Mediterranean Fruit Fly, residents were ordered to strip all fruit from trees and then place the fruit in plastic bags for pick-up by the City, Sherman McCormick, real estate agent and appraiser and former property agent for the City, was named "Citizen of the Year" by the Chamber of Commerce. New Fans with motors that produce 135,000 horsepower have been installed in the world's biggest wind tunnel at NASA Ames Research Center. Grand Central Sauna and Hot Tubs, 170 El Camino Real East is the only business of its kind in Santa Clara County. It has 26 rooms which rent for $6.00 per person per hour after 5 pm and $4.75 before 5. Each room is equipped with sauna, shower, four-person hot tub, a bed and security system. Prohibited are liquor, picnics and any one under 18 years of age. STREET TALKBY BARBARA KINCHEN College, University, Stanford and Leland are streets in the Castro City area, just south of the railroad tracks at Rengstorff Avenue. This was once 'mown as University Park, developed to attract professors from Stanford and perhaps others from San Francisco. The small lots were meant for summer or vacation homes. Mario was born September 27, 1916 in Cupertino. He graduated from Mountain View High School in 1934. He is survived by his wife of 64 years, Kathryn Volarvich Gemello; daughter, Patricia Ferguson of AM..•• Belmont; son, John Gemello of San Mateo; son, Mark Gemello of San Jose; his sister, Celestine Traverso of Mountain View; six grandchildren and one great-grandchild. Mario's family originally had 35 acres of vegetables, fruit and a homestead that was between Rengstorff and El Monte on the West side of El Camino Real. Quite a few acres were sold during prohibition, but in 1934, the family started the Gemello Winery at 2003 El Camino Real (next to Bob's Big Boy and behind a bowling alley and a small shopping center). Upon his father's retirement in 1944, Mario took over full control of the winery. Mario retired in 1982 and the awardwinning Gemello wine label retired with him. The winery was sold to his niece and husband, Sandy and Paul Obester, who had their own winery under their own name in Half Moon Bay. Mario was a member of the St. Francis High School Men's Club, the Elks Club of Palo Alto and St. Joseph's parish. He served as president of the Eagles of Mountain View, the Santa Clara Valley Wine-growers Association and the Kiwanis Club. He was a member of the Mountain View Historical Association. BECKY McREYNOLDS ' I"N SUNDAY, NOVEMBER 6, 2005 AT .2:00 PM Ms. McReynolds is an 'Asian Civilization' instructor at DeAnza Community College in Cupertino. This discussion will be based upon a study and thesis that Ms. McReynolds wrote for her Master's degree from Stanford. It documents and describes the earliest settlement of Chinese in Mountain View by piecing together the story of Yuen Lung, his family and business connections with early residents, such as Jake Mockbee, who provided personal and financial assistance. The author will discuss new evidence of a vibrant Chinese community with networks stretching throughout California as well as into other parts of the U.S. and China PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE BY NICK GALIOTTO What a pleasure it was to represent the Historical Association on September 24 at the commemoration of the Mountain View Library's 100 years of service to our community. And, Barbara Kinchen was on hand to make sure the stories related by the various speakers about the Library coincided with its actual history. It was a very enjoyable program that included the planting of a Centennial Crabapple tree, since such a tree had grown next to the earlier library building. The ad hoc committee studying the feasibility of establishing a Mountain View History Museum has been busy. Wally Erichsen reports that they have visited the local museums in nearby cities and gathered a lot of information. A mission statement for the committee has been developed. The committee consists of Wally, Anne Bakotich, Al Jehning, Barbara Kinchen, Vivian Schatz, John Viscovich, and Bob Weaver. If any other members are interested in joining this committee, Wally says that you're most welcome. Hip Telmont again coordinated the MVHA's participation in the recent Chamber of Commerce Art & Wine Festival. Those of you that worked with Hip on this definitely gave our organization a positive presence at another major community event. Also, of course, it was an opportunity to sell a few books and to sign up several new members, which is always a plus for our organization. Your Executive Committee met on September 7th to plan the association's final activities for this year. (Wow, this year is almost over). And, we give Trudi Tuban a very big "thank you" for all that's involved in getting the Newsletter to our members. Once again, my standard closing: Encourage your friends to attend our meetings. They will learn of Mountain View's colorful past and mingle with some of those that have lived it. That's what we're about. See you on November 6th!! The Train Depot was described as "dreary." The old buildings were surrounded with weeds and dust in the summer and weeds and mud holes in the winter. The newspaper editor suggested a public park be considered for the area between the station and Castro Street. 50 YEARS AGO (1955): The new Los Altos High School opened in September and First Western Bank moved from 201 Castro to new quarters at 565 Castro. Plans were announced for a bowling alley on Gemello's El Camino property. Based on a novel by James Edmiston, Jr., of Palo Alto, a movie, "Home Again," about a Japanese family returning to their flower-growing business in Mountain View after 3-1/2 years internment at Heart Mountain, Wyoming. Background scenes were being shot around Mountain View. (Does anyone have personal knowledge about this movie?) Widespread wind damage, power outages, flooding and evacuations occurred throughout Northern California in a series of storms the week before Christmas. There were deaths; with most lost in the levee break at Yuba City. In Mountain View, both Permanente and Stevens Creeks caused flooding, along with especially high tides. Parts of Bayshore Highway were closed as well as the El Camino-El Monte Intersection. The North Bayshore area was hard hit and the city dump was under water. 25 YEARS AGO (1980): Mountain View-Los Altos High School District trustees, acting on Superintendent Paul Sakamoto's recommendation, voted to close the Castro Street high school in June 1981. Victor Calvo was honored upon retirement from the California State Legislature. His 22 years of public service included councilman, county supervisor, three terms at the state level and member of the California Public Utilities Commission. The Italian Catholic Federation of Mountain View held a testimonial dinner for Ugo Mancini for his many accomplishments and services to the community. The president of Trinity College, Washington D.C., traveled to Portland, Oregon to personally present a graduation certificate to a lady who had been "too busy" to pick it up some 76 years before. Mrs. Jessie Johnson Fretz, age 100, a former resident of Mountain View, was that lady. (Jessie Lane is named for Mrs. Fretz and Paul Avenue for her son, Paul Fretz.) Open house was held in the new Police and Fire Administration Building on Villa Street. After being vacant ten years, there was finally an agreement to finish and lease out the International Environmental Design Building (IED) at Castro and Mercy Streets. Neighbors protested the noise from mock bull fights and other events put on by rental groups, including Hells Angels, at the I.F.E.S. Portuguese property on Stierlin Road. Arrow Development, makers of the Boomerang, Corkscrew, Lock Ness Monster and Logger's Run amusement park rides, was bought by Huss Trading Corporation of Switzerland. Operations are to be moved to Salt Lake City and to Germany. STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN What street is named for one of Mountain View's early Baptist ministers? Reverend Orrin Crittenden (1814-1903), came to our area in 1853 and owned 160 acres where Crittenden Lane runs from Shoreline Boulevard, east to Stevens Creek. Crittenden Middle School is named for Reverend Crittenden's adopted son, Albert M. Crittenden. Albert owned the family land until it sold and became part of Moffett Field in 1929. (3) Old storage building on alley behind Valley Electric. It was once used as the Swall Butcher Shop at the corner of Castro and Villa; it had been moved up the street for Mr. Peterson's Plumbing Shop and later moved to the alley when Peterson had a new building constructed.
