See you on August 7th!! OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 YEARS AGO (1905): A Farmers and Merchants Bank has just been incorporated and 500 shares of stock, at $100 per share, sold. W. H. Bates, a local contractor, has been awarded a contract for a bank building at the corner of Castro and Villa Streets, to be built of San Jose sandstone. Father Cullen presided at the cornerstone-laying ceremony at the site of the new St. Joseph's Catholic Church at Hope and Church Streets. A large tent was erected on Castro Street where members and visitors were served both lunch and supper. Spicer and Mesa started an ice business. The ice, made from pure distilled water, came from Sacramento. Residents had to depend in the past on an ice wagon from San Jose. Miss Jessie Lovejoy won the Goddess of Liberty contest. Her attendants at the Fourth of July parade were May Dunsford and Annie Campen. 75 YEARS AGO (1930: July prices at Mountain View's Blue and White Stores: Butter @ 42 cents a pound Watermelon @ 2 cents per pound Sugar @ 45 cents for ten pounds Local tomatoes @ 17 cents for 3 pounds "The most innovative cafe on the Peninsula," the Bird Cage, opened on El Camino, just south of D&S Lumber. Mr. A. Clark, proprietor, has dozens of singing canaries, bright colored parrots and many other valuable birds to entertain his customers. A daytime fire burned a number of cabins on the Gallimore ranch, near South Shore Port, occupied by Filipino cannery workers. There was one death of a man who had been ill and remained home from work. Recently, there had been letters threatening to destroy any property housing Filipinos. Federal agents arrested Battista Bordi at his Stevens Creek ranch for possessing more wine than he was supposed to have. Over 3,800 gallons were seized. It was later returned and charges dismissed because of a faulty warrant. An audience of Japanese enjoyed a movie in Swan's Hall until the film caught fire. According to regulations, a fireman was stationed in the hall that night, Ed Demezze, and everyone was escorted out with no injuries. 50 YEARS AGO (1955): Disneyland opened in Anaheim and five of the rides had been made by Arrow Development Company, 243 Moffett Boulevard, Mountain View. A new business office for Pacific Telegraph and Telephone was constructed at 707 California Street, at the corner of Hope and California. James Gard was manager. Trustees of the Mountain View Elementary School District condemned the 27-year old Highway Grammar School. A detailed structural survey showed it was not up to State regulations for safety. Nine hundred students attended that school and will have to be accommodated in other schools, possibly by running double sessions. George Sohler, long associated with the City of Mountain View, retired. Over a period of nearly 30 years, he served ten years on the city council, two terms as mayor, superintendent of water works, building inspector and part-time engineering inspector. 25 YEARS AGO (1980): Senator Alan Cranston was present for the dedication of Monte Vista Terrace, the new $5.8 Million housing development on Grant Road, former site of Monte Vista Drive In Theatre. One hundred eighty low income seniors and handicapped residents moved in and there is a long waiting list for future openings. While other libraries are cutting back hours because of funding problems, Mountain View added one additional hour of service. Library hours are 10 to 9 Monday through Thursday, 10 to 6 Friday and Saturday and 2 to 5 on Sunday. Await High School's Jazz Ensemble and the Reflections, jazz vocalists, traveled to Mexico and for one week performed in Mexico City and at the University of Mexico. Raffles and car washes helped raise the $500 for each of the performers, aides and chaperones, 34 total making the trip. Plans were approved for James and Francine Dale to reconstruct Cherry Chase Golf Course and to construct seven three-story buildings for condominiums around the greens. Dominating the news all summer were stories of deadlocked negotiations over salary and pension demands by fire and police personnel. Pickets were placed at City Hall and firefighters went on strike for 39 days. All but one tire station was ciosed and out-of-town firemen hired. Special security measures went into effect for city buildings and city officials. Threatened with the loss of jobs, firemen went back to work the first week in September. Police did not strike, but held a one day "blue flu" sickout in support of firemen and signed a contract in August. Salaries were increased but neither firemen nor police gained the pension packages they had demanded. Send This Form With Your Check to: MVHA Barbecue 107 Del Monte Los Altos, CA 94022 Number of Adults @ $ 10.00 = Please Mail By: Number of Children @ $ 5.00 = July 23, 2005 Total Amount Enclosed Thank You MEMORIES OF LIVING IN MOUNTAIN VIEW BY MEMBER LORRAINE (SIEBER7) MARTIN While my family was not a pioneer family, it is hard to believe it was 60 years ago that we settled in Mountain View. My older sister and parents relocated to Mountain View from Illinois when they decided to stay after a visit. I arrived at the end of the semester in my freshman year of high school and graduated from Mountain View Union High School in 1948. The war was still on but my parents decided to build their own home on the corner of Mariposa and Latham, which was outside the city limits. Building materials were nearly impossible to obtain, so they bought an army barracks on Page Mill Road near where HP now stands. They took it apart board by board, window by window. While they built our home, we stayed in the old Mountain View Hotel in the first block from the railroad tracks on Castro Street. The hotel was above the first Chinese restaurant and we would fall asleep listening to Chinese music. The home was completed sometime in late 1945. I have manypleasant memories of MVUHS. Stan and Edna Thompson worked there at that time as did Eva(Monk) Mockbee. Mr. and Mrs. Blalock both were teachers there and later became my cousin's in-laws. Mr. Blalock steered me in the direction of higher math which qualified me for breaking into a computer career. Miss Froehlich taught chorus which I became very active in. Very pleasant memories. Another activity was organizing a Girl Scout Mariner Troup. We had many dances with the Mountain View Sea Scouts who had their boats at the Palo Alto Harbor. The Sea Scouts were sponsored by the Mountain View fire department, which were all volunteers at that time. The Scouts were active volunteers also. I have pictures of them helping dedicate the "new" post office which had moved from Castro Street to Dana. During lunch hour on Wednesdays, my friend June Andrews and I would go across the street to the hall on the corner to serve lunch to the Kiwanians. Bay Hayes (the local mortician) was the Secretary/Treasurer and he paid us $0.50 per luncheon, a free meal and we were able to skip PE class. Mrs. Peracchi, whose son ran the grocery store "Food City," was the Cook. Mr. Cooke, our high school principal was also a Kiwanis member. What a wonderful place to live. The towns in the area were separated by orchards and the local teens could always get jobs picking prunes or slicing apricots. I remember one September when the opening of school was delayed because the prunes were still to be picked. Across the street from our house, I used to work in the flower beds at $0.25 per hour. I lived in the Bay Area until 1989 and have been a member of the MI/HA for a number of years. EDITOR'S NOTE: Many thanks to Lorraine for her article. We are looking for additional stories. STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN The Josef Sladky family from Bohemia, Austria, owned many acres between Mira Monte and Springer Roads, now occupied by Blossom Plaza Shopping Center and subdivisions. What is now the part of Cuesta Drive between Springer and Mira Monte was opened in 1910 as Sladky Road. Much later, the road was extended to Grant Road. About 1955, there was a name change to Cuesta Drive. Today's Sladky Avenue was once Central Avenue and was so named after the 1944 death of Miss Marie Sladky, last of the family, here since the mid 1880's. This street almost lost the name when, about 1960, residents petitioned to have it changed to Amber (as in Liquid Amber trees). While the City Planning Department favored the residents, the Council refused to erase the old family name. MOUNTAIN VIEW SHELL OIL DEPOT BY MEMBER LOUIS BECK Manny Esparenza, Jack Tutman and Louis Beck were part of the crew working at the Shell Oil Company Depot located at Evelyn and Calderon Avenue, Mountain View. In the 1920's, railroad cars or barges brought goods to a terminal and delivery by trucks was only used for the last 15 to 20 miles because trucks had a limited range because many of them were still using solid tires. For example, barges brought goods to the South Shore Port and then trucks delivered them though out Santa Clara County until the late 1920's. There were Shell Oil Company depots in San Francisco, Redwood City, Mountain View, San Jose, Salinas and Santa Cruz until after World War II. A depot was established at the Redwood City Port in 1949. Gasoline was brought to the Depot by barge from the refinery at Martinez and delivered by truck as far south as San Luis Obispo. My father, Louis Beck, started working at the Mountain View Depot in 1930. Between 1934 and 1940, he worked at the Redwood City, Santa Cruz and San Jose Depots. He was called to active duty in the U. S. Navy in April 1940 and served until the spring of 1948. He returned to Shell until he retired in 1958. Mountain View also had a Standard Oil Company Depot and there was a strong rivalry between Shell and Standard before World War II. I worked for Otto Krebs at his Standard station at El Camino Real and Castro Street in 1944 while I was in high school. It was suggested to my mother that my working for Standard might affect my father's job when he returned from the service. Member Louis Beck, now living in Fresno submitted this article. Louis graduated from Mountain View High School in 1945 and his father, Louis Beck, graduated in 1926. IN MEMORIAM MILAN MATT POPOVICH: Passed away at home in Saratoga on January 20, 2005. Milan was born on June 25, 1920 in Mountain View and grew up on the family fruit ranch on Bryant Avenue. He is survived by his wife of 58 years, Desanka Galeb Popovich; daughters, Paula Smith and Linda Roderick; sister, Olga Batey and brother, Donald. Preceded in death by brother, Robert and sister, Ruby. Milan attended local schools and graduated from Mountain View Union High School in 1937. He was an orchardist for the Popovich ranch on Bryant Avenue and later on the Galeb ranch in Saratoga. He was also an independent insurance agent. He was a veteran of World War II and the Korean War. He was a 67 year member of the Croatian Fraternal Union, a Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association and many other organizations. ELIZABETH "BETTY" E. STODDARD: Passed away on February 3,2005. A native of Mountain View. Preceded in death by her husband John Stoddard. Survived by son, Eric Stoddard; daughter, Allison Stoddard (Lenarcic) and sister, Ellen Downing. Mrs. Stoddard graduated from Mountain View High School in 1940 and later was a secretary with the Los Altos School District. She was a current member of the Navy League of Santa Clara County, Quadalco and a member of the Mountain View Historical Association. MARGARET VIDOVICH: Passed away in Los Altos on February 20, 2005. Survived by nieces and nephews, Margaret Taylor, Susan Taylor, Lois Vidovich and Mark Vidovich. A native of Mountain View, age 90 year, Margaret retired from Ferry Morse Seed Company after 30 years as an executive secretary. She was a member of the Y.L. I., the Quota Club and was a life member of the Mountain View Historical Association. MARY LOU ZOGLIIV: Born September 30, 1928 in York, PA and died in Mountain View on March 11, 2005. She was executive director of the non-profit, Healthy Ventures. She served on the California Community Colleges Board of Governors and the Foothill-DeAnza Community College Board. She was a life member of the Mountain View Historical Association. PATRICIA KLEIN SNOW The Klein family had an inipotta- nt place in the history of Mountain View as well as in other parts of California. Victorine Klein was a primary school teacher and vice principal of the Dana Street School for a period of 32 years ending in 1934. She was recognized as an outstanding and well loved teacher and humanitarian when the (now destroyed) Victorine J. Klein School was built at the corner of California Avenue and Ortega. The site is now Klein Park. Victorine's father, Pierre Klein, was an important influence on the recognition of quality California wines at a time when Europeans felt they had a "corner on the market." Our speaker, Patricia Snow, as the granddaughter of Pierre, is well qualified to tell the story. She is the author of a recent book about the Klein family. After the presentation, there will be our usual opportunity for coffee, cookies and good fellowship. Please join us at the Adobe Building, Sunday, February 6, 2005 at 2pm. February 2005 Page 1 of 8 MVHA PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE BY NICHOLAS GALIOTTO 2005 — A new year, a new President for the Association. I'll start with my best wishes to you all for an enjoyable and productive 2005. Many thanks are due our outgoing President, Craig Holden, and the members of his executive committee. Theft accomplishments over the past two years have been very important: securing the Adobe Building for Association meetings; revising the Bylaws; publishing a new MVHA brochure; promoting "Milestones" sales; creating an MVHA display at the City Transit Center; and, certainly very important, providing entertaining and informative programs at our membership meetings. Ralph Faravelli assured me that the previous officers of our association had done the heavy lifting, so my first year as President would be a light load. However, at the meeting of the new executive committee, Wally Erichsen immediately launched a challenge to explore the possibility of establishing a permanent Mountain View History Museum where artifacts and other memorabilia of earlier Mountain View beyond that of the Library's History Room could be exhibited. Another challenge for the New Year was the replacement of the association's newsletter editor. Hilton Brown had done a great job and was signing off from that role. Fortunately for us, Trudi Tuban Bly agreed to Craig's persuasion and is taking over as editor. This connection to our members is essential, so please thank Trudi. Wally is arranging some interesting programs for our regular meetings in February and May. The August Barbecue and Raffle coordinated by John Viscovich will again be our main event followed by the Annual Meeting in November. Encourage your friends to attend our meetings. They will learn of Mountain View's colorful past and mingle with some of those that have lived it. That's what we're about. Let's share the experience. THANK YOU TO HILTON BROWN III BY CRAIG HOLDEN The Executive Committee of the Mountain View Historical Association, on behalf of the entire membership, wishes to express our profound gratitude to you for your dedicated and skillful service as Treasurer and Newsletter Editor for many years. The people of Mountain View have greatly benefited from your choice of our city as your home. Your volunteer work for the community-at-large, as well as for our Association, stands as an inspiration for all of us. We thank you. Shoreline Blvd., MV 94043 -- $25/5 vouchers OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHE1V 100 YEARS AGO (1905): Young Howard Beverly died of consumption at age 20. He and Edward Green were the first graduates of Mountain View High School, June 1904 and were credited with naming the "Blue and Gray" yearbook. Howard was the son of Justice of the Peace Frank P. Beverly and his wife, Carrie. Mountain View's City Attorney, Arthur M. Free, was appointed postmaster by President Theodore Roosevelt. Mr. Free was later County District Attorney before going on to serve six terms in Congress. Charles Pearson opened a grocery store on Castro Street. In 1918, it became Erichsen Grocery and later the building was moved to make way for Campen's Mountain View Theatre, which opened in 1926. 75 YEARS AGO (1930): Mrs. Lyllis Lundkvist, High School vocal music teacher, will accompany two local students to Chicago. Analee Camp will play cello in the National School Orchestra and Henry Norman will sing in the National High School Chorus. Only about 20 California students were chosen to participate with those from the rest of the nation. By using water from a swimming pool, Fire Chief Jack Mockbee and his crew prevented Marymeade, the Fretz residence on Grant Road at Fremont, from burning. Only the garage and servant's quarters were destroyed. •••••••.. February 2005 Page 3 of 8 MVHA The McDonald and Burke Blacksmith Shop has been in business on Castro Street for over 35 years. First at Castro and Villa in the old Jake Mockbee Blacksmith location, it moved to 363 Castro in 1906. The Prune and Apricot Exposition building at Castro and Mercy Streets was sold to the Redwine family as a new and larger location for its Mountain View Garage and Ford franchise. 50 YEARS AGO (1955): Chester F. Awalt was named Chamber of Commerce Citizen of the Year for his long service in United Crusade, Salvation Army, Kiwanis and many years on the school board. Here are several businesses advertising in the Register Leader. Do you remember any of these names? Radio Norris, Franjo Fashions at the corner of Hope and Dana Streets, Latin Barn at Bayshore and Stierlin Road, Country Boy on El Camino Real, Workingman 's Store at 150 Castro Street. Mrs. Wyllien Pinny Fox opened her Wyllien School of Dance in the Adobe Building. J.C. Penny had Nation Wide sheets, 8" x 108," at $1.59 each and matching pillow cases at $0.37 each. Glenn Stillens was re-elected Assistant Fire Chief for the 25th consecutive year. Mountain View's newest service club is Civitan International with Vern Laveroni as president. For 1954, the Pacific Press reported $5,000,000 income from book publication. One book alone, "The Great Controversy," sold 350,000 copies and used over "seven carloads of paper." 25 YEARS AGO (1980): Mountain View's Arrow Development Company was internationally famous as a manufacturer of amusement rides which are in use at Marriott's Amusement Park, Great America, Disneyland and Disneyworld. Santa Clara County Board of Supervisors would like Mountain View to absorb the unincorporated pockets of land around the city which are now being served by the volunteer Fremont Fire District and have the City's Fire Department respond to all fires. Fremont District headquarters and equipment, formerly on Sleeper Avenue, are now at the end of Stierlin Road, next to the dump. Mountain View has 11 mobile home parks, containing 1, 2655 spaces. Dave Olmos was named Peninsula Times Tribune Athlete of the Week after he won the 123-pound Santa Clara Valley Athletic League Wrestling Championship. Declining enrollment, inflation and lower revenue are forcing a decision on possible closing of one of the three Mountain View-Los Altos High School District's schools. A 26-member committee, representing teachers, parents, students, administration and community, has been formed to make recommendations to Superintendent P. Sakamoto. February 2005 MVHA Page 4 of 8 STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN ,•••••••, In the last Newsletter, there was a question about Front Lane and Minton Lane. After the old Minton Lumber Mill and offices were torn down, a new housing complex, Town Square, was constructed on the block bordered by Evelyn, Bush, Villa and View Streets. Minton and Front Lanes, each only a block long, run between Bush and View Streets. Front Street was the former name for Evelyn Avenue and, obviously, Minton is named for the former Minton Company and the Minton family. NEW QUESTION- What do you know about the name Sladky Avenue? NEW TO THE MOUNTAIN VIEW HISTORY- CENTER FROM MEMBER GEORGE HOLDEN: "Our Stories," a 517 page book by George and Alice Holden about themselves and their ancestors. Also George's 133 page book, "Reference Book — The Writings and Work of George R. Holden at NACA and NASA." FROM MEMBER VIVIA1V SCHATZ. 1963 C of C map of Mountain View. A 1973 brochure, "Shoreline Regional Park Historical Outline." A 92-page MA thesis by Becky McReynolds entitled "Chinese Lives in Early Mountain View." FROM MEMBER WALLY ERICHSEN: A booklet on the history of Westinghouse's Marine Division. Authorization was given to purchase tables, chairs and a tent to use when we sell our books at functions. 2005 DUES A reminder that the annual dues for 2005 are now due. February 2005 Page 5 of 8 MVHA IN MEMORY OF MADELEINE CHARGIN MALOVOS: Passed away November 21, 2004. She was born in 1912 in San Jose, California. Preceded in death by her husband of 58 years, Kenneth Richard Malovos, her sisters Frances Chargin Torelli and Geraldine Chargin Caveney. Beloved mother of Gerald Andres Malovos, Kenneth Mark Malovos and Marian "Mitzi" Malovos Konevich. Mrs. Malovos was a former Santa Clara County law librarian (North Branch), past state president, Law Wives of California and active in numerous other organizations, including being a Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association. ROSS ADRIAN NEWFARMER: Passed away November 19, 2004 at the age of 90 in Marysville. California. He is survived by his wife of 69 years, Shirley, daughter, Gail Carpenter, son, Michael, son, Charles and brother, Kenneth. He was preceded in death by a son, Gary Newfarmer, and a daughter, Beverly Neal. He was born in Colorado, moved to California at age 12 and graduated from Los Gatos High School. After moving to Mountain View, he was involved with the volunteer fire department and the Mountain View School Board. Ross and his brother, Ormand, owned and operated the Silver Seal Creamery in the early 1930's at 242 Castro Street. Ross then moved to Oakland and then Marysville. He was a member of the Mountain View Historical Association. FREDERICK HAROLD JARVIS: Born in Mountain View on January 19, 1918 and died in Capitola on October 24, 2004. He graduated from Mountain View Union High School in 1935. One of his ancestors was Isaac Newton Graham, who traveled by wagon train to Mountain View in 1852. He is survived by his wife, Margery, daughter, Marcie Morton, daughter, Susan Jarvis, son, Don and brother, Leland and a sister, Audrey Hoke. In 1945, he joined the Capitola Volunteer Fire Department run by his father, Frederick M. Jarvis, and worked his way up to Assistant Chief. He took over as Chief from his father in the 1960s. The Fire Department had become a fully paid entity when he retired in 1980. He also worked for the U.S. Postal Service and Southern Pacific Railroad Company. He was a member of the Veterans of Foreign Wars Post No. 7263, the Santa Cruz Gem and Mineral Society and the Mountain View Historical Association. fall-2004.text: ORIN MOUNTAIN VIEW HISTORICAL ASSOCIATION NEWSLETTER P.O. Box 252 Mountain View, CA 94042 Hilton U. Brown, III - Editor iwas 4,1 rtU THE SEVENTH DAY ADVENTIST CHURCH IN MOUNTAIN VIEW PRESENTED BY REV. CURTIS CHURCH THE NOVEMBER MEETING The Seventh Day Adventist Church, its schools and the Pacific Press have more than a hundred year history in Mountain View. In our history book, Milestones, we note that "second only to the railroad, the most significant influence on Mountain View during the first century of growth came from the divine inspiration of a religious woman, Mrs. Ellen White, one of the founders of the Seventh Day Adventist Pacific Press Publishing Company." Our speaker, Reverend Curtis Church will expand on the impact of the Seventh Day Adventist Community upon the growth and prosperity of Mountain View. ELEVENTH ANNUAL BARBECUE & RAFFLE THE AUGUST MEETING The August 1, 2004 meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association was our Eleventh Annual Barbecue & Raffle. Eighty-eight members and friends attended the successful event, held in the Adobe Building on Moffett Boulevard. It was a great opportunity to meet old friends and make new ones. Attendance included honored member Chris Castro and friend from Discovery Bay California. Chris is a great grandson of Crisanto Castro, owner of the Castro land grant. Credit is due Barbecue Committee Chairman John Viscovich and his committee consisting of Margaret Petersen, Dorothy Holden Rich and Ann Cozzolino. The able cooks included Al and Audrey Jelming, Ma-yor Matt Pe,?'r. and city Councilraan Mike Kasperzak. We also wish to recognized Sunnymount Produce, Sunnyvale, CA, donor of the vegetables and watermelons. PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE We will be electing a new slate of officers at our November 7 meeting. I will be retiring from my tenure as president. These past two years have been a very fulfilling experience for me in many ways. I am truly grateful for the friendship and support I received from everyone. The pas-president becomes a member of the Executive Committee so I will still be active in the functioning of our Association. Recently MVHA proposed to the City a project to place an exhibit about Mountain View's history in the replica of the S.P. Depot at the Centennial Plaza area. Thanks to the City's favorable response and support from City staff, we have placed an exhibit at the Depot. We plan to expand and improve this exhibit. Go by and take a look. NOVEMBER 2004 MVHA PAGE 1 OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 125 Years Ago (1879): Extracts from a description of Santa Clara County, "The Garden County" of the State: Of the 832,000 acres within the county, three fourths are mountainous and sparsely settled. There is every variety of soil in the valley. The west side foothills are particularly suited to vineyards. Along the marshy lands near the bay, strawberries are grown. During the summer season, 30 to 75 tons per day are shipped from Alviso to San Francisco. The leading productive industry is fruit culture. Carloads of fresh fruit are shipped east. Two drying and one canning factories give employment to hundreds of women and boys from May to November. San Jose has a population of 17,000 and Santa Clara 3,000. Mountain View and Mayfield are on the line of the San Francisco and San Jose Railroad and in the midst of a rich farming district and yearly adding to their wealth and importance. 100 Years Ago (1904): More than 50 families are living in tents, as no houses are available. A row of houses are expected to be erected on grounds adjoining the Pacific Press (Might these be Adventist families here from Oakland to work at the Pacific Press Publishing business?) Alta Mesa Cemetery has just opened for burials. Brown's Dairy, Whisman Road, employs eight men to care for 180 head of cattle. Manuel Seimas has just opened a dairy on Charleston Road with 70 cows. 75 Years Ago (1929): Mr. K. Kawamoto is proprietor of the Peninsula Goldfish Hatchery, with all kinds of goldfish and birds, on the State Highway (El Camino Real.) A parsonage for the Methodist Episcopal Church South has just been completed at 994 Villa Street. A three-year subscription to the Mountain View Register-Leader was $1.00. The city now has a dial telephone system, in the new quarters at Hope and Dana Street. Palo Alto, Mountain View and Los Angeles are the only cities in California with dial phones. Admission to the local theatre was 250 for adults and 100 for children and there were shows at both seven and nine each evening. A "local retail firm has a dynamite and powder warehouse in the middle of the garbage dump, believing it is as safe a place as the county affords for the storage of explosives." However, a grass fire invaded the dump, at the end of Stierlin Road, and it took both fire departments, City and Fremont District, to keep the fire away from several tons of dynamite and giant powder. 50 Years Ago (1954): This was a record-breaking year for growth and development. New shopping centers: San Antonio, El Monte, Blossom Plaza. New schools: Bubb and Los Altos High School. New buildings included: First National Bank of San Jose, Bank of America, Sprouse Reitz, Pep's Barber Shop and Lawson Real Estate and Insurance (all in the 300 block of Castro Street) and Sylvania plant. New territory: 700 acres were annexed to Mountain View, much slated for industrial use, bounded by Moffett Boulevard, Bayshore Highway, Bernardo extension and present city limits. New family homes: dozens and dozens of permits issued for dwellings in existing or new subdivisions with names like Blossom Valley Estates, Springer Meadows, Sunshine Glade Tract, Miramar Tract, Varsity Park, Yorkshire Homes and Calderon Park. West Coast Door Manufacturing Company, 1701 Villa Street, which opened in 1952 is now shipping 15 to 18 thousand doors a month — "a door-a-minute." Mr. And Mrs. John Gemello celebrated their golden anniversary with three generations of Gemellos in attendance. Bettencourt Miracle Market had local lettuce at three heads for 220, eggs 490 per dozen and filet mignon sold for 690 per pound. NovemBER 2004 MVHA PAGE 2 IN COMMEMORATION Earl Vaslie Masse: Passed away August 25, 2004. Born June 3, 1914 in Sidney, Nebraska to George and Laura Masse. He was preceded in death by his beloved wife of 63 years (Clotilda "Tillie" Masse) on April 7, 2004. Survived by one daughter (Maxine Harrison of Palo Alto), one grandson (Steve Rickman of Sunnyvale), two sisters (Mary Brown and Virginia Denton both of San Diego) and a nephew (Scott Hinrichs of Milpitas). Also survived by numerous other nieces and nephews throughout the United States. Employed by Union Pacific Railroad in the 1930's before settling in California, 38 year employee of Kaiser Permanente cement plant in Cuppertino prior to retirement in 1979. A 60 year member and Past Grand Master ofI.O.O.F. Lodge 244 Mtn. View, CA. Both Earl and Tillie were active members of the Mountain View Historical Association. Paul Mardesich, Jr.: Died at El Camino Hospital August 12, 2004 at age 91. A native of Komiza, Yugoslavia, he belonged to numerous clubs associated with his birthplace including: Am-Slav Men's Club, Jugo-Slav Napredak Club, Napredak Club and Slavonian-American Benevolent Society. His wife was the late Anne Mardesich. He is survived by: daughters Betty Moore and Pauline King, grandchildren Brenda Phillips and Darci King. Both Paul and Anne Mardesich were members of the Mountain View Historical Association. NEW TO THE MOUNTAIN VIEW HISTORY CENTER From Member George Holden: A 1939 Commencement Program for Mountain View Union High School; several student newsletters by Dana Street School second graders in 1928; a 1935 Highway Grammar School "the Owl" publication. Also George contributed an early, undated Moffett Field brochure. From Member Lou Beck: Information about the Shell Oil Depot on Evelyn Avenue where Lou's father worked in the 1930's and pictures of 1925 athletic teams at Mountain View Union High School. NOVEMBER 2004 MVHA PAGE 3 Included in the various teams is not only Lou's father, but also the father of our member Chris Castro. From Member Anne Bakotich: A 1947 Southern Pacific Time Table showing cost of tickets, frequency of trains, and other information on the San Jose - San Francisco line. From Member Patricia Klein Snow: The Klein Family History written by Pat. From Members Ruth and Wally Erichsen: The Erichsen Family Record in Denmark and the United States and several photos of the lighted MOUNTAIN VIEW signs which once week at Castro Street and El Camino Real. In addition Ruth has typed out from her aunt Martha Job's journal about the 1927 political situation in China. Martha Job was there from 1919 to 1930 as a YWCA teacher and social worker. In 1930 Martha visited Mahatma Ghandi in India and Ruth has copied out the diary entries for us to read. From Member Gracie Larsen: Various items from her participation on the Cultural Arts Commission and on the committee to celebrate the Nation's Bicentennial in 1976. From Member Gladys Robinson: An 18 X 24 inch framed watercolor painting by Gladys herself showing memories of the Portuguese Holy Ghost Parades on Castro Street. STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN The August Newsletter asked about a special plaque and memorial located at 2865 Marine Way, near San Antonio Road and north Highway 101. The answer: In 1990, Frank Golzen went back to Germany, from which he had emigrated in 1931, and acquired two 12-foot high sections of the Berlin Wall. They can be found in a corner of a parking lot in a small office building complex at 2865 Marine Way, Mountain View. New Ouestion: In 1996 two new streets were created within the block bordered by Evelyn, Bush, Villa and View Streets. What is the significance of Front Lane and Minton Lane in this location? MVHA emo0 PAGE 4 EDITOR'S GOODBYE It has been a good and enjoyable run but I must call it quits and turn in my eyeshade and sleeve garters. This is the forty-fifth quarterly newsletter under my editorship, but family issues are taking more and more time and energy. Flora is a middle stage Alzheimer's patient, and she is my first priority for the unforeseeable future. I've truly enjoyed doing the Newsletter. We've covered a lot of interesting material. We've supported the creation of the Mountain View War Memorial, which now of course needs updating. We pushed for the creation of the Stevens Creek Trail. We have remembered the earthquake of 1906 and urged preparedness for future shocks. We backed eleven summer barbecues, which have been a satisfying addition to civil life. We helped unveil the new marker for the Pioneer Memorial Park and honored the first residents of the area ,the Ohlone Indians. We've dealt with the Spanish Influence in the Valley. We heard about Trudi Odbert's experiences in the Peace Corps in Hungary. One of our major efforts, to Save the Adobe was a great success. We've talked about agriculture in the Valley. We'v,-, heard from two sailor,: who served on the airship Macon. We backed the drive for the new Library. We have discussed fighting fire and dealing with disaster. We joined with the City in celebrating the city's 95th birthday, a sort of warmup and get ready for the Centennial Celebration. We have heard from the Police Department and the history of policing in Mountain View. NOVEMBER 2004 In the midst of the controversies over the "privatization" of El Camino Hospital, we heard from one of the founding doctors. Did you know that Mountain View was the home of the beginning of the semiconductor industry? Our meeting spearheaded the drive to get the recognition tablet placed at the old Shockley Semiconductor factory building. We had another meeting on agriculture in the valley, and we talked of the family industries in the valley. In an effort to stir up a little friendly controversy, we had a meeting to talk about a former suburb of Mountain View, the newcomer city of Los Altos. The author of our history of Mountain View, Mary Jo Ignoffo spoke to us about California's first Legislature. In an unusual meeting we met with a man who collects fire engines. We had a meeting to talk about an important early but now almost forgotten industry in Mtn. View, Olive Oil. We helped celebrate the 150th anniversary of the First Presbyterian Church and the 100th anniversary of Saint Joseph Catholic Church In November of 2001, we celebrated the renovation of the Adobe Building, an accomplishment in which we played a significant role. In 2002 we celebrated with the City, Mountain View's Centennial. It's been a great and exciting decade, and I regret the necessity of stepping back, but time marches on. I thank you, the membership of the Mountain View Historical Association for the honor of being your editor this past decade. I wish as much success and gratification for my successor. summer-2004.text: INN MOUNTAIN VIEW HISTORICAL ASSOCIATION NEWSLETTER P.O. Box 252 Mountain View, CA 94042 Hilton U. Brown, III - Editor Soo!Aeon Ascilie Ofiri Aftsninin vinaN (JaiOnnini built in NW ELEVENTH ANNUAL BARBECUE & RAFFLE AUGUST 1, 2004 The August 1, 2004 meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association will be our Eleventh Annual Barbecue and Raffle. The place this year will again be the beautifully restored Adobe Building and its patio and lawn area. For an eleventh anniversary, a little nostalgia may be pardonable. At that first BBQ in 1994 our membership was 225 including 16 Life Members. This year our membership has increased to 381, including 114 Life members. Along the way we noted the passing of68 of our members most notably during the last year, Special Member Lena Marie Alameda and Life Member Eva Mockbee. The membership was sent a flyer recently, reproduced as page three of this Newsletter, providing the menu and agenda for the meeting. If you lost or misplaced the flyer, don't despair! Let any of the officers know you're coming so that we can have the correct amount of food available. The most important part of the affair is that hour of socializing and working up your appetite at the beginning of the meeting, so come early. Bring your friends, they will be welcome whether they are members or not. We'll see you on Sunday, August 1, 2004 at the Adobe building, for the Eleventh Annual Barbecue & Raffle. PRUNES AND APRICOTS AGRICULTURE IN SANTA CLARA VALLEY THE SUNSWEET STORY PRESENTED BY MR. RICHARD AZEVEDO THE MAY MEETING Mr. Richard Azevedo's family and forebears were pioneers in raising prunes in Santa Clara Valley. Mr. Azevedo spent 39 years with the prune cooperative, eventually as a member of management of Sunsweet Growers in San Jose and Yuba City. He discussed the growth of the industry, the establishment of the farmers cooperatives such as Sunsweet, the changes that occurred over the years including the decline of the orchard period in Santa Clara Valley with the growth of World War II and the computer industry's forcing the movement to other areas in California such as Sacramento and the San Joaquin Valley. Our President's Message, printed elsewhere in this Newsletter, reminisces about this period in the i'alley of Heart's Desire as I am sure many other members of the MVHA do. AUGUST 2004 MVHA PAGE 1 MOUNTAIN VIEW'S LOVING CUP RETURNS HOME REPORTED BY BARBARA KINCHEN Found in the basement of a home in King George, Virginia, was an old dirty, tarnished, 7" tall, metal cup with the following inscription: PRUNE 8c APRICOT EXPOSITION HELD AT MOUNTAIN VIEW FIRST PRIZE FOR IMPERIAL PRUNE WON BY DR. BARKER 1917 WM. BUBB 1918 C.F. GROSS 1919 Li-tsuN 1920 1921 The John J. Donegan family, after 26 years in their King George home, were getting ready to move to South Carolina. Mr. Donegan, cleaning out his basement, found this interesting object. He had never seen it before and had no idea who might have placed it there. The inscription does not identify Mountain View as being in California but Mr. Donegan did contact our city and talked to Mayor Matt Pear. The cup arrive in April and the sender was properly thanked. Recognizing the historical value of this trophy, Mayor Pear presented it to the Historical Association President Craig Holden for safe keeping. The Mountain View Register Leader newspaper for Sept. 23, 1917 yielded interesting information about that year's Prune and Apricot Exposition. The twoday affair featured exhibits of farm and orchard products, flowers and needlework. There were foot races, cooking demonstrations and special sales in Castro Street stores. AUGUST 2004 Not only was there a parade of decorated floats and autos, but another called a "baby parade." Specifically mentioned were little Doris Awalt representing California with a yellow dress pushing her doll buggy, also in yellow, while Alice Spencer was in electric blue. Frances and Roberta Bubb (Our member, Mrs. Roberta Bubb Sweeney.) represented prunes and apricots, their dresses being made of colored crepe paper with hair ribbons to match. (Their father, Wm.F. Bubb was awarded the loving cup in 1918.) "Silver loving cups" were given for best displays of Blenheim apricots, Moorpark apricots, French prunes, sugar prunes and Imperial prunes. The cups were to be give permanently to a person winning two years consecutively. Dr. A.M. Barker of Cupertino was the first winner for Imperial Prunes. In addition, over 400 ribbons were given other event winners. The first of Mountain View's thirteen annual events was held September 4, 1915. The Commercial Club, an organization of business and professional men, wanted to promote local businesses, recognize the importance of the fruit industry and show off the club's newly-installed project — a huge sign across Castro Street, near the railroad tracks, with MOUNTAIN VIEW spelled out in electric lights. With free movies at the Glen Theatre and exhibits of fruit on \awl display at the club's headquarters in the former Bank of Mountain View's building, "Bargain Day" was a complete success. The next year there were more sponsors, additional activities, prizes, music street decorations and a dance. Produce exhibits filled the Commercial Club building and a stage was constructed at the corner of Castro and Villa Streets. Schools declared a holiday so students could participate in the parade and athletic events. It was apparent that this would become a yearly celebration, so a permanent committee was organized to plan ahead for the next "Prune and Apricot Day." You already have read something about the 1917 affair which was held in two large tents just next to the City Hall at 401 Castro Street. Los Altos, Sunnyvale and Cupertino participated that year. Each year more people came to exhibit, shop, visit and have fun. In 1919 activities were held in the large garage just competed for Redwine Automobile Company. It was a dry and secure location for the MVHA PAGE 2 now three-day event. The next year Redwine's offered their old building for the Exposition. The Exposition Association, in 1921, purchased property at Castro and Mercy Streets, where Mountain Bay Plaza now stands. Tents had to be used until a building was constructed two years later. Admission was charged, for the first time, to enter the tent exhibits. A street carnival and automobile and tractor show were new attractions. Finally, in 1923 a permanent building housed the popular festival. The lumber came from a San Carlos racetrack after a fire had partially destroyed a grandstand. The thirteenth annual Prune and Apricot Exposition, Industrial Fair and Automobile Show was held during a five-day period in September 1927. P. Milton Smith, editor of the Mountain View Register Leader told why this was the last Exposition held. "Street carnival companies had been employed as special crowd pleasing attractions, and the attendance grew into many thousands. Mr. Earl D. Minton had persistently caused the arrest of the street carnival people for conducting gambling games for two or three succeeding years." Smith goes on to say that Mr. O.W. Whaley, President of the Exposition for a AUGUST 2004 number of years "became so disgusted with the whole thing that he announced that he was all through, and would never try to hold another exposition." Mr. Minton was Mountain View's mayor from 1924 to 1928, Mr. Whaley was associated with the local Farmers and Merchants Bank. In 1930 Redwine Motor Company bought the Exposition lot, did some remodeling and added an auto showroom and service station. A grand opening was on October 18, 1930. Previously the company had been located at 256 Castro Street, with the sale and repair of farm equipment at the corner of Dana and Bryant Streets. This latter building was changed into the Cinema Theatre. Pearson Automotive Company last occupied the exposition site, 1939- 1964. Demolished in 1965, the new high-rise I.E.D. building was constructed there in 1970. As mentioned before, we know this as the Mountain Bay Plaza location. The loving cup triggered this research about a part of Mountain View history. We hope soon to use it in an exhibit at the Library's Mountain View History Room. Do any of you readers have ribbons, pictures, or loving cups for that matter, we might include in a Prune and Apricot Exposition display? MVHA PAGE 3 PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE The summer season reminds me of my growing-up years in Mountain View when I worked in the fruit harvest. I reluctantly qualify as a "prune picker" and am acquainted with most aspects of apricot harvesting and processing (as it was done in those days!) I still enjoy eating apricots and cherries in any form and even prunes once in a while. The agricultural part of Mountain View's earlier history, along with the commercial enterprises and community development that accompanied it, is an important part of Mountain View's history. I was born in Mountain View at 217 Pettis Ave. And have lived here most of the time since. My present "adventure" as MVHA president is a very rewarding experience. The spirit of friendliness and community among the members of MVHA has been very supportive. I thank everyone for their willing help and counsel. Our BBQ and Raffle, to be held August 1 at the Adobe, gives us an opportunity to enjoy our community. Come and enjoy. . . Beloved wife of 63 years to Earl Masse; dear sister of the late May Bontempi and Hortense Pritchard. Loving mother of Maxine Harrison and grandmother of Steve Rickman. STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN The May Newsletter asked about a different name for the present portion of Dana Street between Bush Street and Calderon Avenue. It was named Dexter Avenue when it was opened in 1905. At that time the street did not go all the way through to Calderon, but only to the rear line of Andrew J. Dexter's property. The city's 1928 block map shows it cut through, but still labeled as Dexter Street, not yet Dana. RICHARD AZEVEDO THE MAY MEETING The May 2, 2004 meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association will be back at the Adobe Building, Moffett Blvd. and Central Expressway. The speaker will be Mr. Richard Azevedo. Mr. Richard Azevedo's family and forebears were pioneers in raising prunes in Santa Clara Valley. Mr. Azevedo spent 39 years with the prune cooperative, eventually as a member of management of Sunsweet Growers in San Jose and Yuba City. He will discuss the growth of the industry, the establishment of the farmers cooperatives such as Sunsweet, the changes that occurred over the years including the decline of the orchard period in Santa Clara Valley with the growth of World War II and the computer industries forcing the movement to other areas in California such as the Sacramento and San Joaquin Valleys. Join us for snacks and fellowship after the formal meeting. MAY 2004 SILICON VALLEY PRESENTED BY MR. DAVID A. LAWS THE FEBRUARY MEETING The February, 2004 General Meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association was held in the in the Mountain View Library Community Room. Mayor Matt Pear, Past Mayor Mike Kasperzak and Council member Nick Galiotto were recognized. New member Peggy Crowder and guest Dave Nakamura were introduced. Life member certificates were presented to Nick and Rebecca Galiotto and to David Greene, Anthony Radisich and Marion Reginato. Programs and Publicity Chair Wally Erichsen introduced Mr. David A. Laws, our guest speaker. Mr. Laws talk was based upon his photo essay and guide to Santa Clara Valley landscape and communities. Copies of Mr. Laws book were made available for sale, and a copy of the booklet is available in the History Center. Around 40 people attended the meeting, and Mr. Laws presentation was very well received. MVHA SAVE THE DATE! Sunday, August 1, 2004 is the date for the Eleventh Annual MVHA Barbecue. The Alta Mesa Company, organized to found a cemetery to serve Palo Alto, Mayfield and Mountain View, has bought 30 acres on Arastradero Road. 75 Years Ago (1929): Foundations have been laid for a $20,000 building at the corner of Hope and Dana Streets to house the Telephone Company's dial system equipment. Dedication of the new Highway Grammar School was held in the auditorium. After musical numbers and speeches by Roger Sherman, Board of Trustee President, and Kenneth Slater, Principal, visitors were taken on tours. The telephone operator can alert the night policeman by ringing the phone on a power pole at Castro and Villa streets, which will now turn on a newly-installed red signal light high above the intersection. Dr. H.W. Milo will continue his private practice, but sold his interest in the Mountain View Hospital to Mrs. Elsie Fisk and Mrs. Vera Grant, registered nurses. The hospital on El Camino Real near Castro Street, will now be available for all physicians and their patients. Wally Sohler, Mountain View's star baseball pitcher, is being wooed by both Turlock and Sonora. The Blue Bird Beauty Parlor offers permanent waves, including shampoo and setting for $6.00, and has a new machine called a "reducer and health belt" which you may try, without charge, before buying "Treatment Cards." Classes for Whisman School students are being held in the basement of St. Joseph's Catholic Church after a fire destroyed the school on Stierlin Road. The church's school bus is used for transportation. Postmaster Frank Huff says that "Frank Bacon is the most illustrious citizen we ever had in the community and it is high time we took steps to honor his memory." (Frank Bacon died in 1922) Huff is trying to get the State Automobile Association to erect signs directing people to Baconia, the Bacon home on Berry Road, and he thinks tat Gray Line sightseeing tours should include this house. 50 Years Ago (1954): Palo Alto Consumers Cooperative Society has a building under construction at El Camino and San Antonio Road. (This was the first business in what is now San Antonio Shopping Center.) New on Castro Street: the Lawson, Campen, Martinez building at 376-380-384, to be occupied by Lawson Real Estate and Insurance Agency, Pep Martinez Barber Shop and Malovos, Mager, Newcomer and Chasuk, attorneys. The five people at that meeting were Eleanor Dale, who let the group, Elizabeth Forbes, Eldora McCarty, Irma Winter and Marie Hugo. Laws is a travel writer/photographer who has worked for Silicon Valley semiconductor companies for more than 30 years. Mr. Laws talk will be based upon his photo essay and guide to Santa Clara Valley landscape and communities where scientists and engineers learned how to turn sand (silicon) into gold (computer chips). He will show slides and a presentation that uses signature buildings and landscapes, from missions and orchards to factories and high-tech offices, to tell the story of this extraordinary region that nurtured a world wide revolution in the way we live, work and play. Copies of Mr. Laws' book will be available for examination or purchase. Note that the place for the meeting will be The Mountain View Library Community Room. 585 Franklin Street in downtown Mountain View. CONGRATULATIONS Roberta and Joseph Sweeney were married January 26, 1936, In New Jersey. That makes January of 2004 their sixty-eighth anniversary! They are both long timemembers of the Mountain View Historical Association, and both are past Presidents. Congratulations, and best wishes for many more happy years. MVHA PAGE 1 PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE I wish for each of you a "Happy and Prosperous 2004". In 2003 we revised our By-Laws and published a new brochure that presents MVHA. It also serves as a membership application and Milestones order form. John Viscovich headed up our successful Barbeque and Raffle in August. The general meeting programs throughout the year, arranged by Wally Erichsen, were outstanding. 2004 events will include our regular meetings in February and May with the Barbeque and Raffle in August and the Annual Meeting in November, featuring the election of officers to serve through the next two years. Promotion of "Milestones" sales will continue with the A La Carte and Art Festival in May and the Art and Wine Festival in September, as well as at the Mountain View High School Alumni Picnic at Cuesta Park on the first Saturday in October. Recently I needed to check some information regarding past events in the historj- IVIVILIA. Thanks to help from our resourceful historian, Barbara Kinchen, my task was quite easy. The document Barbara showed me was written about the founding and development of the Mountain View Pioneer and Historical Association, written by historian Mildred Winters, probably in the mid to late 1980's. The word "Pioneer" was deleted from our name in 1990 via a By-Laws change. Other important dates for our Association: Our Association was founded in 1954 with Eleanor Dale initiating the project. In 1957 the Association was incorporated as a non-profit organization in accordance with the laws of the State of California. In 1964 we were listed as a non-profit organization under Section 501 C) (3) of the Internal Revenue Code. I found the four-page article by Mildred Winters to be interesting and informative. It is available for reading at the Mountain View History Room at the FEBRUARY 2004 Library on any Tuesday from 1 to 5 p.m. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1903): The Carlin's Blue Front Restaurant is very popular. Upstairs the family has eleven rental rooms and the only public bath room in town. The charge for a bath is 250. A Government Experimental Wine Vineyard has been established on the Distel farm on El Camino Real. The purpose is to find which variety of grapes is best in the soil and climate of the country. The new brick cooperative Fruit Packing House fronts off the railroad tracks near Franklin Street. It is 50 X 150 feet and equipped to handle the expected prune crop of 300 tons. During the month of November 100 train loads of young oysters have been shipped from the East to transplant into the Morgan Oyster Co. Beds along San Francisco Bay, from Belmont to Aiviso, including those at Mountain View. The ordinance licensing slot machines was repealed by the town trustees. Rev. Ingram, Cyrus P. Berry and Albert M. Crittenden had asked that all 15 machines be banned. They estimated that residents were putting $100 each quarter in each machine, money which should have been spent on family needs. 75 Years Ago (1928): Each classroom in the new Highway Grammar School is equipped with a radio connection and each Thursday morning students will be listening to lectures on music, sponsored by Standard Oil. "Love makes the world go round, besides turning a good many heads." Capt. Delbert Brunton, teacher of science at Chico State, was hired as principal at the high school to replace Mr. Otto who resigned. Joseph C. Rose was found guilty and sentenced to MVHA PAGE 2 one to twenty-five years in San Quentin for setting the fire which destroyed St. Joseph's Church on March 18th. Edward E. Myrea, local baritone, has been invited to be official soloist at the Eastern Star convention in Sacramento. 50 Years Ago (1953): An early November storm with gale-like winds dumped over two inches of rain on the area. Street lights were damaged in Mountain view and the roof of the Ben Franklin store on Castro Street flooded, sagged and then split open. Building permits were issued for two new $10,000 homes to be built at 1331 and 1453 Lloyd Way. Roof replacement costs were approximately $250. Doughnuts were 350 a dozen at Food City bakery department. Groundbreakings reported: Two hundred Eichler homes started at the old Mountain View Airport property near San Antonio and Middlefield Roads. The three-bedroom, two-bath house will be available with no down payment and $80 a month. St. Paul Lutheran Church is going up on El Monte Avenue. A v25,000 nffic- building at 180 Castro Street will house Lawson real estate and insurance, law offices for Malovos. Mager, Newcomer and Chasuk and Pep Martinez's barber shop. The Kitty Kelly Begonia Gardens, 2042 El Camino Real, held a "Going Out of Business" sale. Fire gutted the Veterans of Foreign Wars Hall on Moffett Boulevard. The probable cause was cigarette butts emptied into a cardboard container. 25 Years Ago (1978): Ed Henderson, "Mountain View's Friendly Cop", is turning in his badge after 30 years service in the local police force. Mountain View's first Mexican-American councilman, Joe Perez, resigned for health reason in December and died shortly thereafter. Special ceremonies marked the beginning of a fivemonth $780,000 revitalization project in the downtown area. Included were a small gateway park at eNN Castro and Evelyn Streets, new street lighting and traffic signals, brick crosswalks and intersection, IN COMMEMORATION Lena Marie Alameda: — Passed peacefully at Milpitas Care Center on December 26, 2003. A native of Centerville, CA, born April 2, 1898. Raised in the Centerville area, she moved to Mountain view where she lived for 85 years. She was a clerk at Wagner's Drug Store in Mountain View for 60 years. Lena Alameda celebrated her 105th birthday April 2, 2003, at a party held at the Milpitas Care Center, her home. She was surrounded by long-time friends and family members. MVHA President Ralph Faravelli read a proclamation, much to Ms. Alameda's delight, signed by Mayor Sally Lieber. Lena was a Special Member of the Mountain View Historical Association, a Native Daughter of the Golden West, for 60 years treasurer of the Young Ladies Institute and a member of IFES. The MVHA recognized her birthday by the presentation of a beautiful orchid plant. and landscaped mid-block plazas. The long labor dispute between firemen and the city dominated newspaper headlines the last three months of 1978. Threatened strikes, court injunctions, paydocking, work slow-downs, disciplinary hearings and restraining orders and petitions were all reported in detail. Council did grant a 6% pay raise and slight increases in medical and dental insurance in December. And residents would be voting in 1979 on whether future negotiations would be subject to arbitration. STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN The August (2003) Street Talk question was: Paul Avenue and Jessie Lane are named for what Mountain View family? And the answer is: Paul Fretz, realtor and developer, honored his parents by naming two streets for them. Paul Avenue is named for Commander Paul H. Fretz and Jessie Lane for Mrs. Jessie Johnson Fretz. The Fretz family home, Marymeade, was at Grant Road and Fremont FEBRUARY 2004 MVHA PAGE 3 Avenue and eventually was occupied by the Medical Mission Sisters. New Question: True or False: Peacock Avenue was named for the farm where peacocks were raised in the late 1980s for their feathers. SOME CASTRO FAMILY GENEALOGY FROM BARBARA KINCHEN It was a pleasure having Cris Castro at the August meeting, along with his son, daughter-in-law and their young son. Crisanto Roque Castro IV is a member of our Association and a descendant of the Mountain View Castro family. Mariano Castro who acquired the land which later became Mountain View and Sunnyvale, had a son, Crisanto, who lived and raised his nine children here. One of his sons he named Crisanto Roque Castro, Jr. This Crisanto never married, but Joseph Roque Castro, a brother, did and carried on the name with a son, Crisanto Roque Castro III, the father of our member. We have pictures of Crisanto Roque Castro III as a grammar school student in Mountain View as well a his graduation photo in the high school 1925 Blue and Gray. He sang in the chorus and played tackle on the football team. 7.• FEBRUARY 2004 NEW TO THE MOUNTAIN VIEW HISTORY CENTER BY BARBARA KINCHEN From Craig Holden: Group photo of 18 young people, members of the Trinity Methodist Church Youth Fellowship in 1946. BROWN, III EDITOR A CENTURY OF CHANGE PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE GROWING UP IN MTN VIEW IN A JAPANESE AMERICAN FAMILY BY MARGARET NAKAMURA COOPER At our May 2003 meeting, Victor Calvo told his interesting story of growing up in Mountain View in a Spanish American family. Our November 2, 2003 meeting will be the story of Margaret Nakamura Cooper growing up in Mountain View as a member of a Japanese American family. Although her life in Mountain view was interrupted by the relocation of Japanese Americans to concentration camps during World War II, she returned with her parents and brothers in 1946. graduating from Mountain View Union High School with honors. She obtained her degree and teaching credential from San Jose State College, graduating again with honors. She married Frederick Cooper in 1953 at a ceremony in Los Altos. The couple spent a year traveling in Europe before the addition of three sons. The couple now lives in Santa Maria, California. Margaret visits the Mountain View/Los Altos area frequently since her mother and brother are longtime residents of this area. Margaret's mother, Nellie, is an active 101 year old. A book about the family entitled A Century of Change is available in the Mountain View and Los Altos libraries. Come and hear a story of the growth of an individual in a family with strong values, who has led a productive life influenced by her ancestry. The MVHA November meeting is our Annual Meeting. Thanks to Wally Erichsen and Pat Figueroa, we now have our new MVHA brochure. It is an attractive presentation, in color, of MVHA and our Milestones book. Copies will be on hand at the meeting. As mentioned in the August Newsletter, the revision of the by-laws will be up for vote by the Association members at this meeting. We are currently looking for a new location for our Association meetings. The City of Mountain View recently changed their requirements for our use of the Adobe which includes a significant fee increase. As a result, we must find a more suitable location to meet. If anyone has information that might help our search, please let us know. Can you help? The old library card file cabinet in the History Room at the Library is full and therefore the files of 3 x 5 cards are overflowing int "the likes" of shoeboxes. So far we have been unable to find any additional old-style card files for information storage. People come to the History Room for information from the past about events, places, people and family history. Many of them leave with their quest fulfilled and likely pleased at the extent of the resources available. Thanks to our City Historian Barbara Kinchen and staff of volunteers, a significant service is being provided to the community. Pay a visit to the History Room on any Tuesday from 2 to 5pm. Craig Holden, President PAGE 1NOVEMBER, 2003 MVHA NOTICE TO ALL MVHA MEMBERS To comply with MVHA by-laws, you are hereby notified that the revised by-laws of our Association will be voted on at the November 2, 2003 meeting of MVHA. A two-thirds (2/3) majority by the members present is required to approve. The meeting will be held at the Adobe in Mountain View Beginning at 2 P.M. Copies of the amended by-laws with a comparison to the present by-laws will be available at the November meeting. WHAT HAPPENED? EXPLANATIONS AND EXCUSES FROM YOUR EDITOR, HILTON BROWN On the world news front, my problems may seem small, but to me, with medical problems to deal with, bills to pay, and the Newsletter to produce, they seem pretty overwhelming. Three weeks ago, my trusty computer passed on into that great and mysterious silicon heaven. I could have mourned its passing for it has served me well, but it took all of family's medical records, financial records, and, at the moment worst of all, the templates and formatting information for the creation of the MVHA Newsletter, and worst and most tedious, the MVHA membership database. This is the database from which the mailing labels for the Newsletter are produced. A week ago a beautiful replacement machine arrived. It's fast, user friendly (sort of) and very handsome, but doesn't know anything. My hard drives have been sent out for data recovery operations, but the information won't be available to me until some unknown future date. NOVEMBER, 2003 By good fortune, our Membership Chair had in her possession a marked up paper printout of the database. So, I have been sitting at the keyboard entering the name and address of each of the three hundred or so people and organizations who receive the Newsletter. The task is particularly critical right now because Dues are Due, and so the current status of each of our members needed to be made available. In trying to put together a presentable Newsletter, of course none of the standard pictures are available, and even such mundane stuff as heading and body fonts, column layouts, and the "boilerplate" stuff like the list of officers, the Life Members List, etc., etc. The net is, I'm leaving out a lot of material that I would ordinarily include. Please consider this substitute Newsletter as a sort of glorified "Meeting Notice". I intend to put together the "real" Newsletter in a few weeks, as soon has I have my act back together. In the meantime, thank you for your forbearance NOTICE - DUES ARE DUE Dues are now payable for the 2004. The white mailing label on the outside of your Newsletter indicates the year thru which your dues are paid. The year is the number in parenthesis, for example (2002). If the number is 2004 or higher, your dues are paid. If the number is 2003 or lower, dues are due! The code in the adjacent parenthesis indicates your membership class. (AS) is single membership, $7.00 per year. (AF) is family membership, $10.00 per year. A return envelope is for your convenience. Thank you! MVHA PAGE 2 IN COMMEMORATION John K. Stoddard: Born March 9, 1922 in Mason City, Iowa. Died July 29, 2003 of multiple complications at El Camino Hospital in Mountain View. He is survived by his wife, Elizabeth "Betty"; son Eric and daughter-in-law Jewel of Danville; his daughter Elizabeth; and his son-in-law Paul Lenarcic of Mountain View. A native of Iowa, he moved to Chicago with his parents as a young child, the to Arizona, and eventually to Mountain View. Mr. Stoddard served in the Navy in World War II, then graduated from Santa Clara University. Mr. Stoddard was active in civil affairs. He was a member of the Elks Lodge, the Santa Clara Valley Navy League, served on the Mountain View Parks and Recreation Commission, was active with Little League and was a Religion Teacher at St. Joseph School. John Stoddard and his wife Betty were long time members of the Mountain View Historical Association. Susan Mary (Lackey) Ozubko: Born May 15, 1953 to Arthur and Joy Hobbs Lackey in Deep River, Ontario, Canada. Died July 22, 2003 at Kaiser Foundation Hospital in Fontana, California. Survived by husband Gene Ozubko of Hemet, CA; her father Arthur Lackey of Canada; her daughter Rhea Bourgeois of Ottawa, Canada; her son Ryan Ozubko of San Jose CA; her brother Brian Lackey of Georgetown, Ottawa; and three grandchildren. She served as Director of Library Services for the City of Mountain View for fifteen years, and during that time oversaw the construction of the City's outstanding new 60,000 square foot new Public Library. Mrs. Ozubko was active in community affairs and enjoyed golf, quilting, reading, gardening, Cajun dancing and cooking. After she and her husband moved to Hcmet, CA she became very active with the Fieme.L Library iounctation and played a leading role in the construction of the new Hemet Public Library, which was dedicated shortly before her death. Eva Mockbee: Born December 8, 1920 in Vienna, Austria. Died August 11, 2003 in her Mountain View home. Ms. Mockbee immigrated with her parents to California in 1938. After graduating from Santa Barbara State College, she earned a Masters Degree from San Jose State College and did further graduate work at Mills College. She worked for the Mountain View-Los Altos Union High School District from 1943 to 1983 where she was a physical education and science teacher, dean of girls, counselor and head of the counseling department. Active in civic affairs, she was a member of the Quota Club, Business and Professional Women's Club and a Life member of the Mountain View Historical Association. She received the Woman of the year award from the BPWC, the Women of Achievement 'award from the Women's Forum. She spearheaded the Mountain View War Memorial Effort. Ms. Mockbee was preceded in death by her husband Bud. She is survived by a step son John Mockbee. EL CAMINO HOSPITAL BOND ISSUE Tuesday, November 4, 2003 is another election. The El Camino Hospital District Bond issue will be on the ballot along with the election of Governing Board Members for the Foothill-De Anza Community College District. Many local City Council and other local officials are also on the ballot. You should have received a sample Ballot from the Registrar of Voters. Read, learn and then vote! IUI LOCAL BOY MAKES GOOD VICTOR CALVO'S OWN STORY THE MAY MEETING Victor Calvo will tell the story of growing up in Mountain View - incn.1 Boy Makes Good. His story will begin with his ancestor's emigration to California via Hawaii, his early years in a hard working, successful farming family, culminating in a fruitful career in local and state politics as Assemblyman and Member of the State Public Utilities Commission. Victor's early years were full, working on his father's farm and obtaining a good education in Mountain View schools. He is a 1942 graduate of Mountain View Union High School and after service in World War II obtained an AB degree in Political Science from Stanford University. From 1943-1945 he saw combat as a B24 pilot. Post war he established a successful local area business, served on the Mountain View Planning Commission and served two terms on the City Council, of which three years were as Mayor. At the county level he was on the Board of Supervisors for District 5. Subsequently he served in the California Assembly for the 21' district. He was appointed to the Public Utilities Commission by then Governor Brown. Truly a "local boy who made good." After the presentation, there will be our usual opportunity for coffee and cookies and good fellowship. Please join with us at The Adobe Building, Sunday, May 4, 2003 at 2:00 P.M. PLANS FOR THE CITY THE FEBRUARY MEETING At the February 2, 2003 meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association, Margaret Nakamura Cooper presented a copy of the autobiography of her 100 year old mother, Nellie Yae Samiye Nakamura, a remarkable review of one hundred years of local history. The book is available to inspect at the Mountain View Public Library History Center. Mountain View's City Manager, Kevin C. Duggan, gave a presentation about the City's plans for the future, with particular emphasis on the Senior Center and the Community Center. The National, State and Local fina'ncial prospects will of course greatly influence just how much can be done and the schedule for accomplishing it. MAY 2003 MVHA PAGE 1 IN COMMEMORATION William Charles Garliepp: Born in Mountain View January 20, 1921, died February 11,2003 at his home in Oxnard. He was the oldest grandson of William Martin Garliepp, one of the signers of the original petition to incorporate the town of Mountain View. William, more commonly known as "Bill," was the son of William Louis and Nellie Ella Garliepp and was born in their home on Bryant Street in Mountain View. He attended local schools with many of his 22 cousins, and graduated from Mountain View High School in 1938. Bill then joined the Navy before his 18th birthday, finishing his stint with the Navy in three years. He signed on to the Military Sea Transport Group where he served until retirement. His work moved him around from Seattle, Washington to Virginia, Florida and finally to Oxnard, CA where he retired. Bill's wife Louise, predeceased him and leaves his son Bill, Jr.,living in Southern California. He also leaves a sister, Margaret Sideroff of San Rafael, CA and two brothers, Ken of Marina, CA and Jon of Cupertino, CA. William Garliepp was a member of the Mountain View Historical Association. Laura Dale Gentry: Born in Mountain View March, 1916, died in Fresno February, 2003. Laura was the youngest of four children of James Jackson Dale, Sr. and Eleanor (Custer) Dale. Siblings were James Jackson Dale Jr., Dorothy and Claire. Laura was a great granddaughter of Edward Dale who came to this area by 1850 and was one of the founding members, with his wife Elizabeth, of the earliest protestant church here, Cumberland Presbyterian, now the First Presbyterian Church of Mountain View. Laura graduated from Mountain View Union High School in 1934 and married Ellis Anderson, Jr., a 1925 graduate of MVUHS. They had two children, Donald Dale Anderson, born 1941 and Stanley Anderson, born 1945. Laura later married Lawrence Gentry, a Los Altos Architect. Laura was a Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association. Doris Mary Ebere: Died February 10, 2003 in Mountain View. Daughter of the late Chester F. Awalt. Beloved mother of Gary Ebere and wife Betty of Mountain View, Judy Ludlow and husband Terry of Livermore. Grandmother of Maureen Martin, Cathy Etheridge, Vicki Ebere and Lori Ludlow. Sister of Patricia Reyburn and the late Robert Await. Born March 14, 1911 in Santa Cruz and moved to Mountain View when she was one year old. Graduated from Mountain View High School in 1928. Met her future husband Gilbert (Bud) Ebere and they were married in 1936. An active member of the Miramonte Chapter #141 of Eastern Star for 73 years and a Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association.
