OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1903): For sale at $150 an acre, 688 acres, part of the Ynigo Rancho. Situated on the Alviso and Jagel's Landing Road with 25 acres of sugar prunes and the rest in cultivation. There is a nine room house with bath, large barn with room for 24 horses, 50' X 100' barn that will hold 500 tons of hay, blacksmith shop, good buildings for hired help and 5 artesian wells ranging from 96 to 180 feet deep. N.H. McCorkle has just opened a furniture store on MAY 2003 MVHA PAGE 3 Castro Street. He also offers undertaking services. J.J. Dale held dancing classes in Olympic Hall. Regular classes met twice a week for one month, for which men paid $3.50 and women $2.50. Private lessons were 500. Miles of sweet peas bloomed on the San Francisco Road just west of Santa Clara. "They are planted in strips about 50' wide and are nearly a mile in length, each color to itself (white, scarlet, lavender, etc.). They resemble banners." 75 Years Ago (1928): At Penneys in Palo Alto Lady-Lyke brand girdles were $1.98-$2.98 and "apron frocks to make housework a pleasure" sold for 490. Mountain View Theatre announced that three great films would be coming soon: Harold Lloyd in Speedy, Old Ironsides with Wallace Beery and The Circus starring Charles Chaplin. In the same newspaper was a quote from Professor F.D. Tyson of Pittsburgh University: "Persons who enjoy the average moving picture have an intelligence of about12 years." Dr. Richard T. Glyer has organized a community band of Mountain View and Sunnyvale musicians. An arson fire destroyed St. Joseph's Catholic Church early in the morning of March 18th. Playing at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco was The Desert Song, a romantic operetta featuring sheiks, dancing girls and French Foreign Legionnaires. Both Perry and Earl Askam, grandsons of Henry Rengstorff, were in the production, with Perry in the leading role of the Red Shadow. Mr. Shiraki and Mr. S. Hon hosted a picnic for bayarea Japanese, most natives of the province of Fukuako, Japan. Approximately 2,000 enjoyed the contests, games and refreshments at the Abbott ranch, just across the highway (El Camino Real) from Mountain View Avenue. 50 Years Ago (1953): All Chamber of Commerce members agreed to close their businesses on Good Friday from noon to 3 p.m. MAY 2003 Earl "Bud" Mockbee was chairman of the Easter Egg Hunt sponsored by Lions Club and City Recreation Department. Over 700 youngsters participated, the smaller ones at the Woman's Club, others across Castro at City Park. Bank of America honored Miss Gertrude Lewis for her 30 years of service. In 1923 she started as a bookkeeper for Farmers and Merchants National Bank, at the corner of Castro and Villa Streets. In 1926 the bank became Bank of Italy and soon Bank of America. Miss Lewis is now in charge of statements and safe deposit boxes. City Manager James Thomas predicted that income for 1953-54 would reach a new high of $700,000 and assessed valuation could go to $12 million. Eighty-six year old William McCall left Mountain View on a Greyhound bus for New York. There he will board the superliner "United States" and sail to Scotland where he was born. He lives with his daughter and son-in-law, Mr. And Mrs Louis Beck when not off traveling. After years of trying to persuade Southern Pacific to renovate or replace the 1888 train station, Council authorized City Building Inspector Milton Christiansen to post a formal notice condemning the building as a safety hazard. 25 Years Ago (1978): Police raided a cock fight one afternoon, confiscating 39 roosters and spurs and spur holders. Of the 38 men present, only the owner of the Stierlin Road property where the event took place was arrested. The State has turned down a request for funds to restore the Rengstorff House. It was estimated that $128,000 in private funds will now need to be raised. A court suit was brought against the Seventh Day Adventist Church and the Church-owned Pacific Press Publishing Association regarding a pay scale favoring men over women employees. The Church claims exemption from civil laws for all of its religious institutions. A former secretary claims that any employee who has brought suit in the past has been fired. With the passage of Proposition 13, Mountain View estimates a loss of $3.3 million in property taxes the MVHA PAGE 4 e"\ first year. Cost-cutting measures under consideration From an Unknown Donor: Mountain View include: salary freeze, hiring freeze, elimination of Union High School yearbooks for 1944, 1945, and capital improvements, positions and travel 1946. allowances, budget cuts for every department, turning off street lights and not offering summer recreation programs. Business licenses, construction taxes and higher real estate transfer taxes are being considered to increase revenue. Dennis Mateo, Jr., was named Athlete of the Year by Palo Alto Times. The Mountain View High School senior is a three-sport star: football, baseball and basketball. In 1957, his father, Dennis Mateo, Sr., was all-star athlete in the same sports at the same school. NEW TO THE MOUNTAIN VIEW HISTORY CENTER BY BARBARA KINCHEN From Cindy Wolverton: A very, very worn, 57" x 80". City of Mountain View flag with the city seal en a blue background. From Margaret Nakamura Cooper: On behalf of the Nakamura family — the book, "A Century of Change — The Memoirs of Nellie Yae Samiye Nakamura from 1902 — 2002." Not only is this a wonderful tribute to the one-hundred-year-old mother of the family, it is a wealth of information about many locations and their residents, including the Los Altos and Mountain View area. Many photos are included of family and friends, including the Minton family. From Godfrey Baumgartner: Paper on "History of Mountain View and Sugar Beets" telling of the operation of the sugar beet shipping facilities by railroad cars to Alvarado. His father worked there, not far from the Baumgartner orchard. Also given was a sack in which beets from each load were set aside to be tested for sugar content, which would determine the price to be paid the grower. From George R. Holden: Contributed extracts from his memoirs about Mountain View's sugar beet "dump." MAY 2003 STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN The February Street Talk question was: In 1892 a 250 acre subdivision, called the Miramonte Subdivision, was put on the market with road names of Ada, Alice, Gladys, Louise and Stella, said to be named for members of the land owners. What was that family name? Only Ada, Alice and Gladys exist today as reminders of John Sullivan (1824-1882), who bought over 400 acres of land from Maria Josefa Castro Davidson and her husband, Peter Davidson, in 1853. The property ran northerly from our present El Camino Real to Moffett Field and was adjoining the Murphy lands. Sullivan came to California in the Townsend Stevens - Murphy overland party in 1844. He was founder of San Francisco's Hibernia Bank, a generous donor to his Catholic church, including land for the original St. Mary's Church in San Francisco and in 1868, land on El Camino Real in Old Mountain View for the first St. Joseph's Church. New Question: Can you guess what the missing letters are in the following statement? In 1906 there were so many new houses on Mountain View Avenue occupied by young newly-married couples that it was called "H "Avenue. MVHA PAGE 5 A MODEST REQUEST FROM YOUR EDITOR A grandson (William Garleipp) of one of the signers of the original petition to incorporate the Town of Mountain View died recently. Do any of our readers know of other direct descendants of signers of that document still living in the area? Let us know about them. MAY 2003 MVHA LENA ALAMEDA CELEBRATES HER 105 TH BIRTHDAY Lena Alameda celebrated her 105th birthday April 2, 2003, at a party held at the Milpitas Care Center, her present home. In attendance were many of her family and friends including Father Di Nardo, Villa Siena Chaplain and Father Oscar Tabujara of St. Joseph's Catholic Church. Lena is a Special Member of the Mountain View Historical Association, a citizen of Mountain View for more than 85 years and a Native Daughter of the Golden West. The MVHA recognized her birthday by the presentation of a beautiful orchid plant. Brown, III - Editor Sordsam Aseitte Depfht alametaiw Wry Odiflowsta, ANhLL As t US PLANS FOR THE NEW SENIOR & COMMUNITY CENTERS THE FEBRUARY MEETING The next Regular Meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association will take place at The Adobe Building at 2:00 PM, Sunday, February 2, 2003. Mountain View City Manager Kevin C. Duggan will describe the plans and progress for the new Senior Center and Community Center for the City of Mountain View. Both of the present structures are old, need upgrades to meet current seismic standards and are only marginally able to meet the needs of the residents of the community. Mr. Duggan will bring us up to date on just where the City is headed with these important projects. Please join us for cake, coffee and fellowship after the presentation. CENTENNIAL PARTY AND ELECTION OF OFFICERS THE NOVEMBER MEETING At the November 3, 2002 Regular Meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association outgoing President Ralph Faravelli was presented with a beautiful tray in recognition of his many services to the Association and the City of Mountain View. In FEBRUARY 2003 accordance with the bylaws, the Nominating Committee submitted its slate of candidates for election as officers of the Association. A call was made for nominations from the floor, but none were forthcoming. The Nominating Committee's slate was then elected unanimously. The new officers are: PRESIDENT VICE PRESIDENT SECRETARY TREASURER Craig Holden Pat Figueroa Margaret Peterson Hilton Brown The Association had the opportunity to preview the Centennial Video Production outlining the history of Mountain View. We then adjourned to partake of refreshments, including a Centennial Cake. PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE FROM CRAIG HOLDEN As the new president of the Mountain View Historical Association, I appreciate the opportunity to become better acquainted with the members of our association. My experience in the MVHA has provided a new realm of sociality for me — new friends, new responsibilities, the fun of working with others on a common project. Being a native of Mountain View, as many of you are, has meant renewing some former acquaintances and friendships. Also, I want to pay tribute to Ralph Faravelli, our outgoing president, for his outstanding service to the MVHA and to our city. MVHA PAGE 1 Each of us is profoundly influenced by her/his own family heritage. Events and the lives of people from the past have shaped our present day society. Perhaps this is a simple truth, but this fact is likely at the root of why we are members of MVHA. We are curious about the past history of our city and enjoy the sociality of sharing common values with others who live in Mountain View. Here are a few items coming up in 2003. By-laws are being revised and you will soon be informed of the changes and can cast your vote. "Milestones," a history of Mountain View, will continue to be sold at various events. Here's an opportunity to volunteer your help. Our August meeting will be our annual Barbeque and Raffle. I look forward to working with the members of our organization in the coming year. Craig Holden, President, MVHA STREET TALK BY BARBARA KINCHEN The November Street Talk question was: On early maps Bush Street had a different name. What was it called? The Answer: On early town maps Bush Street was shown as Live Oak Street. New Question: In 1892 approximately 250 acres was subdivided and put on the market as Miramonte Subdivision. The original map had roads named Ada, Alice, Gladys, Louise and Stella, said to be named for members of the land owners. What was that family name? This was the same family which gave the land in 1868 for the first Catholic Church in Mountain View. It was situated on El Camino Real near Stevens Creek and was within the later Miramonte Subdivision. MOUNTAIN VIEW CENTENNIAL QUIZ Carol Fischer, a Life Member of the Historical Association and the Librarian in charge of the History Center, has been responsible for a regular column in this Newsletter. She either wrote the column herself, or arranged for some other library staff member to write it. Carol passed away in December, but she had written a set of Centennial Test Questions which we began publishing in the November issue of this Newsletter. In Carol's memory, the balance of the Quiz and the answers are printed below. Carol will be sorely missed. 1. How much did the United States pay for the land that became Moffett Field? 2. What was the plunge? Where was it located? 3. Who donated his land for the establishment of the first Whisman School? 4. How did Eagle Park get its name? 5. What used to occupy the land upon which Fire Station One is built on Shoreline Blvd.? 6. What local landmark once occupied the corner of Castro Street and El Camino Real — the site of today's Washington Mutual Bank? 7. What was NASA originally named when it came to Mountain View in 1939? 8. Who was Mercy Street named after? 9. When was the first Mountain View High School opened and where was it located? 10. How many buildings have carried the name Mountain View High School? 11. Who was the first mayor of Mountain View? 12. When was the first Art and Wine Festival held in Mountain View? 13. Where was Mountain View Airport located? FEBRUARY 2003 MVHA PAGE 2 14. What was the Castro Mound? Where was it located? 15. There was one Ohlone Indian who owned land in this area. Who was he and where was his land located? 16. When was the Mountain View Historical Association incorporated and who was the first president? 17. When was the Mountain View History Center (then known as the Pioneer Room) established? 18. What was the name of the grammar school teacher whose father owned an award-winning vineyard? 19. At one time this Mountain View street was called Pumpkin Alley. Which street had that nickname? 20. The Bank of America (now Red Rock Coffee Co.) At 201 Castro Street was once bombed. Why? By whom. Answers to the Centennial Questions: 1. The land that became Moffett Field was transferred to the United Sates Navy at a cost of $1.00. Local fund-raising campaigns had raised enough money to pay each of the landowners $450 an acre. That in turn allowed the Santa Clara County Consolidated Air Base Committee to offer the land to the government at such a reasonable price! 2. The plunge, known as the Kingsport Plunge, was the largest open-air salt-water swimming pool in Santa Clara County. It was opened in 1925 and measured 50 feet by 120 feet with a depth of 2 to 9 feet. At night, colored lights illuminate the bottom of the pool. Admission was 10 cents. The plunge was located along the bay on land that is now part of Moffett Field. By the late 1920s, the company had gone bankrupt. 3. Henry Rengstorff donated one acre of his land for the establishment of Whisman School. The oneroom school was located on Stierlin Road (now Shoreline Blvd.). IN COMMEMORATION Carol A. (Westphal) Fischer: — Born in San Francisco, January 27, 1954 to Ethel and Charlie Westphal, died suddenly December 22, 2002 in Mountain View. Carol Fischer is survived by her parents, Ethel and Charlie Westphal of San Francisco, her brother Robert of Mann, her husband Chuck, and three sons Ross, Daniel and Jack. She attended San Francisco State University and San Jose State University and obtained a Masters Degree in Library Science. Mrs Fischer worked for 23 years for the Mountain View Public Library as a reference librarian and overseer of the Library History Center. She was a Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association and contributed regular columns for the Association Newsletter. In memory of Carol, donations may be made to the MVHA Memorial Fund, P.O. Box 252, Mtn. View, CA 94042. The Memorial Book is located in the History Center at the Mountain View Public Library. 4. Eagle Park was built on land that once served as the athletic fields of Mountain View High School. When the park was dedicated in 1989, it was named in honor of the former school's eagle mascot. 5. The Dana Street School sat on the land now occupied by Fire Station 1 on Shoreline Blvd. The school was built in 1917 and only kindergarten thru third grade children attended class there. The school was condemned in 1955 and razed in 1960. 6. A 52-foot tower and globe was the local landmark that occupied the Castro street and El Camino Real intersection. The globe was part of the Chrysler Exhibit at the world's fair on Treasure Island in San Francisco. Ugo Mancini dismantled the exhibit and brought it to Mountain View in 1940 for the grand opening of his new car showroom. The globe and tower graced that corner until 1974 when the business closed and the familiar sight was demolished. 7. The National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) was the original name when Ames was first established in Mountain View in 1939, In 1958 NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Agency) absorbed NACA. FE BR UARY 2003 MVHA PAGE 3 8. Crisanto Castro, who inherited Rancho Pastoria del las Borregas from his father, Mariano, laid out the streets of Mountain View. He named Mercy Street for his youngest daughter, Mercedes. Crisanto also had a sister, Mercedes Castro Calderon. Calderon Avenue is name in honor of this sister and her husband, Andres. 9. The first Mountain View High School was located on El Camino Real at Calderon Avenue. It opened in 1902. Before that time, Mountain View high school students had to travel to Santa Clara or beyond in order to continue their education. 10. There have been three buildings that have used the name Mountain View High School. The first was located on El Camino and Calderon Avenue, built in 1902, razed in 1927. The second was located on Castro Street, built 1923-1924, and razed 1987. The third school is located on Bryant and Truman Avenues. It was formerly called Awalt High School when it was built in 1961.111 1981, it was renamed Mountain View High School when the Castro Street campus closed to high school students. 11. Daniel Benjamin Frink served as Mountain View's first mayor from 1902 until 1904. Mr Frink was born in California in 1857 and died in Mountain View in 1912 For many years he was in the "gent's furnishings goods", notions and hat business on Castro Street. He was married to Mary Alice Hitchcock (died in 1909 at the age of 51) and couple had two sons, Lester and Louis. 12. The first Mountain View Art and Wine Festival was held in 1971. The Chamber of Commerce sponsors the annual event and it is one of the oldest and best attended of any such events in the area. 13. The Mountain View Airport was located at today's San Antonio and Middlefield Roads in 1936. It was owned and operated by Ted Simonic. The airport was closed in the early 1950s and a housing subdivision now occupies the area. 14. The Castro Mound was the name Stanford and University of California archaeologists gave the remains of an Indian village found in the area of today's Central Expressway and San Antonio Road. The mound was discovered and excavated FEBRUARY 2003 MVHA at the turn of the century and was dated back to 760 B.C. The Castro mound was destroyed to make way for housing in the 1940s. 15. Lope Inigo (1781-1864), an Ohlone Indian, was raised at Mission Santa Clara. When he was emancipated in 1839, he moved to the Mountain View area and petitioned the Mexican governor for land. He was granted 1,700 acres that he named Posolmi. This area eventually became Moffett Field. Inigo was married twice but survived both wives. Most of his children didn't live to be adults. By the time of his death, he had sold much of his land and squatters had taken over the rest. It is not known whether he had any survivors. 16. The Mountain View History Pioneer and Historical Association, now the Mountain View Historical Association was founded in 1954. Clarence Taylor served as the first President. 17. The Mountain View History Center, then known as the Pioneer Room, was established in 1967. It was then that the Mountain View Historical Association's collection of artifacts, books, pictures maps and manuscripts was placed in the Mountain View Public Library. 18. Victorine Klein taught grammar school for 32 years. Much of her career was spent at the Dana Street School from which she retired in 1934. Klein School on Ortega Avenue was named in her honor in 1966. The school closed in 1978 and was torn down in 1987. It is now the site of Klein Park. Ms. Klein's father, Pierre (1855-1922) was a native of Alsace, France. In 1888, Mr. Klein purchased 160 acres of land on the Montebello Ridge, approximately in today's CupertinoSaratoga area. He named his vineyard Mara Valle and raised Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc Grapes. In 1895 Mr. Klein won his first medal in Bordeaux, France. This was followed in 1896 by the highest award given at the Brussels Exposition. Finally the Mara Valle vineyard was awarded two gold medals at the 1900 Paris Exposition for its claret and burgundy. These medals are on display in the Mountain View History Center. 19. Calderon Avenue was once nicknamed Pumpkin Alley because of the abundance of pumpkins PAGE 4 grown on this thoroughfare. Calderon Avenue is named for Anders Calderon who was wed to Mariano Castro's daughter, Mercedes. Mr. Calderone, a native of Buenos Aires, Argentina, arrived in California in 1849. The street was laid out in 1886 and because it was smooth and level, horse racing used to occur on the newly excavated road. 20. At 3:00 am on Friday morning, August 19, 1938, Lorenzo (Louis) Cerutti dynamited the Bank of America. The culprit was soon caught and confessed to the crime saying he was getting even for the foreclosure of his home on Center Street. The bank opened as usual Friday morning with damage estimated at $3,000. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1902): The local oyster company dredged out its bay beds and people gathered up any oysters which had been overlooked. Wandering willies and blanket packers (tramps and beggars) gather around the train station. Several automobiles are being built at the machine shop, which has been in existence for under a year. The brickyard, just east of town, now has its own railroad stop. The Ames Building is nearing completion and Parkinson Brothers Lumber and Hardware Company is moving from Olympic Hall into the lower story. A sidewalk has been laid, but problems are predicted as it is six inches lower than the adjoining walk. New organizations in town: Grange and Patrons of Husbandry. 75 Years Ago (1928): New Year's Day the postoffice moved into its new building on Castro Street at the railroad. Fire destroyed the Minton Box Factory on Front Street and wiped out $40,000 worth of canned fruit being stored for Clark Canning Company in an adjoining FEBRUARY 2003 MVHA PAGE 5 warehouse. Judge E.L. Maxwell, Justice of the Peace for Fremont Township, resigned to do missionary work in South America. James Atkinson was appointed to fill the unexpired term of office. A petition went to County Supervisors asking that Grant Road be realigned to run straight north from the foothills to a point just opposite Calderon Avenue. The new Glumac subdivision, Orchard Park, offers 50 lots between View and Bush Streets, Church Street and the State Highway, a part of the old Ehrhorn orchard. At Penneys annual January White Sale Penco Sheets, 72 x 99", sold for $1.59 and Wizard pillow cases for 190. Mountain View Union High School showed off the new gym and pool with an open-house for the public, followed by a program and dance. 50 Years Ago (1953): The new eight-room Slater School opened at Gladys Avenue and Whisman Road, bringing an end to double sessions at Highway Elementary School. City Planner Warren Terriberry has designed a new city seal decal for city automobiles. Blue, red, yellow and black are used in the circular design, which shows an oak tree within a wide valley and a mountain range in the background. Firemen are busy restoring the 1917 fire truck and it will be featured at a Lions' Club convention in San Francisco. Knight's Drug Store, 288 Castro Street, was badly damaged when a compressor, running a refrigerator unit, exploded. Dr. William Wright, Optometrist, has been chosen to head the Mountain View Chamber of Commerce for 1953. 25 Years Ago (1978): Birds, drunk from eating fermented pyracantha berries, have caused problems for years by flying near into cars along Central Expressway near Rengstorff. Spraying to inhibit berry growth has not been satisfactory, so 800 pyracantha shrubs are being removed. Water rationing, in effect since April 1977 because of severe drought in California, has been lifted. Whisman and Mountain View School Districts will again study merger. Parks and Recreation Department has established a nature study and recreation area, Deer Hollow Farm, on 393 acres, part of the Permanente Creek Preserve. Council turned down a Library Board request for longer open hours on Fridays. The library will be open on Fridays from 2 to 6 p.m., the same hours which went into effect in 1972. Vandals have five times uprooted newly planted trees between Highway 85 and Stevens Creek, off El Camino Real. Nurseries have donated several hundred trees which city employees have planted and cared for. In the latest incident, approximately 200 trees were torn out, some of which will be salvaged and replanted SoiciAaan Aciihe Dopoi FEBRUARY 2003 .Council's Transportation Committee asked for a study and financing plan to link San Antonio Shopping Center, Old Mill Specialty Center and Mayfield Mall by a shuttle bus system, bicycle lanes and a pedestrian overpass at Central Expressway. NEW TO THE MOUNTAIN VIEW HISTORY CENTER BY BARBARA KINCHEN From Mrs. Jean Gard: Donated three scrapbooks with information about the Quadalco Club — snapshots, newspaper clippings, member directories and program booklets. Quadalco members participated in both civic and social activities. It was started in 1940 as the 20 — 40 (ages) section of the Mountain View Woman's Club. In 1944 it became a separate orgnization known as Quadalco Club. Brown, III - Editor SweA•4.4 Aseikte Depot ab•OSiON Waft 011 14. 444g1 1...2t hi 18U CENTENNIAL PARTY CELEBRATING MOUNTAIN VIEW THE NOVEMBER MEETING At our November 2001 meeting we celebrated the restoration of the Adobe. This year we will celebrate the Centennial of the incorporation of Mountain View. President Faravelli is baking a cake and arranging a panel to talk about Mountain View's first hundred years, with emphasis on the City's own celebration. We will hold our biennial election of Historical Association Officers, revel in the Adobe Building, and perhaps glance across Central Expressway at the Train Depot. The Association has played a significant role in reviving interest in Mountain View's past and this is a chance to revel in the things we have helped to accomplish. Come join us for cake and coffee and a little show of civic pride. DON'T FORGET TO VOTE! TUESDAY NOVEMBER 5, 2002 NOVEMBER 2002 BARBECUE fic RAFFLE THE AUGUST MEETING The Ninth Annual Barbecue & Raffle for the Mountain View Historical Association took place Sunday, August 4, 2001 at the Adobe Building. It was probably the largest attendance in the series, in part I am sure, due to the ambiance of the Adobe Building and its grounds. Thanks for all of the volunteers whose efforts made the event a success MVHA 2002 ELECTIONS REPORT OF THE NOMINATING COMMITTEE It is time to elect MVHA officers for the 2003/2004 biennium. In accordance with our bylaws, a nominating committee was selected at the August meeting, charged with selecting aslate of candidates for MVHA Office. The Nominating Committee consisted of Ralph Faravelli (Chair), Edna Thompson and Wally Erichsen. The committee nominees are as follows: PRESIDENT VICE PRESIDENT SECRETARY TREASURER Craig Holden Pat Figueroa Margaret Peterson Hilton Brown The bylaws specify that nominations for each office may be made from the floor at the annual meeting. MVHA PAGE 1 Therefor, if you are a member of the Association and would like to nominate someone else for any of the Association offices, feel free to do so. NINTH ANNUAL BARBECUE & RAFFLE ACCOUNTING August 3, 2002 Income: 103 Adults $ 1,030.00 Raffle Proceeds 360.00 Total Income $ 1,030.00 Expenses: Food $ 45.00 Printing - Flyers 89.39 Postage 120.25 Total Expense $ 254.64 Profit: $ 1,135.36 There would be no profit without the hard work and dedication of our many volunteers and the generous support of the merchants and individuals who contributed gift certificates and food to our annual fund raiser. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1902): A reception was given students at the newly opened high school at Calderon Road and El Camino Real. A musical and literary program was presented, followed by ping pong games and refreshments. Rooms and halls were decorated in red and lighted with red Japanese lanterns. Voting for incorporation of Mountain View took place on Saturday, November 1. Eighty four voted in favor and sixty four against. Elected to the Board of Trustees (Council) were Dr. C.O. Gates, D.B. Frink, George Pattbery and George Swall. Native sons of the Golden West organized a parlor NOVEMBER 2002 with 24 members. Victor Anzini purchase the Junction Inn, corner of Moody Road (El Monte) and El Camino Real, and hoped to make it an attractive family resort. 75 Years Ago (1927): The new California Apartments, Hope and California, built by Minton Company, were advertized as "six of the most modern and completely equipped apartments in Santa Clara County" with new and improved Rip Van Winkle wall beds, electric ranges, garbage chutes, steam heat, radio plug connections and Frigerator refrigerators. Watkin Evans, night policeman, was made Chief of Police and Wilson Brinton was hired to bring the force up to three. The Chamber of Commerce was preparing a petition asking for Souther Pacific to build a new train station at the corner of Castro Street and the tracks, a block north of the present depot. Objections were because of mud holes I the parking lot, absence of cement walks and the fact there were no paved streets leading to the station. The public was invited to visit the new Rarnona Rabbity at the Junction. It specialized in fresh killed grin fed rabbits. Lawson Brothers celebrated six years in Mountain View. Three prizes were offered for the three nearest guesses to the time it would take for pigeons release at the store to fly to their loft in Santa Cruz. The pigeons were owned by Sperry Flour Company. 50 Years Ago (1952): James H. Thomas, City Administrator here for over six years, was named the first City Manager under the new Charter. He will also act as Finance Director until the end of the fiscal year. Thomas appointed Arthur C. Nielsen as Chief of Police and Clarence Lawson as Fire Chief. Ringlee's Yardage opened at 216 Castro Street and featured flannelette for 390 a yard. Council denied permission for a card room to open in the 100 block of Castro Street. Chief Nielsen and twelve businessmen in the block had recommended a permit not be give because of the four bars, two MVHA PAGE 2 package liquor stores and one card room already there. Pasarow Foods Company of Lo Angeles bought the Hunt Foods plant (pickle works) in Mountain View. The Sunnyvale club on Escuela Avenue (Senior Citizens Center now) invited the public to Saturday night dances in the ballroom and family-style dinners Sunday evenings. 25 Years Ago (1977): Residents responded to need to conserve water during drought conditions by using 26% less water than in 1976, therefore mandatory rationing will not be required. Millard Sheets, famed architect and artist from Clarement, is responsible for the 31 foot mural being installed on the front of the new Home Savings Bank building on El Camino. The mural shows the history of Mountain View. City Hall now has a Hewlett-Packard HP300011 computer and ten display terminals. The first program fed into the data bank was a fire incidents system, a planning tool for the fire department. Mountain View Historical Association celebrated the 75' birthday of Mountain View's incorporation at the Community Recreation Center with a birthday cake and exhibit of memorabilia and photo graphs. Ana Jagels Lew, Eileen Gariepp Berryessa, Ethel Emerson and Manuel Vargras told about early days and Assemblyman Victor Calvo presented a resolution from the State Legislature congratulating the City. Certificates were presented to nearly 50 individuals who had been residents here in 1902. NOTICE - DUES ARE DUE! See page six for details NOVEMBER 2002 STREET TALK BY BARBARA K1NCHEN The August Street Talk question was:: In 1902 the county was asked to "layout, open and maintain a public road" to run from Fremont Avenue, on the bank of Permanente Creek, north to the San Francisco Road opposite Castro Street. This became Miramonte Avenue, but originally how was it written? The Answer: Our present Miramonte Avenue was originally Mira Monte. The local chapter of Eastern Star, organized in 1896, is Mira Monte Chapter. In 1931 a new building was constructed opposite the Castro Street High School. It was named Mira Monte Court and contained six stores and two apartments. Lane's Creamery was in one of the front stores when I was in school, a popular place for students at lunch time and after school. (Editor's note: El Camino Real was known as the San Francisco Road at the turn of the last century). New Question: On early maps Bush Street had a different name. What was it called.? Members, how about contributing to Street Talk? MOUNTAIN VIEW TIME LINE COMMENTS & ADDENDUM The four page Mountain View Time Line, included with the May 2002 MVHA Newsletter has brought forth several suggestions, corrections, criticisms and additions which we shall review, study and ponder with a view to revising and republishing the Time Line next year. Please make note of any ideas or suggestions that you may have to make this an ever more useful and accurate document. Pass your thoughts on to Carol Fischer or Barbara Kinchen at the History Center, or mail them to your editor. If you have misplace your copy, you can pick up a replacement at the Mountain View Library History Center. Relative to this, I have received a very interesting note from Godfrey Baumgartner Jr., a 71 year MVHA PAGE 3 resident of Mountain View. Godfrey, depending in part on boyhood memories and in part on research at NASA Ames reports that as a boy, he could barely see the actual first wind tunnel from the top of the water tank tower on his family farm located at what is now Evelyn Avenue and Highway 85. That wind tunnel was built in 1940-1941 and played an important role in the superiority of American aircraft in the war. The big wind tunnel, the 40 by 80 foot tunnel, the largest in the world, was built in 1944. Godfrey viewed the erection process from the water tower. Here is a little test (contributed by Carol Fischer of the Library Staff) to review our readers' knowledge of Mountain View history during this Centennial year. Although several of the answers can be found in the book Milestones: a History of Mountain View by Mary Jo Ignoffo, see how many you can answer before checking the book. You will find the answers at the end of this column. Centennial Test Questions 1. Was Mariano Castro the original recipient of Pastoria de las Borregas — the Mexican land grant that became Mountain View? 2. Who purchased nearly half of Rancho Pastoria de las Borregas in 1849? 3. What creek used to flood Castro Street? 4. Why is the owl the mascot of Foothill College? 5. What Mountain View citizen was credited with inventing baseball's spitball? 6. When was telephone service first established in Mountain View? 7. Between which decades did Mountain View experience its largest population jump? 8. What Mountain View High School graduate became a United States Senator from California? 9. What part of town was once considered Mountain View's Chinatown? 10. What was the name of the woman who promoted the establishment of Moffett Field? NOVEMBER 2002 MVHA Answers to the Centennial Questions: I. The original recipient of Rancho Pastoria de las Borregas was Francisco Estrada. Governor Juan Alvarado granted Estrada the land grant in 1842. Francisco had married Inez Castro, the daughter of Mariano and Marna Trinidad Castro in 1839. Unfortunately, the young couple died early: Inez in 1844 and Francisco in 1845. As they had no children, Francisco's father. Jose Mariano Estrada, inherited the land. He in turn sold the land to Inez' father, Mariano Castro. 2. In 1849 Mariano Castro sold a little over half of his 8,000+ acres to Martin Murphy, Jr. That portion of the rancho evolved into today's Sunnyvale. 3. Permanente Cree overflowed onto Castro Street. In 1878, toddler Willie Cooper was swept away by the pulsing creek. That incident sparked action and by 1880 Permanente Creek had been re-channeled and Castro Street remained dry during he rainy months. 4. The ow1 was the mascot of the Highway School, a grammar school located on El Camino Real and Calderon Avenue from 1928 until 1955. The building was then used as the first Foothill College while its campus was being constructed. In honor of their first home, Foothill College adopted the owl a its symbol. 5. Elmer Stricklett (1876-1964) is credited with inventing the spitball. Stricklett, a native of Kansas, was a professional baseball player who played for the Chicago White Sox and then for the Brooklyn Dodgers. His career lasted only three years, from 1904-1907. Elmer married Mabel Gates (1877-1968) and the couple eventually took over her parents' orchard on Caldeeron Avenue before retiring to the Santa Cruz are. 6. Telephone service began in Mountain View in 1894 with four subscribers. The exchange was located in Dr. Johnson's pharmacy on Castro Street. Miss Lizzie Martin was the first operator. The service grew gradually and by 1906, there were 85 Mountain view PAGE 4 subscribers. 7. Mountain View experienced two huge growth spurts. The largest of which occurred between 1950 and 1960 when the population boomed from 6,548 to 31,313 citizens. The second surge happened between 1960 and 1970 when the population shot from 31,313 to 54,132 people. 8. Alan Cranston, MVHS class of 1932 served as a United States Senator from California between 1968 and 1993. Senator Cranston died in 2000 at the age of 86. 9. Chinatown was located in the area of Villa and View Streets. Yuen Lung, who arrived from China in 1879, anchored the area with his merchandise store. 10. Laura Thane Whipple was the Alameda County real estate agent who was the first to promote the development of the airbase that became Moffett Field. The Navy had decided to establish a West Coast base for its new fleet of dirigibles. Mrs. Thane envisioned the base being built on the land once owned by the Ohlone, Lope Inigo. She convinotd her client, Otto Hirsch, who one owned land a portion of the property that was to become the airbase, that this was the ideal location for such an undertaking. Mrs. Whipple then mustered and organized local realtors and Chambers of Commerce to support the idea. She enlisted the help of Congressman Arthur Free (a Mountain View man) who lent his encouragement in Washington D,C, Even Charles Lindbergh testified in favor of Mrs. Whipple's plan. By the end of December 1930, the airbase contract was awarded to the Mountain View — Sunnyvale location, beating out the rival San Diego site. MVHA PAGE 1 HAMBURGER HEAVEN IN MOUNTAIN VIEW BY CANDACE BOWERS Visitors to the Mountain View Public Library are often struck by the artwork of Mike Carroll that is displayed throughout the building. His vivid paintings of old-time Mountain View scenes have an almost photo graphic realism. His paintings of some of Mountain View's beloved drive-in restaurants — Linda's, Johnny Mac's, and Spivey's — evoke memories straight out of American Graffiti. Linda's Restaurant stood at the corner of El Camino Real and Escuela for almost 30 years. Owners Dean and Rebecca Riggs had named their business after their eldest daughter. A popular local hangout, Linda's was famed for it Parisian burger — a thick burger topped with a "secret recipe" tomato sauce on a hard roll, served with potato puffs (similar to "tater tots"). Dean Riggs died in December 1984, and his widow closed the restaurant in July 1985. The building was taken over by a Photo Drive-up, and is now the site of Wolf Camera. But the Parisian burger disappear entirely. 11 the mid 90s, it was resurrected by Robert Melnuedo and Sam Galvan Jr. At Galvan's Bar and Grill. Located on Evelyn Avenue near the Sunnyvale border, Galvan's closed its doors in May 1996. Johnny Mac's was located at 1313 El Camino, now the site of a dry cleaners and a liquor store. The building retains the glass-fronted, circular shape. The restaurant was opened by John McClain and William Clark in the late 40s, and specialized in "the Big Mac," chicken and steaks. (McDonald's didn't introduce their "Big Mac" until 1968.) There were other Johnny Mac's branches on El Camino Real, in Redwood City and Sunnyvale. Johnny Mac's was heavily damaged by fire in 1961. By the late 60s it had become Lane's Drive-In, and later the Pilgrim Inn. Spivey's opened in the mid-60s at 175 El Camino Real near Grant Road (currently the site of the Bank of Los Altos.) Thomas Spivey started his chain in 1930 and was known for opening the first drive-in Restaurant in Northern California. There were other branches of Spivey's in Sunnyvale, Campbell, Santa Cruz, and downtown San Jose. Their specialty was AUGUST 2002 broasted chicken. Conveniently, they fronted the drive-in movie Theater. STREET TALK The May Street Talk question was: What was the former name of Meadow Lane in the Springer Meadows subdivision off Springer Road? The Answer: In 1955 Council officially changed Jadsco Avenue to Meadow Lane. The original used an initial from each of the four men who developed Springer Meadows Subdivision No. 1 - Peter Jelavich, Lawrence Anderson, Maurice Dubin, Walter Seibert - adding the abbreviation for company. New Question: In 1902 the county was asked to "layout, open and maintain a public road" to run from Fremont Avenue, on the bank of Permanente Creek, north to the San Francisco Road opposite Castro Street. This became Miramonte Avenue, but originally how was it written? Members, how about contributing to Street Talk? MOUNTAIN VIEW: MOVING FORWARD LOOKING INTO THE PAST THE FEBRUARY MEETING As we said in the last Newsletter, The Friends of the Mountain View Public Library provided the funds, The Mountain View Public Library made available the resources, and Mountain View Community Television (Channel 15) provided the skills and direction to create an excellent video titled Mountain View: Moving Forward, Looking into the Past. MAY 2002 MVHA PAGE 1 OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1901): Following is the third and final portion of a description of Mountain View from the San Jose Mercury, December 22, 1901. There are occasional blank spots in the article, but the word or figure was simply impossible to read in the old newspaper. A PROSPEROUS COMMUNITY (continued from previous Newsletters) These vineyards, combined with the grain fields, the immense hay production of the moist lowlands, the dairy and seed gardens, the local fruit cannery, the brickyard and other industries, add yearly to the production and wealth of Mountain View and make it one of the most important shipping points in Santa Clara Valley, the exports by rail of local products averaging two million pounds a month the year around. These figures, however, do not tell the whole story as shipments are constantly being made by schooner from the landings a few miles below the town. The area devoted to the growing of vegetables, strawberries and seeds is increasing from year to year, and the planting of orchards goes steadily on. Probably the finest body of brick clay in all California lies within a quarter of a mile of the station, and from it the bricks were made that were used in connection with building stone in the construction of the original buildings of Stanford University. The brickyards have a capacity of —,000,000 bricks a year, and their product is still used in the new buildings that are being erected at the university. The fruit cannery, which was built about twelve years ago, although not operated for several seasons, was reopened two years ago, giving employment during the fruit season to a hundred or more men, women and children, and the money paid for operating expenses is expended in the town among the merchants and other business houses, all of which is a help to local trade. Business and Other Buildings The town of Mountain View has expanded with the growth of the surrounding country. The Olympic Hall MAY 2002 building, the Martin and Weilheimer store buildings, the Arnold block, the local bank building and others are all evidences of modern progress, while many new residences during the year past attest the substantiality of the town's advancement. A year or so ago the increased Postoffice business warranted the promotion of the office to third class, and this was followed by the establishment of a rural delivery district with a route of twenty-five miles, embracing families and a population of who are served daily with their mail with out cost to themselves. The town has a telephone exchange with more than fifty subscribers, and during the present year its operations have bee largely extended, many of its patrons residing in the country and their residences being connected by wire with the main local office. A section in which the rural residents may enjoy the convenience of telephones and the free delivery of their mail certainly possesses advantages which it is worth while for home seekers to investigate. The bank building, of brick with stone front and in old Mission style of architecture, is one of the most striking business structures in the town, and although the bank has been in operation not much more than a year, it si a full fledged institution, having the confidence and patronage of the business men, farmers and fruit growers of the district. Its capital stock, all subscribed, is $22,5400, and it owns the building and the lot upon which it stands. Various lines of business are carried on in Mountain View, consisting of stores, of general merchandise and furnishing goods, groceries, etc., boot and shoe stores, hotels, restaurants, livery stables, tin and hardware shops, barber shops, meat shops, blacksmith shops, real estate and insurance offices, lumber yards, warehousers, bicycle shops and other kinds of business, all flourishing. School Church and Library The local public school and grounds represent a valuation of more than $ ,000 and, in a general religious way, the Methodist, Cumberland Presbyterian and Baptist denominations and the Catholic Church are represented by neat and well-furnished church buildings. A free public library has been maintained for many years, and another healthful influence in the town, especially for the young men of the community, is the rooms of the Cycles' Club, where innocent recreation and diversion are provided, free from the demoralizing atmosphere of the saloon. A local board of Trade has done much for the adMVHA PAGE 2 vancement of the town, and the local newspaper, the Register, has ever been loyal to its . The alt water swimming baths, on a channel of the bay, only two miles distant are the only baths of the kind in the county, so one of the chief pleasures of the seaside, that of bathing in salt water on clean sands, may be enjoyed by the residents of Mountain View during the summer months right at home. The brief outline of Mountain View here given will convey to the visitor and home seekers some little conception of what the town and its environments are, but nothing short of a personal visit of inspection will enable him to obtain a satisfying knowledge of the many advantages presented by this one of the most attractive sections of Santa Clara valley. STREET TALK We left you hanging with the November Street Talk. The question was: "Stanford Avenue, College Street, Leland Avenue and University Avenue are clustered together in what sub-division in Mountain View?" The Answer: These four streets are in the Castro City section of Mountain View, off Rengstorff Avenue between California Street and the railroad. My understanding was the first small houses were built by residents of San Francisco as summer places. But might they instead have been for professors at Stanford? New Question: What was the former name of Meadow Lane in the Springer Meadows subdivision off Springer Road? NEW TO THE MOUNTAIN VIEW HISTORY CENTER BY BARBARA KINCHEN From Robert Schick: Two of his own pen and ink drawings. He is an artist. One is of the produce farm on Grant Road at Levin Avenue at Halloween and titled The Great Pumpkin. The other is of the water tower on Bryant Avenue. From Mrs. Jean Pawed: A resident of Sahara Village on El Camino Real at Stevens Creek. Four pages of pictures and historical information about Stevens Creek. SPECIAL MEMBER LENA ALAMEDA A great birthday party was held April 2, 2002 for Lena Alameda on the occasion of her 104th birthday. She was surrounded by her long-time friends and family members. Milpitas Care Center, her present home, was festively decorated including balloons marked 104. Delicious ice cream and cake was served. City Councilman and MVHA President Ralph Faravelli read a proclamation much to Ms. Alameda's delight. It was signed by Mayor Sally Lieber. The proclamation honoring her indicated that she was a Native Daughter of the Golden West, having been born in the east bay area, a citizen of Mountain View for more than 85 years. She was a long time employee of Wagner's Drug Store when located in the Julian Building at the corner of Castro and Villa streets and later an employee of Knights Pharmacy well into her eighties. She was recognized as a person with a vivacious personality, "life of the party" and known for her smart hats and stylish dressing. A long time member of St. Joseph's Church, charter member and treasurer for 60 years of the Young Ladies Institute (YLI) and member of IFES of Portuguese tradition. Few have lived thru two centennial celebrations as she has. Ms. Alameda is a long time member of the Mountain View Historical Association and was very active in the early years of the Association. She is carried as a Special Member in the records of the Association. Lena would welcome visitors at Milpitas Care Center, 120 Corning Avenue, Milpitas, California 95035. MAY 2002 MVHA PAGE 3 IN COMMEMORATION Alice Helen Danner Holden — Born in San Francisco, California 1924, died February 24, 2002. Survived by brother John Danner and his wife Pat, husband George Holden and children Robert, Sally, Kathleen and Paul, several grandchildren and three great grandchildren. She taught children with learning disabilities, retiring from school when her husband George retired from NASA Ames. Interests were grand children, great grandchildren and genealogy. She was a Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association. George Daniel Jagels — Died in San Marino CA, September 1, 2001 at the age of 93. A Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association, born in Mountain View, attended local schools graduating from the high school in 1925. Earned a law degree from Harvard. Attained the rank of Commander in the USN during WW II. The Jagels family came to the Mountain View area in 1873. They owned and operated Jagels Landing at the bay-end of Whitman Road from 1880 until 1907. The Landing included wharves, two scows, warehouses, ranch and orchard property. After selling the Landing, the family operated a feed and fuel business at 1058 Villa Street. The business remained in the family until 1949. MAY 2002 George Jagels is survived by Margaret, his wife of 54 years, sons Edward, George Jr., and Jeffrey; his daughter Jean Vaughan; and 13 grandchildren. Mr. Jagels was a Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association. Margaret M. (Peggy) Matthews — Died January 30, 2002 in her home in Mountain View at the age of 84. Eldest of three siblings, she was born in Vegreville, Alberta, Canada. The family immigrated to Mountain View in 1921 and resided on Palo Alto Avenue. She graduated from Mountain View High School in 1934 and attended San Jose State College, where she studied piano and voice. Mrs. Matthews received her 50 year pin in the Eastern Star in 1987. She was active in the Peninsula Symphony Association and a dedicated member of the Mountain View Presbyterian Church. Her special gift was music. She served as organist for her Eastern Star Chapter, and played regularly at sing-alongs at a convalescent hospital. Her cookies and lemon meringue pie were legendary. She was a long time member ofthe Mountain View Historical Association. Mt«, Calaieveks. data MOUNTAIN VIEW: MOVING FORWARD LOOKING INTO THE PAST THE FEBRUARY MEETING The Friends of the Mountain View Public Library provided the funds, The Mountain View Public Library made available the resources, and Mountain View Community Television (Channel 15) provided the skills and direction to create an excellent video titled Mountain View: Moving Forward, Looking into the Past. You can check out a copy from the Library, or you can come see the video with the Historical Association at the February 3,2002 regular meeting. The meeting will be at the Adobe Building, located on the North East corner of the intersection of Moffett Blvd. and the Central Expressway. The Producer/Director for the video, William Nielsen, from the staff at KMVT will be present. He is currently engaged in producing a video for the City, to support the Centennial Celebration, and he may want to solicit our help in that project. The Mountain View Video is very good. I feel sure that you will enjoy this look at our City. Our meetings are an excellent opportunity to greet old friends and meet new ones. Our hospitality hostess, Elizabeth Engberg will oversee beverages and snacks at the end of the meeting. FEBRUARY 2002 CELEBRATING THE ADOBE THE NOVEMBER MEETING The November meeting was held at The Adobe Building, and was the culmination of a six year effort by the Historical Association to help the city preserve and restore this fine landmark building. The effort began in November. 1995 with an Historical Association Newsletter article Save The Adobe Campaign Begins by Eva G. Mockbee. It continued with circulating petitions, staffing booths at fairs, and providing public speakers. It was with great satisfaction that the Association was again able to hold a regular meeting in the beautifully restored facility. MVHA PAGE 1 MILESTONES: A HISTORY OF MOUNTAIN VIEW, CALIFORNIA BY MARY JO IGNOFFO In early 1998, the Mountain View Historical Association commissioned Mary Jo Ignoffo to write a history of Mountain View, to be available in the Spring Of 2002, to honor the City of Mountain View's Centennial. Ms Ignoffo is the Vice President of the California History Center Foundation and the author of several articles and local history books, one of the latest being Gold Rush Politics: California's First Legislature. Milestones: A History of Mountain View, California is nearly ready for publication and distribution. It is filled with wonderful pictures of people and places in old Mountain View. Details concerning publication will be available at our February meeting. In the mean time, an eight page extract is available in the December, 2001 issue of The Californian. FEBRUARY 2002 IN COMMEMORATION Anne R. Craik — A native of Portland, Oregon, born August 20, 1924, died November 10, 2001 in Los Altos Hills. Anne is survived by her daughter, Denise Williams and a son, James Craik. Shad one grand daughter, Alison. Her hobbies were Bridge, Decorating and Gardening. She worked as a Volunteer for the History Center in the Mountain View Library and was a Member of the Mountain View Historical Association. Tony Spily — A native of Cupertino, California, born April 9, 1918, died April 25, 2001 in Rocklin. California. He and his late wife, Ruth Whiting Spily were both graduates of the Mountain View Union High School. He is survived by three children, six grandchildren and four great grandchildren. He was a member of the Mountain View Historical Association. William "Bill" Henderson — A native of Mountain View, California, died December 20, 2001 at age 79. Survived by his wife Eleanor Henderson of Los Altos, brother Ed Henderson of Sunnyvale, daughters Janice Gallagher of Los Gatos, Kathy Newell of Carmel Valley, Peggy Thompson of Sunnyvale and Judy deRegt of Carmel. Grandfather of 13 and great-grandfather of 3. Past President of the Mountain View Chamber of Commerce. Member of the Board of Freeholders preparing a Charter for the City of Mountain View 1951-1952. Past District Chairman for the Mountain View Scouts, past Chairman of the Mountain View United Community Fund, Man of the Year Award 1955. A Veteran of WWII, he received the Distinguished Flying Cross for extraordinary achievement. He was a Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association. MYNA NolV PAGE 2 000"\ THE Hoo Hoo HOUSE BY KATHLEEN LOWE OWEN In August 1926, nearly ten years after being relocated from the Pan-Pacific International Exposition to the hills near Monte Vista, the Hoo Hoo House - a controversial but popular dance resort near Mountain View - was destroyed by a "fire of undetermined origin". Originally the Oregon Building at he PPIE in San Francisco, the Hoo Hoo House had been moved to Monte Vista when the exposition closed. The building was designed by Bernard Maybeck who also created the PPIE' s Fine Arts Palace. It was considered unique in design; huge redwood slabs covered the exterior and the building was surrounded by several immense pillars made to represent giant redwoods. The Hoo Hoo House had been the subject of discussion and censure in the Mountain View Register Leader as early as 1921. It was closed by the County of Santa Clara in 1924. At that time the Register Leader reported that "after many years of practically unrestricted license to do evil the notorious Hoo Hoo House at Monte Vista near Cupertino has had its county license as a resort revoked by the Board of County Supervisors". The closure was the result of various community complaints, including an investigation conducted by members of the Grange in Mountain View and several surrounding towns. The Grange committee complained that "vulgar conditions were prevailing, that liquor flowed as freely as in pre-Volstead days and that the requirements of a county ordinance on lighting were disregarded" by the owners of the Hoo Hoo House. The owners petitioned the county for a new business license several times during 1925 before finally leasing the building to A.H. Oswald of Cupertino and James Wylie of Mountain View in early 1926. Just a few months before the fire Oswald and Wylie reopened the facility as the Peninsular Club. The Peninsular Club was considered a private social organization. Members could pay a $5.00 fee for a three month membership; they could then attend weekly dances at the club. A dance had been held at the club the evening of the fire but the owners said the dancers had gone and the building had been FEBRUARY 2002 locked for at least 30 minutes before the fire was first noticed. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1901): The San Jose Mercury for December 22, 1901 carried a very interesting description of Mountain View. In 1902 the town was incorporated and next year there are many events planned to celebrate. This newspaper article gives a wonderful picture of what was here and some history of the area. We ran the first extract from this long article in the last Newsletter. We continue below, and more will follow in future issues. A PROSPEROUS COMMUNITY (continued from previous Newsletter) The original Mountain View was located about a mile southwest of the present town on the old stage route from San Francisco to San Jose. A hotel was erected there in 1852 by James Campbell and gradually a few stores and business shops of several kinds appeared. A church was built in 1859, by which time quite a large community had been established. But with the advent of the railroad in 1864 conditions were changed. The road passed about a mile east of the town, which was left that distance away from the station, at which point a new village soon made its appearance, and the latter has developed into the thriving and progressive Mountain View of today. The old town, however, still has a hotel, a blacksmith shop and some few other business houses, and a number of handsome residences. The fine Odd Fellows building is at the old town, and near it is the public school, one of the largest and most efficient in the county. The two towns are connected by a broad and well-kept highway, with inviting gardens and orchards on either hand. Many Orchard Homes The growth of Mountain View has steadily followed the cutting up of the extensive grants and ranches by which it was formerly surrounded. It was found long ago that the valley lands in the vicinity, which year after ear had been rewarding their owners with rich harvest of hay wheat and barley, were especially MVHA PAGE 3 adapted to the growth of apricots, peaches, prunes and other fruits and that in the foothills near by the wine grape flourished and produced vintages exceeding in quality and merit even the choicest productions of the valley vineyards. The demand for orchard and vine lands by the many who want to engage in fruit and wine growing, supplemented by prosperous San Francisco residents who wished to provide themselves country homes in the midst of attractive surroundings, necessitated the subdivision of large tracts of land into comparatively small parcels, and sone by one the grain fields of the Emerson, Murphy, Taaffe, Hale and other big ranches have been converted into orchards and vineyards of from five to five to forty acres or more, an on nearly every one of these small tracts a house has been erected, some of them unpretentious but neat and comfortable, and many others costly and with all the luxurious appointments that wealth can supply. The small orchards may be numbered in by the hundreds, while some idea of the extent of the fruit and vine holdings in the district may be imparted to the reader by mentioning those of D.L. Delmas, containing one hundred acres in fruit and four hundred in vineyard; Joseph Sladly, two hundred acres in orchard and vineyards; the John Snyder estate, more than one hundred acres of fruit and vines; B. Distel, one hundred acres in fruit and vineyard, J.C. Campbell, one hundred and thirty acres in fruit and vines; R.C. Kirkwood, one hundred acres in orchard; G.P. Sparks, forty-two acres in orchard; Mrs. Benjamin Bubb, forty acres in fruit; Mrs. J. Abbott, forty acres in vineyard and orchard; Mrs. J. Bergin, one hundred acres in vines and fruit; E.W. Knapp, forty-five acres in orchard; James A. Huff, seventy-five acres in fruit; Mrs F.M. Ehrhorn, fifty acres in orchard, and many others might be mentioned. The growers as a rule dry their own fruit for the market, but there are several driers in the district where the fruit or orchardists who have no private driers is handled and prepared for shipment. The large number of vineyards in the district implies that there must be wineries, and such is the fact. Including the contiguous districts of Cupertino, the West Side country and Montebello, which is picturesquely located far up on the mountain side, and tributary to Mountain View, there are probably not less than twenty wineries in what may be called the (—unreadable words—). (Continued in the next Newsletter) 75 Years Ago (1927): A manual arts building has been completed for the high school. Mrs. Ruckdashel, lady barber formerly employed by Mr. Davidson, has opened her own shop at 1570 Villa Street. The Sunshine Grocery at 172 Castro Street is now a Purity Grocery and advertised Old Dutch Cleanser at 3 cans for 190 and Oval Sardines at 100. Charles Milani opened the New Italian Grocery at 341 Castro Street. Within one month the local Farmers and Merchants National Bank became Liberty Bank of America and then Bank of Italy. E.E. Mylrea and Fred Greenough have leased the new service station being built for L. Arreco at the corner of Castro and California Streets. Twenty-seven Chinese, Japanese and Filipinos were arrested on a Saturday night for gambling at 200 View Street. Police marched them to city hall and called in the Justice of Peace. The men pleaded guilty, posted bail and a trial date was set for the next week. 50 Years Ago (1 952):Miss Helen Froelich, vocal and choral instructor at the high school, was named Citizen of the Year 1951 by the Chamber of Commerce. Sam Galvan was elected President of Sociedad Cervantes Lodge in place of retiring Joe Diaz. Giant search lights were to light up the Chamber of Commerce building and the Methodist Church bell would ring to kick off the "March of Dimes" evening collection for polio funds. Parent and Teacher Association members, under leadership of Mrs. L.R. Forner and Mrs. Warren Grass, will go to homes where residents have turned on porch lights and hope to collect $900. Voters have approved, 664 to 114, adoption of the Mountain View Charter, outlining a Council-City Manager type of government to become effective in April. FEBRUARY 2002 MVHA PAGE 4 Honored for heroism in Korea were Lt. Ambrose Mena and First Lt. Henry J. Nafao. A report from the State Engineer predicts that most Santa Clara county orchards and farmlands will be replaced by homes and industries. The local Chamber of Commerce urged the city to annex large parcels of land for industries, including parts of the Whisman School District and the triangle bounded by Whisman Road, Alviso Road and Bayshore Highway. SoutAaaut &eat& &pat FEBRUARY 2002 EDITOR'S MUSING HILTON BROWN My wife and I have lived in Mountain View twenty one years, this month. When our employer moved us from New York to the Bay Area and we started looking for a home, we found Mountain View the perfect spot: good schools, parks, multi-ethnic, quiet streets, a fine library, respected public safety organizations, and an open and accessible city government. We made an excellent choice when we picked Mountain View.Some of the things that still delight us are the children playing soccer in the street in front of our house, the delightful little mini-park within easy walking distance where we can watch little ones sliding on slides, getting sandy in the sandbox and swinging on swings. We like this town that is large enough to pave and light the streets, collect the trash and provide excellent fire and safety services, but at the same time is small enough so that we know and can reach our elected officials and department heads. Over the years the Mountain View Historical Association has been positive force in the community. We have supported the schools and the library, and we have been outspoken in preserving the best of our heritage. I'm glad I live here, and I'm glad that I have been given this opportunity to serve the Association. A6 m4a. Seat he tin CELEBRATING THE ADOBE THE NOVEMBER MEETING The November, 1995 issue of the Mountain View Historical Association Newsletter featured an article Save The Adobe Campaign Begins by Eva G. Mockbee. The City Council had announced plans to demolish the Adobe Building. The building had served as a community facility, meeting hall, USO and teen center, and even as a National Guard Armory, but the costs of renovation and upgrading to modern building standards were deemed too high. The Mountain View Historical Association asked the City for a reasonable amount of time to study costs of renovation, plans for fund-raising and possible uses for the restored building. Thus began the campaign to save and restore the Adobe. The Historical Association spearheaded the creation of the Save The Adobe Task Force, which circulated petitions, established a speakers bureau, published brochures and established a presence at civic events of all kinds. The May, 1998 issue of the Newsletter was able to report that the City Council had taken the fate of the Adobe Building under study and that the outlook was hopeful. Our optimism was confirmed with the inclusion of funding for the restoration of the Adobe Building in the 1998-1999 budget for the City. Ai the August 1999 Historical Association Barbecue, NOVEMBER, 2001 Mark Rogge, the City Engineer managing the restoration of the Adobe Building shared with us details of the restoration and pleaded for help in finding pictures, programs, articles and artifacts from the early days of the Adobe which might be useful in the restoration. This November, six years after the Mountain View Historical Association started the drive to Save the Adobe we will be meeting in the restored building. Our President is planning a program of reminisces from the early days, and "campaign stories" about the effort to bring about the restoration. He will perhaps even mention some of the people who made it happen! MVHA Celebrating the Adobe, Sunday November 4, 2001, 2:00 PM. A SIGN OF THE TIMES BY CAROL FISCHER In 1920 when Mountain View was a small town of about 2,000 citizens, a plan was formed to build two electric signs at the entrance to Castro Street at El Camino Real (then known as The Highway). The purpose of these signs was to advertise to travelers along The Highway that "Mountain View was a town and not a few cottages and a blacksmith shop". Matt Burdett, a local blacksmith, was instrumental in fund-raising for the project. (Mr. Burdett lived on Hope Street, the site of today's Post Office). Citizens were asked to drop off their donations at Mountain View's two banks: The Farmers and Merchants Bank and the First National Bank, both located on Castro Street. Names of donors and their contributions were listed in the local newspaper. It was estimated that the project would cost 44,500 with each of the four pillars priced at 4100 a piece. The City got into the spirit by purchasing two crescent pieces of land from Mr. Polley on one side and Mr. Graham on the other so that the entrance NOVEMBER, 2001 MVHA PAGE 2 would spread out in a fan configuration. Two iron, electrified signs that read "Mountain View" would be constructed on either side of Castro Street. Pillars mad of special rocks supported these signs. Iron seats or benches complemented the project so that local citizens could "wait for auto buses or watch traffic". At least 30 individuals mad a long trek to the Pacific Ocean to gather unique rocks for the pillars. The January 21, 11921 headline of the local Mountain View Register Leader read: "Brave Men and Fair Women went down by the Sobbing Seas for to Gather Spoil unto Building Monuments". The group considered these stones distinctive "as they have been rolled and tossed about in the sea salt for 7 million years." After all the trucks and automobiles had been loaded, the crowd had a large picnic before heading back to Mountain View. In May 1921, the signs were dedicated. A three-day carnival was held to commemorate the event and ro raise additional funds to pay for the new "monument". A motion picture was even made to capture the celebration! These electric signs graced the corner of Castro and El Camino Real MIA/ 1962 when it became necessary to dismantle them in order to widen El Camino Real. MVHA PAGE 3 OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1901): The San Jose Mercury for December 22, 1901 carried a very interesting description of Mountain View. In 1902 the town was incorporated and next year there are many events planned to celebrate. This newspaper article gives a wonderful picture of what was here and some history of the area. Because of its length we will run some extracts for the next several issues. A PROSPEROUS COMMUNITY Mountain View is Growing Vigorously in Business and Population It Lies in the Midst of Orchards, Vineyards and Broad Acres of Fertile Fields The town and district of Mountain View may be cited as a notable example of the development of Santa Clara county that has been going on during the last decade and in the first year of the new century. Other examples there are — villages that have sprung up in fields which until recently were devoted to stock raising or the growing of grain — but Mountain View was one of the first towns in the valley, and as for a quarter of a century it had remained p:actically stationary, the vigor of its later growth is all the more marked by contrast. That Mountain View was content for so many long years to doze in the sun and be comfortable was not due to any lack of local advantages. Quite the contrary, its apparent apathy grew out of the very richness and abundance of its natural resources. The early settlers were attracted there by the beauty of the landscape, the evenness of the climate, and the many evidences of an inexhaustible soil, and the cereal crops were so large and remunerative that the fortunate owners of ranches and farms in the district, supplied with all the comforts that rural life could afford, had no incentive to join in the stir and activities that characterize the life of the more modern community. But progress is a law of nature, and the placid existence of the fanning element and of the little village which it NOVEMBER, 2001 MVHA sustained finally yielded to influences which had begun to transform the entire Santa Clara valley from a region of grain fields, pastures and natural parks of giant oaks to a vast stretch of orchards and vineyards whose fruits and wines have become a household word in every country in the civilized world. Beautiful Environments Mountain View is located in the Northwestern section of the county, about midway between the western range of mountains and the bay of San Francisco, the width of this section of the valley being 10 miles or more. The town is 11 miles from San Jose and 4 from Stanford University and gazing out from it at the magnificent sweep of mountains on either side of the valley one is struck with the significance of the name "Mountain View". The mountains, foothills, valley and bay by which the landscape is diversified make up a picture whose charm must be experienced to be realized, and once seen, the picture will never fade from memory. Stevens and Permanenty creeks, both heading far back in the wooded canyons of the Santa Cruz range, flow by the town, emptying their waters into an arm of the bay. These streams are lined with oaks, maples, alders, sycamores and other timber, and they are among the best trout streams in the country, affording during the long summer months, sport and recreation for those who delight in outdoor life. There are many quail in the foothills, and a few deer still range the ridges and canyons sides within 5 or 10 miles of the town. MVHA PAGE 1 THE DAY THE EARTH SHOOK IN MOUNTAIN VIEW BY CAROL FISCHER The plane crash occurred on Friday, February 1, 1957 at 3:25 p.m. Capt. Robert S. Mulvehill was attempting a routine landing at Moffett Field when his Air Force jet exploded and smashed into the home of Opal and Les Wright at 1039 California Street. Mrs. Wright was preparing to go shopping when the Thunderjet ripped into the back of her home. She was able to escape safely through a front bedroom window. Immediately she reentered her home to retrieve her purse but the house was in flames and she made another quick exit. In the meantime, Les Wright was at work at his store at 181 Castro Street when he heard the explosion. Seeing the flames erupting from the vicinity of his neighbor hood, he rushed home where he found Opal standing outside their fireengulfed home with a swollen anlde, a cut on her leg and a broken toe. He took her to Dr. Cody on Castro Street for treatment. The explosion and fire completely destroyed the home that had been in the Wright family since 1919. Wreckage and debris affected other areas around town. Fires occurred at apartments at 420 and 424 Franklin Street as well at the Larex Meyers home at 1075 California Street. The second story of the Pedro Cabajal house at 427 Franklin Street was severely damaged by fire. Newspaper accounts report that this part of town resembled a wartime battle scene. Miraculously no one was injured. More wreckage rained down on Pearson Automobile Company at 492 Castro Street. Salesman E. I. Swanson and customer, Phillip Seaton, ducked for cover inside one of the cars as falling metal and shrapnel struck several other cars. As the editorial for the February 4th edition of the Mountain View Register Leader pointed out, the plane crash could have been a true catastrophe as the accident occurred near a very congested area of town. Students and faculty of Mountain View High, Dana Street School or the Mountain View Academy could have been victims of the disaster. The merchants and shoppers of downtown Castro Street also escaped without incident. The editorial also pays tribute to Capt. Mulvehill, a young man of 32 and the father of four children. February 1, 1957 was a day of miracles and a day of tragedy for Mountain View. A site at the corner of Villa and Franklin Streets has been selected for the new police headquarters building. STREET TALK Do you have questions or information about Mountain View's street names? Please contact the Newsletter Editor. Eunice, Franklin and Sleeper Avenues are named after members of the early Sleeper family. Fran Sleeper (1822-1872) and Eunice Sleeper (1814-1901) owned several hundred acres running from El Camino Real at Grant south to include the above named roads. The Sleepers came from Boston in the early 1850s. Mr. Sleeper was a Santa Clara County Supervisor from 1864 to 1868. Frank P. Beverly, Justice of the Peace in Mountain View for many years, was raised by his aunt, Mrs. Sleeper. The 1926 directory shows that Alfred Wilcox and a Max Wohlberg both lived on that Avenue. Those names and that avenue do not appear in the 1930 directory.
