MAY, 2001 NIVHA PACE 2 y BY KATHLEEN LOWE OWEN For many years Mountain View was the home of many canneries and food processing plants. One of those plants was known locally as the "pickle works". It was located at the corner of Franklin and Villa Streets. The first of several "pickle works" buildings was constructed in 1915 for the California Supply Company, a San Francisco canning firm. The plant was expanded throughout the 1920s until it became on of the largest employers in Mountain View during the period between the world wars. California Conserving Company and Hunt Foods, Inc. also owned and operated the "pickle works" during it 47 years in Mountain View. California Conserving Company bought the plant in the 1940s and Hunt Floods Inc. was operating the plant by 1950. At one time more than 200 persons were employed during the peak season, which was June through September. At times there were as many as 30 year-round employees who maintained the property and equipment used in making pickles. In later years fewer individuals were employed because cucumbers were sorted at locations other than Mountain View. Many of the fall time employees performed such specialized jobs as barrel making or coopering. Most of the tomatoes and cucumbers processed during the 1920s and 1930s were grown on the Holthouse and Thompson ranches, which are now the site of Lockheed's Sunnyvale facility. Each year cucumbers were delivered directly to the factory and then prepared into various pickle products. These were placed in salt brine for up to three months. The pickles were brined in 5000-gallon wooden vats before being transferred to 500+ pound barrels. The barrels were shipped to other facilities where the pickles were bottled: Between 50 and 100 barrels were produced each day. Until the 1950s the plant also processed tomato catsup. Residents in Mountain View always knew when the tomatoes were in — steam rising from the cooking house at the plant carried the aroma all over town! Like the pickles, the catsup was either sold in bulk or shipped to other facilities for bottling. Chasuk — Born June 19, 1923, died July 29, 2000. Beloved husband of Dolores Chasuk for 53 years. Survived by children Annette, Suzanne, Tom, John, Robert, Patricia, Margaret and Jeanette, 15 grandchildren and a sister. Born in Alabama, Mr. Chasuk served in the Navy in World War II. He attended San Jose State and University of Santa Clara Law School. In 1966 he was admitted to practice law before the U.S. Supreme Court, where he successfully argued a landmark case on eminent domain. Mr Chasuk served for 25 years on the Board of Trustees of the Foothill-DeAnza Community College District. He was a member of Rotary, Catholic Social Services, Knights of Columbus. He was the Mountain View Citizen of the Year for 1966. A Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association. Mathilde Moore — 83, died August 5, 2000 in Mountain View. Wife of the late Hon. Warren C. Moore (1989). Mother Anita Moore Chiles of Atherton and the James B. Foster. Sister of Fernando F. Herrero of Modesto and Trudi Odbert of San Jose. A native of San Francisco. Virginia Ralston — Born February 19, 1923 in San Mateo, died July 9, 2000 in Windsor, CA. Wife for 58 years if Robert Ralston. The family home from 1943 to 1999 was on Sleeper Avenue. Interests were in the Children's Health Council, Scouts, the Mountain View Woman's Club and the DAV Auxiliary. She was a Forest Service Volunteer and a member of the Mountain View Historical Association. Joseph A. Reginato — Born Jan 30, 1917 in Delta, died September 20, 2000, in Menlo Park. Member of the only undefeated football team in San Jose State University history.Served in the South Pacific with the Marines during World War II and retired from the Marine Corps Reserve as a Lieutenant Colonel in 1977. Survived by his wife of 58 years, Marion, son James, daughter Janet Reginato Holmes, brother John and five grandchildren. DON'T FORGET TO VOTE! Arrada had become incensed after hearing he had been called a cattle thief by King's son and threatened to kill both father and son. Three days later Arrada was killed when he rode by the hotel. There were no witnesses to what was said just before the shooting. The father was arrested and admitted to the killing and the Coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide. King asked for a trial to clear his name but the Grand Jury dismissed the case. In the meantime, the well-liked King was elected Justice of the Peace by a large majority vote. White men received $1.50 a day, $1.00 if with board. Chinese and Japanese boarded themselves and got $1.15 — $1.25. Many families set up tents in the orchards and the entire family would work. Children were paid by the box. Duke, the St. Bernard belonging to William Costello, made his Thanksgiving dinner on neighbor Merriman's prize Jersey cow. Witnesses stated that the plane circled and landed at Moffett but authorities at the field said that no plane carrying that kind of bomb was in the air at the time of the accident. PAGE 4 \•,/ \awl CHESTER AWALT BY CAROL FISCHER Await High School (present-day Mountain View High School), was named after a remarkable gentleman, Chester Await. Mr Await was outstanding for many reasons; he served as trustee on the high school board for almost four decades (with two brief interludes), he was station master at the Southern Pacific depot, he worked for the Bank of America, served as City Treasurer, was a charter member of the Mountain View Kiwanis, named Mountain View's Citizen of the Year in 1954, and was father of three and the grandfather of eight! By all accounts, he was a gentle, smiling man who supported local sporting events, loved children and was obviously devoted to his community. Mr. Await was born in Hanford, California on January 5, 1883. His family moved to Santa Cruz where graduated from Santa Cruz High School. He received a scholarship to the University of California, where he received his B.S. from the College of Commerce in 1907. Mr. Await continued to be loyal to the Cal Bears his entire life. In 1912, Mr. Await was named Southern Pacific station agent for Mountain View. He and his family actually lived on the second floor of the depot for several years. Mr. Await is quoted as saying that his three children, Patricia, Doris and Robert, were the envy of their friends because they lived amidst all the excitement, hustle and bustle associated with a busy train station. One of Mr. Awalt's scariest memories occurred when he witnessed a shoot-out in 1915. Two men had robbed a San Jose tavern of $38.50, commandeered a San Francisco-bound train where they held the passengers and engineers captive. The engineer was able to brake in Mountain View where the robbers were met by waiting police who opened fire. One of the thugs was killed and the other wounded. It was while he was station agent that Chester Await decided to run for the school board. By some fluke, he was elected to both boards — the elementary and high school boards. He served on the elementary board for five years but remained as a high school trustee for nearly 40 years. One of his happiest moments was handing out diplomas to his three NOVEMBER, 2000 MVHA children and to two of his grandchildren. Another proud occasion happened when the school board named the new high school in his honor in 1961. Chester Awalt was present at the groundbreaking ceremonies of all three high schools, Mountain View High (on Castro Street), Los Altos High and Await High. After leaving their quarters above the depot, Chester and Estella moved to their home at 630 Bailey Avenue (now Shoreline Blvd.) Where they were often visited by former students. The couple continued to be interested in local schools long after Mr. Awalt's retirement. They also enjoyed attending Stanford football games — although Chester always wore his blue Cal necktie! Mrs. Await died in 1972 and Chester in 1975. Several generations of fortunate Mountain View students have been touched by Chester Awalt's years of service and dedication. Recently, the Mountain View History Center has been given some Await High School yearbooks. The Center has a complete set of Mountain View High School yearbooks and would to have such a collection for Await High. If any readers are thinking of tossing their copies, please donate them to the Mountain View History Center instead of the Goodwill! AUGUST 2000 MVHA PAGE 1 MANCINI'S TOWER BY CANDACE BOWERS An eye-catching landmark once stood at the gateway to downtown Mountain View. Ugo Mancini's Chrysler dealership, with its 52-foot tower, occupied the corner of El Camino and Castro Street. The Mancini Motors tower is still instantly recognizable in old street scenes of the 1940s, 50s, and 60s. A native of Italy, Mancini had been in this country 10 years when he opened a Nash dealership in Mountain View in 1921. In 1933, he changed to selling Chryslers. Coincidentally, the Chrysler Corporation was staging an exhibit at the 1939 World's Fair at Treasure Island. By that time, Mancini was ready to build new business offices at a different location, and arranged to buy the materials of the former Chrysler exhibit. He paid $3000 for the entire exhibit, then sold some unwanted material for that same purchase price. That money was used to buy the land at the corner of El Camino and Castro Street (the current site of Home Savings.) To further recoup his expenses, Mancini was able to sell part of his plot of land to another company, for use as a service station. The main expense was therefor the transportation of the remains of the Chrysler exhibit from Treasure Island, across the Bay Bridge to Mountain View. The move cost Mancini about $2000. The stainless steel tower weighed in at 20 tons and literally stopped traffic as it traveled across the bridge in the middle of the night. The tower, topped by a globe that was 9 feet in diameter, was a Mountain View landmark from 1940 until the early 1970s. Mancini AUGUST 20u0 relocated his business to Sunnyvale in April of 1971, leaving behind the tower that featured his name running vertically down its length. The site was eventually sold to Home Savings in 1974, and subsequently demolished. EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE MEETING The Executive Committee of the Mountain View Historical Association met June 29, 2000. A program of spelling matches, musical numbers and recitations took place on the last afternoon. Population of Santa Clara County is estimated to be 31,000 with 8,997 registered voters. "The Fourth of July was honored in a very appropriate manner. S.P. Taylor made the valley ring with the sound of the old mountain cannon, which, for the last twenty years has been used on the occasion of waking up the citizens of Mountain View." Threshing is over and more than 40,000 sacks of wheat and barley are now stored in the railroad company warehouse at Mountain View Station. Mountain View is in "receipt of a butcher shop, a harness shop, and Chinese wash house, within the past two weeks." 100 Years Ago (1900): Pierre Klein, Montebello district vineyardist and winemaker, received a gold medal for his exhibit of wines at the Paris Exposition. (On display at the Mountain View History Center.) The brickyard was supplying bricks for the new buildings at Stanford University as it had done for the original buildings. Only a quarter of a mile from the train station, the yard's brick clay is said to be the finest in California. An explosion in a shed at the rear of the Weilheimer General Store destroyed the shed, a barn and many windows in nearby structures. A hole had been punched in a 25-pound can of blasting powder, a fuse inserted and lit. Much of the downtown could have been destroyed if other powder, dynamite, gasoline and coal oil in the shed had caught fire or exploded. A young feeble-minded teen-ager was immediately suspected and confessed. Sometime in the past the store had refused him credit. The Bank of Mountain View opened for business on AuGuST 2000 MVHA September 12, in its brick mission-style building on Castro Street. (This was the first bank in the town Railway Express later occupied the Building.) 75 Years Ago (1925): Glen Theatre showed "The Lighthouse By The Sea" staring Rin Tin Tin, the wonder dog. State Highway Garage, Renaldi and Mancini proprietors, has outgrown its building. Ugo Mancini has purchased property at El Camino and Ehrhorn Avenue where he will have a showroom built for Nash auto sales, while Mr. Renaldi will remain at the present location. Miss Martha Job, who has been on furlough from her position with the Y.W.C. A. in China, was honored at a reception at the Baptist Church. Property owners have petitioned for a road to run from the Bubb and Glen pumping plants on Grant Road to the highway opposite Calderon Avenue. This would shorten the distance into town for residents along Grant Road. During July and August the Baptist, Methodist, Adventist and Presbyterian Churches were holding union services on Sunday evenings. Anway Undertaking Company has purchased the office and residence property of Dr. A.H. MacFarlane, at 340 Castro, and will transform it into a mortuary. Some residents protested, but as the area was already designated a business district Mr. Anway received a permit. Olin W. Tait was issued a season ticket to the new Kingsport Plunge for his winning slogan to be used in advertising - "The King Sport at Kingsport." (Does anyone have pictures of this salt water plunge at the end Whisman Road?) Mrs Gonzales of Santa Clara had her hair bobbed. Her husband objected and threw her out of their house and sued for a divorce. The judge granted it, ruling that a "woman past middle age should not bob her hair without her husband's consent." Six new houses are under construction and nine families are already living on Loreto Street, in the new Palmita Park subdivision. PAGE 4 50 Years Ago (1950): Service station operators expected the price of gasoline to go up two cents a gallon. At present, ethyl costs 260 a gallon and regular sells for 240 Headlines told of North Korean troops crossing the 38'h parallel toward Seoul. Jim Thomas, Superintendent of Public Works, was given a new title of City Administrator. He will still have the same responsibilities - all public works departments, personnel administration and most fiscal matters. The local Greyhound bus depot, at 216 Castro for twenty years, has opened up the street at 374 Castro. According to manager John Parmelee, over 600 passengers a day go through this station. Receiving prizes at the State Fair were Frank Takamoto for chrysanthemums and Mountain View Greenhouse, on Bailey Avenue, for carnations. County Floral winners were Leonard Oku, Yoshio Mishimoto and G. Imamura. Mrs. Jeannie Julian Holtzclaw won recognition for her zinnias. Young Adventist men were urged to sign up for a Cadet Medical Corps Training course at Mountain View Academy. A new auditorium at the school has been named for Principal C.H. Baker. He is leaving to become head of the Academy at Loma Linda. Foster's Old Fashion Freeze celebrated its first anniversary in Mountain View on August 4. Hunt Foods, Inc., estimates that 1200 tons of cucumbers will be processed into pickles this season by the 27 workers employed in the plant in downtown Mountain View. Kiwanis Club introduced plans for a Scout Center to be built on a three-acre site off Leksich Avenue. Money for land and buildings are to be raised by public subscription. Membership in Mountain View scouts totals over 500 — Cubs, Brownies, Boy Scouts, Girl Scouts, Mariners, Sea and Air Scouts August 4, was the date for the grand opening of Monte Vista Drive-in Theatre on Grant Road near El Camino, with the largest screen on the peninsula and spaces for 825 cars STREET TALK FROM BARBARA KINCHEN The May Street Talk Puzzler was: For whom was Calderon Avenue named? Mercedes Castro, sister of Crisanto Castro, married Andres Calderon in 1856. In 1883 the Castro and Calderon families sold about 120 acres to A.M. Stoddard, who then laid out a road from the railroad tracks to Church Street with five acre lots on each side. At first the road was called Stoddard, but by 1886 it was Calderon Avenue and said to have been as smooth and level as a race track. And this leads to the November Street Talk Puzzler — To the west of town there was also a Calderon Road. This caused much confusion until 1948 when the Board of Supervisors approved a name change What was the name selected? ELMER STRICKLETT BY CAROL FISCHER "Take me out to the ballgame, take me out to the crowd, buy me some . .. " Ah, spring is in the air and to many sports fans that means baseball. This year is particularly exciting for Bay Area baseball fans with the opening of PacBell Park, the new Giants stadium in San Francisco. For local enthusiasts, a little known baseball trivia fact revolves around Mountain View resident Elmer Stricklett who is credited with being the father of the spitball. A spitball, now illegal, is a pitch in which saliva is surreptitiously applied to one part of the ball, so as to make it break or swerve unpredictably. Elmer Stricklett was born in Glasco Kansas on August 29, 1876. He made his major league pitching debut for the Chicago White Sox in 1904 but was traded to the Brooklyn Dodgers the following year. He played with that team until 1907. Elmer five feet six inches, weighed 140 pounds and pitched and batted right handed. His career average ERA (earned run average) was 2.84. Elmer introduced the overhand spitball —diiring a Dodgers/Giants game on May 29, 1905. He taught the pitch to "Big Ed" Walsh of the Chicago White Sox who went on to become one of the best spitballers in all of baseball. How is Elmer Stricklett related to Mountain View? He married a local girl, Mabel Gates. Mabel's parents, Mary Julia Burk and Benjamin Gates, came to Mountain View in 1885 when Mabel was eight years old. The family settled into a home on Calderon Avenue. Mrs. Gates was a writer of local history. She wrote one of the first histories of the area in 1895 as well as articles for the Mountain View Register Leader on local Indians, the various landings on the bay, and about such prominent families as the Castros and the Estradas. Benjamin Gates was believed to have been one of the first orchardists in the area. Mabel Stricklett's uncle, Dr. Frederick Burk (or Burke) was the president of the State Normal School in San Francisco (now San Francisco State University) for many years. In 1912, Elmer Stricklett tried to make a pitching comeback but never made it back to the big leagues. MAY, 2000 MVHA PAGE 2 He and Mabel retired to Santa Cruz where he died in 1964 and she in 1968. Visitors to the Mountain View History Center can see a picture of Elmer Stricklett in his 1906 Brooklyn Dodgers uniform. There are also photographs ofMabel Gates Stricklett and her parents, Mary Julia and Benjamin Gates in the collection. Perhaps one can even catch a whiff of".. . peanuts and Cracker Jacks . . . STREET TALK FROM BARBARA KINCHEN The February Street Talk Puzzler was: Where is Eldora Drive, and for whom was it named? Well, it's off Calderon between Church and Dana. Eldora Freeman married Jack McCarty, whose parents had bought land on Calderon Avenue in 1885. Jack was a surveyor and Eldora was a teacher. Subdivision of their land began in 1940 and two streets carry on their names: Eldora Drive and McCarty Avenue. And this leads to the May Street Talk Puzzler —For whom was Calderon Avenue named? MAY, 2000 MVHA PAGE 4 MOUNTAIN VIEW CITY COUNCIL ACTIONS OF SPECIAL INTEREST ADOBE RESTORATION On January 11,2000 the Mountain View City Council approved the plans and specifications for the Adobe Building Restoration and authorized staffto advertise for bids. The restoration will include structural and seismic improvements to bring the building into code compliance, concealed heating, ventilation, power and communications, renovated kitchen, and retrofitting of the fireplace. A perimeter wall, designed to appear as the original adobe wall will be built. The architectural consultant has prepared documentation to upgrade the Adobe Building's historic designation and nominate it to the National Register of Historic Places. If all goes according to plan, the City will award the construction contract in April, work will commence in May, and should be completed in January, 2001 SHOCKLEY SEMICONDUCTOR COMMEMORATIVE MARKER On April 11, 2000 the Mountain View City Council approved the placement of a commemorative marker recognizing the historical significance of the Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory located at 391 South San Antonio Road. The building, know as the barn to those who worked there is the point of origin for the commercial transistor, and therefore a cornerstone of modern computer technology. PIONEER PARK IRRIGATION AND GROUNDS IMPROVEMENTS. Pioneer Memorial Park, located off Church Street between Franklin and Castro is an oasis in the midst of downtown Mountain View. It was once the primary cemetery for Mountain View, and the remains of many of the city's pioneering residents are still buried there. Irrigation and Grounds Improvements are required, and the Council approved the work on April 11, 2000. The Council required assurances that the work not disturb the remains. The council also asked that additional benches be included in the park. HOSPITALITY! A substantial part of the collection is that of the Mountain View Historical Association. Several Association members regularly volunteer here. The following has been abstracted from the April 2000, vol.45 no .4, of the Newsletter of the Santa Clara County Historical and Genealogical Society, by Peggy Rossi. The Mountain View Historical Association in conjunction with the Mountain View Public Library, maintains a local history reading room and local exhibits. The History Center is located at the Mountain View Public Library, 585 Franklin St. The center is open on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday from 1 PM to 5 PM.. Whether you have family from Mountain View or not, this center is worth a visit, not only to have a chance to see the beautiful new Mountain View library but to look at the historical exhibits and photographs For those whose families hail from Mountain View, there is a wealth of information to be found here. Among the resources here are: microfilm of Mountain View newspapers (such as the Mountain View Register and the Leader) dating from 1903 into the 1960s, (found in the main library collection); Assessment Rolls from 1903-1930s; Indexes to Voter Precinct Registers, early registers ofbusiness licenses (pre-1930), and city directories A particular treasure is the Winter's Collection. Mildred Winter, a retired history professor from San Jose State University, had gathered volumes of information in preparation for the publication ofa book on the history of Mountain View. Unfortunately, she passed away before the book could be published. However all her notes are available in binders and include material from 1849 to 1929, such as clippings, probate and deed extracts. MAY, 2000 There are extensive versicle files with a large collection of photographs and clippings. The photographs are all being scanned at this time so they will be available to researchers via computer. This process is allowing the Association the opportunity to make sure each photograph is identified and dated when that information is available. This is an excellent collection, in an attractive and comfortable setting and well worth a visit, especially if your family lived in Mountain View. MVHA 77Re4,44.91V 04.4. PAGE 6

WHERE IT ALL STARTED SILICON VALLEY 8c THE BARN In 1947 William Shockley, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain developed the transistor, the basic device for the semiconductor industry. They were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for this work In 1955 Shockley moved to Palo Alto and recruited a team of engineers and scientists to work for a new company, Shockley Semiconductor. Shockley opened his research and manufacturing facility in a building located at 391 San Antonio Road in Mountain View, adjacent to the San Antonio Mall. To those who worked there, the building was known as "The Barn" . Shockley's vision was of the commercial production of transistors. He recognized the technical superiority, for commercial purposes, of silicon as the semiconductor material for the fabrication of transistors. One group of Shockley Semiconductor engineers left to form Fairchild Semiconductor, the birthplace of the integrated circuit. Nearly every semiconductor and integrated circuit company in the Bay area can likewise trace its origins to The Barn at 391 San Antonio. William Shockley may not have been a very nice human being, but honoring William Shockley the man would not be the primary objective in memorializing the barn. Rather, it would be marking the location where a very significant turn in the direction of industrialized society took place. There is a garage in Palo Alto that is properly regarded as a memorial to the beginnings of the modern commercial electronics industry. The barn is an equally important memorial to that other leg of modern technology, the commercial transistor. We should do everything we can to assist the City of Mountain View in recognizing this important historical site FEBRUARY, 2000 M VHA PAGE 5 RENGSTORFF HOUSE 1"-- — • ••• • • : i f : . • ••;.:11••" ib .y .0•4...••^,...• • • "1...• • Thg RevaaAti We". MONDAY Much of the early history of nineteenth century California revolves around development of the railroads Although they are alternately seen as either the facilitator of modern commerce or as the octopus which swallowed the land and wealth of the state, no one can deny the impact of the iron horse on the nation, the state, and even on our own locality. Mountain View, occupying an important position almost midway between San Francisco and Jose, had its own unique role in California railroad history and one which deserves to be remembered In an agricultural area like Santa Clara Valley, the problem of delivering produce to market has always been of pnmary importance While water transport was available from Alviso and other ports along the bay, the problem of getting the crops to the ships remained, and the additional time required for loading and unloading hade railroad service seem even more attractive. Yet railroad construction required a great deal of initial capital, and even in a rich state like California it was not always easy to come up with the necessary cash. Even so, it was not surprising that some of the movers and shakers of the growing city of San Jose began to think of the potential profit of such an endeavor. In 1851, Davis Divine, a judge in San Jose began to raise money for the construction of a San Jose to San Francisco railroad service. While the project was ultimately stillborn ( in spite of the interest expressed in it by the Rothschild family ), this did not discourage Divine. A year later he was back with anew company, under the grandiose title "Pacific and Atlantic Rail Road," and even began surveying the route north, part of which ran through property owned by the Castro family. Divine was soon pushed out of the project by bigger investors, but even though more capital became available, the railroad idea was again abandoned. It was not until 1860 that a railroad route became a serious possibility once again. A professional promoter named Peter Donahue began work on a new line, the San Francisco and San Jose Railroad, and with considerable skill he began amassing the money, men and materials to make the steel highway a reality. By October 1863, this new line offered service from San Francisco to Mayfield (Palo Alto), with connecting stage service the remainder of the way into San Jose. The inaugural journey was made by city officials of San Francisco, who were seated on open flatcars and were whisked along at an amazing speed of nearly sixty miles an hour! On the 17th of that same month, a more elaborate transit was made with nearly four hundred passengers, including Governor Stanford and Governor Gibbs of Oregon. The question remains whether the railroad proceeded only as far as Palo Alto (coincidentally the boundary of Castro property) only due to delays in construction, or whether it experienced problems gaining right-of-way over that family's land. The historical record seems to be unclear on this point. The Castro family was certainly aware of railroad practices which legally "stole" land that could not be otherwise be obtained, yet they no doubt also recognized the potential good which railroad service might bring. What is known is that by January 1864, the San Francisco and San Jose Railroad Company commenced service all the way into San Jose itself, and a deed was signed August 20 of that same year by Crisanto Castro and his mother giving right of way for a payment of $500. Along with the cash settlement, the railroad was also required to construct and maintain a station near the Castro home (located at Alma and Rengstorff Avenues) at which trains would stop twice a day, and allow any member of that family to stop any local train merely by flagging it down as long as the railroad was in existence. It is also believed that the railroad was required to build a spur line which led right up to the family's hay barn. Interestingly, this deed was signed some seven months after track was laid across their property, and it has been speculated that this delay was because the Castro's were waiting to see if the railroad would hold up their end of the bargain! Whatever the exact nature of the agreement, right of way was granted, and Saturday, January 16, 1864, nearly two thousand people crowded into six coaches and a number of cattle and box cars on two different trains for the first regular service from San Francisco to San Jose proper. At 1:30 P.M. this merry excursion ended at the San Joses' depot to the roar of the crowd and the tunes of a brass band in a celebration which was remembered by people all along the route for many years. Like so many other aspects of our local history, the study of the role of the railroads is one which offers many fascinating stories and much room for future research. Each day we listen and watch as trains rush through the city, but how often do we wonder how it all came about? Perhaps this brief introduction will serve to make us all stop once in a while and think of all those people, scoundrels and dreamers' alike, who NOVEMBER, 1999 MVHA PAGE 2 helped bring the steel rails to Mountain View. OLD NEWSPAPER ITEMS COMPILED BY BARBARA KINCHEN 100 Years Ago (1899): San Jose's YMCA building, 82 N 2" Street, was purchased by funds from the Sleeper Trust and dedicated as Sleeper Hall, headquarters for the Spiritualist Union of San Jose. Frank and Eunice (Beverly) Sleeper had lived in Mountain View since 1851 and Mr. Sleeper had served on the County Board of Supervisors. They were both Spiritualists and after his death in 1872, she established a trust with all proceeds, except a small yearly sum for her living expenses, to support their beliefs. Dedication ceremonies for Sleeper Hall were November 26, 1899, Mrs. Sleeper's 85th birthday. Several years later her funeral services were held there also, after which she was buried in Mountain View, as were her husband and young daughter. Sleeper, Eunice and Franklin Avenues are part of former Sleeper properties. 75 Years Ago (1924): W.C.T.U. ladies chose an individual's name for the local branch and honored a charter member, Mary Julia Gates of Calderon Avenue, for her years of loyalty and devoted service. More than 26 hundred tons of freight were handled by South Shore Port in October. The Company operated one steamer and six trucks and had contracted for a second ship to cost $40,000. California's only Deciduous Fruit Research and Experimental Station is located in Mountain View. The 10th Annual Prune and Apricot Exposition featured an "Illuminated Street Parade" and Tom Dale's Riders of the Gray Sage. Fred Jarvis was appointed to the police force as traffic officer. Another part of his job was as inspector of new sidewalks and curbs Minto Company advertized lots on Ehrhorn Avenue at $8.00 per front foot. Dr. D.E.Davenport was in charge of the Mountain View Hospital and Sanitarium on the "Highway near the Castro Entrance." He had installed a c"chlorine chamber for treatment of respiratory disorders." California Supply Company, commonly called the Pickle Factory, bought more land on Franklin Street on which to build a large factory for making dill pickles. The company located here in 1917. Fruit cake and mince pies for holiday dinners were available at Hirschbek Bakery, 168 Castro Street. 50 Years Ago (1949): The minimum wage went from 400 per hour to 750 Walt Keene sold the Daily Register, which he had owned since 1937, to Mr. and Mrs. Sutton Christian. A weekend of events was planned for the 3 annual Mexican Fiesta of Guadalupe The Crab Kettle, 2011 El Camino, sold three crabs for $1.00 and on Escuela Avenue William Joseph had 30 pound lugs of canning tomatoes for 500 Halloween events included a Spook Parade for costumed children which was sponsored by Recreation Department and Highway School P.T A., Dance Party at Veterans of Foreign Wars Hall on Moffett Boulevard and the theater had vaudeville acts on stage and The Spider Woman, with Bella Lugosi, on screen Anthony Radisich and Ivan Vojvoda organized Anrad's Travelers, a semi-professional basketball team. Whisman District's new Crittenden School held an open house and celebrated the 89th birthday of Albert Crittenden, for whom the school is named He was in the first class of the original Whisman School when NOVEMBER, 1999 MVHA PAGE 3 it was built in 1871 New Businesses in town included Mary Ann Dress Shop at 819 Villa, Diaz & Sons Shoe Store at 200 Castro, Craig Furniture, El Camino at Ehrhorn, Sue Berry Salon and Romero's Florist Shop in the 800 blocks of Castro. Dana Washette, Mountain View Cycle and Toy shop and J. Bennett Company Stationers were all new on Dana Street. After ten years at Castro and Dana, J.C. Penney moved into a new building at 274 Castro. After occupying three temporary locations the past year, Chamber of Commerce moved into new headquarters on Castro at Mercy, built from money willed by Mary Rose Sladlcy. Pre-colored oleomargarine could be sold for the first time on October 1. Until this time it was white and you added yellow coloring for it to resemble butter. 25 Years Ago (1974): Victor Calvo was sworn in as Democratic Assemblyman for the new 21' district. Until November 30, he served on the Santa Clara County Board of Supervisors and previously was a Mountain View councilman and mayor. The Fire Department wound up its Centennial Celebration by placing a time capsule at Fire Station Four, 231 Whisman Road It is to be opened in 1999. After standing in line at a local bank, a young man said to the teller, "Oh, I left it in the car." He reappeared a few moments later and showed the young lady a card with the word gun written on it. He got away with an undisclosed amount of cash in a late model convertible. Headlines read "Forgetful Bandit Comes Back." From Lisetta Jansen Mieth Challen: Mrs. Lisetta Jansen Mieth Challen, of Capitola, died this year and willed our Association a beautiful, large, ornate and valuable wardrobe or armoire. Mrs Challen was a great grand-daughter of Christopher Conrad Stierlin (1826-1900) and Clara Laux Stierlin (1834-1904). In 1851 Mr. Stierlin settled in the area later known as Old Mountain View. In 1864 he bought a large ranch closer to the bay on a road later named for him, Stierlin Road. The property and large were near present Shoreline Boulevard (formerly Stierlin Road), 101 Highway and L'Avenida. The Rengstorff family became their neighbors to the north. Wally Erichsen arranged for the armoire to be moved to Mountain View and has been in contact with one of the executors who has promised to share information and pictures from boxes found in Mrs. Challen's home We hope to find some definite proof that the armoire was once part of the Mountain View household of Mr. and Mrs. C.C. Stierlin. NOVEMBER, 1999 14#1VHA PAGE 4 IN COMMEMORATION Joseph Phillip Cusimano — Age 82, died July 17, 1999. Beloved husband of Margaret Cusimano (formerly Margaret Jory) and the late Emma Sue Cusimano of 49 years. Survived by children Matthew, Joseph, Sherri and Peter Cusimano and by numerous nieces, nephews and friends. Resident of San Jose since 1919 and of Mountain View since 1957. Graduate of San Jose High School, San Jose State College, California College of Mortuary Sciences. Retired Major of the U.S. Army (Medical Corps), veteran of WWII (Battle of the Bulge). 22 years in the Army Reserves. Mr. Cusimano was a Mountain View City Council member from 1968 to 1976 and served as Mayor in 1974. A member of the American Legion, Eagles and the Elks. Founder and First President of the Sierra Club of Mtn. View. A member of numerous other social, religious and service organizations. Past President of the Chamber of Commerce and Citizen of the Year in 1976. Founder (with Sue Cusimano) of the Cusimano Family Colonial Mortuary, established in 1957. Joseph Phillip Cusimano was also a member of the Mountain View Historical Association. Reynolds W. Camp — Age 81, died August 20, 1999. Born in Palo Alto. Married Juanita Murdock in June, 1942. Survived by his wife, two sons, Dennis and David, daughter Elaine, and seven grandchildren. Mr. Camp graduated from Mountain View High School and attended Menlo College and Stanford University. He graduated from UCLA in 1941 and went on to serve as a flight instructor in the US Army Air Corps during WWII. Mr. Camp was self-employed as a real estate and insurance broker until his retirement in 1972. Mr. Camp was a founder and President of the Mtn. View Board of Realtors. Mr. Camp served on the Mtn, View Planning Commission and was Mtn. View Citizen of the Year in 1964. Reynolds W. Camp was a Life Member of the Mountain View Historical Association. Betty Nelson Fahs — Age 83, died July 29, 1999 in Mountain View. Widow of F. Robert Fahs. She is survived by her children Barbara Fahs and Beverly Shepherd, granddaughter Jennifer Sheperd, son-in-law Steve Sheperd and her cousin Frances B. Collins. Mrs. Fahs graduated Phi Beta Kappa from the University of Wisconsin and remained active in the Alpha Chi Omega Sorority. She was honored by the Mountain View-Los Altos Union High School Division as the Senior Student of the Year in 1997. Mrs. Fahs a regular volunteer in the History Center of the Mtn, View Public Library. AUGUST, 1999 PERIODS OF INDUSTRY FAMILY INDUSTRIES IN MOUNTAIN VIEW MAY, 1999 MEETING The Sunday, May 2, 1999, meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association was the second in the series on Periods of Industry in Mountain View. The program included two family enterprises: A presentation by Trudy Herrero Odbert about the Herrero family and Spanish Sausages, and a presentation by Mario Ambra and his sister Cathy Ambra, and described the production of Olive Oil. Trudy's father was born in Spain. Her parents were married in 1914, and had three children, all born in San Francisco. In 1921 they moved to Mountain View at the corner of what is now Shoreline and US 101. The family Spanish Sausage business was started on the ranch in 1930 in a 40 by 60 foot building with two rows of stainless steel tables. A sample sausage press was on display at the meeting. The sausage was smoked for two weeks and then delivered to customers in Mountain View, San Francisco, Sunnyvale and Oakland, In 1938 the family opened a store at the corner of View and El Camino. Trudy's father retired in 1962. Mario Ambra and his sister Cathy's grandparents were from Sicily and arrived in San Francisco in 1909, where he was employed as a carpenter, In 1923 they bought the property offRengstorff, near US 101. By 1933 they were in full olive oil production. The last production of olive oil was in 1993. The olive MVHA PAGE 1 trees were beaten to cause the fruit to drop to the ground. The fruit was then trucked, cleaned, dried, pulped and pressed. The oil was pumped to tanks and a separator, then filtered and bottled. 125 pounds of olives were required for each gallon. Olives sold for $120 per ton. Two very interesting and informative presentations. He will give us a progress report and tell us what we can do to help with the restoration You can help preserve -hist-iffy, and assist in making records accurate and complete During the Rengstorff House restoration artifacts and photographs helped accurately restore the building's architectural features AUGUST, 1999 Important pieces were received from people who removed them for preservation These donations were vital in completing details that enrich the House's historic and architectural integrity. Please share your photographs, artifacts, records or clear recollections of the Adobe Building. Of particularly interested are photographs, interior and exterior, in the period from the Adobe's construction in 1934 until 1954. Also in preparation is a timeline of the activities that occurred at the Adobe Building. Let us know what activities you participated in. Of interest are newsletters, notices or announcements for meetings or other events at the Adobe Building. Information, photographs, or personal recollections may either be donated to the Mountain View History Center at the Public Library or we can arrange to copy them. We can arrange to photograph artifacts not suitable for the History Center collections. With the approval of the City of Mountain View, librarians Michael Lapointe and Carol Fischer have been busy organizing all the photographs belonging to the Historical Association. Each photograph has been placed into archival sleeves and then organized into appropriate subject areas. The next step is to catalog and scan each photograph so that it will appear in the library's on-line catalog. Since this catalog is also accessible through the Internet, these photographs will be available for viewing worldwide! This project has been funded for two years. Eventually the library's photographs will receive the same organizing, cataloging and scanning as is being done with the Historical Association's collection. It was decided to begin with the Historical Association's photos because they are older and best capture the flavor of our city's heritage. The scanning process does not harm these precious photographs. They look very clear on the computer screen and can be zoomed in for a more detailed look. However the images do not print of a quality that can be used in books or papers. It is hoped that when people see the delightful images found in the Mountain View History Center, they will be enticed to come look at the real photograph and use the many resources of our collection A few of the images have been catalogued and scanned already. If you are interested in seeing them on your computer, here are the directions: Go to the library's catalog by typing in: library.ci.mtnview.ca.us 2. Click on "Search the Catalog" 3 Choose "Call Number" 4. Type in "pha" — this abbreviation stands for "photographs Historical Association" Because these photographs have been given full cataloging, they can be searched by such keywords as "baseball teams Mountain View" When all the photographs are cataloged, you will be able to search a person's name and a picture of that person will AUGUST, 1999 appear or perhaps a match will be made for their house or business Images of Castro Street, Moffett Field, schools, orchards and buildings are only a few of the photographs that will soon be available. HIGH-TECH TOOLS FOR HISTORICAL RESEARCH By Candace Bowers When one thinks of genealogical research, the image that probably comes to mind is that of intimidating stacks of musty, dusty books. Faced with that prospect, it can be difficult to know how to get started on your family history project Why not use the latest high-tech tools to help you on your way? The Internet can provide a wealth of genealogical information, and getting started might not be as difficult as you think A group of volunteers has created a huge, free website that serves as the ideal gateway to genealogical information on the Internet. The USGenWeb Project (http: www.usgenweb.org) is a comprehensive site that provides links to genealogical websites for all 50 states. Each state website is further broken down by county. In addition, USGenWeb sponsors several projects that help you with research that may span state or county lines. This includes an archive of public records; census data, and an ongoing project to transcribe tombstones. When you choose a state to research, you will find the name of that state's genealogical information coordinator. In turn, you will find a coordinator for each county. Please note that the coordinators are not able to do your family research for you, they are in charge of organizing the information you see on the website. Each county website provides links to a vast array of information to help you trace your "roots" For example, you may be able to locate volunteers who can do local "look-ups" for you, obituaries, biographies; a list of surnames and their current researchers, old maps, newspaper archives; and information on veterans and battlefields. You might find a forum where you may post inquires, and you might also be able to join an electronic mailing list, where you can communicate with other like-minded researchers via e-mail (Tip! You might meet some "locals" from your ancestors' home towns.) One feature that could be especially helpful in your research, is a listing of all cemeteries in a particular county or town • (Remember, each county's website has been compiled by local volunteers, so the level of information at each site will vary.) If you're lucky, you might find that the volunteers have gone so far as to walk the cemeteries and record the information on the tombstones If all this information still seems to overwhelm to you, the USGenWeb project has information to help beginning researchers get started PRIVATE NOTE On your Newsletter address label you will find a number following your name. ADOBE ARMORY FROM JOSEPH DE LA FUENTE The Adobe Building was the first and only armory in Mountain View. In April, 1949, the State of California leased the building to house the newly organized Battery B, 637th Field Artillery Battalion, California National Guard. The Battalion headquarters was located at 240 N. Second St. in San Jose. The unit was federally recognized on April 26, 1949. Capt. John S. Vai was the first battery commander. Vai was assistant manager of the Bank of America Joseph de la Fuente was the administrative assistant (NCO) and Robert R. Sullivan was the unit caretaker (Supply Sergeant) The two NCO's were full time technicians. The supply room was a small room on the left side of the entrance to the building It was reinforced with metal landing strips for the protection of the weapons, tools and clothing stored there The orderly room occupied the old pump building (razed in 1997). The building was known then as "The Armory" and/or "The Adobe Shack" The Mountain View High School Teen Club used to hold Friday and Saturday night dances there and called it "The Eagle Shack." The active members of the Battery were mostly from Mountain View, Los Altos, Palo Alto and Menlo Park. The unit participated in Mountain View's Centennial parade in 1949. In January, 1950 the unit was alerted by the Governor of California to report to the Armory for standby alert on the flooding of Alviso. In July of 1953 Battery B, 637th Field Artillery was relocated to the armory at 251 W. Hedding St. in San Jose. With that the city of Mountain View MAY, 1999 MVHA PAGE 5 lost its one and only National Guard Unit. Brown, III - Editor • .-411.414" ne• C.1461.14.• &alit ria PERIODS OF INDUSTRY AGRICULTURE IN MOUNTAIN VIEW FEBRUARY, 1999, MEETING The Sunday, February 7, 1999, regular quarterly meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association will begin a series on Periods of Industry in Mountain View. In the early part of the twentieth century, Mountain View was the heart of a thriving agricultural area. Fertile soil and adequate water made for the growing of premium fruits and vegetables. The presence of packing, icing and loading facilities for the shipping of agricultural products made Mountain View the natural center of the area. The heyday of the Agricultural Period was from the beginning of the century up through World War II. The February 7 program will be a panel discussion moderated by Wally Erichsen John Viscovich will discuss orchards and cherry farming, Leo Kalcic will describe the events in a year of an apricot grower, and Ralph Faravelli will cover the truck farming activities of his family. They will all undoubtedly reminisce about some of the more memorable experiences in the life of local farmers including some that will be amusing, revealing and interesting. After the program, plan on joining your friends and acquaintances for refreshments and good conversation WHERE IT ALL STARTED SILICON VALLEY & THE BARN NOVEMBER, 1998, MEETING Our speaker at the November, 1998 meeting was Consulting Engineer Jacques Beaudouin, one of the engineers and scientists present at the birth of Silicon In 1947 William Shockley, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain developed the transistor, the basic device for the semiconductor industry. They were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for this work. In 1955 Shockley moved to Palo Alto and recruited a team of engineers and scientists to work for a new company, Shockley Semiconductor. Shockley opened his research and manufacturing facility in a building located at 391 San Antonio Road in Mountain View, adjacent to the San Antonio Mall. To those who worked there, the building was known as "The Barn". Shockley's vision was of the commercial production transistors. He recognized the technical superiority, for commercial purposes, of silicon as the semiconductor material of choice for the fabrication of transistors. One group of Shockley Semiconductor engineers left to form Fairchild Semiconductor, the birthplace of the integrated circuit. Nearly every semiconductor and integrated circuit company in the Bay area can likewise trace its origins to The Barn at 391 San • FEBRUARY, 1999 MVHA PAGE 1 Antonio The Electronics Industry, which was well established in the Bay Area, and two great universities provided a pool of great talent which Shockley was initially able to organize and direct Your automobile, your electronic coffee maker, your cellular phone, your home computer, your television set, would all be impossible in their present form without the semiconductor devices and integrated circuits which stem from work begun at The Barn. Without The Barn the area might well be known as electron gulch, but Silicon Valley, with its tens of thousands of skilled workers would be vastly different. The Mountain View Historical Association has been asked by the Mountain View City Council to consider jointly sponsoring some sort of historical marking for The Barn. Our November speaker, Consulting Engineer Jacques Beaudouin, worked for several years with William Shockley at The Barn, and has been a long time advocate for memorializing the structure The November meeting was an opportunity to gain some insight into the origins of what may be the most profound revolution of modern times. William Shockley may not have 1)-e-en a very nice human being, but honoring William Shockley the man would not be the primary objective in memorializing The Barn Rather, it would be marking the location where a very significant turn in the direction of industrialized society took place There is a garage in Palo Alto that is properly regarded as a memorial to the beginnings of the modern commercial electronics industry. The Barn is an equally important memorial to that other leg of modern technology, the commercial transistor. As an association created to record and remember the significant events in the Mountain View area, the Mountain View Historical Association should do everything we can to assist the City Council in recognizing this important historical site. IN COMMEMORATION James Jackson Dale. Jr. — of Nicolaus, CA, died at age 85, October 27, 1998. Born in Mountain View in 1913, a descendant of Edward Dale, who came to this area in 1850, and the son of the late James J. Dale and Eleanor (Carter) Dale. Eleanor Dale was a founder and the first President of the Mountain View Historical Association. Preceded in death by his wife Francie and sisters Dorothy Arnold and Claire Stevenson. Survived by sons William Dale and Ronald Dale, both of Nicolaus, CA. A member of the Masonic Lodge #129, the Central Sacramento Valley Shriner's, the Yuba City Moose Lodge and the Native Sons of the Golden West He was a long time member of the Mountain View Historical Association. Thank you, FEBRUARY, 1999 MVHA PAGE 4 FRANK L. HUFF BY KATHLEEN LOWE OWEN When Huff School reopened after being closed for 18 years there was much local publicity about the event. Since the school has reopened, it seems appropriate to refresh our memories about Frank L Huff Frank L. Huff was born in 1867 off Charleston Road near Mountain View. His parents, James and Emily Huff, had come to the Mountain View area in the early 1860's. They came from Michigan and were part of a wagon train that took five months to reach California. Most of the members of the group settled in the Napa Valley, but James and his family came to Mountain View and began farming After attending Whisman School and Washington College at Irvington (Fremont), Frank Huff entered the first class at Stanford University. He was head of the Department of Business at Washington College for two years, then took the teacher's examination in Santa Clara County. He taught school for six years in Boulder Creek, two years in San Jose, and 18 years at the Highway School on El Camino here in Mountain View. He was the principal of the Highway School for most of his years there. In addition to his involvement with the local schools, Frank Huff was involved in a variety of community organizations in Mountain View. He was active in the Presbyterian Church and the Prune and Apricot Association. He also participated in the Mountain View Grange, IOOF, the Native Sons of the Golden West, the Masonic Lodge, and Kiwanis International, After his teaching career ended, Frank Huff was appointed the postmaster in Mountain View from 1922 until 1934. He received his appointment from President Warren G. Harding. After retiring from this position, Frank Huff continued to farm his prune orchard on Levin Avenue in Mountain View until his death. In 1938 Frank Huff was killed in a train accident at Rengstorff Avenue. He was killed instantly when his car was struck by a southbound Southern Pacific locomotive as he was crossing the tracks To commemorate his service to the local school district, an elementary school was dedicated in his honor in 1958 SAVE THE ADOBE FEBRUARY, 1999 IMV1-1A PAGE 5 EDITOR'S RAMBLINGS Flora and I moved to Mountain View in January, 1982. This Mountain View home is our fourteenth, and this seventeen year residence is the longest we have ever spent in one house in our forty-eight years together I became interested in the Historical Association while doing some research prior to the construction of our neighborhood Gemello Park. I was given the opportunity to become Editor of this Newsletter when Mary Lentz decided after seven years as Editor to move on to other challenges. This issue is the twenty second under my auspices, the second issue in my sixth year as Editor. In my first issue I said I want to use the office of Editor to forward the aims of the Association. I take these to he: to make us more aware of the richness of our culture and heritage, to support the institutions and activities which will make Mountain lieu,' a more culturally rich and diverse place, and to speak out boldly on issues which run counter to the aims (as I see and interpret them) of the Association. Mary Lentz and I have had, up until this issue, a common problem. Finding enough space in each issue for all of the articles and announcements needing to be published. This time I found myself with a whole page needing to be filled. I've decided to review my incumbency and try to see how well or ill I have performed against those goals. To begin with, aside from Barbara Kinchen who can always be relied upon to deliver interesting material on a timely basis, the staff of the Mountain View Library has been amazingly prescient in identifying issues The staff gave us an article on Shockley Semiconductor in November of 1993, a topic which 'turned hot' in 1998 The staff described the Adobe Building in November of 1994, which 'turned hot' in 1996. The staff has also delivered interesting and timely sketches of prominent residents Maxwell, Slater, Stevens, Kennedy, Bruner, and Askam. Altogether, a total of twenty articles from the Library Staff, in the twenty-two issues I have edited. The Newsletter has featured the history of the El Camino Hospital, the Fire Department, the Police Department, the Shockley Semiconductor Barn, the Adobe Building, the Peralta Adobe, the Pioneer Cemetery and earthquake preparedness Let me strike a bargain with all you who have any interest in the Newsletter. Send me articles, and if they are relevant I'll edit and publish. Send me notes and references, and if they are relevant, I will write them up. In short, I welcome the participation of anyone in the community who has something relevant to say. Beyond just the editorial content of the Newsletter, I welcome comments and suggestions about layout, composition and content Anything which will help make this a more interesting and attractive package for our readers I'm reasonably satisfied with what we have done I strive to do better in the future. In the mean time, you see what happens when you don't feed me enough material, so get busy! STREET TALK The November, 1998 Street Talk Puzzler was: Cousins, Margaret Sharp Peterson and George Holden, lived for a number of years on Main Street. This is now incorporated into which expressway? Your Editor had never before noticed that Mountain View is a town without a Main Street! The answer for the November puzzler is. Main Street was on the north side and parallel to the train tracks and ran east from the Castro Street crossing only to Stevens Creek. West from the same crossing was Alma Street. Now, both streets are incorporated into the Central Expressway. For this issue the Street Talk Puzzler is: Until 1930 Alma Street had a different name. What was it? ELECTIONS ARE TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 3, 1998 NOVEMBER, 1998 MVHA PAGE 2 The Mountain View Historical Association is lucky to have many members who are descendants of pioneer Mountain View families. One of our members, Roberta Bubb Sweeney, has recently written biographies of her parents: Elanor Mabel Cooper Bubb and William Franklin Bubb. Roberta's grandfather, Benjamin T. Bubb, arrived on foot from Missouri in 1850 two weeks before California became a state. The family arrived in Mountain View in 1851. Benjamin and wife, Josephine, had seven children. Their second son, William, was Roberta's father. On his 120 acres, Benjamin first planted wheat. It wasn't until 1889, one year after Benjamin's death from a farm accident, that the Bubb family planted its first prune trees. Soon their entire land became an orchard of prune and apricot trees. Because William's siblings chose careers outside of ranching, it became William's responsibility to tend to the Bubb acreage. The Bubbs were active members of the Cumberland Presbyterian Church located on Castro Street. It was here that William met, courted and married Elanor Cooper in 1908. Roberta and sister Frances were born a few years later. The Bubb family home was located at what is now Begen Avenue and Leona Lane. However, William and Elanor made their home at the corner of Grant Road and Cuesta Drive (once known as Bubb Road) — much of what is now occupied by St. Timothy's Episcopal Church. It is interesting to read Roberta's first-hand account of a young girl growing up in Mountain View. Roberta recalls her father's difficulties of maintaining a successful fruit ranch. Spraying trees for insects and fungus and lighting smudge pots on frosty evenings was a dirty and smelly job. The Bubbs owned on of the first dehydrators in the Valley and were able to employ the local youth. During the summer, the girls were busy helping can fruits and vegetables. Roberta also describes how difficult it was to be an orchardist during the Great Depression. Mrs. Elise Haag, daughter of Henry Rengstorff, helped out the family when times were rough. A SPECIAL SET OF MEMORIES Roberta attended local schools, graduating from Mountain View High School in the early 1930s She by Carol Fischer then continued her education at San Jose State During this time, Roberta met a dashing young man from New Jersey who had come to Mountain View to work at the new Naval Air Station Joe Sweeney and Roberta fell in love and were married in 1936, shortly after Roberta's graduation from college. The Bubb family was active in the early beginnings of the little town of Mountain View. Their efforts contributed to the local economy; they worshiped at the local Presbyterian church; their children attended local schools (Roberta's father was a trustee for Mountain View High School); and both Roberta and Joe have been active in the Mountain View Historical Association. Thank you Roberta for making your memories a permanent record. We invite the members of the Historical Association to come to the Mountain View History Center to read Roberta's biographies. Our staff would enjoy sharing this special collection devoted to our City's heritage. MONDAY To most of us today, the origin of Veteran's Day is little more than a hazy recollection of something to do with past wars and the Veterans who fought in them. Yet the significance of November llth and the five years, 1914-1918, which led to the establishmert of what was formerly called Armistice Day, still impacts us down to the present. The beginning of the eat War" sent out ripples that were soon felt far beyond the lands of Europe and, by 1917, were even affecting life in California. The United States had traditionally tried to avoid foreign entanglements, but the rapid growth and prosperity of the young nation soon encouraged some to feel that America deserved a place among the major powers of the world. The outbreak of World War I would be the stage upon which the country would play its first major role. As America drew closer to war, the Federal Government began to study how the population could be mobilized. The idea of a draft was still relatively unfamiliar to most Americans. There had been a draft during the Civil War of course, but it had sparked riots, particularly in New York City, which resulted in many deaths and injuries. Would the same be true this time? No one could be sure, but there seemed to be no practical alternative, and so on May 18, 1917, the Selective Service Act (which still exists in a modified form) became law. On registration day, June 5, 1917, California registered 298,989 men between the ages of 21 and 31 as eligible for military service, with no disturbance of any kind. The mood of Mountain View and of Santa Clara County as a whole over the course of the next year and a half is clearly reflected in a volume titled War History of Santa Clara County, published by the Santa Clara Historical Society in 1919. The History Room of the Mountain View Public Library recently obtained a photocopy of this fascinating pamphlet, which details how the people of this area threw themselves into the war effort with tireless enthusiasm. Volunteer organizations of every description quickly appeared, involving everyone from small children to senior citizens. Among the names listed are many which will be familiar to students of local history, as well as many more who were just "average" people trying to help as best they could. The greatest sacrifices, however, were of course those of the men and women who left the peace and security of home for the distant battlefields of Europe, or for many other far-flung outposts around the world. Ultimately, more than 135,205 Californians actually served in the armed forces, more than three thousand of whom enlisted or were drafted from Santa Clara County. Among the servicemen from Mountain View were three young men of the Robart family: August, Eugene and Leon. After joining the Army, August and Leon were assigned to Camp Lewis, Washington, where many California men were sent to fill the ranks of the 91 ("Evergreen") Infantry Division. Leon eventually went overseas as a member of that Division's 363rd Infantry Regiment (H Company). Unfortunately, he was never to see home again. Killed in action, he became Mountain View's only combat casualty of the war. In later years his sacrifice would be commemorated with the establishment of the Leon Robart Post of the American Legion. The stories of Leon Robart and his fellow veterans of the Great War still remain, for the most part, unwritten. Santa Clara County can boast of many interesting tales, including that of Sing Kee, a Sergeant in the 306th Infantry Regiment (77th Division), who became the first Chinese—American to win the Distinguished Service Cross. While photographs of the parade given in his honor through the streets of San Jose's Chinatown may still be seen in the History Room, the records of te service of most of his comrades are still unrecorded. Perhaps readers of this newsletter will be able to add to our knowledge of this understudied portion of Mountain View's history, and future generations will have a better understanding of the significance of "the eleventh hour, of the eleventh day, of the eleventh month." Brown, III - Editor s'-' 4""` alimiam oacova". ha< tlia EL CAMINO HOSPITAL AND THE PRACTICE OF MEDICINE AFTER WW II The May 1998 Meeting Our speaker for the May 3, 1998 meetin& of the Mountain View Historical Association will be Dr. ij j riIughl 'Coon, M.D. Dr. L.Tpton did 1-iis residency at the USN Hospital Mare Island and at the San Mateo Community Hospital He established his practice in the Los Altos—Mountain View area in the early 1950's and has practiced here ever since with his special interest being in family medicine. In the mid 1950's he became aware of the acute need for a central medical facility in the Mountain View area and became involved in the early committee work which led to the creation of the El Camino Hospital District and eventually the development of El Camino Hospital, one of the premier medical facilities of the entire Bay Area Dr. Upton has served as Chief of Staff for the Hospgal and continuously on various committees and Task Forces overseeing the operation of the hospital Dr. Upton will talk about the early days in creating the El Camino Hospital, and the medical, economic and political environment surrounding this fine institution COMMUNITY ACTION YOUR POLICE AT WORK The February 1998 Meeting At the February meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association, Sergeant Richard Elias, Community Action and Information Officer for the Mountain View Police Department give us an excellent overview of the history and development of Mountain View's Police Department. He shared with us a wealth of old pictures and documents which called up many memories from the audience. Sergeant Elias spoke at some length about the concept of Community Policing and about the Citizens Police Academy. Community Policing is an effort to get the public more involved with the Police Department and to build a partnership for policing the community. The Citizens Police Academy is a major effort at building a closer relationship and greater understanding between the people and their police It was a very interesting a provocative meeting MAY, 1998 MVHA PAGE 1 FREMONT FIRE DISTRICT BY CAROL FISCHER Two fire districts in Mountain View? Well, not exactly. In 1928, the Fremont Fire District was formed to protect those areas on the outskirts of Mountain View not within the sphere of the established Mountain View Fire Department. This area also included the unincorporated land of Los Altos and Los Altos Hills. The new district was accountable to the Santa Clara County Board of Supervisors. The manpower was completely volunteer. The men were proud of their new American La France pumper which was capable of pumping 500 gallons per minute. Shortly after the district was formed, the company responded to an explosion of a Prohibition still in a two-story house on Jordan and San Antonio Road. Although the volunteers couldn't save that house, they were more successful at extinguishing a nearby grass fire on Mariposa Avenue. Thus began the accomplishments of the new Fremont Fire District. As Mountain view grew and began annexing more land, it was often thought that the two districts would merge. However, by 1977, the Fremont District was still in existence as an all-volunteer department. The firefighters were very excited because the district had just purchased a $46,000 American La France fire engine from the La France factory in Elmira, New York. Because the department was a frugal and resourceful one, they decided to save funds by driving the new engine back to Mountain View rather than paying someone else to do it. The adventure began in New York for Captain Will Radcliff and fireman Brad Lutts on April 26th. The men drove in shifts, making about 600 miles a day. Since the engine drove better when fully loaded, it was filled with 750 gallons of water. Radcliff and Lutts decided to fight any fires they might spot along the way. They certainly got strange looks from the locals whenever the showed up at a fire! The two made stops in Fremont, Ohio and Mountain View, Wyoming. The latter station was nothing but an old barn spray-painted "Fire Station" on the side. The only mishap occurred in Reno Nevada when the windshield wipers broke. While being repaired, the men spent their time playing the slot machines. What impressed the local MAY, 1998 citizenry the most during the journey? The engine's capacity to take on gas. Radcliff quipped, "We filled up at one gas station and made the attendant happier than he had ever been in his life!" The new La France arrived safe and sound in Mountain View on May 2, 1977. After more than 3,000 miles, Radcliff and Lutts were glad to be home but were pleased that they had undertaken such a unique odyssey. By 1982, the Fremont Fire District remained small but active. however it was shrinking in size. It was estimated that there were only 400 residents in nine small pockets of unincorporated land. This area included the region now known as North Bayshore and parts of Mountain View bordering Los Altos. At the time there were 22 volunteer firefighters who received no pay but a minimal $5.00 for each response they attended. The Mountain View Fire Department felt they would trouble responding to the fires in the Fremont District without additional manpower or operational costs. So it was in August of 1982 that the Fremont Fire District ended 54 years of dedication to the Mountain View/Los Altos area. Local residents should feel proud of this tiny, independent district whose firefighters cared enough to volunteer their services as well as to drive their new fire engine across the country home to Mountain View! MAY, t998 MVHA PAGE 4 HISTORY OF MOUNTAIN VIEW The Mountain View Historical Association Executive Committee is exploring the idea of commissioning the creation of a History of Mountain View. Your executive committee has appointed a subcommittee with the goal of publishing the History of Mountain View by the year 2002 (the 100th anniversary of the city) or possibly sooner. The committee consists of our City Historian, Barbara McPheeters Kinchen, Trudy Herrero Odbert, Margaret Vidovich and Wally Erichsen as Chairman. Initial activity involves study of some typical local history books of nearby cities and formulation of coverage quality and objectiveness. The Committee has met with Kathleen Peregrine, Director of the California History Center at DeAnza College and Mary Jo Ignoffo, author of the book on the history of Sunnyvale, to establish the possibility of help from professional historians in writing and publishing such a book. Preliminary thoughts are that the book should be well illustrated and factual, and should relate the history of the Mountain View area from prehistoric times up to the present. A CELEBRATION THE FIRST 95 YEARS The November 1997 Meeting On Sunday, November 9, 1997 the Mountain View Historical Association and the City of Mountain View jointly celebrated the 95th anniversary of the day Mountain View became a Municipal Corporation. Celebrating a 95th birthday is a little unusual but Mountain View is a part-j- town, and we enjoyed our 75th so much that we decided to celebrate every ten years. A "hidden agenda" reason for the celebration however, was as_a sort of warmup and practice for the Centennial of Mountain View! The City and the Historical Association have begun thinking about the Centennial, and you may notice that the Executive Committee has started a review aimed at making all of our publications current and available by 2002. Highlights of the meeting were a presentation by Barbara McPheeters Kinchen relating the history of the City, and the introduction of many of our past Councilpersons and other civic leaders. The first and second floors of City Hall wei-e filled with exhibits of scenes from the City's past, and punch and cake made it into a very pleasant afternoon. The 95th anniversary celebration followed by only two weeks the grand opening of the City's new Library. The Library includes greatly expanded and improved space for the Mountain View History Center; the new name for the Pioneer Room. As I saia earlier, Mountain View is a great party town. Its time to start getting ready for a really big one, the Mountain View Centennial.' February 1998 THE MAYFIELD DUEL BY CAN DACE BOWERS MVHA More than a hundred years ago, men from the nearby community of Mayfield were involved in a dispute over property rights that ended in an old-time duel and left three people dead. The Seale brothers, Thomas, Henry, and Joseph, had settled in the area and were involved in helping the Soto family of rancheros get a clear deed to their property — 2200 acres in what is now Palo Alto In return for their help, the Sotos gave the brothers half their land. In 1858 or 59, Thomas Seale was involved in a dispute with brothers Paul and Richard Shore, who were squatting on Seale land in the Mayfield area. Seale and his hired man, Alexander Robb, went to Paul Shore's cabin to eject him. In the ensuing argument, Paul Shore was shot and killed. Thomas Seale immediately turned himself in to authorities in San Jose, claiming self defense. Also arrested as a accessory to the killing was Scale's friend Samuel Crosby, who underwent a preliminary examination and was discharged. Several months later, Thomas Seale and Alexander Robb went on trial for the Shore killing, at the Courthouse in San Jose. Samuel Crosby was also present as a witness. Other supporters of Thomas Seale, as well as Shore's brothers Thomas and Richard, were gathered outside. Thomas Shore called out to Crosby in an apparent challenge to a duel. Crosby was mortally wounded, but not before he was able to fire a few haphazard shots. One of his bullets killed an innocent bystander miner from Grass Valley named L. Posey Fergusson. After firing the shot that killed Crosby, Thomas Shore fled and was never prosecuted — but the Shores vowed revenge on Thomas Seale. Both Thomas Seale and Alexander Robb were acquitted of Paul Shore's killing. Seale left for Nevada and later lived in Australia Years later he returned to live in the house that his brother Henry had built on Webster Street, near the Oregon Expressway. (This house later became an orphanage, and was destroyed in 1937.) When Thomas Seale died in 1907, it is said that Thomas Shore removed the gun he'd worn since the trial and said, "Sorry I never had a chance to use it" Page 2 EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE MEETING DECEMBER 17, 1998 Ti-.
