Join with us, Refreshments will be served BARBECUE fic RAFFLE THE AUGUST MEETING August was the Annual Barbecue & Raffle for the Mountain View Historical Association. We assembled in the Patio Area of the Mountain View Senior Center. The weather was glorious California, and we had enough umbrellas to provide some shade. There were -.bout one hundred of us in attendance. Art Walton's potato salad was up to expectations, and Al lehning flips hamburgers like a professional. We had apple pie and ice cream, and there were baked beans and salad. Everything for a great traditional picnic! The musicians were able to dredge up all of those great old songs from back when we were young and dating. There were dozens of great prizes for the Raffle, and I am going to keep going back until I win something! The Event could not have been the success it was without the generous support of many businesses and individuals. You will find the list of people and organizations that contributed in the Newsletter, but ultimately this kind of thing happens because a few individuals work very hard. A few of those people are Ralph and Art and Al and Wally and Edna and Bobby, and they drafted family and friends. It was a team effort, and great fun, and we will do it again. MTN. VIEW INCORPORATED 95 YEARS A CITY BY BARBARA MCPHEETERS KINCHEN Mountain View became a Municipal Corporation of the sixth class on November 7, 1902 Gustavus K. Estes, lawyer and editor-publisher of the Register, was the principal backer of incorporation. He urged citizens to support it because of financial advantages. Some $2,000 a year was going into the county treasury from local road taxes and business licenses Estes estimated that $1,000 was enough to run the town, including sprinkling all the streets, and there would be money enough for improvements like a park and a library. Following the procedures prescribed by law, a petition was prepared and circulated Signed by seventy-two supporters, it was presented to Santa Clara County Board of Supervisors in August of 1902. Benjamin E. Burns and Walter A. Clark, both influential businessmen of Mountain View, accompanied Mr. Estes to the formal hearing in September. Nc one appeared in opposition and so a special incorporation election was ordered for Saturday, November 1, 1902. Polls were open from 6:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. at Olympic Hall, at the corner of Castro and Front Streets. Front Street is now Evelyn Avenue. Registered voters within the proposed town limits voted for or against incorporation and, at the same time, indicated choices for five trustees and three officers. There were 156 votes cast, 88 for incorporation and 64 against, with four rejected for "irregularities" Elected as Town Trustees were Benjamin E. Burns, Daniel B. Frink, Dr. Charles 0. Gates, M.D., George A. Pattberg and George Swall. Paul J. Schwab had the most votes for Town Clerk and exofficio Assessor. Alvin Rogers was selected as Treasurer and Richard C. Waits won as Marshall and ex-officio Tax and License Collector. Supervisors canvassed the vote and forwarded an order for incorporation to the Secretary of State where it was received and officially stamped November 7, 1902. The Board of Trustees and elected officers met for the first time at 7:30 p.m. on November 10 in the law offices of B.E. Burns. After electing Mr. Frink as President, Ordinance No. 1 was introduced and adopted which set amounts for bonds required for the three officers. Committees were then appointed to design a seal and to draft ordinances. The handwritten minutes show that before adjourning "a contribution of one dollar each was given by each member of the Board & Officers-elect and placed in the hands of the Treasurer." The sketch following this article shows the 1902 town limits. Within the area of approximately one square mile the population count was 610. Pop Smith, editor of the Mountain View RegisterLeader, wrote in 1927 that the 1902 boundary lines had been carefully drawn so as to exclude some areas populated by incorporation objectors and to include large orchards whose owners favored forming a town The small area defined by San Jose Road, Montgomery and Centre was the school lot on which had been a grammar school since 1858 and, now, the high school building just opened in September of 1902. The Mountain View Historical Association sponsored the 75th anniversary of incorporation with a Diamond Jubilee Meeting on November 6, 1977. Panel members told of happenings in the past and Victor Calvo, at that time an Assemblyman, presented certificates to more than 40 invited guests who had been living in and near Mountain View in 1902. Rengstorff Community Center auditorium was filled with members, guests, friends and representatives from city and community organizations. As befitted birthday celebrations, there was a very large and beautifully decorated cake for all to enjoy. Maryce Freelen was chairwoman for the party on November 7, 1987. An estimated crowd of 7,000 gathered on Castro Street where merchants, schools, organizations and industries arranged exhibits and activities for all ages. These included a gallery of old photos, a walking tour, displays in historic downtown buildings, stagecoach rides, music by two bands and painting of a mural at November, 1997 MVHA Page 2 Castro and California Streets. A biplane towed a AWE birthday greeting sign overhead Special ceremonies at 2:00 p.m. under a big tent featured cutting the two 4X8 foot birthday cakes by Mayor Bob Scats, assisted by honored guest, Mrs. Helen Horton Madden, 93 years old life-long resident Now, after another decade of growth and change, it is again time to celebrate and learn, or recall, our local history. And it's not too early to begin planning for that biggie in 2002 — our 100' birthday. SPRR U. SAVE THE ADOBE Mountain View was only three decades old when the Adobe was built. It is the last remaing public building of any significance left in the area.. It was a building built with style and grace, designed to bridge the transition from old mountain view and our Spanish traditions and the modern world. -1 ..1111K-4, 21,,t 1St - Parishioners were raising money for a new building at Hope and Church Streets, next to their newly constructed parsonage. On Christmas afternoon the Cyclers' Club played the high school football team and won 5 to 0 (5 touchdowns?) A petition was sent to the Board of Supervisors asking that a branch County jail be placed in Mountain View. Howard A. Streight of El Monte Avenue, one of America's foremost landscape painters, is exhibiting his paintings in San Francisco, including a recent one of Mt. Shasta. It would be very appropriate if the Adobe could grace this primary entrance into downtown Mountain View when we celebrate our 100th aniversary. The building sits almost at the terminus of the light rail system as it will exist in 2002, and that makes it seem a particularly appropriate symbol of the old and the new, and our connections to our roots. OLD AND PRECIOUS This graceful old home now overlooks Shoreline Regional Park. It embodies a good deal of Mountain View's history, and it is very much too the credit of the community that they chose to preserve it. It provides an island of calm in our midst, and an opportunity to reflect upon just how we got here, and where we have been. We are a multi-cultural society now, and in particular here where generations of peoples have come for the agricultural work, for tie climate, for the high tech work. We are red, yellow, brown and white in our roots, and soon there will be no one race or nationality which constitutes a plurality. If you haven't visited Rengstorff House you are missing out on some important insights in too who we are. For these very reasons we also need to preserve the Adobe. FIGHTING FIRE & DISASTER THE MAY MEETING Battalion Chief John Fetz was the speaker for the May 4, 1997 Regular Meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association. He presented an illustrated history of the Mtn. View Fire Department. Chief Fetz will be remembered as a speaker on earthquake preparedness at the May 1994 meeting. The history of the Mountain View Fire Department begins with a meeting of 50 volunteers April 1, 1874 to form Hook and Ladder #1. The volunteers purchased the equipment themselves. It was probably housed at the Rogers and Rogers store. May 17, 1905 the Mountain View Town Council passed a resolution formally creating the Volunteer Fire Department, and on June 7, Hose Company #1 was formed. Hose Company #1 fought its first fire on October 29, 1905, and in April of 1906 it fought a fire at the Rogers and Rogers store. After that fire, a second fire company was formed. The first Fire Station was built in 1924. It was replaced by Fire Station 1, which was built in 1953. The bell was the 1905 volunteer bell. A new Fire Station 1, located at the corner of Dana and Shoreline was dedicated in 1996. (See Fire on page 2) August, 1997 MVHA Page 1 (From Fire on page 1) Fire Station 2 was dedicated in 1953 and is scheduled to be rebuilt in 1998, Redwine Motors built the city's first fire truck in 1917. This truck is still in use for parades and musters. By 1924 the City had acquired a LaFrace engine, and in 1930 Redwine Motors built still another engine. The current fleet includes six engines and one truck, all 1990 Seagraves. In the early days the dispatchers worked 24 hour shifts. For a time, the dispatchers worked from Palo Alto, but they returned to Mountain View in 1980. The new Communications Center is located on the lower level of the Public Safety Building at 1000 Villa Street. This modem center provides 911 service and dispatch for Fire, Police, Public Services and Rangers. The whole operation is computer supported today. The Volunteer Service was disbanded in 1964. Today a minimum of 18 persons are on duty. The Department now provides emergency medical services, deals with hazardous materials, performs fire safety inspections, fire investigations, water rescue, fire fighting, and mutual aid within and outside the county. Public education is a major activity of the Department which includes public event and school appearances for Sparky the Dog and Pluggy. Chief Fetz showed pictures of the 1941 Junction Inn fire and the Chinatown Fire of 1946. One of Mountain View's worst disasters was the Jasco Chemical fire and explosion in April of 1965. 28 Firefighters were treated at El Camino Hospital. The most serious fire of recent times was the 6 Alarm Minton Lumber Fire. Units from as far away as Gilroy lent assistance. The Mountain View Fire Department has been a proud and integral part of the City of Mountain View for more than one hundred years. The City is indeed fortunate in having the services of these dedicated men and women. EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE MEETINGS JUNE 7, JUNE 18, JULY 8, 1997 The Executive Committee of the Mountain View Historical Association has met several times since the May Regular Meeting. We have reached agreement considering the collections to be housed in the new library. The collection space will be known as the Mountain View History Center. The Library Collection will contain items relating to the immediate vicinity of Mountain View which can be readily stored in filing cabinets or shelves. The Historical Association collection will also include these types of items but will continue to include some larger pieces. Where appropriate these pieces will be displayed in the Mtn. View History Center, but where they cannot be displayed the City will continue to make the fourth floor of City Hall space available. The Executive Committee decided to oppose the proposed construction of a new office for the Chamber of Commerce in Pioneer Park. The tentative proposal would not have damaged any of the Heritage trees, and after removal of the present building a more useable park would remain. The objections are primarily to any sort of further encroachment on Pioneer Park, and the unknown impact upon interred remains. The Executive Committee continues to support the Save The Adobe Task Force in its efforts to preserve and restore the Adobe Building. Emerson 56,285 Henry Rengstorff 48,578 John Snyder 34,829 John Sullivan 30,950 L.P. Collins 27,318 Jeff Bailey 25,280 Frank Sleeper 24,925 There were 141 pupils attending public school. A petition was submitted to the Board of Supervisors asking that Charleston Road be made a public road 75 Years Ago (1922): Wages for apricot pickers were set at 40¢ an hour. There were only two fires on the Fourth of July, both due to the combination of small boys and firecrackers. A $197,000 bond election for buying land and building and furnishing a new high school carried by a vote of 684 to 188. The opposition came from an area where residents had wanted to unite with Palo Alto High School District. An average of 77 patrons a day used the library which was open afternoons and evenings, except for sundays and holidays. Theatrical Cold Cream, made by Owl Drug Company, sold locally at 750 a pound tin. Powell Brothers Grocery hoped to entice customers with "Buy a dollar's worth of groceries and get a 25¢ watermelon free." P G & E would install a gas system if 500 residents signed up for service. A string of Percheron horses, 3 stallions and 3 mares, from the Rosehall Percheron Farm on Charleston Road, won the Grand Reserve Champion Ribbon at the California State Fair and 11 first premiums and 4 seconds. The Woman's Club raised over $200 for its building fund with a Lady Minstrel Show and a Prize Cakewalk. Pop Smith congratulated the all-local entertainers for one of the best shows he had seen in his 30 years with the RegisterLeader. "Traffic violations continue to increase. People of all ages and conditions seem to take a sinister delight in defying the laws to protect human lives. In addition to the increasing menace from the traffic violators in the streets, we also have to contend with bicycle riders on the sidewalks. Lately we have heard of two ore more instances in which ladies were forced off of the sidewalks by men on bicycles." 50 Years Ago (1947): Many local people report seeing flying discs or saucers. All Navy blimp activities along the Pacific coast are being discontinued and Moffett's blimp squadron is being transferred to North Carolina. The local theatre showed The Egg and I starring Claudette Colbert and Fred Mac Murray. The Sunnyvale Club, an organization of Italian families, has applied for a permit to build on Castro Avenue. (Now the Senior Center on the renamed Escuela Avenue.) The play, I remember Mama, now running in San Francisco and also being filmed in Hollywood, was written by Katherine Anderson who graduated from Mountain View High School in 1925. She wrote under the name of Kathryn Forbes and was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Leon Ellis Anderson. A midnight blaze lit the sky for miles when the three-story feed and storage barn burned at the Lawrence dairy farm on Charleston Road. The volunteer fire department fought the fire for 12 hours, assisted by Los Altos and the Division of Forestry at Alma Station. The 625 tons of hay were expected to burn for several days. All 25 cows and 2 bulls were led to safety. However, the bulls battled each other in the pasture where they were placed and when one escaped Officer Ed Henderson and Sgt. Art Nielsen had to quickly scramble over a barbwire fence. Chief Clarence Lawson badly injured a foot when he stepped on a nail. This was the fourth hay barn fire in the area in the last six weeks! 25 Years Ago (1972): An anonymous tip led to the discovery of 48 marijuana plants growing in a cornfield on Tyrella Avenue. Mrs. Ruth Lawson replaced Mrs. Edith Duke as August, 1997 MVHA Page 4 Librarian. Budget cutbacks had kept the library closed on Fridays and. Sundays for the last year, but now Friday hours were restored. Garbage collection rates rose from $1.62 to $1.86 a month, but there would no longer be backyard pickups. Instead, an unlimited number of cans could be placed at curbside. Mrs. Christi Penkoff became the first female police officer for Mountain View. The Chamber of Commerce-sponsored Mountain Views first Art and Wine festival, La Fiesta de Sierra Vista, featuring 40 artists and craftsmen. The two-day event drew 15,000 visitors. A crowd of 1,000, including numerous local school children, greeted Mrs. Pat Nixon when she visited Ames-Research Center. The Holy Cross High School for girls and St. Francis High School for boys consolidated on September 11, 1972. Chick Taylor retired after serving 12 years as Fire Chef at Moffett Naval Air Station. Previously, he had been with the Mountain View Volunteer Fire Department for 13 years. Brown, III - Editor FIGHTING FIRE & DISASTER The May Meeting The history of fires and disasters in Mountain View and the men and women who have dealt with them will be the themes of the May 4, 1997, meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association. Battalion Chief John Fetz of the Mountain View Fire Department will be our speaker. The Fire Department, initially a volunteer organization, and now a thoroughly professional and modern emergency services team, has been an important part of Mountain View since the City's earliest days. By coincidence, the Old Newspaper Items column in this Newsletter from 100 years ago describes the construction of a building which was to include the Fire Department. From about the same period, the obituary for Pauline Bellew mentions the wedding celebration which the Department provided for one of its own. Chief Fetz will talk about some of those early days of the Department, some of the disasters they had to deal with, the growing pains, and something about the range of services the Department now provides. The Historical Association meeting should be of particular interest since many members of the Mountain View Historical Association participated in one way or another with the Department in its earlier days. HISTORY OF THE MOUNTAIN VIEW PUBLIC LIBRARY The February Meeting Susan Ozubko, Director of Library Services for the City of Mountain View, was our speaker at the February 2, 1997 meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association. Her presentation covered the history of the library in Mountain View from the early pioneer days up to the present. The presentation included many illustrations. The first Library and Reading Room in Mountain View was opened to the public December 1, 1890. By 1892 the collection included about 700 books. Judge B. E. Burns acted as Librarian and continued to sponsor the Library for many years. In 1903 the Library moved from the basement of the J. S. Mockbee residence at Hope and Villa Streets to the Library of the new high school in Old Mountain View. In 1903 Mr. B. C. Nichols, owner of the Mountain View Register opened a Circulating Library. A membership subscription was $3.00 per year. In 1908 William Garliepp opened the Tarbad Inn Circulating Library. There is no record as to the duration of either of these ventures. On March 10, 1905, the Mountain View (See Library on page 2) May, 1997 MVHA Page 1 (From Library on page 1) Woman's Club successfully petitioned the Town Board of Trustees for a Free Public Reading Room. On April 14, 1905, the Free Public Library and Reading Room opened over Rogers & Rogers General Store. Earthquake damage in 1906 necessitated finding new quarters for the Library. After a succession of temporary rooms, the Library moved into the Swell Building in September 1907. Miss Laurabelle (Dolly) Graham, for whose father Graham Middle School is named, became Librarian. An open house was held when the Library was established on the first floor of the thennew City Hall, April 9, 1910. There were 300 books on the shelves and there were one thousand cardholders. Mr. A. L. Palmer assumed the office of Librarian in 1919. In 1929 the Library was moved to the second floor of City Hall. Mr. Palmer retired in 1944, but lived to a grand old age of 105. Mrs. Edna Roth succeeded Mr. Palmer and served until retirement in 1957. In 1952 the Library moved to a converted store at 939 Dana Street. The collection numbered 17,000 volumes. In 1956 a $160,000 bond was passed for the first Library building, an 8,400 square foot structure with a capacity of 65,000 volumes. Mrs. Edith Duke was appointed Librarian and assumed the responsibility of completing the building on Franklin Street. In 1968 a threestory, 22,800 square foot addition was added, bringing the capacity up to 160,000 volumes. Ruth Lawson was appointed City Librarian in 1973, and served until her retirement in 1981. She was succeeded by Ruth Stilwell, who served until 1988, when Susan Ozubko was appointed as Library Services Director. After many efforts, in 1993 a $14 million bond issue to fund construction of a new library was placed on the ballot, but the measure failed by a very narrow margin. Alternate funding was found and in 1996 work commenced on the new Mountain View Public Library. The library is presently located in temporary trailers at the corner of Moffett Boulevard and Middlefield Road. Excavation for the new Library forced the relocation of about 34 graves from the old Presbyterian Church Cemetery. It proved impossible to precisely identify these remains, but they have been respectfully re-interred. The new Library will blend with the architecture of the Civic Center, and yet be a good neighbor to the residents of Franklin Street. The new Library will be equipped to deal with the age of technology with fiber optics, cabling and computers. The expected opening date is December 1997. MOUNTAIN VIEW'S `RED SHADOW' by Carol Fischer What do the famous lyricist, Oscar Hammerstein and the City of Mountain View have in common? Would you believe the dashing "Red Shadow" in the operetta, The Desert Song, was Perry Askam, the grandson of Henry Rengstorff? Perry Askam, the Broadway matinee idol of the 1920's, was the son of Helena Rengstorff (one of Henry's seven children) and Dr. Oliver Perry Askam. Both Perry and his older brother, Earl, were orphaned as children. Perry was then raised by his mother's sister, Mrs. Elise Rengstorff Haag. As Mrs. Haag had no children, Perry inherited the family home, Rengstorff House, at the time of her death in 1952. Before becoming a Broadway star, Perry ventured to Alaska in 1915 in pursuit of gold. Not finding his fortune, he went to Europe and volunteered with the French army during World War I. While driving a Red Cross ambulance in Italy, Perry was hospitalized for malaria. In the bed next to him was another young ambulance driver recuperating from shrapnel wounds—Ernest Hemingway. The two young soldiers became friends and enjoyed each other's company as they toured the small eateries of Milan. Immortalizing his experiences, Hemingway later wrote a novel entitled "A Farewell to Arms" depicting wartime Italy with an ambulance driver as the story's hero. (see Red Shadow on page 3) May, 1997 MVHA Page 2 (From Red Shadow on page 2) Perry Askam's baritone kept him employed beyond the lights of Broadway. After touring the United States for five years with The Desert Song, he sang solos for both the San Francisco Symphony and the Los Angeles Philharmonic. In one 1956 interview, Mr. Askam admits to leads in a "couple of small movies" with Warner Brothers in the 1930's (Palo Alto Times, September 27, 1956). Earl Askam, Perry's older brother, actually had signed a contract with Cecil B. DeMille but died in 1940 before reaching stardom. Even though Perry Askam was friends with the likes of Al Jolson, Ernest Hemingway and Ezio Pinza, it was to his childhood home in Mountain View that Perry and his wife, Frances, retired. Perry spent his last years at his 165-acre ranch at 1737 Stierlin Road "singing to the cows." Perry found great contentment wearing "jeans and an old shirt instead of grease paint and an operatic wig." (Mountain View Register, May 3, 1953). Perry died at the age of 60 in 1961. .'" 1114 Ape.* . ".; 0,, IN COMMEMORATION PAL/LINE IvANcovicti BELLEw: 91, in Sunnyvale, February 24, 1997. Born in Watsonville, she was a member of the first graduating class from the new Mountain View High School on Castro Street in 1924. Her parents immigrated from Croatia. She married Kyrie Bellew, at the time a volunteer with the Mountain View Fire Department, and the firemen drove them up and down Main Street in celebration. She leaves a brother-in-law James Bellew of Fremont, and numerous nieces and nephews. She was for many years a member of the Mountain View Historical Association. ALBERT S. MILLER: 76, in Yountville, March 13, 1997. Lived at the Veteran's Home in Yountville. He leaves a brother and sister, both out of state, and a niece, Lynn Cohen of San Francisco. He was a member of American Legion Post #248 and the Mountain View Historical Association. CHIEF ROBERT K. SCHATZ: 69, at El Camino Hospital in Mountain View, March 29, 1997, of emphysema. Born in Pocatello, Idaho, he grew up in Oakland. He served in both the Army and the Navy. He earned a degree in criminology from San Jose State University and was also a graduate of the FBI National Academy. Bob Schatz served 34 years with the Mountain View Police Department, the last thirteen as Chief. Chief Schatz served for nearly nine years on the Mountain View City Council, and served as Mayor for two terms. Bob Schatz was a man of warmth and good humor, and always caring for his fellow humans. Chief Schatz was a member of many civic organizations, and a very active and supportive member of the Mountain View Historical Association. May, 1997 MVHA Page 3 SAVE THE ADOBE TASKFORCE MISSION STArrme-Nr: The mission of the "Save the Adobe Task Force" is to restore and preserve Mountain View's historic Adobe Building for use as a vital community resource. The task force has continued to meet regularly and has formulated some important positions. The future use of the Adobe Building should be as a cultural center based upon its design, site, historical value and architecture. Restoration keeping the integrity of the original structure would provide for a variety of cultural uses such as a museum, a place for special exhibits, handicraft shows and meetings of other interest groups. It could serve as a place for dinners, wedding receptions, dances and sirnifar events. Renovation and site development would greatly enhance this gateway to the historic downtown area. We have reviewed the preliminary engineering and architectural studies and we are convinced that a safe, attractive and historically valuable addition to downtown Mountain View is viable. We need the support of every interested Mountain View resident. We must raise substantial amounts in cash and pledges to preserve the Adobe and make it into the Mountain View asset that it should be. If you can help, or if you have ideas that may help, contact the Task Force at; Save the Adobe Task Force P.O. CaLqes•ia. imas .14 riff THE MOUNTAIN VIEW LIFE AS A CREWMAN LIBRARY ON THE USS MACON The February Meeting The November Meeting The Mountain View Public Library has been an integral and vital part of the City of Mountain View since the very early days. Founded and endowed by a group of citizens, it prospered thru the support and efforts of many volunteers. Since it's incorporation into the City, it has had several homes, but it has continued to outgrow the facilities provided. A new library building is now under construction and should be ready for occupancy by the end of this year. Our speaker on Sunday, February 2, will be Susan Ozubko, Mountain View's Library Services Director. She will review the history of the library, particularly as it relates to the people and organizations that "made it happen" over the years. She will describe the growth and problems which made the current expansion necessary, and will touch on some of the unique problems associated with building a new facility on the location of the old and in the vicinity of some of the City's most hollowed ground. She will end with describing something about the future of our library, and libraries in general. TT T (see - IVA V LAVILlq - on page z) The November meeting provided an unusual insight into what it was like to live aboard those great and beautiful airships. As the US Navy operated them, they were submarines of the air, complete with wheel, rudder, diving planes, and speaker tubes. Life aboard, even for the enlisted men, provided comfortable accommodations and good food. There were three crews, one flying. one doing maintenance and housekeeping and the third on break, and they normally rotated every 72 hours. When they were flying, they worked four hours on and four hours off, with hot bunking. (A single bunk alternated between two crewmen.) Accommodations were surprisingly spacious. The Macon could make 75 knots, which doesn't seem fast in comparison with the airplanes, even of the thirties, but this ship was the size of a cruiser. The Macon carried a crew of more than eighty, and had five aircraft which it could launch and retrieve. It could carry eighty tcgia, and had an operational range of 7500 miles and normally stayed operational for 72 hours at a time. (see - Macon - on page 2) February. 1997 MVHA Page 1 - M V Library - on page 1) Our library is a vital educational, research and cultural asset. It belongs in a unique way to people of the area. Come to the meeting with your thoughts, opinions and questions ready. Susan is perhaps the best qualified person around to deal with them. (from - Macon - on page 1) Of particular interest were the comments of George Weldy and Pete Calande, both of whom served on the Macon. There were also several persons in the audience who had first hand experiences with the Macon to relate. Ben deBolt put together an entertaining and informative afternoon for us, and we are grateful. If you would like to delve further into the life and times of the great airships, the Pioneer Room on the fourth floor of City Hall has lots of information, and the Moffett Field Historical Society has even more. MOUNTAIN VIEW LIBRARY FOUNDATION One of the advantages of being a Newsletter Editor is that you can occasionally get on your soap box for a favorite cause. You may have noticed that I have taken an interest in the Mountain View Public Library, supporting bond issues, calling attention to construction activities, et cetera. Well, at the February 2 meeting you will have an opportunity to share in my enthusiasm. The Mountain View Library Foundation is a new not for profit corporation. Its objectives are summarized in it mission statement. MISSION STATEMENT The purpose of the Mountain View library Foundation is to raise money to benefit the Mountain View Public Library. Private gifts made through the Foundation are used to enhance library materials, facilities, and services by supplementing the library's public finding. The MVLF was able to salvage some of the bricks used in the old library, and most of the carved wooden letters which were on the wall in the children's area. They will be available as mementoes in exchange for a fifty dollar donation to the MVLF. Each object will be accompanied by a certificate attesting to its provenance, and if you would like. an actual sheet of the blueprints for the new library. Since the objects have no real intrinsic value, and the MVLF is an IRS approved charitable organization, your donation will be tax deductible. Stop by the display table and take a look! It may be just the thing to recall many fond memories of your visits to the old library. February, 1997 MVHA Page 2 SAVE THE ADOBE TASK FORCE Mission Statement: The mission of the "Save the Adobe" Task Force is to restore and preserve Mountain View's historic Adobe Building for use as a vital community resource. The Task Force continues to meet on a regular basis. On December 11, 1996, the task force reported to the Mountain View City Council on the results of its year long efforts to ascertain the level of public support for preserving the Adobe. Results so far have been encouraging, and the Council urged the Task Force to try to find non-public funding to participate in the seismic upgrade and renovation work. The Task Force has recruited some additional volunteers and is preparing to imbark on a campaign to enlist corporate and foundation support. The Task Force must report back to the Council with the results of this campaign within six months. In the mean time, garnering additional public support is a prime objective. A presentation kit has been developed, and the Task Force can arrange for a 30 minute presentation on very short notice. To schedule a presentation to your group contact Wally Erichsen or Hilton Brown. The Task Force is also prepared to participate with displays at conventions or meetings. The Task Force welcomes your ideas and participation. If we are to preserve the Adobe, it will require the support of the entire community: individuals, small business, and corporations. February. 1997 MVHA Page 5 THE MOUNTAIN VIEW 11 TIT FTNTXTel lradr'rTi 1.V.1.M.L. 1 1IN / By Kathleen Lowe Owen Today Mountain View is a virtual molting pot of people who have come here or have ancestors who came from various parts of the world. That was not true until fairly recently and at the end of the 19th century it was almost unheard of. For example, settlers from Japan did not arrive in Santa Clara County until 1898. At that time there were 12 Japanese residents - nine men and three women. Records in the historical collection at the Mountain View Library show that many of the early Japanese settlers in Mountain View were men who worked at Minton's Lumber Yard. By 1912 there was an early Japanese school on the Minton's property where employees and their relatives could learn English. In 1914 an elementary school which served the children of Japanese residents was established at Front (Evelyn) and View streets. There were perhaps five Japanese children in 1915 but by 1920 nearly 40 children attended this school. They were taught English, Japanese and the regular primary curriculum. The school was moved to the corner of Alma and Bailey at the Japanese Seventh Day Adventist Church. The Tr -City Association, which includes members from Sunnyvale and Los Altos, constructed a new Japanese School at View and Dana Streets. In 1929 the Mountain View Japanese Association incorporated this school, and eventually as many as 150 students attended on a regular basis. That school was in operation until the start of World War H in 1941 when all people of Japanese ancestry were relocated to internment camps such as Hart Mountain and Nanzanar. During the war the building was leased to the Girl Scouts. In return the Girl Scouts were responsible for maintaining the property. (continued in next column) It wasn't until 1959 that the Japanese Language School was established. At that time the Tr -City Association of Sunnyvale, Los Altos and Mountain View, began sponsoring the school. Instead of offering a complete elementary education the school began to focus on the Japanese language and culture. It is still located at the Mountain View Buddhist Church on Shoreline Boulevard where as many as 100 students attend classes each Saturday. Though most students are of Japanese descent any student is welcome who has a desire to learn the Japanese language. If you are interested in learning more about the different Japanese schools in Mountain View or in other information about our early Japanese residents you should visit the Historical Collection at Mountain View City Hall. A display of photographs as well as copies of oral histories compiled by some of Mountain View's residents is currently on display. MOUNTAIN VIEW'S MODEL CANNERY By Candace Flowers Among the many fruit canning plants that once operated locally, one was praised as a "model cannery" that had the latest machinery, met the highest sanitary regulations, and provided for the well-being of its employees. This cannery, J.W. McCarthy Jr. and Co., was located on Villa Street just west of Shoreline Blvd., near the railroad tracks. J.W. McCarthy Jr. bought the cannery in 1917 from the Sanguinetti family, who had started the cannery about a dozen years earlier but apparently lacked the capital to keep the business growing and expand. This included building a housing complex for his employees, which was known as the Rose Court cottages. A 1920 photograph of the Rose Court cottages shows neat, one-story bungalows grouped around well-manicured lawns and connected by clean, white sand paths. Employees' children had their own playground that was presided over by a full-time "matron." The ecnnplex also had its own superintendent and boasted of the latest, most efficient electrical, water and bathing facilities. It was hoped that such comfortable living quarters would ensure the "respectability and high morale" of the residents. The cannery was an important factor in the local economy. The operation supported hundreds of men and women on its payroll, which at the peak of the season could mean $10,000 a week paid to workers. It was thought that these busy workers spent most of their money locally. The plant also had a large expenditure for raw materials. In one year they bought 2,000 tons of tomatoes at $12-$21.50 per ton; 400 tons of apricots at $100-$405 per ton; 330 tons of Firestone and cling peaches, which ranged from $55 to $110 a ton; 100 tons of pears at $100 a ton; and 100 tons of apples at $14 a ton, to name several crops. See you Sunday, August 4! AGRICULTURE in the SANTA CLARA VALLEY The May Meeting The May meeting was the first of series highlighting the agricultural past of our area. Mountain View Historical Association Vice President Arthur Walton gave an interesting, informative and data filled presentation discussing the early days of agriculture in the area. He discussed the vineyards and truck farms which once dominated the Santa Clara valley, and the residents of Portuguese and Italian extraction who were the farmers and workers of the are- , Our reckless destruction of the environment of the Valley of Heart's Desire was an important theme The water table in the valley had dropped 200 feet before the creation of the Water District in 1929. We have paved over a large fraction of what once once the most productive agricultural area on the continent. The once pristine air is now often smoggy, and the beautiful vistas of orchards in bloom are only remnants. Future meetings will early on the agricultural theme and bring it up to the present. Brown, III - Editor ' 3 / 444"*" Cokieseseisi isa4 dis is AGRICULTURE in the SANTA CLARA VALLEY The May Meeting The May meeting will be the first in a series of meetings highlighting the agricultural past of our area. Mountain View Historical Association Vice President Arthur Walton views that agricultural heritage as divided into four eras: the Spanish/Mexican, the post gold rush, the transition to modern, and the era of intense horticulture. The growth and demise of the canneries, box manufacturing, warehousing, water, rail and truck shipping, and family and corporate farming can all be related to this framework. Santa Clara County was once a major fruit, wine and general agricultural center for the world. The first few years at IBM's San Jose plant the value of the nuts exceeded the value of the computer product shipped. Art Walton's own and collateral family roots are deep in Santa Clara Valley Agriculture. He will AM, draw on these personal resources as well as the research facilities of the area in bringing us a multi-part overview of what we had and what we have paved over. May, 1996 SAVE THE ADOBE BUILDING The February Meeting The Mountain View Historical Association held its February, 1996 meeting on February 4, 1996 at the Mountain View Senior Center. Arthur Walton, Association Vice President, presented a history of the the Adobe Building and the events leading up to its construction. Art grew up in the area, and was able to draw on his own and family resources to bring the era alive, but he also did his research and brought to his presentation the topical quotes from the journals of the day. Following his own presentation, Art moderated a panel presentation highlighting the significance of the Adobe Building in the cultural, social, civic and historical aspects of life in Mountain View. A brief report on the present condition of the building and what must be done to restore it to a useful condition was made. The panel presented a number of ideas for possible future uses of the building, and concluded with a plea for community involvement in the effort to save and restore this part of Mountain View's heritage. This neat, friendly building was the home of the Mountain View Women's Club. A proud, active 0rgan175ti0n, the Women's Club has been donating its services to the people of our area since its inception in 1904. The Club began with eight members and within six months grew to 23 members. Dues at that time was $1.00 a year. With these initial funds and along with ice cream sales and clam chowder suppers, the club members began their first project— starting Mountain View's first public library. The library reading room opened in 1905 with a total of 88 books and was staffed by Women's Club members. The Women's Club purchased an old church building in 1919 and had it moved to the Castro Street property. It remained a fixture on Castro Street between California and Mercy Streets until 1965 when the Club was sold due to excessive taxes. Since then, the Women's Club has met in the Masonic Hall on Church Street. The Women's Club is more than a social organization. Its members work on many local charitable and community improvement projects. Among their works are donations of food and clothing to the Community Services Agency, gifts to the library, and scholarships for local students. Mountain View has been lucky to have been served so faithfully through the years by the Women's Club. It is important for the community to have the continuity of such an active organization. "Toil is the price of excellence" is the Club's motto— and it is one that our local women have honored these last 92 years! THE ADOBE BUILDING By Barbara Kinchen It was during the Great Depression— thousands were out of work. Bayshore Highway was almost complete from San Francisco to San Jose and the USS Macon was berthed at the dirigible hangar at Moffett Naval Air Station. Farms, ranches, dairies and orchards surrounded the town of Mountain View. The population was 3,308 within town boundaries which stretched from El Camino Real to Washington Street and from Pettis Avenue almost to Calderon Avenue. Most businesses were on Castro Street, clustered in blocks nearest the railroad tracks. At Castro Street and El Camino Real, south of the high school, were the impressive signs spelling out Mountain View in lights. Moffett Boulevard was paved and landscaped within town limits and soon the road would be extended to Moffett's main gate, thus creating a second entrance to Mountain View. At 157 Moffett Boulevard stood the new Junior Chamber of Commerce civic building. The year was 1934. Members of the Junior Chamber raised money for a Spanish-style adobe building, on property owned by the town, for general community use as well as Chamber headquarters. Plans included a large meeting hall, veranda, heavy wooden beams, fireplace and lighting fixtures with wrought iron details, all under a red tile roof. Workers in government work-welfare programs made the adobe blocks on site and started construction in 1933. Work progressed slowly and lack of funds necessitated a temporary composition roof. Opening ceremonies were finally held in December of 1934. Events over three days and nights included tours, teas, a card party, a banquet, a grand ball and formal presentation to the Town of Mountain View. La Casa De Monte Vista was chosen winner in a name-the-building contest, but instead it was called the Adobe building or the Adobe and for over 50 years was used for a myriad of activities. The finest camping grounds in the midst of the most delightful mountain scenery in California may be reached by a drive of from 2 to 20 miles from the town, taking in all the renowned scenery of the Santa Cruz MountBins, and other parts of the coast range. Twelve passenger trains pass Mountain View every day, and all but 2 stop here. Two mails arrive from the south, and 2 from the north daily. The climate is mild, its equableness being due to the combined influence of the mountains on the south which are but 4 miles away, and the bay on the north, distant by 3 miles. The chief products of Mountain View are hay, grain, vegetables, berries, fruits, wines and brandies. There are 18 wineries and distilleries at Mountain View and its vicinity, and no section of the State has a more enviable reputation for the products of its orchards and vineyards. A local brickyard and sawmill furnish the chief materials for building at cheap figures. Brown, III - Editor areAsiii Aro Coldiosida, data lot Ma SAVE THE OLD ADOBE The February Meeting A few years ago we visited with my wife's relatives in Norway. I was struck by the fact that "the new house" was one built before our Civil War, and "the old house" was still in use on one side of the farm quadrangle of buildings. When we lived in New York, the James Fenimore Cooper house was still being lived in, and pre-revolutionary war homes were not unusual. Here in the west there is very little left from even a few decades ago. The buildings have been replaced with structures of little distinction, the meadows and fields paved over, and the farmlands planted to housing developments. Our oldest buildings in Mountain View are a handful in downtown which survived the earthquake. Roots and ties to the past are what builds a sense of belonging and community, and with this sense comes manners and a regard for each other. The facts are that few of us have been here more than a generation, almost none more than two generations. We need some way to tie ourselves back to the past. Not a past of father, grand- father, great-grandfather, but perhaps a past of previous (see - Old Adobe - on page 2) THE PEACE CORPS IN HUNGARY The November Meeting The Mountain View Historical Association held its November, 1995 meeting on 11/05/95 at the Senior Center. A sizeable audience of members and friends heard our President, Ralph Faravelli kick off the "Save The Adobe" campaign (of which more elsewhere in this Newsletter). This was followed by Trudi Herrero Odbert describing her experiences as a Peace Corps Volunteer in Hungary. Trudi is almost a native of Mountain View, having moved here with her parents as a youngster. She grew up in Mountain View, attended local schools, and married a Navy Man from Moffett Field. Navy life took them all over the world, but at retirement they returned to Mountain View, where Trudi obtained a Masters in Education from Stanford and then taught in a local high school. After retiring from teaching, she was inspired by a granddaughter to apply for the Peace Corps, and was accepted. As a Peace Corps volunteer, she spent two years as a teacher at the University at Veszprem, Hungary, teaching Linguistics, American Culture, (see - Peace Corps - on page 2) February, 1996 MVHA Page 1 (from - Peace 0:vs - on page 1) Cross Cultural Conversations and Literature. It was a somewhat lonely assignment since she did not become truly fluent in Hungarian, but she did establish many close ties. A long term project is to establish Vesprem as a "Sister City" with Mountain View. The adjustment in coming home was more difficult than the adjustment in going over. The Hungarians place great emphasis on family, and they took her into a small University oriented town. Trudi is already becoming re-engaged in Mountain View, picking up issues and causes, and with her family. We're glad she's back, and we're grateful for the time she spent telling us of her experiences in the Peace Corps. (see - Exec Corn - next column) (from - Old Adobe - on page 1) generation, grand-generation and great-grandgeneration. If we can do that, it gives all of us roots amongst all of the peoples who have lived here over the last few centuries. How can we do this? Buildings like the Old Adobe can be a start. The building was erected at an economic turning point for the area. The old skills of working with adobe bricks were dying out. The Spanish/Mexican heritage was being overrun by immigrants from the American East and Midwest. So, while the Old Adobe is not an old building by the standards of other areas, in style and feel it is a structure from our past. It is worth preserving simply as an architectural link with the past. There are other reasons for preserving the structure. We're short on good meeting space in Mountain View. Convenient space for club meetings, a bridge tournament, a small convention, a charitable group meeting are all in short supply. A historic role for the Old Adobe might be a revival of teen dances on Friday evenings. We don't yet have a firm handle on what it might cost to restore the Old Adobe to serviceable condition, or what the feasible uses for the building might be. We don't know where the money required might come from, or how the facility would be managed when restoration is complete. We need a strong expression of support from the public for restoring the Old Adobe. We'll take a long step on that road at the Mountain View Historical Association meeting on Sunday, February 4, 1996. Come to the meeting with your thoughts and ideas and lets see what we can and should do. Fobruiary, 1996 MVI4A Paso 2 JOSEPH F. KENNEDY By Shirley Pearson and Kathleen Lowe Owen Many of us have ancestors who came west in the middle of the 19th century. The Pioneer Room has a copy of the diary of one such intrepid traveler - Joseph Finley Kennedy. Kennedy kept a diary of this trip to California in 1863. The diary began two days before he actually left and discussed both the hardships and joys experienced along the way. For example, on June 9, 1863 Joseph wrote "passed several graves today and hardly a day passes but what our attention is arrested by one or two of these solitary mounds. The end of many a poor emigrant's journey." To read more of his diary you can visit the Pioneer Room on the fourth floor of City Hall on Tues., Wed., and Thurs. from 1-5 PM. Kennedy was born in Independence, Missouri in 1843. He left his family's home in Council Bluffs, Iowa by wagon train on May 19th, 1863, and finished his journey on the afternoon of September 3rd, 1863 in Dublin, California. Joseph tried several occupations before becoming a school teacher in Pleasanton. On January 21, 1868, Kennedy married Sarah Margaret Graham of Mountain View. She was the third child of Isaac Newton Graham after whom Graham Middle School is named. The young couple's first child, James Isaac, was born in Pleasanton at the end of 1868 and their second, Frances Winifred, in Mountain View in 1870. They were living in Alvarado, CA, for the birth of their third child Margaret Elizabeth, in March, 1871. Sarah died of consumption on April 5, 1871, and Joseph brought the children back to Mountain View, where the baby was raised by her maternal grandparents, Isaac and Elizabeth Graham. The two older children went to live with their mother's aunt, Mrs. Winfred Mayers, and her husband, also of Mountain View. (see - Kennedy - in next coliann) THE EDITOR'S RAMBLINGS By Hilton Brown The article on Joseph F. Kennedy in this Newsletter indicates that his wife Sarah died of consumption. Consumption is another term for phthisis or tuberculosis, and this disease accounts for one quarter of the known causes of death of the persons interred in Pioneer Cemetery in the last century. Almost another quarter died of pneumonia, bronchitis or typhoid. I'm not sure what to make of this, except to comment upon the amazing strides we have made in dealing with illness, and how poorly we have done in dealing with violence. The young woman, Sarah Kennedy, probably weakened by the stress of her pregnancy, died of tuberculosis within a month of the birth of her third child. (more on page five) SPANISH INFLUENCE The May Meeting Our speaker for the regular May, 1955, meeting of the Mountain View Historical Association was Dr. Chatham H. Forbes, a faculty member at the DeAnza College California History Center. Dr. Forbes joked that he was "issued" at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, New York, but he moved to the area of Menlo Park and Palo Alto very young. His grandfather was the founder of the California Military Academy, established on the grounds of the old Mayfield Farm in 1924. The original farm building dated from 1853, and eventually became a beautiful mansion of some 40 rooms. The mansion burned down about 1932. contributing to the demise of the Academy. There were two main themes to Dr Forbes presentation. The first was for the Mountain View Historical Association to join with the California History Center in some sort of project relating to Mountain View history. To this end he offered the services of the Center in coordinating research involving the Center's own resources, the resources of the Santa Barbara Mission Archives, and the Bancroft Library of the UC San Francisco. He also indicated that the Center was initiating a California Studies Program which might be of interest to the audience. (see - Influence - on page 2) August, 1995 MVHA Page 1 (from - Influence - on page I) The second theme was an effort to refute what he referred to as the revisionist history of the missions in California. Dr Forbes blames the civil and military authorities for the brutalities inflicted upon the local Indians, and feels that the mission conflicts were largely due to the cultural shock incurred when two such different cultures as the civilized, Christian catholic fathers met with and tried to convert the gentile Indians. It was unfortnnote that Dr. Forbes did not spend more time discussing the Spanish Influence in the Santa Clara Valley, and what actually occurred as the two culture met, rather than trying to assess blame. No matter what the cause, a highly successful population of several hundred thousand native Americans was reduced to a few thousands in a a few decades, Spanish was established as the universal language, and Europeanized farming and ranching was established. Perhaps we can try to deal with this subject again in a future meeting. KENNETH SLATER Reported by Carol Fischer Kenneth Norton Slater was one of the most beloved educational figures in Mountain View's past. He was an employee of the Mountain View School District for 40 years. Born in 1893 in Alturas, Modoc County, California, Kenneth was the youngest of Daniel and Jeanette Slater's three children. He and his family came to our area in 1904 and he graduated from Mountain View High School in 1912. Attending San Jose Normal School and Stanford University, Mr. Slater became Chief Administrator of the Mountain View School District in 1917. At this time the district comprised only two schools -- the Dana Street School and the Highway School -- with an enrollment of 275 pupils. Forty years later when Mr. Slater retired, there were seven schools and an enrollment of 2900 students. At Mountain View High School, Kenneth was known as a studious athlete. He enjoyed playing football and baseball. In later years he recounted going to athletic evente on the train. If a member of the team didn't have the train fare, he'd hide on the train and jump off just prior to the destination. Those games must have been very important! Kenneth Slater was a man of many and varied interests. He joined the Navy in 1918. After returning from the service, he became director of the Chamber of Commerce, Commander of the American Legion and a district commander of the Boy Scouts. He also served as the president of the Santa Clara County Theater's Association. On top of these activities, he even had time to court, woo and many Arline BahIs in 1923! The new Mrs. Slater was also a teacher. They settled into a home on Velarde Street. In 1956, shortly before Kenneth Slater retired, the District honored him by naming their new school on Whisman Road for him. After retirement, Kenneth and Arline traveled to Europe. Once at home, he remained active in the Mid-Peninsula Retired Teacher's Association. Mr. Slater died in 1971 at the age of 77. < < August, 1995 MVHA Page 2 MOUNTAIN VIEW HISTORICAL ASSOCIATION P.O. Recent columns have described the "South Shore Port Baths", and early newspapers in Mountain View. Old Newspapers (continued) Three ounce packages of Jello sold for 9C, 12 ounce cam of Canada Dry Soda were 10C and fresh salmon was priced at 79C a pound for half or whole and slices for 89C a pound. IN MEMORIUM Dorothy Petty Reel - April 28, 1995. Dorothy and her husband George operated a mobile home park and resort in Shasta City for a number of years and later worked with the Mobile Missionary Assistance Program, traveling to different parts of the country helping build churches, campgrounds and Christian Centers. She was the dauehter of the late Rollie and Leslie (Redwine) Petty and a cousin of our treasurer, June Redwine de Larios. Rollie Petty was Mountain View's Postmaster from 1933 until his retirement in 1964. Some time ago Dorothy gave us a number of snapshots showing postal employees and events and also an 8X10" photo taken May 19, 1938 at Mountain View Airport showing Mr. Petty beside a small plane which was taking a special bag of airmail to Mills Field, now San Francisco Airport. HONORS The City of Los Altos declared June 4, 1995 as Anna and Joe Fitz Day and honored the couple with a reception at History House. Anna Knapp Fitz, long-time member of the Mountain View Historical Association, is a painter and sculptress, using historical places and people as inspiration. She has used her Los Altos paintings and sculptured heads to teach school children about local history and has now donated these items to the Los Altos History House Museum. STILL MORE THIS 'N THAT "The 1906 Earthquake in Mountain View" by Barbara McPheeters Kinchen, with assistance from the Library and Mr. Jason Chan, is available in the Pioneer Room and will be available at the August 13 Barbecue. August, 1995 MVHA Page 5 EXPANSION PLANNED FOR THE PIONEER ROOM The Pioneer Room is about to undergo a major expansion. With the cooperation and leadership of City Manager Kevin Duggan, Library Services Director Susan Ozubko and MVHA President Ralph Faravelli, the Pioneer Room will nearly triple its space on the fourth floor of City Hall. The new space will be comparable in size to the space the historical collections will occupy in the new library, when that building is completed in the future. The improved facility will allow space for the public exhibition of pictures, documents and other artifacts of old Mountain View and the area. It will greatly increase the accessibility of the historical materials for researchers, business people and students with a need to work with the historical records, and it will give the staff and Pioneer Room Volunteers the "elbow room" they need to carry on the work of preserving and cataloguing the archives of the area. The Pioneer Room serves a number of important ftaictions. For the Mountain -View Historical Association, it is our archive. For the developer or builder, it is an early step in determining the suitability of a site for development. For the person seeking roots and origins, its the place to find out about the history of the area. For the City of Mountain View, it is our collective memory. The Pioneer Room will be expanding into its enlarged quarters over the next few weeks. The library staff, with the leadership of Carol Fischer, and the Pioneer Room Volunteers led by Barbara Kinehen will be working hard to make the Pioneer Room an even more welcoming place for Mountain View residents and visitors. Wally Erichsen reported on the status of the Castro station. The Historical Association Handbook is under development. Trudi Herrero Odbert moved to Mtn. View with her parents in 1921. Her father operated Herrero's Market at the corner of View and El Camino for many years. She attended grade school and High School in Mountain View. She married1t career navy Meteorological Officer, Odbert, and lived the life of a naval wife for 28 years. They had duty stations on both coasts, in Alaska and overseas. When they retired from the Navy, Trudi-really went to work, attending Foothill College, San Jose State, and eventually obtaining a Masters Degree in Education from Stanford University. She taught at Guanigh School for thirteen years, retired, did some traveling, signed up for the Peace Corps, and spent two years at the University at Veszprem, Hungary, teaching teachers to teach English. February, 1995 MVHA Page 1 LIVE ME ADOBE CAMPAIGN BEGINS By Eva G. Mockbee The Mountain View City Council recently announced plans to demolish the Adobe Building located at 157 Moffett Boulevard near Central Central Express Way. The property on which the building now stands was deeded to the City in 1929 by Wallace and Alice Angelo for $ 10. The original adobe bricks were made on location from the soil found on the site. Construction began through the combined efforts of the Junior Chamber of Commerce and the WPA. It was presented to the City in 1934. Through the 30's, 40's, 50's, 60's and the early 70's, the adobe served as a community facility, a place for meetings of the American Legion, USO, Dance Classes, Senior Nutrition Program, Service Men's Hospitality Room and the Eagles's Shack, a teen center - to name a few. In 1987, plans for renovation were proposed, including removal of the adjacent water tower to allow for additional parking spaces. The costs of upgrading the facility were deemed too high and the facility was closed, its future much in doubt. When the Mountain View Historical Association was informed that the Adobe might be demolished, a letter was sent to the City Council, requesting a reasonable amount of time to study costs of renovation, plans for fundraising and exploration for use of the Adobe as a community meeting hall. Presently, Mountain View lacks a suitable locale for community groups and local clubs to hold meetings or social events. The City Council granted the Mountain View Historical Association a three month period to explore opportunities for utilization of the Adobe and sources for fundraising. The study will include the development of a proposal to declare the building a historical landmark. Currently, the City of Mountain View lacks an ordinance regarding designation of historical buildings; a committee, appointed by President Ralph Faravelli is now at work obtaining information from neighboring communities relating to this endeavor. The Mountain View Historical Association is enlisting the support of the membership, local business, community groups and concerned citizens in their efforts to SAVE THE ADOBE, Mountain View's last remaining, public historical building. The October, 1994, issue of the Mountain View Historical Association Newsletter contained an article, "The Adobe Building", by Carol Fischer, giving some of the history of the building. February, 1995 MVIIA Pogo 2 ..•••••• NETTLE MARIA STEVENS Biologist and Geneticist Reported by Loretta M. Jackson Rosamond Bacon, a longtime resident of Stanford, recently brought Nettie Stevens to my attention. Nettie, along with her librarian sister, Emma Stevens, and her father Ephraim Stevens lived on a prune and apricot farm here in Mountain View. Nettie was the first one to arrive, leaving Vermont for California in 1896 to get her education at Stanford. Her father and sister came out to visit her, fell in love with the area and decided to relocate. Nettie Stevens became a scientist in a time when many colleges didn't even allow women to take any science courses because they felt the work would be too hard and potentially damaging to a woman's mental and physical health. After receiving her A.M. Degree at Stanford in 1900 Nettie Stevens got her first paper, of the forty she would eventually produce, published. Oliver Peebles Jenkins and Frank McFarland are probably the professors that led Dr. Stevens to her work in cytological research. Her interest in nuclethr and chromosomes eventually led her to Bryn Mawr where she worked with Thomas H. Morgan. Her most significant paper was published in 1905 and identified the specific chromosome that determines sex. This major breakthrough was discovered simultaneously by another scientist, E.B. Wilson, who published his paper almost in the same week. Both scientists had great respect for each other and referred to each other's work as proof of their own. This discovery was considered quite radical and took some years to be accepted by the scientific community Sadly, by the time it was accepted, Nettie Maria Stevens died of breast cancer at only 51, and most science books credit Wilson with the discovery rather than both of them. Many of the articles I found described Dr. Stevens as scholarly, quiet, earnest and unassuming and her scientific papers were known for their clarity and brevity. Many felt that her untimely death prevented her from receiving the Nobel Prize that her future research would have earned. IN MEMORIUM Elda Frederickson Black, 84, died earlier this year. She attended local schools and then taught 28 years in the Mountain View Elementary School District, d`was a well-known pianist and organist. Anna Knapp Fitz, 82, of Los Altos, was a long-time member and supporter of the Historical Association, and a graduate of Mountain View High School. In later life she did many paintings and studied sculpture. Her oil paintings and sculptured heads were based on our local area's historical people and scenes and were used to help children especially, visualize the past. Angelo Semino, 99, was born in Mountain View, son of Jtalian parents. Their farm was the site later of Wrfield Mall where there is a commemorative plaque foij1i family. Mr. Semino was a Stanford graduate and a mechanical engineer and served as Historical Association president 1980-1982. Ross Spencer, 80, died in August. A native son, he was associated with Sterling Lumber Company. "The school trustees and the principal have been gunning for woodpeckers who infest the school house." "French Dave" was sentenced to 15 days in the County jail by Judge Frank Beverly for disturbing the peace. An early morning fire destroyed seven buildings on the East side of Castro Street between Villa and Front (now Evelyn) Streets. The bucket brigade could not stop the flames and the whole block would have been lost if there had been a wind. All persons sleeping in the buildings escaped and some household goods and stock-in-trade were saved. McDonald and Burke, the blacksmiths, were back to work within hours under a temporary shed roof but it took three days for Mr. Guth to erect a rough shack with dirt floor and start selling drinks. Within one month new structures housed the restaurant, blacksmiths, firmer, carriage painter, barber, saloon and fruit store. Mountain View Cyclers Club gave a smoker for members and guests. Entertainment consisted of card playing, vocal and instrumental music, food, speeches, followed by "impromptu high jinks by some of the less dignified members."
